exp.2:14:
Elisha asks for a musician to be brought to him, one who plays a stringed instrument such as the harp. "Minstrel" is the word for the person who plays an instrument. While the musician was playing, the hand of the Lord came upon Elisha, that is, God acted with power upon him and prepared him to speak his message.

Elisha speaks in the middle of a crisis: three kings, of Israel, Judah and Edom, were without water in the desert, on their way to war against Moab. Elisha does not respect the king of Israel because of his idolatry, but he does respect Jehoshaphat, who followed the Lord. It is not known with certainty why he used music; the text only says that it was then that God spoke.

For today: before you decide or advise, look for a moment of calm to listen to God. A song, a quiet prayer or reading the Bible can help you settle your heart and be attentive to his voice.
exp.7:1:
This verse says the woman obeyed what Elisha, the prophet, had told her. She got up, left with her whole household, and went to live in the land of the Philistines for seven years. The words "é" and "partióse" are old forms: "é" means "and", and "partióse" means "she went away".

Elisha had already warned her that God would bring a famine lasting seven years. This is the woman from Shunem, whose son Elisha had brought back to life. She trusted the prophet's word and left her home and her land. Afterward she came back and went to the king to ask that her property be returned to her.

For today: obeying God may cost comfort and security, but He cares for those who trust His word. When you sense that God is guiding you toward a difficult change, take the step with faith and confidence.
exp.21:6:
This verse says that the men in charge of the temple work were not asked to account for the money they received, meaning no detailed review of every coin was made. The reason was that they worked faithfully, that is, with honesty and loyalty. "Handling" means administration, and "was entrusted to them" means "was handed over to them."

King Josiah ordered the temple repaired, and he sent his secretary Shaphan to the high priest Hilkiah. Money had been gathered from the offerings, and it was to go to carpenters, masons, and stonecutters. These men had a good reputation, which is why they were trusted. Shortly afterward the book of the law was found, and this moved the king to seek God.

For today: trust is earned by being faithful in small and hidden things. If you are entrusted with money or responsibilities at church or at work, act with honesty even when no one is watching. And whoever leads should know how to trust those who have shown integrity.
exp.24:14:
It says the captain of the Babylonian guard carried away from the house of the LORD the firepans and the bowls. The firepans were containers for burning incense, and the bowls were basins used in worship. What was of gold he took away as gold, and what was of silver, as silver. He left nothing of value.

This is part of the historical account in the book of Kings, where the author tells of the fall of Jerusalem. Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of Nebuchadnezzar, looted the temple after the conquest, around 586 B.C. The text presents this as part of the judgment for the people's unfaithfulness.

For today: the most valuable objects are of no use if the heart turns away from God. Take care of your relationship with Him first, because external things can be lost, but God remains faithful.
exp.7:7:
In this passage King Ben-hadad of Syria, who is sick, speaks to his servant Hazael. He orders him to take a gift, go to the man of God (the prophet Elisha), and ask the Lord through him whether he will recover. A "gift" is what Hazael is told to bring, and "ask the Lord through him" means asking Elisha to inquire of God on the king's behalf.

Elisha had come to Damascus, the capital of Syria, and the king heard about it. Although Syria was a rival nation to Israel, Ben-hadad recognizes that the God of Israel has power and that His prophet can speak on His behalf. For this reason he sends a generous gift, as was customary when approaching a prophet.

For today: when we face an illness or a crisis, seeking God is the wisest thing we can do. But let us do it with sincerity and a willingness to hear His answer, even when it is not the one we hope for.
exp.3:23:
She had a female donkey saddled and told her servant to lead the way and keep moving forward without slowing down, and not to stop the pace for her to ride unless she herself told him to. Saddling the animal means putting the saddle on it. The servant is a young attendant, and the donkey is a she-donkey.

The Shunammite woman has just lost her son, and the text suggests she left him dead on the prophet's bed. To her husband she says only "It is well," without giving any details. Now she speaks urgently to her servant, because she wants to reach Elisha, the man of God, on Mount Carmel quickly.

When grief comes, we too can turn quickly to God and to those who guide us spiritually. She did not freeze: she acted in faith and moved toward God. Today we can do the same in prayer, with sincerity, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.15:6:
Ahaz, king of Judah, sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. He told him that he was "your servant and your son," that is, he placed himself under the king's authority. He asked him to come up and defend him from the kings of Syria and of Israel, who had risen up against him. "Messengers" here means official envoys.

Judah was under attack from Rezin and Pekah. Instead of seeking the Lord, Ahaz asked a foreign power for help and paid with silver and gold from the temple and the palace. Isaiah had called him to trust the Lord (Isaiah 7), although this passage does not mention it. Assyria did attack Damascus, but this left Judah subject to a powerful empire.

When we are afraid, it is easy to look for quick solutions that draw us away from God. Before making desperate decisions, let us pray and ask for his guidance. He is more faithful than any human help.
exp.22:12:
This verse says that King Josiah defiled, that is, made unclean and unfit for use, the high places of worship that stood before Jerusalem. Solomon had built them for the false gods Ashtoreth (of the Sidonians), Chemosh (of Moab), and Milcom (of the Ammonites). The "mount of corruption" is probably another name for the Mount of Olives, though some scholars debate this. The word "abomination" points to something that is detestable to God.

The passage is narrated by the author of Kings. It tells of Josiah's great reform, in which he sought to cleanse the land of idolatry and return to the covenant with God after finding the book of the law. It shows that the sin of centuries earlier, even Solomon's, remained present until someone confronted it.

For today: it is not enough to leave what is obvious; God can show you old things that have been left "tolerated" in your life. Ask Him for light and decisively remove whatever competes with Him.
exp.13:27:
The author says he will not tell everything Jeroboam did: his exploits, his strength, and his wars. He mentions that Jeroboam recovered Damascus and Hamath, and that the rest is written in the official book of the kings of Israel. The phrase about Judah is difficult, and it is understood in several ways. It probably refers to territories that had earlier been under the control of Israel.

The author of Kings closes the reign of Jeroboam II with a common formula. Earlier he said that this king did what was evil before God, but that the Lord, seeing the suffering of his people, used him to save them. The king's achievements are due to God's mercy, not to his goodness.

For today: God sees people's pain and sometimes helps even when they do not deserve it. So do not boast in your achievements. Give thanks to God for his patience and use it to do good.
exp.18:18:
King Hezekiah asks God to save them from the power of Assyria. His plea is "save us, I beseech you," which is a humble request. He wants all the nations to know that the Lord alone is the true God. "All the kingdoms of the earth" refers to all the peoples.

King Hezekiah speaks in prayer inside the temple. The Assyrian king Sennacherib had surrounded Jerusalem and was mocking God. Hezekiah acknowledges that Assyria destroyed other peoples and burned their idols, which were made of wood or stone. But he trusts in the living God. Afterward, God responds through the prophet Isaiah and says that he has heard his prayer.

When you face a very great problem, bring it to God with sincerity. Ask him for help, but also ask that his name be honored in whatever happens. Praying this way changes the focus: you are not only seeking relief, but that God be known.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that the money people brought to the temple was handed directly to the workmen who did the job, and with that money the house of Jehovah, that is, the temple, was repaired. The phrase "they gave that to the workmen" in the verse means that they paid the workers with it.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He tells how King Joash and the priest Jehoiada organized the repair of the temple, which had fallen into disrepair. The text stresses that the money was used only to fix the building, not for luxury items, and that those in charge handled it faithfully, without anyone needing to call them to account.

For today: what is dedicated to God should be used with honesty and with purpose. If you handle money from the church, your family, or your work, try to be so faithful that there is nothing to hide.
exp.9:23:
This verse tells how the worshipers of Baal went into the temple to offer their sacrifices and burnt offerings. Meanwhile, Jehu had stationed eighty armed men outside. He warned them that if anyone let one of the worshipers escape, that man would pay with his own life.

The narrator recounts what Jehu, king of Israel, did. God had raised him up to bring an end to the house of Ahab, and he wanted to remove the worship of Baal, which had led the people astray. He used deception and very harsh violence. The Bible describes what happened, but it does not say that every method Jehu used was an example to follow. His heart also did not fully follow God.

For today: it is not enough to remove what is wrong on the outside. Ask God to cleanse your heart too, and to guide you with truth and mercy.
exp.24:20:
This verse says that the king of Babylon ordered the important prisoners to be struck down and put to death at Riblah, a region of Hamath, north of Israel. The word "struck" means that he attacked or executed them. "Was carried away" means that he was taken into exile. With this, the kingdom of Judah was removed from its land.

This is the account of the writer of Kings, who tells of the end of the kingdom of Judah. Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, brought these men before Nebuchadnezzar, who judged and executed them. The book presents this exile as the consequence of years of Judah's disobedience to God, although the execution itself was a cruel act by a foreign king.

For today: God is serious when he warns, but his patience is great. If today you feel you have lost something because of your mistakes, do not harden your heart. Return to God with sincerity, for he remains faithful and can restore what seems lost.
exp.23:12:
The king of Babylon sacked Jerusalem. He carried off the treasures of the temple and of the king's palace. He also cut into pieces the gold objects that Solomon had ordered made for the temple. The text adds that this happened "as the Lord had said."

The narrator of the book of Kings describes how Judah fell before Babylon, around 597 B.C. Jehoiachin surrendered, and Nebuchadnezzar took the spoils. The closing phrase reminds us that God had already warned of this judgment through his prophets, for example to Hezekiah in 2 Kings 20:17. In this way, the people understood that this was no accident.

Today we learn that neither sacred places nor sacred objects protect us if the heart turns away from God. Let us trust in Him himself, and listen to his Word in time.
exp.22:23:
This verse says that King Josiah cleared Judah and Jerusalem of everything connected with the occult and with idolatry. The ones who consulted the dead or spirits, the ones who claimed to predict the future, and the small household idols used to seek guidance were all removed. Josiah removed them to obey what was written in the book of the law that the priest Hilkiah had found in the temple.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings. He recounts Josiah's reforms after the book of the law was discovered. After the Passover, the king kept removing whatever contradicted God. Even so, the text makes clear that the judgment on Judah was not canceled, because of the sins of Manasseh.

Today we might ask what we look to for security or guidance apart from God. Just as Josiah responded to the Word with concrete actions, it is wise to set aside whatever contradicts it.
exp.18:30:
It says that from Jerusalem a group of survivors will come out, people who will escape and settle on Mount Zion. The word "remnant" means those who are left behind or survive. The "zeal" of God is his intense and determined love for his people, and that zeal will fulfill the promise.

The prophet Isaiah speaks, sending a message from God to King Hezekiah. The Assyrians, led by Sennacherib, had invaded Judah and were threatening Jerusalem. God gives him a sign: although the land has been laid waste, they will again eat, sow, and bear fruit. In this way he assures him that the city will be delivered.

When everything seems lost, God can sustain a small remnant and make it flourish again. Trust that his love for you does not give up, and take today the small step that is within your reach.
exp.21:1:
He did what was pleasing to the Lord. "In the sight of the Lord" means "according to God's judgment." "He walked in all the way of David" means he lived with the same faithfulness as David. "Turned not aside to the right hand or to the left" means he did not stray either to the right or to the left, that is, he was steady.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the king's character. Josiah came to the throne as a child, at eight years old. This summary prepares what follows: the repair of the temple and the discovery of the book of the law, which moved the king to reform. The text does not explain how his faith formed as a child, so it is best not to invent details.

For today: faithfulness is lived out with steadiness. Ask God to help you remain firm, without drifting, in the small decisions of each day, regardless of your age or your past.
exp.8:32:
Jehu orders the court eunuchs to throw Jezebel down from the window. They obey, and her blood splashes onto the wall and the horses. Afterward Jehu rides over her with his horses. "Trample" means to step on and crush under foot. "Was splashed" means the blood fell in drops.

Jehu speaks, anointed as king of Israel by God's command to bring an end to the house of Ahab. Jezebel, Ahab's wife, had promoted idolatry and the killing of the Lord's prophets. She greets him with a mocking remark, comparing him to Zimri, a traitor. The eunuchs, who served Jezebel, side with Jehu. Then what Elijah had foretold about her end comes to pass.

For today: God does not overlook injustice, even when he is slow to act. This invites us to trust his justice without taking revenge ourselves, and to use whatever power we have with humility, knowing that we will give an account to God.
exp.12:9:
It says that Jehoash, the son of Jehoahaz, began to rule over Israel, the northern kingdom, from Samaria. He reigned sixteen years. This happened in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of another Jehoash, king of Judah.

The author of the book tells the history of the kings and arranges it by dates, comparing the northern kingdom with the southern one. He has just told of the death of Jehoahaz and now introduces his son. The next verse makes the important point clear: Jehoash did evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the sins of Jeroboam.

For today: God does not only look at how long a life lasted, but at how it was lived. Ask yourself whether there are habits or mistakes inherited from your family that you keep repeating, and ask God for help to walk differently.
exp.24:29:
This verse says that the king of Babylon gave Jehoiachin a ration of food every day, without fail, for as long as he lived. The phrase "was given" means the same as "was given." The word "continually" means "always." Jehoiachin no longer depended on the prison or on scarcity; he received his daily sustenance.

The book of 2 Kings ends with this account. Jehoiachin, king of Judah, was taken captive to Babylon, and years later King Evil-merodach released him from prison and treated him kindly. The author does not say who wrote the book, and does not fully explain why it ends this way. Many see it as a small sign of hope: although Judah was punished, the line of David had not disappeared.

For today: even in difficult times, God can give us provision and hope in simple things. Today, give thanks for what you receive each day, and trust that He continues to care for you.
exp.14:20:
This verse is the formula the writer uses to close the reign of Menahem. It says that the rest of his deeds and all that he did are written in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That book is not preserved today, and we do not know exactly what it was like; it was probably official records of the kingdom.

The author of Kings, whose name we do not know, summarizes each reign and refers readers to other sources. Just before this, he tells us that Menahem paid a thousand talents of silver to the king of Assyria, and that he raised that money from the rich people of Israel. This shows a weak kingdom that buys its stability with money and burdens its people.

For today: our deeds are also recorded, and decisions have a cost. Before seeking security through shortcuts or at the expense of others, it is wise to trust God and act justly, for He knows our whole life.
exp.17:11:
It says that Samaria fell because the people of Israel did not listen to the voice of the Lord their God. They broke his covenant, that is, the commitment of faithfulness that God made with them. Nor did they do what Moses, the servant of God, had commanded them.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. After telling of the fall of Samaria and the exile to Assyria, he explains the reason from the standpoint of faith: it was not only a military defeat, but the consequence of years of disobedience. Meanwhile, the kingdom of Judah, under King Hezekiah, was still standing, but it would also face trials.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; it must be put into practice. Today you can choose one thing that God has already shown you in the Bible and obey it with humility.
exp.2:13:
Elisha swears by the living God, the Lord of hosts, whom he serves. He says that if it were not for his regard for Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, he would not even look at the king of Israel. The expression about regarding someone's presence means honoring or considering a person. Saying he would not look toward him nor see him is a strong way of saying he would ignore him completely.

Three kings, of Israel, Judah, and Edom, are without water in the desert, on their way to fight against Moab. Jehoshaphat seeks a prophet of God and finds Elisha. Joram, the king of Israel, had followed idolatry, and that is why Elisha speaks to him harshly. Even so, God acts because of the faithful king.

For today: the faith and obedience of one person can bring blessing to those around them. And when we are in trouble, it is not enough to cry out to God; it is also good to draw near to Him with humility and sincerity.
exp.9:1:
This verse is the opening of a letter from Jehu. He addresses the leaders of Samaria, who had the care of King Ahab's sons. He reminds them that they have resources to defend themselves: chariots, horsemen, a fortified city, and weapons.

Jehu had just been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab, and he had already killed the kings Joram and Ahaziah. With this letter he challenges the leaders of Samaria to choose a successor and fight. He was probably trying to test their loyalty, and they responded with fear. Some interpreters see a clever move here, and the Bible does not spell out all his intentions.

For today: having resources does not guarantee courage or good decisions. Before acting, it is worth asking ourselves whom we truly trust: what we have, or God.
exp.0:7:
The messengers of King Ahaziah describe the man who stopped them: "hairy," that is, wearing a garment of hair or very hairy, and with a leather belt tied around his waist. On hearing this, the king immediately recognizes that it is Elijah the Tishbite.

Ahaziah had been injured by a fall, and he sent to consult Baal-zebub, a false god of Ekron. God sent Elijah to intercept the messengers with a message of judgment. Some understand "hairy" as clothing made of animal hair; others, as a man with a great deal of hair. The text does not make this clear. What is clear is that the king knew Elijah well.

For today: when we are afraid or in need, let us not first run to sources that do not come from God. Let us seek the Lord first, and live with an integrity so simple and firm that others recognize we belong to him.
exp.1:8:
Elijah and Elisha had already crossed the Jordan River. Elijah offers Elisha to ask for something before God takes him away. Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit. "Taken away from thee" means carried off, away from you. "I pray thee" means "I ask you."

Elijah is the greater prophet, and Elisha is his disciple and successor. According to the law (Deuteronomy 21:17), the firstborn son received a double portion of the inheritance. For this reason many understand that Elisha is asking to be recognized as Elijah's spiritual heir, not to be twice as powerful. Others interpret it as a request for greater power; the text does not fully clarify this.

Elisha did not ask for riches or fame, but to be useful to God in his calling. We can sincerely ask God to give us his Spirit, wisdom, and strength to serve him and serve others, and not only things for ourselves.
exp.1:3:
Elijah again asks Elisha to stay where they are, because God is sending him to Jericho. Elisha answers with an oath: "As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you." That is, he swears by the Lord and by Elijah's life that he will not separate himself from him. Then the two of them arrive at Jericho.

Elijah is about to be taken up by God, and he travels from town to town. Elisha is his disciple and successor. It is not known for certain why Elijah asks him to stay; some think it is a test of loyalty, others a gesture of consideration. Elisha insists and does not part from his master.

For today: faith sometimes calls for perseverance, even when the road is long or uncertain. If you want to grow spiritually, stay close to God and to those who guide you in the faith, without giving up at the first difficulty.
exp.8:36:
This verse says that Jezebel's body was left like dung lying in the field of Jezreel, so decayed that no one could recognize it or say, "This is Jezebel." The word for "dung" in this verse refers to waste left on the ground, and the phrase "the portion of Jezreel" refers to a piece of land that belonged to a family.

The speaker is Jehu, who had just been anointed king of Israel. Jezebel, wife of King Ahab, had promoted idolatry and the killing of innocent people, such as Naboth, whose vineyard in Jezreel was taken from him. Jehu recalls that God had announced this end through the prophet Elijah. Some see here the exact fulfillment of a divine warning; the text gives no further detail about how Jehu felt.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, and his words come true. We can trust that he sees abuse, and this encourages us to live with humility, avoiding taking advantage of others.
exp.2:10:
Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asks whether there is not here a prophet of the Lord through whom they may inquire of the Lord. One of the servants of the king of Israel answers that Elisha, son of Shaphat, is here, the one who poured water on the hands of Elijah. That is, he served him and helped him wash his hands. It was a way of saying that he was his close assistant.

Three kings, of Israel, Judah and Edom, march against Moab and run out of water in the desert. The king of Israel sees only a judgment from God. Jehoshaphat, who was seeking the Lord, asks for a word from Him. Elisha was not yet very well known, but he had a reputation among the servants.

When we are in trouble, it is wise to seek God's voice before giving up or blaming Him. And God often uses humble and faithful people, who serve quietly, to give direction.
exp.3:15:
Elisha tells the woman that, in about a year, she will be holding a son in her arms. "About this season, according to the time of life" means: at this same time of year, when the year comes around again. She answers with disbelief and asks him not to deceive her, calling herself "thy handmaid," out of respect.

Elisha is speaking with a woman from Shunem, who had treated him with generosity and had prepared a room for him. Gehazi, his servant, noticed that she had no children and that her husband was old. She had already left that hope behind, and that is why she fears it may be a false hope.

For today: sometimes we stop hoping for something good so that we will not suffer another disappointment. This scene invites us to bring before God even the longings we had given up for lost, trusting that He can act in His own time and in His own way.
exp.5:24:
It says that the king of Syria surrounded the city of Samaria with his army, and inside a terrible famine fell. Prices became so high that a donkey's head, something normally not eaten, cost eighty pieces of silver. A small measure of "dove's dung" cost five. A "piece of silver" is a shekel. Some believe that this "dung" was an emergency food or a plant with a similar name; it is not known for certain.

The one who narrates is the author of Kings, who describes the despair of the people. Shortly before, God had given Israel a victory over the Syrians without battle. Now Ben-hadad returns with his whole army and besieges the city. The text that follows shows the king of Israel, without hope, speaking with a woman who cries out for help.

For today: in times of scarcity and fear, it is easy to look only for human solutions or to blame others. This passage invites us to bring our need to God with sincerity, and to help generously those who suffer near us.
exp.17:24:
Here Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, asks whether he has come up against Jerusalem without the Lord's knowledge. He claims that God himself told him: "Go up against this land, and destroy it."

Rabshakeh speaks in the year Assyria was besieging Jerusalem, during the reign of Hezekiah. He wants to discourage the people so that they will surrender. He uses the name of the Lord as a psychological weapon. The Bible does not record that God actually spoke to him in this way; it is a claim made by the enemy, and the account that follows shows that God defended Jerusalem.

For today: not everyone who says they speak on God's behalf is telling the truth. Always test what you hear against Scripture and against the character of God. If a message only spreads fear and turns you away from trusting Him, examine it carefully and seek wisdom in prayer.
exp.3:35:
This verse tells how Elisha called his servant Gehazi and asked him to bring the Shunammite woman, the mother of the child. When she came in, Elisha said to her simply: "Take up your son." The sentence explaining the old wording is removed, since the verse reader sees here does not use those words.

Elisha is the one speaking. Earlier, this woman had been kind to him and had given him a place to stay. Her son, who had been a gift from God, died. Elisha prayed and the boy came back to life. Now Elisha gives him back to his mother.

For today: God sees our pain and can act where everything seems to be over. We can bring our losses to him in faith, and also thank him when he gives us hope again, as this woman did when she bowed down in gratitude.
exp.4:13:
He went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, as the man of God had told him. Then his skin was healed, smooth like a child's, and he was clean of his leprosy. "Dipped himself" means that he went fully under the water. "Was clean" means that he was made well.

Naaman was a Syrian commander who had leprosy. He had come to Elisha seeking healing, but he grew angry because the prophet only told him to wash in the Jordan, and he thought the rivers of Damascus were better. His servants persuaded him with good sense: if the prophet had asked him to do something difficult, he would have done it. Here the narrator tells the result of his obedience.

For today: sometimes God asks us for something simple, and our pride resists. Obeying with humility, even when we do not understand everything, opens the door to his blessing.
exp.20:10:
This verse says that God accuses King Manasseh of doing detestable things, worse even than those of the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan before Israel. It also says that Manasseh led Judah into sin by worshiping idols, that is, false images of gods.

The Lord speaks through his prophets. Manasseh was a king of Judah who set up pagan altars and encouraged the people to follow him. For this reason God announces judgment on Jerusalem. The verses that follow show that this punishment would be very serious, although the text also shows that God had warned them earlier with patience.

For today: our decisions affect others, especially if we have authority in the family, at work, or in the church. Let us ask God to help us guide others toward what is good, and let us listen quickly when he corrects us.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that Elisha's disciples, called "sons of the prophets," tell him that the place where they live with him is already too small for them. The word "too small" means cramped, without enough room. The verse says the disciples live with him, and it says they spoke to Elisha, so the wording is clear in the verse itself.

It speaks of a group of young men who followed Elisha to learn about God and serve him. Their community had grown and they needed more room. That is why they ask permission to go to the Jordan, cut timber, and build. Notice that they do not act on their own: first they consult their teacher, and he goes with them.

For today: when God makes your family, your church, or your work grow, it is normal that you need to expand and change. Plan with humility, ask advice from those who guide you, and do not move ahead without seeking God's direction.
exp.20:12:
God says he will bring against Jerusalem the same measure of judgment he applied to Samaria and to the house of Ahab. The "line" is the measuring cord, and the "plummet" is the builders' plumb line; together they speak of a rod of justice. Then he says he will clean out Jerusalem the way a dish is cleaned: everything is removed, and it is turned upside down so that it drains and is left empty.

The Lord speaks through his prophets during the reign of Manasseh, king of Judah. This king promoted idols and wickedness worse than that of the nations who lived in the land before. Samaria and the house of Ahab had already been judged, so Judah knew what it meant. The judgment would come because the people persisted in their sin.

For today: God is patient, but he takes sin seriously. We should not play with it; rather, let us turn to God promptly, confess what is wrong, and allow him to cleanse us.
exp.11:15:
The money that people paid as an offering for a guilt or for a sin was not put into the chest to repair the temple. That money belonged to the priests. "Trespass money" here refers to the guilt offering, and "sin money" means that it was not put into that chest.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, whose name we do not know. He tells how King Joash organized the repair of the temple. He kept apart the offerings meant for the priests, which according to the law belonged to them, from the money for the work. In this way everything was clear and in order.

Today we can learn to handle money with order and honesty. If something was given for a purpose, let us respect that purpose, and let the accounts be clear before God and before others.
exp.3:22:
Here the husband asks his wife why she wants to go to see the prophet today, since it is neither a new moon nor a sabbath. She answers with a single word, without giving any further explanation.

The husband speaks with the Shunammite woman, who had just laid her dead son on the bed of Elisha, the man of God. The days of the new moon and the sabbath were times when some people went to the prophet to receive teaching. She does not tell him about the tragedy; some think she wanted to avoid pain and delay, others that she was acting in faith. The text does not make this clear, but she runs toward Elisha.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, do not stay frozen. Even if you have no clear words, bring your distress directly to God, who can receive you just as you are.
exp.16:9:
This verse describes how the Israelites set up sacred pillars and images on every high hill and under every leafy tree. The sacred pillars were columns or stones set up for worship. The groves were wooden poles or symbols connected with the goddess Asherah, though the older word used for them may cause confusion.

The narrator of 2 Kings explains why Israel, the northern kingdom, was taken captive by Assyria. God had brought them out of Egypt, but they imitated the customs of the nations around them. These places of worship on the hills and under the trees were part of that idolatry.

For today: God is not satisfied with being given only a corner of our lives. We can ask ourselves which customs from our surroundings we have adopted without noticing and that compete with God. With honesty, let us ask Him for help to return to Him with our whole heart.
exp.24:3:
The text says the Babylonians had already broken through the walls of Jerusalem. That night, the soldiers and King Zedekiah fled through a gate between the two walls, near the king's garden, even though the Chaldeans (Babylonians) surrounded the city. The king took the way toward the plain, that is, toward the open country, in the direction of the Jordan.

It is a historical account of the end of the kingdom of Judah, around 586 BC. It is not told through a single character; the narrator explains how Jerusalem fell after a long siege and a terrible famine. For years, the prophets had called the people and their kings to return to God, but they did not listen.

For today: running away does not resolve what has been ignored for a long time. It is better to listen to God and correct our course in time, before the crisis reaches us. His word guides us with love, even when obedience is hard.
exp.21:9:
What it says: Shaphan, the king's secretary, tells King Josiah that the priest Hilkiah has handed him a book. Then Shaphan read it aloud before the king. Words like "scribe" and "shewed" in the verse above mean a secretary or official of the royal court, and one who informed or made the king aware.

Context: The narrator tells us that, while the temple was being repaired, Hilkiah found the book of the law. Many think it could have been all of Deuteronomy or a part of it, though this cannot be known for certain. Shaphan first reported on the money for the work and then added this news. As what follows shows, the king reacted with deep grief when he heard it.

For today: Do not keep the Bible like a forgotten object. Read it carefully and with an open heart, as Josiah did, and let its message correct you and draw you closer to God.
exp.5:14:
This verse tells how the servant of Elisha got up early, went outside, and saw that a large army surrounded the city, with horses and chariots. Frightened, he said to Elisha, "Alas, my master! how shall we do?" The phrase "the man of God" refers to the prophet Elisha, and the servant was a young attendant.

The king of Syria wanted to capture Elisha, because the prophet had been warning the king of Israel about Syrian military plans. So he sent troops by night to Dothan, where Elisha was. The one speaking here is the servant, and he speaks out of fear, because he could only see what was right in front of him.

For today: when problems seem bigger than we are, we can pray as Elisha did and ask God to help us see with faith. His care is real, even though we do not see it with our eyes.
exp.0:8:
This verse says that King Ahaziah sent a captain with fifty soldiers to seek out Elijah. The captain found him sitting on the top of a hill and spoke to him with a command: "Thou man of God, the king hath said, Come down." "Man of God" is a way of addressing a prophet.

King Ahaziah was lying sick in his bed and had sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, a god of Ekron, instead of seeking the God of Israel. Elijah told him that he would die. Furious, the king sent soldiers to bring him. Notice that the captain calls Elijah "man of God," yet gives him an order as if the king were above God.

Today: It is easy to recognize God with our lips and yet not submit to His word. Ask yourself whether you truly obey Him or merely mention Him.
exp.24:24:
In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, a descendant of the royal family, came with ten men and struck down Gedaliah, the governor, so that he died. They also killed the Jews and the Chaldeans (Babylonians) who were with him at Mizpah.

This is a historical account. Judah had just fallen to Babylon, and Gedaliah was appointed governor to look after those who remained. He had promised them that things would go well for them if they submitted. Ishmael, of royal descent, may have acted out of resentment or ambition; the text does not explain his motives. Afterward, the people fled to Egypt out of fear.

For today: when someone seeks peace and order, violence and bitterness can destroy everything. Let us ask God to deliver us from envy and hatred, and to seek peace with humility.
exp.22:9:
It says that King Josiah defiled Topheth, a place in the valley of the son of Hinnom, that is, he made it unclean and unfit for worship. He did this so that no one would again make his son or daughter go through the fire in honor of Molech, a false god. The phrase "go through the fire" is understood to mean offering children as sacrifices, although some scholars debate the details of the rite.

The writer of Kings tells of Josiah's great reform in Judah. His predecessors, such as Manasseh, had filled the land with idols. Josiah, after rediscovering the book of the Law, destroyed altars and places of false worship, beginning with the most scandalous ones.

For today: God values the lives of the smallest and does not share his throne with any idol. Today we can ask ourselves what things we place above God, and protect children with love, time and care.
exp.2:21:
It says that at dawn the Moabites got up and the sun shone on the water that God had sent. From a distance, the water looked to them as red as blood.

This is part of the account where three kings (Israel, Judah, and Edom) were without water for their army, and Elisha announced that God would give them water. It is the narrator who tells what happened. The Moabites, seeing the color, believed that the allied kings had killed each other. Scholars think that the sun, the color of the soil, or both may have caused this effect, but the text does not explain it in detail.

For today: God can use something ordinary, like water, to bless some and confuse others. Let us learn not to draw hasty conclusions from what we see at a distance, and to trust that God cares for his people.
exp.3:13:
Here Elisha asks his servant Gehazi what can be done to show gratitude to the Shunammite woman. Gehazi answers that she has no child and that her husband is old.

Elisha, the prophet, used to stay at this woman's house, and she had prepared a room for him. She turned down the prophet's offer of help, because she lived peacefully among her own people. So Elisha asks Gehazi for advice, and Gehazi notices a need that she had not mentioned. The verses that follow show that Elisha announces a son to her.

For today: sometimes those who serve with generosity ask for nothing, yet they carry hidden needs. Let us learn to look at those who help us with attention and affection, and to bless them with humility. We can also remember that God sees the sorrows we keep silent.
exp.7:28:
This verse tells how King Joram of Israel went back to Jezreel to be healed of the wounds the Syrians had given him at Ramah, during the battle against Hazael, king of Syria. Then Ahaziah, king of Judah, went down to visit him, because Joram was sick.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, reviewing the deeds of the kings. Ahaziah followed the evil ways of the house of Ahab, to which he was related by marriage. The text does not merely report a friendly visit; it shows that Judah had become too closely joined to the royal family of Israel, both in alliances and in conduct.

For today: friendships and alliances influence us more than we think. It is wise to ask ourselves who shapes our decisions, and to ask God for wisdom to choose companions who draw us closer to Him.
exp.13:26:
This verse says that God had not decided to wipe Israel off the face of the earth completely. The word "blot" means to scrape away or erase entirely, the way someone erases a written name. So God saved them through Jeroboam, son of Joash, king of Israel.

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel. Jeroboam II was a king who did evil in the eyes of the Lord, but God saw the suffering of the people, who had no one to help them. So, according to the word of the prophet Jonah, the territory was recovered. This shows God's compassion, not that he approved of that king.

God can show mercy even when we do not deserve it. If today you feel without help or without a way out, remember that God sees your affliction. His goodness does not depend on our being perfect, and he can act through unexpected means. Trust in him and seek his guidance.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the sons of the prophets urged Elisha so persistently to let them search for Elijah that Elisha, embarrassed, finally said, "Send." Urging, as used here, means asking again and again without tiring. The fifty men searched for three days, but they did not find him.

Elijah had just been taken up into heaven, and Elisha had seen it. That is why he had told them not to send anyone. The prophets, who had not seen it closely, thought the Spirit of the Lord might have set him down on some mountain or in some valley. Elisha gave in so that the argument would stop, and the search showed that what he had said was true. Some think his embarrassment came from the pressure of the group; the text does not make this clear.

For today: when God has given you clarity, do not let yourself be pressured by the insistence of others. Listen with humility, but hold your ground with kindness, and if yielding will harm no one, do it with peace.
exp.3:14:
Elisha asks Gehazi, his servant, to call the woman. Gehazi calls her, and she comes and stands at the door.

Elisha speaks with Gehazi because this woman of Shunem had cared for him with generosity, and he wants to thank her. She did not ask the king or the commander for help, since she lived content among her own people. Gehazi notices the need she never mentions: she had no children, and her husband was old. So Elisha has her come in order to give her a promise.

For today: serving with generosity, without asking anything in return, is beautiful. And God often sees and answers the deep needs we keep silent about. We can bring to him with confidence whatever hurts us in silence.
exp.15:11:
He says that when King Ahaz returned from Damascus and saw the altar that the priest Uriah had built, he approached it and offered sacrifices on it. In this case, "the king of Damascus" is a confusing form of the text; from the context, the one who arrives is King Ahaz of Judah, not a king of Damascus.

The account has no speaking character; it is the narrator of Kings who tells the story. Ahaz had gone to meet the king of Assyria and liked a pagan altar. He ordered it copied and placed in the temple of the LORD. Uriah obeyed the king without resisting. The text shows how the king and the priest changed the worship, although the Bible does not say here what each of them thought inwardly.

For today: let us not copy ways of worshiping just because they seem attractive or convenient. Let us always compare what we do with what God has said in his Word.
exp.16:32:
This verse says that the foreign peoples brought to Samaria claimed to honor the Lord, but at the same time kept serving their own gods, just as they had done in their homelands. In this verse, "feared" means worshiping and serving the Lord.

The author of the book of Kings, whom Jewish tradition does not identify with certainty, explains why the northern kingdom fell. Assyria carried the Israelites away and settled other peoples in their land. They tried to add the Lord to their list of gods, but the text says this mixture was not true fear of the Lord, since he had commanded that he alone be worshiped.

Today we may ask ourselves whether we give God a place among other loyalties, such as money, success, or the approval of others. God does not seek one more place in our lives, but a whole heart.
exp.1:0:
This verse announces that God himself decided to take Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, that is, a strong, swirling wind. The verse says that Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal while this was about to happen.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Elijah has been a very important prophet, and his time of service is coming to an end. Elisha is his disciple and successor. The verses that follow show that Elijah tries to part from him, but Elisha will not leave him. Some believe Gilgal is the place near the Jordan, although there is some doubt about which Gilgal is meant.

God directs the beginning and the end of our service. If today you are called to learn from someone with more experience, be faithful and steadfast, like Elisha. And if you are called to teach, prepare others with love, trusting that God will continue his work.
exp.14:16:
This verse says that Menahem, son of Gadi, began to rule over Israel in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, king of Judah. His reign lasted ten years, and he governed from Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom. The word "reigned" means that he began to rule as king.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, noting the kings of Israel and of Judah one by one. Menahem came to the throne after killing Shallum, and the verses that follow tell of his great cruelty against Tiphsah and his evil before God. Afterward he paid tribute to the king of Assyria to secure his hold on power.

For today: reaching a position is not the same as ruling well. We may seek security through force or through money, but God calls us to trust him and to treat others with justice and compassion.
exp.18:27:
It says that God knows the king of Assyria has raged against Him and has challenged Him with pride. Therefore God tells him that He will put a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips. That is, He will control him and make him return by the same way he came. The word "tumult" means noisy commotion or arrogance.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had invaded Judah, mocked the God of Israel, and threatened Jerusalem. King Hezekiah had prayed asking for help. God answers by saying that no human power acts outside of His knowledge. Some scholars see in the image of the hook an Assyrian custom of leading captives with hooks, but this is interpreted in various ways.

For today: when you feel threatened by someone stronger, pray as Hezekiah did and trust that God sees everything and rules over any human pride.
exp.14:5:
This verse is a closing formula. The author says that the rest of the life and deeds of King Azariah (also called Uzziah) are recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." It is a rhetorical question: it means "that is already written there, and you can look it up."

The narrator of Kings summarizes each reign and refers to official court archives. That book has not been preserved, so we do not know for certain what it contained. Earlier, it is said that Azariah had leprosy until he died, and that his son Jotham governed the palace. The author focuses on whether the king followed God, not on all his achievements.

For today: our lives also leave a record. More than achievements, what matters is whether we walk with God with a whole heart. Let us live today so that what is written about us is faithfulness, humility, and love.
exp.16:29:
It says that the foreign peoples whom Assyria brought to Samaria made their own idols. The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth made Nergal, and the men of Hamath made Ashima. "Made" means that they fashioned them with their own hands. Scholars are not sure exactly what each name represented.

The account comes from the author of Kings. It explains why the northern kingdom fell: Assyria carried off the Israelites and settled people from other nations in their land. They wanted to honor the LORD as one more god of the region, but without giving up their gods. That is why the text says they feared the LORD and, at the same time, served their idols.

For today: it is not enough to say we believe in God if we leave room for other things that rule the heart. Let us ask Him to show us which modern "gods," such as money, success, or the approval of others, we need to let go of so that we serve Him alone.
exp.22:6:
This verse says that King Josiah destroyed some rooms that were inside God's temple. Men dedicated to prostitution in pagan worship lived there, and the text calls them by a word from an old usage that refers to them. The women wove tents or garments for the sacred pole, meaning the image of the goddess Asherah, which was an idol.

The one telling the story is the author of Kings, recounting the great reform of Josiah, king of Judah. He had found the book of the law and wanted to clean the land of idolatry. Earlier kings had allowed these practices to enter even the temple itself. Some details of the Hebrew text are interpreted in different ways, but the general idea is clear: these were idolatrous practices.

For today: God wants a clean heart given wholly to Him. Let us ask Him to show us what things we have allowed into our lives that take away His place, and let us remove them with resolve.
exp.20:21:
He abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not live according to the will of God. "Abandoned" means that he turned away from Him, and "way" speaks of the manner of living and obeying.

This is the account of the author of Kings about Amon, son of Manasseh. It is not a speech but a summary meant to explain why his reign was evil. He imitated the idolatry of his father, and he reigned only two years. Then his servants killed him, and the people made his son Josiah king.

For today: it is not enough to inherit a faith or to see good examples; each person decides whether to walk with God. Today you can seek Him through prayer and reading the Bible, so that your faith is personal and not merely a family custom.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that the Moabites came confidently to the camp of Israel, but the Israelites rose up and attacked them. The Moabites fled, and the Israelites pursued them without stopping, striking them down.

The narrator recounts what happened after the miracle of the trenches filled with water, which Elisha had announced. At dawn, the sun made the water look red, and Moab thought the allied kings had killed each other. They believed the only thing left was to plunder the camp. It was a miscalculation that led to their defeat.

For today: it is dangerous to decide in haste and on appearances alone. Moab saw something red and concluded what they wanted to believe. Before acting, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek the truth, because what seems certain at first glance can be very far from reality.
exp.14:15:
This verse describes an act of brutal violence. Menahem attacked the city of Tiphsah and all its inhabitants, and also the surrounding territory, from Tirzah. The reason given was that they did not open their gates to him. He also struck down the pregnant women, ripping open their bodies.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings tells the events without approving of them. Menahem had just killed King Shallum and taken the throne of Israel. This city refused to submit to him, and he answered with extreme cruelty. The text that follows says that he did evil in the sight of the LORD. There is uncertainty about the exact location of Tiphsah.

For today: power without the fear of God becomes cruel. If we have authority, whether at home or at work, let us ask God to make us treat others with justice and compassion.
exp.18:8:
This verse says that the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, received a report: Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, had come out to fight against him. Upon hearing it, Sennacherib sent messengers again to Hezekiah. The name that appears in the verse as "Tirhakah" is the same person, and "Ethiopia" corresponds to Cush, south of Egypt.

Assyria held the threat over Judah. Earlier, God had said through Isaiah that the king would hear a rumor and return to his own land. This news fits that word, although the text does not say it is the only rumor. Sennacherib, though uneasy, still wanted Hezekiah to surrender, and so he sent another message of pressure.

For today: when a threat seems stronger than you are, remember that God governs events, including the news that moves the powerful. Trust in Him, and do not let yourself be persuaded by voices that tell you God will not help you.
exp.21:13:
This verse tells that the priest Hilkiah and four other trusted men of the king went to speak with Huldah, a prophetess. She was the wife of Shallum, who was in charge of the wardrobe (probably the temple's or the palace's garments; it is not known for certain). She lived in Jerusalem, in the second quarter of the city, a newer area that some understand as a separate district.

We are speaking of King Josiah. While the temple was being repaired, the book of the law was found, and on hearing it, the king was distressed because his people had disobeyed God. For this reason he sent these men to inquire of the LORD what would happen. Huldah would give them the answer from God.

For today: when God's word confronts us, we should not ignore it. Let us seek God with humility and obey it.
exp.20:3:
It says that King Manasseh built pagan altars inside the temple of the Lord. That is, he placed objects of false worship in the very place that God had set apart for himself. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem, and "put my name there" means that God chose that place to dwell in a special way among his people.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells the story of Manasseh, son of the good king Hezekiah. Manasseh undid his father's reforms and followed the customs of the pagan nations. The writer stresses that this was all the more serious because it happened in the temple, where God had promised his presence.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are letting other things, such as money, pride, or fame, take the place that belongs to God alone in our hearts. Let us give him first place.
exp.24:19:
This verse tells that Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, took the priests, officials, and other important men of Jerusalem and brought them to Riblah, where the king of Babylon was.

It is the account of the end of the kingdom of Judah, after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem around 586 BC. The author of the book, whom Jewish tradition associates with Jeremiah though this is not certain, narrates the judgment on a people who had turned away from God for a long time. At Riblah, the king of Babylon had these men executed, as the following verse says.

For today: God takes the responsibility of leaders seriously. We can pray for those who guide us and live with humility, remembering that God remains faithful even in very dark times.
exp.18:13:
This verse tells how King Hezekiah received a letter from the messengers sent by Sennacherib. He read it, went up to the house of the Lord, and spread it out before the LORD. The word "letter" here means the written message, and "Lord" refers to God.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, was threatening Jerusalem. In his letter he mocked God and said that the God of Judah would not be able to save them, just as the gods of other nations had not saved theirs. Hezekiah did not respond with pride or with fear. He brought the problem to God. Some see in the act of spreading out the letter a way of laying the case before Him, although the text gives no further explanation.

When something worries us, we can do the same: not only think about the problem, but honestly place it before God in prayer. He listens to us and invites us to entrust to Him what weighs on us.
exp.4:5:
Here the account tells that Naaman brought a letter to the king of Israel. A "letter" is a written note sent from one person to another. The king of Syria wrote that he was sending his servant Naaman so that the king of Israel would heal him of his leprosy.

The one speaking is the king of Syria. Naaman, his military commander, had leprosy, and an Israelite girl had told him there was help in Israel. The king thought that healing depended on another king, so he wrote to the authority he knew. He did not know that the healing would come through the prophet Elisha, not through the palace.

For today: sometimes we look for help in the places that seem most important or powerful. God often works in simple ways and by unexpected paths. Ask him to guide you, and to give you humility to receive his help as and through whatever means he chooses to give it.
exp.20:17:
It says that King Manasseh died, that he "slept with his fathers", a gentle way of speaking of death. He was buried in the garden of his own house, called the garden of Uzza, and his son Amon began to reign in his place.

This is the account of the writer of Kings, who sums up the end of one of the most wicked kings of Judah. Manasseh filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and led the people into sin. It is noticeable that they did not bury him in the tomb of the kings, though the text does not explain why. We also do not know for certain where the garden of Uzza was. Then Amon repeated the same sins as his father.

What we do leaves a mark on those who follow us, above all on our children. Let us ask God that our example draws them close to Him, and does not lead them to repeat our mistakes.
exp.24:16:
Here it says that each bronze pillar of the temple was eighteen cubits high (about eight or nine meters, depending on which cubit is used). On top it had a capital, that is, a decorative piece three cubits tall. Around it ran a network of bronze and pomegranates, also of bronze. The other pillar was the same.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, around 586 B.C. The Babylonian captain of the guard carried off the objects from the temple. The pillars are described in such detail because they were beautiful and symbolic, and now they lay destroyed. Interpreters differ on the exact meaning of their ornaments.

For today: what seems large and secure can be lost. Do not place your trust in buildings, achievements, or visible things, but in God, who remains faithful even when everything falls apart.
exp.4:19:
This verse shows what went through the mind of Gehazi, Elisha's servant. He thought his master had made a mistake by refusing the gifts of Naaman the Syrian. The word "spared" in the verse means that Elisha let go of an opportunity. Swearing by the Lord's life is a way of making an oath. Gehazi decided to run after Naaman in order to get something for himself.

Naaman had just been healed of leprosy through Elisha. He had offered silver, gold and clothing, but Elisha would accept nothing, to show that the healing was a gift from God and not something that could be bought. Gehazi speaks to himself, that is, in secret, and uses the name of the Lord to justify his greed.

For today: let us be careful not to use religious words to cover selfish desires. Before we act, let us ask ourselves honestly: am I seeking to serve God, or to benefit from what he does?
exp.21:12:
This verse says that the king sends his men to inquire of God about the book that was found. He recognizes that the wrath of God is kindled, because the people before them did not obey what was written. "Ask of the Lord" means seeking God's answer; "because" is the meaning of the word that connects the reason.

King Josiah speaks, having just heard the law of God, probably read from the book found in the temple. He tore his clothes as a sign of grief and repentance. Realizing that the people had turned away from what God commanded, he was not content to stay as he was, but sought a word from God. That is why he sends to consult the prophetess Huldah.

For today: when the Bible shows us that we are falling short, let us not ignore it or make excuses for ourselves. Let us respond with humility, ask for forgiveness, and seek God's guidance to change.
exp.9:22:
Jehu went into the temple of Baal along with Jehonadab, son of Rechab, and asked the worshippers of Baal to search carefully and make sure there was no servant of the Lord among them. Only those who serve Baal were to be present.

Jehu, king of Israel, had pretended to be a great devotee of Baal in order to gather all of Baal's followers into one place. Jehonadab was a man known for his faithfulness to God, and he went along with Jehu. What follows is the slaughter of the worshippers of Baal. Jehu acts with deceit, and the Bible does not present everything he does as an example to imitate, since 2 Kings 10:31 says that he did not follow the Lord with all his heart.

For today: God wants a sincere and undivided faith. Let us honestly examine whom we truly serve, and not settle for a half-hearted religion.
exp.16:24:
It says that when the new settlers arrived in Samaria, they did not honor or respect the Lord. Because of this, God sent lions that killed some of them. "Fearing the Lord" means revering him and acknowledging him as God. The word "at the beginning" in the verse simply refers to when they first began living there.

The narrator of the book explains what happened after Assyria carried Israel away into exile because of its unfaithfulness. The Assyrian king brought foreigners into the region, and they did not know the God of that land. The settlers understood this as a failure to know the way the God of the place was to be worshiped. The text presents the lions as an act of the Lord, although it does not explain in detail how or why it happened that way.

For today: God deserves to be taken seriously, and he is not indifferent to how we treat him. We can ask ourselves whether we truly honor him or merely keep outward forms. His desire is that we know him and trust him with reverence and gratitude.
exp.10:0:
This verse tells that Athaliah, the mother of King Ahaziah, learned that her son had died. Then she rose up and ordered the killing of all the royal seed, that is, the descendants of the king's family, so that she could keep the power for herself.

The account is told by the author of the book of Kings. Ahaziah had died shortly before, and Athaliah saw the opportunity to rule. She came from the line of Ahab and Jezebel, and her action threatened the descendants of David, from whom God had promised that the king would come. Even so, the following text shows that Jehosheba saved the little Joash, and God's promise remained firm.

For today: the desire for power can harden the heart to the point of hurting those closest to us. Let us ask God for humility, and remember that even when evil seems to dominate, God continues to watch over his plan and can use brave and humble people.
exp.14:19:
This verse says that King Menahem, in order to pay the king of Assyria, collected a tax from the wealthy and influential men of Israel. From each one he demanded fifty shekels of silver (a shekel was a unit of weight, about eleven or twelve grams). With that payment, the Assyrian king withdrew and did not stay in the land. The phrase "mighty men of wealth" refers to people with a great deal of money and standing.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes Menahem's reign, speaks. Menahem had done evil before the Lord, and he gave a thousand talents of silver to Pul (also called Tiglath-pileser) to strengthen his kingdom. That is why he gathered the money from the rich. The Bible does not say that he sought God; he trusted in a foreign king.

For today: when pressures arise, it is easy to look for quick human solutions. Before paying a high price to secure our position, let us seek God in prayer and trust in Him.
exp.16:4:
This verse says that the king of Assyria invaded the whole territory of the kingdom of Israel and attacked the city of Samaria, the capital. He surrounded it and kept it under siege for three years. The word "went up" is used because Samaria stood on high ground, and "besieged it" means that he kept it encircled.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the fall of the northern kingdom. Hoshea, the last king of Israel, stopped paying tribute to Assyria and sought help from Egypt. That rebellion provoked the invasion. The verses that follow explain the deeper reason: the people had sinned against God and adopted foreign gods.

For today: trusting in human solutions, as Hoshea did with Egypt, does not replace faithfulness to God. When we face pressures, we can return to Him sincerely before the consequences pile up.
exp.8:5:
Jehu got up and went into a house. There the young prophet poured oil on his head and told him what God says: he has anointed him as king over Israel, the people of God. "Anoint" means setting someone apart for a task, and the oil was the sign. The word "entered" is what this means.

The young man had been sent by the prophet Elisha to Ramoth-gilead, where Jehu was with other army commanders. God speaks through the young man and gives Jehu the task of judging the house of Ahab, for its wickedness and for the blood of the prophets. God is the one who gives the authority.

For today: every position or responsibility we receive comes with a call to obey God. Today you can ask yourself how to use faithfully what God has entrusted to you, without forgetting that He is the one who gave it.
exp.14:1:
He says that Azariah, also called Uzziah in other passages, began to reign over Judah at the age of sixteen. His reign lasted fifty-two years in Jerusalem, a very long time. He also mentions his mother, Jecholiah, who was from Jerusalem.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book of Kings, who introduces each king by his age, his years of rule, and his mother. He does this to place each king within the history of Judah and Israel and later to evaluate him according to his faithfulness to God. This king had a long and stable reign.

For today: God can use a young person who takes on great responsibility. If you are called to serve, work, or lead while young, do it with humility and seek God's guidance. Doing what is right also matters across long and steady years.
exp.5:4:
It says that a man was cutting down a tree when the iron head of his axe came loose and sank into the water. He cried out in distress because the tool was not his own.

The word that appears here means "borrowed," so the word in the source has been turned into the plain English word that matches the verse.

The disciples of the prophets needed a larger place to live, so they went to the Jordan to cut wood. Elisha, the prophet, went with them at their request. The one speaking is one of those young men, worried because he could not pay for the axe head or give back what he had borrowed. He was probably poor.

God cares about our small worries, not only the big ones. If something troubles you, such as a debt or a mistake you do not know how to put right, bring it to him with confidence and honesty. And take care of what others entrust to you.
exp.9:30:
Jehu did not make it his concern to walk in the law of the Lord God of Israel with all his heart. He also did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, which had led Israel into sin.

The narrator of the book of Kings is speaking here. Jehu had just carried out God's judgment against the house of Ahab, and God commended him for it. But the text shows that his obedience was partial: he kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Afterward, Israel began to lose territory to Hazael, king of Syria.

For today: obeying God only in what suits us or comes easily is not enough. We can ask him to show us any area we have left unsurrendered, and obey him sincerely, not just for appearance or to check a box.
exp.11:6:
King Jehoash called the high priest Jehoiada and the other priests to account. He asked them why they had not repaired the cracks in the temple. He ordered them to stop keeping the money they received from their acquaintances and to hand it over for the repairs.

The verse says "the breaches of the house," and the word "acquaintances" refers to the people close to them who gave them offerings.

King Jehoash speaks. Twenty-three years had passed in his reign and the temple was still damaged, even though it had been arranged that this money would be used to repair it. That is why the king corrects the priests firmly.

For today: what is dedicated to God should be used faithfully and openly. Let us check whether we are doing what we promised, and give an account with humility.
exp.5:17:
This verse tells how the soldiers of Syria came down toward Elisha to capture him. Then he prayed to God and asked that they be struck with blindness. God did what Elisha asked.

The king of Syria was at war with Israel and wanted to seize Elisha, because this prophet was revealing his plans. Elisha had already shown his servant the army of God that protected them. Now he prays again. Some think this blindness was a confusion of sight that kept them from recognizing where they were, not necessarily total darkness.

When we face threats or people who want to harm us, we can first turn to God in prayer, instead of acting out of fear or violence. He knows how to care for us and guide the situation.
exp.10:5:
This verse describes how the guards would be divided. One third would watch the gate of Sur, and another third the gate behind the guard, that is, the entrance where the guards were stationed. With this they would protect the temple so that no one would break into it by force.

The priest Jehoiada is speaking. Athaliah was ruling Judah illegitimately, and Jehoiada had secretly kept the young Joash, the rightful heir to the throne, hidden. In the seventh year he organized the soldiers, made a covenant with them in the temple, and gave them precise orders to protect the child king. Some details of the names of the gates are difficult to pin down.

Today, this passage reminds us that caring for what is precious requires order, commitment, and teamwork. Each person must fulfill their place well, whether in the family, in the church, or at work.
exp.5:2:
One of the disciples asks Elisha to go with them, and Elisha agrees. Where the wording of the verse is concerned, the request is simply "Be content, I pray thee, and go with thy servants." The phrase "I pray thee" is a polite way of asking, and "thy servants" is a humble way of referring to themselves. Elisha's reply is brief: "I will go."

The sons of the prophets were a group of disciples who lived together near Elisha. Their house had become too small, so they decided to go to the Jordan to cut timber to build a larger one. They already had Elisha's permission, but one of them also wanted his company. Elisha did not stay behind giving orders from a distance, but went with them. What follows shows that his presence was very valuable.

For today: it is not necessary to be perfect to invite God and spiritual leaders into our projects, even ordinary ones. Asking for companionship with humility, and offering it with generosity, strengthens the community.
exp.5:6:
He says that Elisha, the man of God, told the man, "Take it up," and that the man reached out his hand and picked up the iron axe head that was already floating. "Reached out" means stretched out, and "picked up" means took it.

The prophets' disciples were building a place to live beside the Jordan. One of them dropped a borrowed axe into the water, and he was distressed because it was not his. Elisha made the iron float by means of a stick. Here Elisha speaks, and the account shows that God cares even about a small problem and about the honor of someone who owes something to another. Scholars see in this a miracle, not a natural explanation.

When you face a need, however small it may seem, bring it to God with confidence. Then take the step that is yours to take, like that man who had to reach out his hand.
exp.14:33:
It says that Jotham, king of Judah, did what pleased God. "Did that which was right in the sight of the Lord" means doing what God sees as right. He followed the example of his father Uzziah, who was also a king who, in general, honored God.

The narrator of the book of Kings summarizes the reign of Jotham, which lasted sixteen years. His good conduct is highlighted, but the text goes on to clarify that the high places, where the people offered sacrifices, were not removed. So his faithfulness was real, though not complete. Jotham also built the upper gate of the temple.

We can be thankful for and follow the good examples of those who came before us, but we should also examine whether there are "high places" in our lives: customs or habits we have left unchanged. Let us ask God for help to obey Him wholeheartedly, not only in part.
exp.9:25:
The verse tells that Jehu's men brought out the images from the house of Baal and burned them. The word "images" refers to sacred pillars or stones that were used in the worship of Baal. This is not described as simple disorder: it shows how they destroyed the objects of worship that were inside the temple.

This takes place after Jehu, who had been anointed king of Israel, gathered the worshippers of Baal by deceit and ordered them put to death. The account is told by the author of the book of Kings, who shows Jehu ending the Baal worship that the house of Ahab had promoted. Scholars differ in their views on his violent methods, and the same book notes that Jehu did not follow the Lord wholeheartedly.

For today: if something in your life occupies the place that belongs to God alone, be honest and remove it without leaving a trace. Let it be God, and nothing else, who holds your first trust.
exp.17:15:
It says that King Hezekiah cut the gold off the doors of the temple and from the frames that held them, and gave it to the king of Assyria. Here "the frames that held them" refers to the posts or frames on which the doors turn.

The speaker is the narrator of the book. Assyria had invaded Judah, and Hezekiah, who had earlier been faithful to God, tried to buy peace by paying a heavy tribute. To gather it, he took even the gold from the temple that he himself had put there. Even so, the Assyrian king later sent a great army against Jerusalem, so the payment solved nothing.

When we are afraid, we may try to fix everything with hasty solutions, even giving up what is sacred. This passage invites us to trust God first and not to hand over what is most precious out of fear.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that God saw the very bitter suffering of the people of Israel. No one was protected or left to their own fate with the strength to hold on, and there was no one to help them. "Saw" means that God looked on them closely and had compassion. The phrase "shut up nor left" is hard; it probably refers to the idea that everyone, whether bound or free, was without strength. It is understood that no one could rescue them.

The author of the book of Kings recounts that King Jeroboam II did what was evil, yet God used this king to recover territory, as spoken by the prophet Jonah. The verse explains the reason: it was not because of the king's merit, but because God saw the pain of his people and decided not to blot out their name.

God can see our pain and act with mercy even when we do not deserve it and there is no one else to help. We can come to Him honestly, trusting in His compassion, and thank Him for His undeserved help.
exp.4:3:
One of Naaman's servants went in and told his lord, the king of Syria, the message he had received. The verse reports that Naaman, commander of the army of Syria, went and repeated to his king what the young Israelite girl had said. The phrase "told his lord" means that he passed on the whole account to him: that there was a prophet in Samaria who could heal him of his leprosy.

Naaman speaks with the king of Syria, his lord. The girl was a captive, taken by force by Syrian soldiers, and she served Naaman's wife. Even so, she spoke with goodwill. Naaman took her words seriously, and that moved the king to send him to Israel in search of healing.

God can use ordinary people, the young, or those in difficult circumstances to give a word of hope. Let us not look down on anyone because of their age or condition. And when someone offers us good guidance, let us listen with humility.
exp.6:12:
A servant of the king offers a practical solution: that they take five of the horses that are left in the city and send some men to investigate. He says that those horses and the men who ride them are in the same situation as everyone else: in any case they are at risk of dying of hunger, so they lose nothing by trying.

The king suspected that the Syrians were pretending to have withdrawn in order to set a trap for them. Samaria was under siege and the people were dying of hunger. One of his servants, who speaks with realism, proposes sending scouts to find out the truth instead of remaining paralyzed by fear.

When we are in a difficult situation and everything seems uncertain, it is often better to take a prudent step and check the reality than to remain motionless. Doing so with faith, asking God for wisdom, can open unexpected doors.
exp.2:5:
This verse tells that King Joram went out of Samaria, the capital of Israel, and numbered all Israel. That word means he reviewed or counted his troops to see what forces he had. It was preparation for war.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Moab had been paying a huge tribute to Israel, but when Ahab died, his king Mesha rebelled. Joram, son of Ahab, wanted to regain control, and so he gathered the army. Right away he asked Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, for help. It is striking that at this point it is not mentioned that Joram sought God's counsel.
