For today: before making plans, counting resources and setting out, it is wise to stop and seek God's guidance. Preparing well is wise, but it must not take the place of prayer.
exp.18:21:
God asks Sennacherib two questions that carry a sharp rebuke: whom do you think you have insulted and offended? Speaking with contempt and offending are what the words "reproached" and "blasphemed" describe. "Lifted up your voice" and "lifted up your eyes" describe pride and arrogance. The answer is plain: he offended the Holy One of Israel, that is, the holy and only God.

Here God speaks, through the prophet Isaiah, to the king of Assyria. King Hezekiah had prayed for help, because Sennacherib was mocking Jerusalem and its God. God answers that these mockeries did not go unheard.

For today: when someone mocks your faith, or you feel small before powerful people, remember that God hears and rules over all. Pray with confidence, as Hezekiah did, and avoid the pride that forgets God is holy.
exp.24:6:
This verse describes the cruel punishment that the king of Babylon gave to Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. First they killed his sons in front of him, and then they blinded him. Then they took him, bound in chains, to Babylon. The last thing Zedekiah saw was the death of his sons.

The narrator of the book tells of the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. Zedekiah had tried to escape, but they caught up with him near Jericho. He had broken his oath to the king of Babylon, and the book presents this fall as the result of Judah's rebellion against God and of the warnings the prophets ignored. It is a harsh account, not an approval of cruel violence.

Today we can learn that ignoring the voice of God has painful consequences. If God calls us to correct something, it is better to obey today with humility than to wait until it is too late.
exp.1:9:
Elijah tells Elisha that his request is "a hard thing", that is, something Elijah cannot grant by his own power. He gives him a sign: if Elisha sees him when he is taken away from his side, he will receive what he asked for. If he does not see him, he will not receive it.

Elijah speaks as the senior prophet to his disciple, shortly before his departure. Elisha had asked for a double portion of his spirit, which many understand as the share of the firstborn or heir (Deuteronomy 21:17), though some interpret it in other ways. The answer places the gift in God's hands, not Elijah's. Then Elisha sees the chariot of fire.

For today: we may ask God for great things, but it is He who gives them. And it is wise to remain attentive and faithful, with our eyes fixed on Him, so that we can recognize what He is doing.
exp.3:5:
It says that, when all the vessels were full of oil, the woman asked her son for another vessel. The son answered that there were no more, and at that moment the oil stopped flowing. "Stayed" means that it stopped. "Yet" here means "still."

A widow, in debt and in danger of losing her sons as servants, had asked the prophet Elisha for help. He told her to borrow vessels from her neighbors and to shut herself in with her sons and pour out the oil she had. The account relates that the oil lasted as long as there were vessels available. Afterward, Elisha told her to sell the oil and pay her debt.

God often provides according to the faith with which we take concrete steps, even when what we have seems small. We can obey and prepare our "vessels" with confidence: praying, working, and waiting. We can also remember that his provision is sufficient for every need.
exp.22:27:
This verse is a closing formula that is repeated throughout Kings. It says that the rest of what King Josiah did, and all his deeds, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. That book is not the Bible we know, but an ancient court record that is not preserved today.

The narrator closes the account of Josiah, a king who reformed the country and turned the people back to God. Even so, the verse before shows that God did not withdraw his judgment because of the sins of Manasseh. Right after this, the story tells of Josiah's death at the hands of Pharaoh Necho.

For today: our deeds matter, and God remembers them. Serve God faithfully, even when you do not see all the results, and leave your life in his hands.
exp.3:26:
She says that the Shunammite woman came to Elisha, the man of God, on Mount Carmel, and caught hold of his feet. Gehazi, the servant, came near to push her away, but Elisha stopped him. This verse says that her soul was vexed within her, meaning she was suffering a very deep pain, and that the reason had been hidden from her by God.

Elisha speaks. The son of this woman, whom God had promised earlier, had just died. She had said nothing about the reason as she traveled, but before the prophet she showed her distress. Elisha admits that he does not know everything: God did not always reveal things to him.

For today: when someone suffers, it is not necessary to have all the answers. Sometimes the best thing is to let the person pour out what they feel, to listen to them with patience and stay beside them, while we bring them before God in prayer.
exp.13:28:
It says that King Jeroboam died. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is an old, gentle way of saying that he passed away and was laid to rest with his ancestors. Afterward, his son Zachariah became king in his place. With this, the account of Jeroboam's reign comes to an end.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the history of the kings of Israel. This Jeroboam, the second of that name, reigned for a long time and was strong in matters of war. But the biblical text also presents him as a king who continued in the sins of the first Jeroboam. God showed patience with Israel and did not yet want to blot out their name. That patience does not mean that he approved of everything that was being done.

For today: no power, success, or position lasts forever. Let us live with humility, using well the time God gives us, and take hold of his patience to turn back to him with sincerity.
exp.24:0:
In the ninth year of the reign of King Zedekiah (as the following verse makes clear), on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came with his whole army against Jerusalem and surrounded it in order to attack it. "Surrounded it" means that he encircled the city to keep anything from going in or out. The war machines, such as towers or siege ramps, that they raised all around the city were the siege equipment.

The text is a historical account, not a speech. The author of Kings tells the story of Judah's fall and presents it as the result of the people and their kings turning away from God, after many warnings from the prophets. This verse marks the beginning of the final siege against Jerusalem.

For today: God's warnings are not cruel but an opportunity to return to Him in time. If you feel that God is calling you to correct something, do not put it off; answer Him with humility and trust in His mercy.
exp.15:3:
This verse says that King Ahaz offered sacrifices and burned incense in the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree. The word for perfumes means incense, and the high places were places of worship on elevated ground.

The author of the book, who tells the story of the kings, describes Ahaz, king of Judah. He compares him with David and concludes that he did not do what was right. He adopted practices from pagan peoples, and those places were tied to idolatry. The text presents him this way to explain the spiritual decline of Judah, just before the attacks from Syria and Israel arrived.

For today: it is not enough to be religious; what matters is to whom we direct our hearts. Let us examine whether we worship God alone or whether we copy customs that draw us away from him. Let us ask him to guide us into a sincere faith.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that Ahaz, son of Jotham, began to reign as king of Judah in the seventeenth year of Pekah, king of Israel. "Began to reign" means that he started to govern. At that time there were two separate kingdoms: Israel to the north and Judah to the south.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, recording the reigns of the kings of both kingdoms. His purpose is to place each king in time and to judge him by his faithfulness to God. The verses that follow show that Ahaz did not follow the example of David, but practiced idolatry. Some scholars debate how to match the exact dates of these reigns, and there is no single solution accepted by everyone.

For today: what we inherit does not decide what we will do. Ahaz had a good father and a good example, but he chose another path. Each day we can decide to follow God wholeheartedly.
exp.12:8:
This verse tells us that King Jehoahaz died. The expression "slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died and was joined to his ancestors. They buried him in Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and his son Joash took the throne.

It is part of the historical account in Kings, written by an author who is not named. It summarizes the end of Jehoahaz's reign, a weak king whose army was nearly destroyed by Syria. According to the context that follows, his son Joash also did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam. The text shows how one king after another kept to the same wrong path.

No office or power lasts forever, but our decisions leave a mark on those who come after us. Today we can ask ourselves what example of faith and obedience we are leaving to our family, and ask God to help us live in a way that others will want to follow.
exp.16:6:
This verse explains why the northern kingdom fell. It says that the people of Israel sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt and freed them from the power of the Pharaoh. Even so, they "had feared other gods," that is, they honored and worshiped false gods.

The author of the book of Kings, whose identity is not known for certain, is the one speaking. After telling of the fall of Samaria and the exile to Assyria, he stops to explain the reason. For him, it was not only a military defeat, but the consequence of having abandoned the covenant with God.

For today: remembering what God has done for us helps us not to give our hearts to other things. Ask yourself what thing today has taken the place that belongs to God, and trust Him again.
exp.17:3:
This verse tells us that King Hezekiah cleared the land of false worship. He removed the high places (places where rituals were held, often mixed with idolatry), broke the images, and cut down the groves (poles or trees tied to the worship of false gods). He also destroyed the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because the people were burning incense to it. He gave it the name Nehushtan.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes Hezekiah's reign. That serpent came from Numbers 21, when God healed the people through it. Over time, something that had been a reminder of God's help became an object of worship. The author shows that Hezekiah sought to obey God, even when that meant breaking something of historical value.

Today, it is worth asking ourselves whether something good, such as a tradition, a memory, or a ministry, has taken the place that belongs to God alone.
exp.4:22:
Naaman, the commander of the Syrian army, now healed of leprosy, insisted that Gehazi accept two talents of silver, double what had been asked. Gehazi tied up the silver in two bags, and with it he received two changes of clothing. Naaman's two servants carried everything on their backs, to bring it before Gehazi.

Gehazi, servant of the prophet Elisha, had run after Naaman and lied, saying that Elisha was asking for this gift for two young prophets. Earlier, Elisha had refused all payment, so that the healing would be seen as a gift from God. Gehazi wanted to take advantage of that, and his deception would soon be discovered.

For today: greed can lead us to lie and to use what belongs to God for our own gain. Let us ask God for an honest and thankful heart, one that serves without seeking hidden profit.
exp.7:2:
It says that, when the seven years of famine had passed, the woman returned from the land of the Philistines. Then she went to ask the king for help to recover her house and her lands. Here "cry out" means to ask for help with urgency, like someone demanding justice.

The narrator tells what happened after Elisha warned her about the famine. She was the woman whose son Elisha had brought back to life (2 Kings 4). She obeyed and stayed away for seven years. On her return, we do not know for certain why she had lost her property; probably others occupied it while she was gone. The passage shows how God cared for her and brought her before the king at just the right moment.

For today: obeying God may cost us leaving things behind, but he does not forget us. We can act with courage, ask for what is just, and trust that he guides the timing.
exp.3:9:
She says to her husband that they should build a small room with walls, on the upper part of the house or next to it. There they would put a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick (a lamp on a stand). That way, when Elisha passed by, he would have a place where he could rest and stay.

The woman of Shunem, described as "a great woman," probably means someone of good standing. She had already noticed that Elisha passed by often and recognized him as a holy man of God. So she is not content just to give him food; she wants to offer him a quiet and dignified place to rest.

For today: simple hospitality is a way of serving God. You do not need much; it is enough to notice the needs of those who serve others and offer them rest, food, or a space of peace.
exp.24:23:
Gedaliah, the governor, promises the officers and their men under oath that they need not fear submitting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). He tells them to stay in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with them. "Servants" here means being under their authority.

Jerusalem had fallen and many had been taken captive. Babylon left behind in Judah the poorer people and appointed Gedaliah governor at Mizpah. He tries to calm the military leaders, who feared reprisals. His counsel agrees with what Jeremiah taught: accept the judgment and live peacefully in the land. But shortly afterward Ishmael murdered him, and the people fled to Egypt out of fear.

For today: when we go through difficult consequences, fear pushes us toward hasty decisions. It is wise to listen to God's voice, act with humility, and seek peace, without being carried away by violence or by panic.
exp.11:17:
The verse says that Jehoash king of Judah took all the holy things that Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, his ancestors, kings of Judah, had set apart, along with his own holy things and all the gold found in the treasures of the house of the Lord and in the king's house, and sent it to Hazael king of Syria. With that payment, Hazael stopped attacking Jerusalem.

It is part of the historical account in Kings, where the speaker is not a character but the narrator. Hazael had already conquered Gath and was threatening Jerusalem. Jehoash, who had earlier repaired the temple, now buys peace with what had been set apart for God. The text does not say he sought God in that crisis; the end of his reign was tragic.

When fear arrives, it is tempting to resolve it quickly by giving up what we should not give. Before taking an easy way out, it is wise to pray, seek wise counsel, and trust God.
exp.4:4:
This verse tells how the king of Syria says to Naaman that he should go to Israel, and that he himself will send letters to the king of that country. Naaman sets out with a great gift: ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of fine clothing.

Naaman was commander of the Syrian army, and he had leprosy, a serious disease of the skin. An Israelite girl who served in his household said that a prophet in Samaria could heal him. The king of Syria thought the proper course was to go to the king of Israel, not directly to the prophet. That is why the letter and the costly gift.

For today: sometimes we look for God's help by the paths of power, money, or influence. This story invites us to remember that healing comes from God, and that he often acts more simply than we expect.
exp.22:26:
God says that he will remove Judah from his presence, just as he earlier removed Israel. He will also reject Jerusalem, the city he himself had chosen, and the temple, of which he had said, "My name shall be there." Here, "reject" means to turn away firmly.

The Lord speaks. This comes right after praise for Josiah, the king who turned to God with all his heart. Even so, the judgment had already been decided because of the people's sins, above all those that Manasseh encouraged years earlier. Israel, the northern kingdom, had already been taken into exile by Assyria.

For today: sincere obedience is always worthwhile, even when it does not change everything around us. Josiah was faithful in spite of everything. It also reminds us that sin leaves long-lasting consequences, so it is wise to seek God today without putting it off.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that the leaders of Samaria were filled with great fear. They reasoned that if two kings could not stop Jehu, they would not be able to either. The word "stand" in the verse means to stand against him, to face him or oppose him. The two kings are Joram, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah, whom Jehu had already defeated.

Jehu, anointed to destroy the house of Ahab, wrote to those in charge of the seventy sons of the king. He challenged them to choose a successor and fight. The ones who answer here are the city's leaders, and fear leads them to submit without a struggle. What happens next is very harsh, and the text only narrates it.

For today: fear of powerful people can lead us to stay silent or give in. Let us seek first what pleases God, and ask him for the courage to act rightly, without letting ourselves be moved by fear alone.
exp.8:12:
They say that the army officers, on hearing that Jehu had been anointed king, quickly took off their cloaks and spread them beneath him, on the top of the steps. Then they blew the trumpet and shouted, "Jehu is king!" The horn was a wind instrument, like a ram's horn or trumpet. Quickly means fast. The high place probably refers to the steps or to an elevated spot.

The prophet Elisha sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu in God's name. Jehu's companions first called him a madman, but when they heard the message, they recognized him as king. Thus began the fall of the house of Ahab.

For today: when we recognize that God speaks, it is fitting to respond with humility and promptness. The officers hesitated for a moment, but then they acted. Let us ask God to help us obey his Word without delay, even when at first it seems strange or uncomfortable to us.
exp.16:12:
The Lord warned Israel and Judah again and again. He did this through all the prophets and all the seers (men who saw what God showed them). "Testified against" means that he gave a solemn witness, a serious warning. The message was clear: turn from your evil ways and obey my commandments and laws, the same ones I gave to your fathers.

The author of the book of Kings explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell to Assyria. The people worshiped idols, just as the nations around them did. God did not leave them without warning; he sent them prophets, patiently calling them to return.

Today, God still speaks before the consequences arrive. If we sense a warning in his Word, let us not ignore it. Obeying in time is worth more than regretting later.
exp.9:34:
This verse says that Jehu died. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is a respectful way of saying that he passed away, as the kings before him did. They buried him in Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and his son Jehoahaz became the new king.

The author of the book of Kings, who is not named, sums up Jehu's reign here. Earlier he spoke of Jehu's conquests and of how he lost territory to Syria. Jehu destroyed the house of Ahab, but he did not follow the law of God wholeheartedly (verse 31). In the end, his life is recorded briefly.

For today: our life also has an end, and what remains is what we did in obedience. Achievements and power do not last, but a sincere faith does matter. Today you can ask yourself: am I following God wholeheartedly, or only in part?
exp.16:0:
This verse says that Hoshea, son of Elah, began to reign over Israel, the northern kingdom, in the twelfth year of the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. His capital was Samaria, and he ruled for nine years. The words "began to reign" simply mean that he came to the throne.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, recounting the history of the kings of Israel and Judah. Hoshea was the last king of the northern kingdom. According to the text that follows, he did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord, though not as much as the kings before him, and he ended up paying tribute to Assyria. The author presents this fact to show the end of a kingdom that had turned away from God. The dating calculations between the kings are debated by scholars.

For today: God sees our decisions, even when we are not as bad as others. Let us not be content with comparing ourselves; let us seek to obey Him from the heart and return to Him in time.
exp.7:26:
This verse says that Ahaziah, king of Judah, followed the bad example of the house of Ahab, king of Israel. "He walked in the way" means that he lived and acted as they did. "Did evil in the sight of the Lord" means that he did what God saw as wickedness. The reason the text gives is that he was "son in law" of that house, that is, he was related to them by marriage. His mother, Athaliah, came from that family.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. He explains why Ahaziah failed: the family alliance between Judah and Israel also brought the spiritual influence of Ahab. Then we see him join Joram in the war and visit him in Jezreel.

For today: the people closest to us influence us greatly. It is wise to take care of our friendships and bonds, and to choose to be faithful to God even when bad examples surround us.
exp.2:1:
Joram, king of Israel, is said to have done evil in the sight of the Lord, but not as much as his father Ahab and his mother Jezebel. He removed the image of Baal that his father had made, which means the sacred pillars or stones that his father had set up to worship that false god. The phrase "in the sight of the Lord" means "in the eyes of God," according to his judgment.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, evaluating each king by his faithfulness to God. Joram carried out a partial reform, but the next verse makes clear that he continued in the sins of Jeroboam, such as the worship of the golden calves. Some think he removed those images for political reasons; the text does not explain this.

For today: God looks at the heart, not only at outward changes. Removing a bad habit is good, but it is not enough if everything else stays the same. Ask God to lead you to complete obedience.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign. The word "á" is only the old spelling of "a," so that sentence should simply be left out. Let me restate: the sentence about "á" is deleted and nothing replaces it. It is a short detail, but a very important one: the king of Judah was only a child.

The author of the book tells the story. Athaliah had seized power and killed much of the royal family. Jehoash survived and was hidden in the temple, until the priest Jehoiada presented him to the people as the rightful king. In this way Athaliah's rule came to an end, and the people rejoiced.

For today: God can work through people who seem small or weak. And if we are young or inexperienced, it is wise for us to surround ourselves with wise and faithful counselors, as Jehoiada was for Jehoash.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that the Israelites burned incense in all the high places, just as the peoples whom God had driven out of that land before them had done. In this way they did very wicked things that angered God. The word "carried away" here means that God had removed them or taken them away from there.

The author of the book explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell before Assyria. Here he describes their sin: they imitated the religion of the neighboring nations and worshiped idols, even though God had forbidden them to do so. The verses that follow say that God warned them many times through the prophets, calling them to return to Him.

Today we can ask ourselves which customs around us we are copying without thinking, even though they go against what God says. Listening to His Word in time helps us return to Him before our hearts grow hard.
exp.6:15:
What it says: The people of Samaria went out of the city and took everything the Syrians had left in their camp. With so much food available, prices dropped sharply. "Fine flour" is high-quality flour. Everything happened "according to the word of the Lord," that is, just as God had announced it.

Context: Samaria was under siege by the Syrian army and suffered terrible famine. The prophet Elisha had announced that the next day there would be cheap food at the city gate. An officer of the king did not believe it. Then four lepers discovered that the Syrians had fled, and the news reached the whole city. The narrator stresses that what had been said was fulfilled.

For today: God can change a desperate situation from one day to the next. When everything seems closed off, trust what He has promised and keep moving forward with hope and patience.
exp.16:33:
They say that, up to the day this was written, the people living in Samaria still kept their old customs. Although they claimed to fear the Lord, in reality they did not obey him. "Fear" here means to honor and obey. The commands and rules that God gave are his statutes and ordinances.

The narrator of the book explains what happened after Assyria carried the kingdom of Israel off into captivity. The Assyrian king brought foreigners to live there, and they mixed the worship of the Lord with their own gods. The text recalls that God had made a covenant with Jacob, also called Israel, and demanded complete loyalty. Some scholars think the writing was composed or edited during or after the exile, though this is debated.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we say we believe in God while letting other things rule our hearts. God does not want a half-hearted faith, but a sincere trust that shows in daily obedience.
exp.20:5:
This verse tells of the very serious things King Manasseh did: he made his son pass through the fire, meaning he offered him in a pagan ritual, probably as a sacrifice. He observed times and used enchantments, which refers to trying to read signs and omens in order to foretell the future. He dealt with familiar spirits and wizards, who were said to speak with the dead, and the wizards were those who claimed to know hidden things. In this way he provoked the anger of God.

The narrator of the book of Kings describes the reign of Manasseh. He led Judah into idolatry, even within the temple, the place where God had placed his name. The writer shows that the problem was not an oversight, but an open rebellion against the law given through Moses.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom we turn for direction when we feel fear or uncertainty. Instead of turning to horoscopes or superstitions, God invites us to pray and to trust in his Word.
exp.17:32:
In this verse, the spokesman for the king of Assyria boastfully asks whether any of the gods of the nations has been able to save his land from the power of Assyria. By this he means that no one has been able to stop him, and that the God of Israel will not be able to either. The word "nations" in the verse is the one that carries this sense of peoples and lands outside Israel, and "delivered" means "rescued" or "saved."

The speaker is Rabshakeh, envoy of King Sennacherib, at a time when Assyria was surrounding Jerusalem. He wanted to frighten the people into surrendering and into abandoning their trust in King Hezekiah and in the LORD. He placed the LORD on the same level as the idols of other nations, and that was a serious error.

For today: when the voices of fear say that your situation has no way out, do not measure God by human measures. Bring your fear to Him in prayer and trust His faithfulness, even when you cannot yet see the answer.
exp.1:23:
He turned around, saw the young men who were mocking him, and cursed them in the name of the Lord. Then two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of them apart.

The narrator tells this right after Elisha received Elijah's mantle. The young men may have been youths rather than small children; the Hebrew word covers a broad range of ages. Their mocking of the bald man and their call to "go up" may have been contempt toward him and toward God, whose prophet he was. There are several interpretations, and the text does not explain every detail. Nothing indicates that Elisha acted out of simple personal anger.

For today: this passage reminds us that despising what God has placed as his voice is a serious matter. It also invites us to watch our words, to respect others, and not to mock them.
exp.24:12:
It says that the Chaldeans, that is, the Babylonians, destroyed the two great bronze pillars of the temple, the bases (the stands with wheels), and the "bronze sea," a huge basin of water used by the priests. Then they carried the metal off to Babylon. "Lord" is the name of God, and "broke in pieces" means they smashed it to pieces.

The author of the book, as narrator, recounts the fall of Jerusalem in about 586 B.C. Babylon destroyed the temple that Solomon had built. The book presents this as the consequence of years of the people's unfaithfulness, although the text here only describes the event with sorrow and detail.

For today: what seemed firm and sacred, like a building, can disappear. Place your trust in God himself and not in places, traditions, or things that he never promised would last forever.
exp.1:21:
This verse says that the waters of that place were left clean and good, and that they stayed that way "to this day," that is, up to the time the account was written. This happened just as Elisha had spoken it. The word "healed" means made well or made wholesome, and the phrase "according to the saying of Elisha which he spake" means the same as "in keeping with what Elisha had said."

The narrator is the one telling the story, and he closes the episode at Jericho. The people had told Elisha that the water was bad and the land did not bear fruit. Elisha threw salt into the spring, but he made clear that the healing came from the LORD, not from the salt. The text shows that God backed Elisha as his prophet, after Elijah had been taken up into heaven.

For today: God can bring healing and renewal to damaged places, such as a home, a church, or a community. We can get to work with humility and trust that his word is fulfilled.
exp.18:11:
Here it is asked whether the gods of other nations were able to save their peoples when the kings of Assyria attacked them. Places are mentioned such as Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar. The question "Did they deliver them?" is the point of the verse, and "fathers" refers to the earlier kings of Assyria.

The one speaking is the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, through messengers and a letter. He wants King Hezekiah to surrender. He compares the God of Israel with the gods of other peoples, as if He were just one more, in order to sow fear and doubt in Jerusalem.

For today: when the voices of fear or pressure tell you that God cannot help you, do not argue with them. Do as Hezekiah did: bring your worry to God in prayer and lay it before Him with confidence.
exp.3:27:
Here the Shunammite woman speaks with Elisha, the man of God. She asks him two questions in her pain: "Did I desire a son of my lord?" and "Did I not say, Do not deceive me?" The word "deceive" in the verse means to mislead someone with false hope.

Her son, born through a promise of Elisha, has just died. She does not ask for explanations calmly; she pours out her grief and almost accuses the prophet. Elisha does not rebuke her, for he understands that her soul is in bitterness. He himself admits that God had not revealed to him what had happened.

For today: when you suffer, you can bring your pain to God with complete honesty, even with hard questions. He is not frightened by your anguish. Moreover, she does not walk away; she clings to the prophet and keeps seeking help.
exp.13:10:
Amaziah, king of Judah, did not pay attention to the warning from Jehoash, king of Israel. The phrase "did not listen" simply means that he did not heed the advice. So Jehoash marched out with his army, and the two kings faced each other at Beth-shemesh, a town that belonged to Judah.

The author of the book of Kings recounts this episode. Amaziah had defeated Edom and felt very strong. Jehoash answered him with a fable: a small thistle thought itself equal to a cedar, but the wild beasts trampled it. It was a warning not to get involved in a war. Even so, Amaziah insisted, and Judah was defeated.

For today: pride in a success can make us deaf to wise counsel. When someone advises us with wisdom, it is good to listen with humility before taking a step that could harm others.
exp.17:34:
Here the envoy of the king of Assyria asks with pride which god of any country was able to save his people from the power of Assyria. From this he concludes that the Lord will not be able to deliver Jerusalem either. The words "deliver" and "delivered" mean to rescue or save, and "country" refers to a land or nation.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a high official of King Sennacherib of Assyria. He stands before the walls of Jerusalem and wants to frighten the people into surrendering. He places the Lord on the same level as the gods of other nations. The people keep silent, just as King Hezekiah had commanded.

For today: when threats or voices of doubt compare God to the things of this world, there is no need to argue with them. We can remain silent, bring the matter to God in prayer, and trust that he is different and greater.
exp.2:3:
This verse presents Mesha, king of Moab, as a sheep breeder. Every year he gave the king of Israel a huge tribute: one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams, with their wool. The phrase with the wool refers to the fleece still on the animals. It was a heavy payment that showed Moab was under Israel's control.

The narrator of the book explains the political situation before the war. Moab had been paying this tribute since the days of Ahab. When Ahab died, Mesha rebelled, and that is why Joram, king of Israel, prepared his army. The text also says that Joram did evil, although he removed the statues of Baal. This sets the scene in which God would then act.

For today: a half-done reform is not enough. Joram removed one visible sin, but he stayed tied to others. Let us ask God to help us obey him completely, not only in what is easy or what others can see.
exp.17:33:
Here the spokesman of the king of Assyria mockingly asks where the gods are of several cities that Assyria had already conquered: Hamath, Arphad (or Arpad), Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivah. He says that none of them could save their cities. He even adds that the gods of Samaria did not deliver it either. To "deliver" means to rescue or save, and "out of mine hand" means out of his power.

The one speaking is Rabshakeh, sent by King Sennacherib, in front of the walls of Jerusalem, during the reign of Hezekiah. He wants to frighten the people so that they will surrender and stop trusting in the LORD. He places the God of Israel on the same level as the idols of the defeated nations, which was a serious mistake.

For today: when the voices of fear or mockery tell you that God will not sustain you, do not compare them with your past history or with what others have lived through. Instead, pray and trust in the living God, who is different from any idol.
exp.18:17:
This verse says that the kings of Assyria threw the gods of the peoples they conquered into the fire. Those gods were not true gods, but objects made by human hands, of wood or stone, and that is why they were easy to destroy. Here "destroyed" means that they were made to vanish completely.

The one speaking is King Hezekiah, praying to the LORD. Assyria was threatening Jerusalem, and its king Sennacherib mocked the God of Israel as if he were just one more among the gods of the nations. Hezekiah acknowledges what Assyria did, but he points out a difference: the LORD is the living God, not a lifeless image. That is why he asks Him to save them.

Today we can ask ourselves what things made by us we try to put in God's place, such as money or success. In great troubles, we can pray with Hezekiah's confidence: God lives, listens, and can act.
exp.14:26:
Pekah, son of Remaliah, began to rule over Israel from Samaria in the fifty-second year of Azariah, king of Judah. His reign lasted twenty years.

The book of Kings tells this as a narrator who keeps track of who ruled each kingdom and when. Pekah came to the throne by killing his king, Pekahiah, whom he had served as captain. The verses that follow say that he did what was evil before God, and that Assyria carried off several cities as captives. Some scholars debate the exact chronology of these years, so the dates are understood in different ways.

For today: power taken by violence, and without fear of God, does not bring lasting peace. We can ask God to give us integrity to serve honestly in what is entrusted to us, and trust that He guides our future without our needing to use unjust means.
exp.19:13:
Here the prophet Isaiah goes to King Hezekiah and asks him two questions: what those men said, and where they came from. The word "men" in the verse is the one the verse refers to, and it simply means men. Hezekiah answers plainly that they have come from a far country, from Babylon, and he does not mention that he showed them all his treasures.

Hezekiah had just recovered from a serious illness. The envoys of the king of Babylon arrived with letters and gifts, and the king showed them everything he had. Isaiah does not ask out of curiosity: he is the voice of God confronting him. Later he announces the consequences. Some think Hezekiah acted out of pride or in search of alliances, although the text does not say so clearly.

For today: when God blesses us, it is easy to boast about what we have or to put our trust in the wrong people. We can ask him to give us humility, and listen to those who speak to us with truth, even when their questions make us uncomfortable.
exp.24:15:
It says that the Babylonians carried off the two bronze pillars, the great basin called the "sea," and the movable stands that Solomon had had made for the temple. There were so many objects, and they were of so much metal, that their weight could not be measured. The "bases" are the stands on which the water basins were placed. "Vessels" here means utensils.

This is the account of the writer of Kings about the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the temple, and his captain Nebuzaradan plundered what Solomon had made centuries before. The text presents this as part of the judgment for the people's long-standing disobedience.

For today: What is most beautiful and seemingly secure can be lost when the heart turns away from God. Let us place our trust not in buildings, traditions, or achievements, but in the Lord himself, and seek to obey him sincerely.
exp.23:14:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took Jehoiachin, king of Judah, as a prisoner from Jerusalem to Babylon. He also took the king's mother, the king's wives, his officers (the court officials) and the mighty men of the land. The people taken away were prisoners of war.

The book of 2 Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. Here the narrator recounts the first great deportation to Babylon, around 597 B.C. The text says this happened as the Lord had said, that is, as judgment for the disobedience of the people and their kings.

God is faithful to his word, both in his warnings and in his promises. Today we can take his voice seriously, turn back to him in time, and trust that, even in difficult times, he still has control.
exp.4:11:
Naaman, commander of the army of Syria, compares the rivers of Damascus, the Abana and the Pharpar, with the waters of Israel. He thinks they are better and that he could wash in them and be clean. When the text says he "turned and went away in a rage," it means he turned around and left furious.

Naaman had leprosy and had come to Israel looking for healing. Elisha did not even come out to meet him; he only sent word that he should wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman expected something more spectacular and was offended in his pride. Afterward his servants persuaded him to obey, and he was healed.

For today: sometimes God works in simple ways that do not match what we expect. Our pride or our ideas can keep us from receiving his help. Obeying with humility, even when we do not understand everything, opens the door to his blessing.
exp.3:18:
This verse tells how the boy, while out in the fields with the reapers, suddenly feels a strong pain and cries out to his father: "My head, my head." The father does not stop to attend to him himself, but orders a servant (a servant of the household) to carry him to his mother.

This is the son God gave to the Shunammite woman, as Elisha had announced. The boy had already grown and had gone out to see his father. The father speaks calmly and hands the boy's care to another. What follows is painful: the boy dies in his mother's lap. The text does not say what caused his illness, so it is not wise to claim anything more.

When someone suffers, let us not leave them alone or overlook their pain. A timely gesture of attention and closeness can be a true act of love.
exp.22:5:
The verse tells that King Josiah had the grove brought out of the temple. It was a wooden pole or tree that stood for the goddess Asherah, a Canaanite idol. He took it outside Jerusalem, to the brook Kidron, burned it, ground it to powder, and threw the powder over the graves of common people. Crushing it to powder and scattering it over burial places was a way of showing his complete contempt for that object.

The account is told by the author of Kings. After finding the book of the law, Josiah wanted Judah to worship the Lord alone, and he cleansed the temple of all the idolatry that his predecessors had allowed.

For today: ask yourself what things in your life have taken the place that belongs to God, and do not tolerate them halfway. Josiah did not hide them or keep them stored away; he removed them completely.
exp.14:30:
This verse closes the account of the reign of Pekah, king of Israel. The writer says that everything else Pekah did is recorded in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That phrase means there was another record, now lost, where more details of his deeds were kept.

The author of Kings summarizes the reigns of many kings and refers the reader to those court archives. Just before this verse he tells the essentials: Assyria invaded the north and carried many captives away, and Hoshea conspired against Pekah, killed him, and reigned in his place.

We all leave a written trace, even if only in the memory of others. Pekah was remembered for his violence and his fall. Ask yourself today what will be recorded of your life, and live so that God and others remember faithfulness, not destruction.
exp.6:5:
This verse tells how God made the Syrian army hear, at night, the sound of chariots, horses, and a great multitude, though there was none. The Syrians thought the king of Israel had hired other kings (the Hittites and the Egyptians) to attack them. To "hire" here means he had brought them in as military help.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. Samaria was under siege and the people were dying of hunger. Four men with leprosy, with nothing to lose, went to the enemy camp. There they discovered that God had already acted, just as Elisha had announced.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, we can take a step of faith, even a small one. God may be at work where we cannot see it. And when we receive good from Him, let us share it with others who also need it.
exp.22:31:
Explanation of 2 Kings 23:32

It says that Jehoahaz, the new king of Judah, did what was evil in the eyes of God. The phrase "in the sight of the Lord" means "in the sight of God," that is, according to God's judgment. And "according to all that his fathers had done" means that he followed the same wicked path as his ancestors.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who sums up each reign with a spiritual evaluation. Jehoahaz came to the throne after the death of his father Josiah, a king who had sought God. His reign lasted only three months, and then the Egyptian pharaoh took him prisoner. Some think that "his fathers" refers to earlier kings such as Manasseh; the text gives no further details.

For today: a good inheritance does not guarantee a good life. Each person must decide to follow God for themselves, without relying on the faith of their parents.
exp.8:16:
This verse tells that a watchman, standing on the tower in Jezreel, saw in the distance a group of people approaching. A watchman is a lookout, and a company is a group or troop. King Joram ordered a rider sent out to ask them: "Is it peace?", that is, whether they came with good intentions.

The narrator describes how Jehu, anointed by a prophet to bring an end to the house of Ahab, was advancing toward Jezreel. Joram was wounded and was recovering there, not knowing that Jehu was coming as his enemy. Joram asks about peace, but the house of Ahab had carried much idolatry and violence, so the peace was not real.

For today: it is not enough to ask whether there is peace; we must examine whether we are truly living with God. We can ask him to show us what we need to correct before judgment comes.
exp.7:9:
Elisha tells Hazael to go and say to King Ben-hadad, "Thou mayest certainly recover." But right away he makes clear that the Lord has shown him the king will die all the same. The word "howbeit" means "but," and "shall surely die" means that his death is certain.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was sick and sent Hazael with a large gift to ask the prophet whether he would recover. There are different ways to understand Elisha's words: some think the illness was not fatal in itself, and that death would come from another cause. The text does not explain this in more detail, but it does show that God knows what is coming.

For today: when you seek answers, ask God for the truth, not only for what will comfort you. And remember that He sees the future and the heart of every person, so we can trust His justice.
exp.21:16:
God says he is going to punish Judah because they abandoned him. The phrase about burning incense means offering incense to false gods. Provoking him to anger means making him angry by doing this, and the works of their hands refers to the idols and to all their conduct. His burning anger will not go out, which means the judgment has already been decided.

The prophetess Huldah speaks on behalf of God. King Josiah had found the book of the law in the temple, was frightened when he read it, and sent to ask God what would happen. The answer is harsh: the people have persisted in their sin, and punishment will come. However, the verses that follow show that God did listen to Josiah's humble heart.

For today: do not neglect the Word of God or put other things in its place. When you read it and it confronts you, respond as Josiah did, with humility and repentance, because God listens to the one who turns back to him.
exp.13:5:
He says that King Amaziah, after punishing the men who had murdered his father, did not put their children to death. He obeyed what is written in the law of Moses: the fathers should not be put to death for the children, nor the children for the fathers. Each person would answer for his own sin. The word "but" introduces the contrast, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. He tells how Amaziah, as soon as he had established his reign, executed the servants who had killed his father, King Joash. But the account emphasizes that in this he followed the law (Deuteronomy 24:16) and did not practice family vengeance, which was common in those times. Even so, the passage makes clear that he did not remove the high places, so his obedience was only partial.

For today: let us not make others pay for the wrongs of their relatives. Even when we have been hurt, let us seek justice without bitterness and without punishing someone who has no guilt.
exp.5:3:
It says that Elisha, the prophet, agreed to go with the sons of the prophets to the Jordan River. When they arrived, they began to cut down wood. The words "went" and "wood" in the verse refer to the logs or beams they needed for building.

The sons of the prophets formed a group that followed Elisha, and their place had become too small. So they proposed building another place to live. Elisha gave them permission, and when one of them asked him to go with them, he said yes. The text does not explain why they asked him to come, but what follows shows that his presence was important.

For today: when you make plans or work on something important, invite God to go with you. He does not stay far from ordinary tasks, and He can help you even in small and unexpected problems.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that the two groups of guards whose shift ended on the Sabbath, and who would normally go home to rest, were to stay and watch over the temple ("the house of the Lord") alongside the king. "That is to say" means "in other words," and "watch" refers to the guard duty they kept.

The priest Jehoiada is speaking to the commanders of the guards. Athaliah, the queen mother, had seized the throne, and young Joash, the rightful heir of David, was hidden in the temple. Jehoiada carefully arranges complete protection so that he can be crowned. He takes advantage of the Sabbath change of shifts to gather more men without arousing suspicion.

For today: when what is right must be defended, order, courage, and commitment are needed. Ask yourself where God is calling you to stand firm, even when it would be more comfortable to rest.
exp.22:11:
It says that King Josiah destroyed the pagan altars that were on the roof of Ahaz's upper chamber, and also those that Manasseh had made in the two courts of the temple. The word "roof" refers to the flat top of the building. Then he took the remains, ground them to powder, and threw the dust into the brook Kidron, a stream near Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. He tells of the great reform of King Josiah, who wanted to cleanse Judah of idolatry after rediscovering the book of the Law. Earlier kings had filled even the temple with false worship. Throwing the dust into the Kidron showed a complete rejection of those idols.

For today: if something in your life takes the place that belongs to God, it is not enough to merely hide it. Ask Him for help to remove it at the root and give Him first place once again.
exp.17:21:
Here the chief cupbearer of the king of Assyria speaks, and he wants to discourage the people of Jerusalem. He tells them that if they answer that they trust in the Lord their God, they are wrong, because Hezekiah took away the high places (the places of worship on the hills) and the altars, and commanded them to worship only before the altar in Jerusalem. The high places were sites of worship, and the name Hezekiah is the same as the name you know from the verse above.

The speaker is a spokesman for King Sennacherib, and he is pressing Judah to surrender. His argument is that Hezekiah offended God by removing those altars. But the Bible presents that reform as an act of faithfulness, not of offense. The Assyrian does not understand Judah's faith well and uses half-truths to sow doubt.

For today: when someone uses arguments that sound convincing in order to weaken your trust in God, do not let yourself be carried away. Compare what you hear with what God actually says in his Word.
exp.14:9:
It says that a man named Shallum, son of Jabesh, plotted against King Zechariah. He attacked him before the people, that is, in plain view of everyone, killed him, and made himself king in his place. The word "conspired" means he secretly agreed with others to overthrow him, and "smote him" means he struck him down.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is telling the story of Israel. Zechariah, the last descendant of Jehu, reigned only six months and followed the sins of Jeroboam. His death fulfilled what God had told Jehu: that four generations of his sons would sit on the throne. Shallum did not last long on the throne either.

For today: violence and ambition build nothing lasting. If we seek influence or success, let us pursue it with honesty and trust in God, not by trampling over others.
exp.20:4:
This verse tells that King Manasseh built altars to worship "all the host of heaven," that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He placed them in the two courts of the temple, the open areas surrounding the holy building. With this he mixed the worship of the heavenly bodies with the place dedicated to God.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the reign of Manasseh. His father Hezekiah had removed the places of false worship, but Manasseh rebuilt them. The author stresses that this happened in the temple, the place where God had said he would put his name. For this reason he presents it as a very serious offense.

For today: God deserves the first place, not a shared one. We can ask ourselves which things, even good ones, occupy in our hearts the place that belongs to Him alone.
exp.13:9:
Amasías won a battle against Edom, and his heart was lifted up with pride. Joash advises him: enjoy your victory, but stay at home. He asks why he is looking for trouble that will bring him down, and Judah down with him.

Joash, king of Israel, is answering the challenge of Amasías, king of Judah. Earlier, Joash had used a parable: a small thistle thought itself equal to the cedar, and wild beasts trampled it. Amasías did not listen, went to war at Beth-shemesh, and Judah was defeated. Joash was not a king faithful to God, but his warning proved true.

For today: success can puff up our hearts and lead us into rash decisions. Before we rush into a new challenge, it is wise to stop and act with humility, to seek counsel, and to listen to warnings, even when they come from an unexpected source.
exp.14:6:
It says that King Azariah died. "Slept with his fathers" is an old, gentle way of saying he died. He was buried with the kings before him in the city of David, which is Jerusalem. His son Jotham took the throne. Azariah is also known as Uzziah in other passages.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes the end of each reign. Azariah had spent his last years with leprosy, living apart in a separate house, while Jotham governed in practice. That is why the account moves naturally from one king to the next. Afterward the text turns its attention to the northern kingdom, Israel, which was still living in sin.

For today: no one remains in his place forever, not even a king. This invites us to live with humility and to think about what legacy we leave. With our children and those who come after us, we can sow faith and good example, trusting that God continues to govern from one generation to the next.
exp.14:14:
This verse is a closing note about King Shallum. It says that the rest of his deeds, including the conspiracy by which he seized the throne, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. A conspiracy is a secret plot, and to conspire means to agree with others to overthrow a ruler.

The author of Kings summarizes each reign and refers readers to official records from that time. That book is not preserved today, so we do not know its contents. Shallum reigned only one month and was killed by Menahem, in a time of violence and coups in the northern kingdom.

For today: power taken by force or deception does not last long. It is better to seek what is right with honesty, because in the end our lives are also recorded before God.
exp.10:7:
They were to surround the young king on every side, with their weapons ready in hand. If anyone tried to break through their ranks, that person was to be put to death. They were also to stay with the king wherever he went, both when he went out and when he came in.

The word "ranges" in the verse means the rows or lines the soldiers formed.

The priest Jehoiada speaks to the commanders of the guard. Athaliah, the queen mother, had seized the throne by killing the royal family. Joash, the child heir, had been hidden in the temple for six years. Jehoiada prepared a plan to proclaim him king and to protect him.

For today: when God entrusts us with something precious, such as faith, family, or a vulnerable person, we should guard it with courage, order, and steadiness, never neglecting it.
exp.4:10:
Naaman goes away angry because he had expected something different. He thought Elisha would come out to meet him, stand up, call on the name of the Lord his God, wave his hand over the diseased part, and heal him. The phrase "went away" appears in older spellings in the source, and the word for the Lord is the divine name. Leprosy was a serious skin disease.

Naaman was a commander of the army of Syria. He had arrived with his chariot and his horses at the house of the prophet Elisha. But Elisha only sent him a messenger with the instruction to wash himself seven times in the Jordan. Naaman felt insulted, because his pride and his ideas about how God should act clashed with the simplicity of the command.

Sometimes we want God to work in our way, with something great and visible. But He may ask us for simple steps of obedience and humility. If we set pride aside and trust His word, we can receive what He wants to give us.
exp.3:20:
She went up, and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut the door upon him, and went out. Here the verse says that the Shunammite woman carried her dead son up to the room of the prophet Elisha, the man of God, and laid him on the bed. Then she shut the door and went out.

It is part of the story of a woman who had generously looked after Elisha, and God had given her a son. The child fell ill in the field and died in his mother's arms. She tells no one what has happened and acts with calm. The text does not say why she chose that place, but it seems she brought him to where the prophet was, hoping to find help.

For today: in the midst of pain, bring what hurts you most to God and seek help in faith, even when you do not understand everything. Acting with trust does not take away the pain, but it places it in the right hands.
exp.8:0:
Elisha calls a young prophet and gives him an urgent order. The phrase "Gird up thy loins" means to pull up the robe and fasten it with a belt so that you can run without anything getting in the way. He is to take a small flask of oil in his hand and go to Ramoth-gilead.

Elisha speaks as a prophet of God at a time of great wickedness in Israel, under the house of Ahab. Oil was used to anoint kings, and this mission would lead to anointing Jehu as the new king. Elisha does not go himself but sends someone else, which shows that God works through different people.

For today: when God entrusts you with something, obey promptly and without excuses. You may not be the main figure in the story, but your faithfulness in a small task can be part of what God is doing.
exp.22:35:
This verse tells us that Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign and that he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. It also names his mother, Zebudah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah.

The phrase "began to reign" is simply the verse's way of saying that he became king.

The narrator here is the writer of the book of Kings, who records the official facts about each king of Judah. Jehoiakim came to the throne because Pharaoh Necho put him there and changed his name, after taking his brother Jehoahaz away as a prisoner. His reign began under foreign pressure and with heavy taxes laid on the people. The next verse says that he did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord.

For today: reaching a position or a place of authority does not guarantee that we will use it well. Let us ask God for wisdom to serve with justice and to care for others, even when others press us or demand the opposite.
exp.14:4:
This verse tells that God struck King Azariah (also called Uzziah) with leprosy, and he had it until he died. He lived in a separate house, isolated, because that was how lepers were treated. Meanwhile, his son Jotham was in charge of the palace and governed the people.

The book of Kings is a historical narrative, not a speech. It summarizes Azariah's reign as generally good, but with one flaw: he did not remove the high places of worship. This verse does not explain the reason for the leprosy. Another book, 2 Chronicles 26:16-21, connects it to his pride when he entered the temple to burn incense.

For today: even those who serve God with a good heart can stumble if they leave things uncorrected or become proud. Let us ask God for humility and courage to remove what does not please Him, and trust that He cares for His people even when leaders change.
exp.22:18:
This verse says that King Josiah did not stop with destroying the altar at Bethel. He also took away all the houses of the high places that were in the cities of Samaria. The kings of Israel had built them, and in doing so they angered the Lord. Josiah did to them the same thing he had done at Bethel.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. He tells of Josiah's great reform, the king of Judah who returned to God's covenant after the book of the law was found. His reform reached even into the territory of the old northern kingdom. In this way, what the man of God had announced years before was fulfilled.

Today we can learn that truly obeying God means removing at the root whatever takes his place in our lives, not only what is most visible. Let us ask him to show us what "high places" there are in our hearts.
exp.18:7:
This verse tells how Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, returned from Jerusalem and found his king fighting against Libnah. The king had left Lachish, another city he had been attacking.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Rabshakeh had threatened Jerusalem and King Hezekiah. Isaiah had already announced, on God's behalf, that the Assyrian king would hear a report and return to his own land. This verse shows that the king's movements were already beginning to change, just as God had said.

For today: when threats seem enormous, remember that God keeps working even when we cannot see it. His word is fulfilled in its time, so we can wait with confidence and prayer.
exp.3:19:
This verse tells that the servant carried the boy to his mother, and that she held him seated on her knees until noon. Then the boy died. The words "having taken him" refer to the servant, and "died" is the meaning of the old form "murió".

The narrator relates the story of the Shunammite woman, to whom God had given this son through the prophet Elisha. The boy suddenly fell ill in the field, with a severe headache. His father, not knowing how serious it was, sent him home to his mother. She held him until the end.

For today: when grief comes, we are not alone. This mother suffered in silence, but she immediately sought out the man of God. We can bring our deepest sorrows to God in prayer, even when we do not understand what is happening.
exp.8:11:
His servants ask Jehu what the prophet wanted, and they press him with the words "tell us now," as if to say, "Do not deceive us; tell us." Then Jehu reveals what the young prophet said to him on behalf of God: that the Lord had anointed him king over Israel. To be "anointed" means that oil was poured on him as a sign that God was setting him apart for that office.

Jehu is a commander of the army. Elisha sent a young prophet to anoint him in secret, and Jehu at first wanted to make light of it. When he saw the insistence of his companions, he spoke. God was thus judging the wickedness of the house of Ahab.

For today: when God speaks to you through His Word, do not hold it back out of fear or belittle it. Obey it with courage and humility, remembering that all authority and every calling come from Him.
exp.22:21:
This verse says that no Passover had been kept like the one under Josiah, neither in the time of the judges nor during the reigns of the kings of Israel and of Judah. The sentence about the wording is removed here, since the reader's verse uses "holden" for "kept" and it need not be explained. The Passover was the feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt.

The author of the book tells what happened when Josiah, king of Judah, came upon the book of the law in the temple. He cleansed the land of idolatry and commanded the people to keep the Passover as it was written. It is said that it was different because the law was followed faithfully. We do not know with certainty all the details of the earlier Passovers.

For today: when we rediscover the Word of God, it is not enough to admire it. We can obey it with humility, remove what keeps us from God, and remember with gratitude what He has done for us.
exp.19:17:
God announces, through Isaiah, that some of Hezekiah's descendants will be taken away. There they will be "eunuchs," that is, servants in the palace of the king of Babylon. The word "begotten" means that they are his own children by blood. "Take away" means that they will be carried off by force.

Isaiah speaks to Hezekiah after the king proudly showed all his treasures to the envoys from Babylon. The prophet warns him that this wealth, and even his family, will end up in Babylonian hands. Hezekiah responds with acceptance, though he is glad that there will be peace in his days. Some see this as humility; others, as a certain indifference toward the future. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: what we do and boast about has effects on those who come after us. Let us consider the legacy we leave, and trust in God more than in our riches or achievements.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the Syrian army fled at the start of the night. They left everything behind: their tents, their horses, their donkeys, and the camp just as it was. The phrase "fled for their life" means they thought only of escaping with their lives.

The account tells what happened while Samaria was suffering a terrible famine because of the Syrian siege. Four lepers, shut out of the city, went to the enemy camp and found it empty. The text says that the Lord made a great noise like an army marching, and the Syrians, frightened, believed that allies were coming against them.

For today: God can deliver in unexpected ways, even when the situation seems impossible. And when we receive good news or help, we should not keep it to ourselves, but share it with those who need it.
exp.4:8:
Naaman, a foreign army commander with leprosy, came with his horses and his chariot and stood at the door of Elisha's house. The word "stood" here means he came to a halt or stood up, which fits the picture of him arriving in full display of his power, expecting to be received with honor.

Naaman was commander of the army of Syria. A young Israelite girl who had been taken captive spoke to him about the prophet, and the king of Israel was alarmed when he received the letter. Elisha stepped in so that Naaman would know that there was a prophet of God in Israel. The account does not explain in detail why Elisha did not go out to meet him, but what follows shows that God was working in a way that broke Naaman's pride.

For today: God heals and helps those who come to Him with humility, not with pride or demands. We can ask ourselves whether we are asking God for help on our own terms or whether we are willing to obey Him as He directs.
exp.2:25:
He saw that he was losing the war. So he took seven hundred soldiers with swords and tried to break through to the king of Edom (Idumea), but he failed to do it. The word "saw" in the verse is rendered as "saw," and the phrase "break through" means to cut through the enemy lines.

It is part of a story in which Israel, Judah, and Edom attack Moab, and the prophet Elisha had announced water and victory. Moab, surrounded in Kir-hareseth, makes one last attempt to escape. The text does not say why he chose Edom; some think they saw it as the weakest point, but the text does not explain this. What follows is very harsh: the king sacrifices his son, and the exact meaning of the wrath that falls on Israel is interpreted in several ways.

For today: desperation can lead to extreme and useless decisions. Before acting out of fear, let us seek God and his counsel with calm.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the king's messengers returned to him sooner than expected, and the king asked them why they had come back. The question shows surprise, because they were not supposed to return so soon.

It speaks of King Ahaziah of Israel, who was injured in a fall and sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, a false god of Ekron. On the road, Elijah stopped them with a message from God: the king would die. That is why they returned at once. The king wants to know the reason, not realizing that God had already answered him.

When we are in trouble, it is easy to look for help anywhere but in God. Before running to other sources, it is wise to go first to the Lord and listen humbly to what he tells us, even when it is not what we want to hear.
exp.1:18:
The men of Jericho tell Elisha that their city is in a good place, as he can see for himself, but that the water is bad and the land is unproductive. This means the water was harming the fields, so they did not yield good crops. The word about the city's location refers to where the city sits.

The residents of Jericho are the ones speaking. Elisha was there after Elijah had been taken up into heaven. They come to the prophet because they recognize that God works through him. Continuing the account, Elisha throws salt into the spring and declares that God heals those waters. Scholars explain the use of the salt in several ways, but the text emphasizes that the healing comes from God.

Today we can speak honestly before God about what is not working in our lives, even when everything else seems good. He is not shocked by our problems, and he can heal from the root.
exp.14:17:
He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord: throughout his reign he never turned away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin. "Led into sin" means that he guided the people into idolatry. "In the sight of the Lord" means "in the eyes of God."

The narrator of the book is giving a judgment on Menahem's reign. Shortly before, his violence against the city of Tiphsah is recounted. Jeroboam had set up golden calves as centers of worship, and many kings after him followed that path. It is then told that Menahem paid tribute to Assyria to secure his power, and he collected that money from the wealthy of Israel.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we repeat harmful habits simply because others began them before us. God invites us to examine what we have inherited and to return to Him with humility, without trusting in power, money, or alliances.
exp.18:22:
This verse says that the king of Assyria, through his messengers, spoke with contempt against the Lord. He boasted that with his many war chariots he had gone up to the highest mountains of Lebanon, and that he would cut down its tallest cedars and its finest trees. The phrase "spoke insults" means saying offensive words. The "fir trees" here are commonly understood as choice trees, though some translate them as "cypresses." "Carmel" speaks of a fruitful forest.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel as if he were just one more of the gods of the nations. God answers that these mockeries were directed against the Holy One of Israel himself.

Today we can learn that pride, power, and achievement do not make us greater than God. Before boasting of what we have accomplished, let us remember that everything is under his hand. And if anyone feels threatened, they can trust that God hears and answers.
exp.23:6:
It says that Egypt never again sent its army out of its own borders. Babylon had conquered all the Egyptian territory between the stream of Egypt (a brook on the southern edge of Canaan, not the Nile) and the Euphrates River to the north. Before this, Egypt had dominated that region.

The speaker is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the reign of Jehoiakim. Egypt had been Judah's ally, and with its defeat, Judah was left without support. The text explains why Judah fell under the power of Babylon. The exact dates and details of these events are interpreted in several ways, but the shift in power is clear.

For today: empires seem eternal, but they are not. Trusting in money, in allies, or in human power leaves us without a foundation. Today we can place our security in God, who holds history in his hands and sustains those who trust in him.
exp.2:18:
It says that Israel, together with its allies, would defeat Moab and do it great harm. They would attack the walled cities, the fine towns, cut down the good trees, block up the springs, and ruin the good fields by covering them with stones.

The prophet Elisha speaks on God's behalf. Three kings (of Israel, Judah, and Edom) had run out of water in the desert while they were marching against Moab. Elisha promises them water and also victory. These acts of war were part of the customs of that time, and the text describes them; it does not present them as an example for us.

For today: when you lack what is essential and see no way out, God can act in ways you do not expect. Seek Him first, obey Him, and trust that He knows how to help you.
exp.14:22:
This verse says that Pekahiah, son of Menahem, began to rule as king of Israel in Samaria in the fiftieth year of Azariah's reign over Judah. Pekahiah ruled for only two years.

The verse does not speak through a character but through the narrator of the book, who records the order of the kings of Israel and Judah. Pekahiah inherited the throne from his father. The verses that follow explain that he did evil in the eyes of God, and that his captain Pekah killed him. Some scholars note that the dates of these reigns are hard to fit together, and they explain this in several ways.

For today: having a position or an inheritance does not guarantee a good ending. What counts is following God with sincerity. Let us ask him to help us live in a way that leaves a good example, not bad habits.
exp.17:5:
It says that King Hezekiah held fast to God. "Clave to the Lord" means that he clung to him, and "departed not from following him" means that he did not turn his back on him. Furthermore, he kept the commandments that God gave to Moses. His faith showed in what he did, not only in what he felt.

The speaker is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the life of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Earlier it is told that he removed the forbidden places of worship and destroyed the bronze serpent, because the people had made it an object of worship. The text presents him as a faithful king, and then says that God was with him.

For today: faithfulness to God means removing from our lives whatever takes his place, even good or inherited things. Examine which habit or custom pulls you away from him, and take a concrete step to obey him.
exp.9:14:
Jehu, as he left that place, came upon Jehonadab, son of Rechab. After greeting him, he asked whether his heart was sincere toward him, as his own heart was toward Jehonadab. Jehonadab answered that it was. Then Jehu asked him for his hand, as a sign of agreement, and lifted him up into his chariot. Here the word "right" means sincere and loyal.

Jehu speaks in the middle of a violent purge against the house of Ahab, which God had announced through Elijah. Jehonadab was known for his simple life and his faithfulness to God (Jeremiah 35). Jehu seeks his support, perhaps to lend credibility to his work. The Bible does not make clear whether Jehu's zeal was entirely pure; later it says that he did not follow God with his whole heart.

For today: before we join ourselves to someone or to a cause, let us ask whether the heart is sincere. And let us also examine our own, because religious zeal needs humility and love.
exp.9:28:
Here it says that, although Jehu put an end to the worship of Baal, he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam. In other words, he went on worshiping the golden calves that were in Beth-el and in Dan. The sentences explaining the old wording are removed, since the verse above has no such phrases; the remaining explanation is translated as follows.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings, who evaluates Jehu, speaks. Jehu had just eliminated the family of Ahab and the worship of Baal. But Jeroboam had set up those calves centuries earlier so that the people would not go up to Jerusalem to worship. Jehu kept them, perhaps for political reasons, though the text does not say so.

For today: it is not enough to remove an obvious sin if we leave others hidden. Let us ask God to examine our heart and to obey him completely, not only in what suits us.
exp.19:10:
The prophet Isaiah prayed to the Lord with urgency, and God caused the shadow to go back ten degrees on the "dial of Ahaz." That dial was probably a staircase or a set of steps that marked the passing of time by the shadow of the sun. "Cried" means that he prayed aloud and with urgency.

King Hezekiah was seriously ill, and God had promised to heal him. He asked for a sign to confirm that promise. Isaiah let him choose, and Hezekiah chose the harder one: that the shadow would go backward. How exactly it happened is not explained; the text only says that God did it.

God knows that at times we find it hard to believe, and He can give us confirmations that strengthen our faith. But the following passage reminds us that, after receiving His help, we should keep trusting in Him and act wisely, without forgetting Him.
exp.16:26:
This verse says that the king of Assyria ordered one of the Israelite priests who had been carried into captivity to return to Samaria. There he was to live and teach the new inhabitants the manner of the God of the land, that is, the correct way to worship the LORD. The words "thither" and "there" refer to Assyria and to Samaria. "Brought" means "carried away."

After conquering the northern kingdom, Assyria brought foreign peoples to live in Samaria. They thought that each land had its own local god.
