When lions attacked them, the text presents this as a judgment from the LORD, because they had not respected him. So they asked the king for help, and he sent a priest to teach them.

For today: knowing about God is not the same as truly fearing him. The passage shows that those peoples learned rituals, but they kept following their own gods. Let us ask God for a whole heart, one that obeys him and worships him alone.
exp.17:31:
He says the king of Assyria promises to take the people to another land, rich in grain, wine, bread, vineyards, olive oil and honey. He assures them that by going they will live and not die. He asks them not to listen to Hezekiah, whom he accuses of deceiving them when he says that the Lord will deliver them.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, spokesman for King Sennacherib, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. His aim is to break the people's trust in God and in Hezekiah so that they will surrender. He offers deportation disguised as a kind offer. He measures the Lord as he would the gods of other nations.

For today: not every voice that sounds reasonable and promises well-being deserves your trust. When someone invites you to stop trusting God in exchange for comfort, compare their words with what God has said, and pause to pray before you decide.
exp.17:12:
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. "Came up" means that he advanced with his army toward Judah, which lay on higher ground.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings. Shortly before, he tells how Assyria carried the northern kingdom of Israel away into captivity for disobeying God. Now the threat reaches Judah. Afterward, Hezekiah acknowledges his mistake and pays a heavy tribute. Scholars debate how to date these events exactly, but the text shows a moment of great pressure.

For today: when strong trials come, do not rely only on your own defenses or your own solutions. Seek God with humility, learn from the mistakes of others, and ask Him for wisdom before you decide.
exp.17:13:
Here King Hezekiah of Judah sends a message to the king of Assyria, who was at Lachish. He says, "I have offended," asks him to withdraw, and promises to bear whatever he puts on him. The Assyrian king demands three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold. "Return from me" means "withdraw from me"; "put on" here means to demand a payment.

Hezekiah speaks as a king who had sought to please God. Sennacherib had already taken the fortified cities of Judah, and the pressure was enormous. It is not clear what he means by "I have offended": it could be rebellion against Assyria or a miscalculation. To pay, he emptied the treasures of the temple, and later the account shows that God rescued him.

For today: when we are under pressure, it is easy to look for quick solutions that cost us dearly. Before giving in out of fear, pray and seek God's guidance. He can deliver us in ways we do not imagine.
exp.3:25:
Elisha tells his servant Gehazi to run to meet the woman and ask her three questions: whether she is well, whether her husband is well, and whether the child is well.

Elisha sees the Shunammite woman coming from far away, the woman who had earlier hosted him and to whom God gave a son. Her child had just died, but she does not tell Gehazi and goes straight to the prophet. Some understand her answer as faith that still trusts, others as a way of holding back her grief until she speaks with Elisha. The text does not make this clear.

When we are deeply hurt, we do not always need to explain everything to just anyone. We can bring our pain directly to God and seek out people of faith who will walk alongside us with wisdom and love.
exp.5:8:
The prophet Elisha sends a warning to the king of Israel: do not pass by a certain place, because the Syrians are hiding there. "The man of God" is another way of saying prophet. The "Syrians" are the people of Syria, and "beware that thou pass not" means "be careful, do not go that way."

Syria was at war with Israel. The Syrian king planned ambushes and set up his camp in secret places. But God revealed those plans to Elisha, and the prophet warned the king of Israel. In this way the king escaped danger several times. The Bible does not explain here how Elisha knew, but the text presents this as help that comes from God.

God sees dangers that we do not see. When we receive wise counsel, whether from the Bible or from a person of mature faith, it is good to listen with humility. And praying for direction helps us not to walk in the dark.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that God spoke through his prophets, whom it calls "his servants." The phrase "by the hand of" is an older way of saying "through."

The verse is only an introduction: God's message comes in the verses that follow.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, and says that the Lord himself spoke. This happens during the reign of Manasseh, king of Judah, who led the people into idolatry and into doing more evil than the nations that God had driven out of that land. The text does not name the prophets of that time. God warns before he acts, and he does so with patience.

For today: God still speaks to us, today above all through his Word. Listening in time prevents much pain. If God shows you something in the Bible, do not put it off; obey him with humility.
exp.3:4:
She went away from him, shut the door behind her and her sons, and began to do as she was told. Her sons kept bringing the jars to her, and she kept pouring oil into each one. The sentence about the quoted phrases must be removed, since those words do not appear in the verse.

Elisha the prophet had given this instruction to an indebted widow. Her creditors were threatening to take her sons as servants. She had only a little oil in her house. Elisha told her to borrow empty jars, and she did what she was told. It appears that the oil was enough to fill all the jars she managed to get.

God often asks us to take a step of obedience with the little we have. This woman did not see the miracle before she acted; she saw it while she was obeying. Today we can begin with what is within our reach, trusting that God knows how to supply what is lacking.
exp.24:2:
On the ninth day of the fourth month (the text does not name the month, but the context makes it clear), the hunger grew very severe in Jerusalem. The sentence says the famine spread until it covered everything. There was no longer any bread for the people of the land, meaning ordinary people.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings, who recounts the fall of Jerusalem. Babylon had surrounded the city for nearly two years. The book presents this siege as the result of Judah's long disobedience to God, although the suffering fell mostly on ordinary people.

For today: the decisions of leaders affect many people. We can pray for those who govern, help those in need, and listen in time to God's voice, before the difficult days arrive.
exp.5:31:
Elisha was sitting in his house with the elders, that is, the leaders of the people. The king of Israel sent a man to kill him. But Elisha already knew this and warned the elders. He called the king "son of a murderer," and asked them to shut the door and not let the messenger in, since the king was coming up behind him.

The kingdom was under a terrible siege and there was extreme hunger. The king, in despair, tore his clothes and was found to be wearing sackcloth beneath them, a rough garment of mourning. Then he swore to kill Elisha, perhaps blaming him for the tragedy. Many believe that "son of a murderer" refers to Ahab, the king's father, although the text does not say so in so many words.

For today: in the midst of pain, it is easy to blame others or even God. Instead of reacting with anger, we can stop, pray, and seek God with humility and trust.
exp.23:2:
These misfortunes that fell on Judah were no accident. They happened by the command of the Lord, who meant to remove the people from his sight, that is, to drive them out of their land. The cause was the sins of Manasseh, "according to all that he did," or in other words, according to all the evil he committed.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who explains why Judah suffered attacks during the reign of Jehoiakim. Manasseh had ruled decades earlier, and his idolatry and violence left a deep wound. Although there were reforms afterward, the people continued on the same path. Some scholars point out that the rebellion of the following generations also played a part.

For today: our decisions can affect others for a long time. Let us ask God for wisdom to live with integrity, and let us remember that he is just and also patient.
exp.14:7:
This verse says that Zachariah, son of Jeroboam, began to reign over Israel, the northern kingdom, in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah's reign over Judah. His rule lasted only six months. Azariah is also called Uzziah in other passages.

The author of the book of Kings moves back and forth between the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah, and that is why he dates Zachariah by the year of the king of Judah. This Zachariah was the fourth descendant of Jehu, and with him that line of kings came to an end. The following verses explain why his reign was so brief: he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord and was murdered.

An important position does not guarantee stability if there is no obedience to God. Zachariah inherited a throne, but he followed the sins of his ancestors instead of seeking the Lord. Today we can ask ourselves what we are inheriting from our family and decide, with God's help, to break bad patterns and build on what pleases Him.
exp.8:34:
It says that when they went to bury Jezebel, they found only her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands. Nothing else was left. The word "skull" is the top part of the head.

The narrator tells what happened after Jehu, anointed as king of Israel, ordered Jezebel thrown from a window. She had promoted idolatry and injustice, as in the case of Naboth. Jehu sees in this the fulfillment of what God had said through the prophet Elijah: the dogs would eat Jezebel in Jezreel. The details of the end are told with stark directness, and the text presents it as God's judgment.

For today: God's word is fulfilled, even if it takes time. This invites us to trust his justice without taking revenge, and to take sin seriously, since power and fame do not last forever.
exp.10:10:
These verses describe how the temple guards took their positions, each with his weapons in his hand. They were stationed along the temple, from the right side to the left, near the altar and the building, surrounding the king. The word "round about" means "around." The king here is Joash, a child.

The account is narrated; it is not a speech. The priest Jehoiada organized this plan in secret to protect Joash, the heir of David, who had been hidden away. Queen Athaliah had seized the throne and tried to destroy the royal family. Jehoiada wanted to restore the kingdom to the rightful descendant, and so he used the weapons of King David that were kept in the house of the LORD.

For today: protecting what God has placed under our care requires courage, order, and teamwork. It may be a family, a church, or the faith of someone weaker than ourselves. Let us do our part faithfully, without acting alone.
exp.19:16:
This verse is a declaration from God. Isaiah tells King Hezekiah that a time will come when everything in his palace, and everything his ancestors stored up, will be carried off to Babylon, and nothing will be left.

The prophet Isaiah speaks here, sent by God. Envoys from Babylon had visited Hezekiah, and he showed them all his treasures. Isaiah warns him of the consequences. The texts do not explain the reason in detail, but many understand that there was pride or excessive trust in wealth and in human alliances.

For today: what we accumulate is not secure forever. It is good to give thanks for what we have, to use it with humility, and to place our trust in God, not in our possessions or in what others think of us.
exp.19:1:
This verse tells how King Hezekiah, on receiving the news that he would die, turned his face to the wall and began to pray to the Lord. "Face" is the front of his head, and "Lord" is the name of God. What follows is the content of his prayer.

The prophet Isaiah had just told Hezekiah, on God's behalf, to put his house in order because he was going to die. Hezekiah was seriously ill. Many believe he turned toward the wall to find privacy and pray without distractions, though the text does not explain the exact reason. It is the narrator who describes the scene, and it shows the king responding to the bad news by seeking God.

For today: when you receive hard news, you do not have to fix everything alone or stay silent. Find a quiet moment apart from the noise, and speak to God honestly. He listens to anyone who comes to him with an open heart.
exp.22:32:
Pharaoh Necho of Egypt imprisoned Jehoahaz at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, and so his reign in Jerusalem came to an end. He also forced Judah to pay a fine: a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. The phrase "put him in bands" means "had him bound," and "fine" here is a tribute imposed by force.

This is the account of the writer of Kings, who tells the story of Judah. Jehoahaz had reigned only three months and, according to the text, did evil in the sight of God. After the death of the good king Josiah, Judah fell under the power of Egypt. The people paid the price, since the money was taken from the people of the land.

For today: the decisions of those who lead affect many people. Let us pray for our authorities and, if we are called to guide others, let us do so with uprightness and the fear of God, for our decisions also weigh on others.
exp.13:8:
Here Jehoash, king of Israel, answers Amaziah, king of Judah, with a parable. A thistle from Lebanon (a small, prickly plant) asks the cedar (a huge tree) to let his daughter marry the thistle's son. But a wild beast passes by and tramples the thistle underfoot. The word for "trode down" means trampled or crushed.

Amaziah had just defeated Edom and challenged Jehoash to a fight. Jehoash, who speaks here, calls him a thistle that thinks it is a cedar. With this story he warns that his pride is ridiculous and dangerous. Scholars debate who is who in the image, but the general meaning is clear: Amaziah thought himself greater than he was.

For today: a success does not give us the right to think we are invincible. Before getting into an unnecessary conflict, it is wise to listen to advice, even when it comes from someone we do not like. Humility protects us.
exp.16:19:
This verse says that God rejected the whole people of Israel, that is, the northern kingdom. He punished them with suffering and allowed raiders to defeat them, until they were removed from their land. The word "rejected" means to reject or set aside. "Seed" means descendants. "Afflicted" means "afflicted them," and "delivered" means "delivered them into the hand of." "Spoilers" are those who steal and destroy.

The author of the book of Kings, whom Jewish tradition associates with an anonymous prophet, explains why Israel fell before Assyria, around 722 B.C. It was not bad political luck: the people followed the sins of Jeroboam and turned away from God again and again. The text also warns Judah, which imitated those same practices.

Today, this passage reminds us that God is patient, but not indifferent to sin that becomes a habit. If there is something you know is drawing you away from God, do not ignore it: confess it and correct it soon, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.14:2:
He is said to have done what pleases God, just as his father Amaziah had done. The phrase "in the sight of the Lord" means what God sees as right. The word "according to" means "in agreement with" or "just like."

The book of Kings has no narrator who identifies himself; it is a historical account that evaluates each king by his faithfulness to God. Azariah reigned 52 years in Judah. The text clarifies right away that the high places were not removed, so his obedience was real, but incomplete. It then says that the Lord struck him with leprosy. The text does not explain the reason here; another book, 2 Chronicles, gives more detail.

For today: Following God truly does not mean doing it perfectly, but it does mean paying attention to the details. Ask God to show you which "high places" you have left standing in your life, and remove them with humility.
exp.7:16:
This verse says that Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and that he ruled eight years in Jerusalem. It is a brief fact, like an official record of the kingdom of Judah.

The author of the book of Kings is telling the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. Here he introduces a new king of Judah. Some scholars think Joram ruled alongside his father Jehoshaphat for a time, and that would explain how the years are counted, though not all of them explain it the same way. What follows shows what matters most: he married a daughter of Ahab, and his life took a wrong turn.

For today: the people we bond with and the environments we choose shape us. Let us seek relationships that draw us closer to God. And let us remember that God remains faithful, even when we fail.
exp.18:31:
He says that God speaks about the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, and promises that he will not enter Jerusalem. He will not shoot so much as an arrow against it. Nor will he come before it with a shield, nor raise a siege ramp against the walls.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. King Hezekiah of Judah had prayed in desperation, since Assyria had already conquered other cities and was threatening Jerusalem. God answers that he will protect the city for the sake of his own name and because of the promise made to David. The preceding passage speaks of a remnant that would survive and bear fruit again.

When you feel that a problem surrounds you, you can bring it to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. His promise to Jerusalem is not a guarantee that there will never be difficulties, but it reminds us that God is faithful to his word and cares for his people.
exp.12:16:
Elisha tells the king to open the window facing east, and to shoot an arrow. The old words are explained this way: the word that means "arrow" refers to the arrow, and "deliverance" here means victory or rescue. Elisha declares that this arrow is a sign that God will give victory over Syria. Aphek was a place where Israel would fight, and "consume them" means to finish off the Syrian threat.

Elisha, a prophet already old and sick, speaks with Joash, king of Israel, who was weeping because Syria was oppressing his people. Elisha placed his hands over the king's hands to show that the power came from God. Then the king struck the ground only three times, and the prophet was angry because he lacked zeal. Some understand that he did not fully believe.

For today: God gives us promises, but he expects us to respond with faith and commitment. Let us pray and act with all our heart, without holding back halfway.
exp.20:18:
It says that Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign over Judah, and that he ruled only two years from Jerusalem. It also names his mother, Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz, from a place called Jotbah.

It is part of the account in the book of Kings, which briefly presents each king of Judah: his age, how long he reigned, and his family. The narrator does not speak personally but records the history. Amon comes to the throne after the death of his father Manasseh. The following verses explain that he followed his father's evil ways, and for that reason his reign was short.

For today: our decisions also influence those who come after us. Amon followed the bad example he received, but each person can seek God and choose a different path. Ask yourself what example you are leaving and whom you are imitating.
exp.5:12:
He says that the king of Syria gives an order to his servants: they are to go and find out where Elisha is, so that he can be seized. Soon they report to him that the prophet is in Dothan.

It is the king of Syria speaking, and he was at war with Israel. He was frustrated because his secret plans kept failing. One of his servants told him that Elisha, the prophet, was letting the king of Israel know what was being said in private. For that reason the Syrian king wanted to seize him.

For today: the king believed that an army could stop a servant of God. When you feel surrounded by problems bigger than you are, remember that God sees what you cannot see. Trust that He takes care of His own, even when the situation seems impossible.
exp.8:20:
It says that King Joram ordered his war chariot to be made ready. They found him right in the field that had belonged to Naboth, in Jezreel.

Joram asks because the messengers he had sent did not come back, and the watchman reported that Jehu was coming at full speed. God had anointed Jehu to bring an end to the house of Ahab. It is significant that the meeting takes place in Naboth's field, the man whom Ahab and Jezebel unjustly put to death so they could take his vineyard (1 Kings 21). The text does not explain more, but the scene seems to show that this sin was not forgotten.

For today: God sees injustice, even though he may be slow to act. We can trust that he is just, and also examine our hearts so that we do not take advantage of anyone.
exp.13:19:
It says that the body of King Amaziah was brought from Lachish to Jerusalem on horses. There he was buried with his ancestors, in the city of David, which is the oldest part of Jerusalem. The words "brought" and "buried" here are how the verse reads in this translation.

The author of the book of Kings recounts the end of Amaziah, king of Judah. Some men conspired against him, he fled to Lachish, and there they killed him. Even so, he received an honorable burial among the kings. Afterward, the people made his son Azariah, also called Uzziah, king in his place. The text does not explain why there was a conspiracy against him.

Our life passes, and no one remains forever. What matters is how we walk while we live. Today you can ask God to help you live with humility and faithfulness, knowing that he cares for his people from generation to generation.
exp.9:19:
Jehu gives the order to proclaim a special feast in honor of Baal. The word "proclaim" means to announce a day set apart for a religious act, and "assembly" means a sacred and formal gathering. Those who heard the order carried it out and called the people to gather.

Jehu, king of Israel, had just wiped out the family of Ahab. He pretended to be devoted to Baal, but it was a trap, as the text says: he acted "with cunning." He wanted to gather all the worshipers of Baal in order to destroy them. Interpreters debate whether his method was an example to follow, since his obedience to God was incomplete (v. 31).

For today: the truth does not need deception. Let us ask God to give us wisdom to serve him with honesty and a whole heart, not only with actions that merely look right.
exp.1:4:
The sons of the prophets who lived in Jericho came to Elisha and asked him whether he knew that God would take away his master that very day. The phrase about taking him "from your head" means that Elijah, who had been over him as his guide, would be taken. Elisha answered that yes, he knew it, and asked them to keep quiet.

The sons of the prophets were groups of disciples who gathered to learn and to serve God. Elijah and Elisha went from place to place, and in Bethel the same conversation had already taken place. Elisha did not want to talk about the matter, because the pain was great and he wanted to focus on staying with Elijah until the end.

There are moments when God prepares us for a farewell or a difficult change. Rather than discussing it at length, sometimes the right thing is to stand firm, pray, and stay close to what God has given us to do, as Elisha did.
exp.13:0:
This verse marks when Amaziah began to reign in Judah. It was in the second year of Joash, who was king of Israel, the northern kingdom, and the son of Jehoahaz. Amaziah was the son of another Joash, king of Judah, the southern kingdom. The phrase about him beginning to reign means that he started to govern.

It is the narrator of the book of Kings, who does not identify himself, who speaks. His purpose is to place each king in his time by comparing the dates of the two kingdoms. The verses that follow show that Amaziah did what was right, but not wholeheartedly as David did.

For today: God looks not only at what we do but also at how complete our commitment is. Amaziah followed the example of his father, who had both good and bad moments. We can ask ourselves whom we imitate and whether we truly seek to follow God with our whole heart.
exp.6:18:
This verse recalls what an official of the king said when Elisha announced that there would be plenty of food and that it would be cheap. The official did not believe it and asked, mockingly, whether such a thing could happen even if God made windows in the sky, that is, even if He made food rain down. Elisha, the man of God, answered that he would see it with his own eyes, but would not eat of it.

Samaria was under siege and suffering great hunger. Elisha had announced that the next day food would be cheap at the city gate. God caused the enemy army to flee, and the people went out to plunder the camp. The official, whom the king had put in charge of the gate, was trampled to death by the crowd.

For today: God can fulfill what seems impossible. Doubting His word with mockery is dangerous, but trusting Him, even when we do not see how, opens us to His help and His faithfulness.
exp.1:17:
It says that the fifty men came back to Elisha, who had stayed behind in Jericho, without having found Elijah. Elisha reminds them of what he had already warned them: "Did I not say unto you, Go not?"

Elisha is speaking, the successor of Elijah. Elijah had just been taken up into heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha had seen it. The sons of the prophets believed that perhaps the Spirit of the LORD had set him down on some mountain or valley. Elisha knew they would not find him, but he gave in to their insistence so that they would be at peace.

For today: sometimes God has already shown us something clearly, yet we want to check it for ourselves. Trusting what God has already revealed spares us useless efforts and helps us move forward in peace.
exp.16:3:
This verse tells how the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea, king of Israel, was plotting against him. Hoshea had sent messengers to So, king of Egypt, and he no longer paid the yearly payment owed to Assyria. For this reason the king of Assyria seized him and shut him up in prison. A "conspiracy" is a secret plan against a ruler, a plot. The "payment" was a sum owed each year to the stronger king.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who explains why the northern kingdom fell. Hoshea was a vassal of Assyria, but he looked for help in Egypt instead of trusting God. No one knows for certain who "So" was; scholars interpret the name in several ways. Shortly afterward, Samaria fell, and the people were carried into exile.

For today: when we are in difficulty, it is tempting to seek quick and doubtful ways out. This story invites us to turn first to God, with humility and honesty, before leaning on human resources.
exp.13:17:
This verse is a closing formula that is repeated throughout Kings. The author says that the rest of what King Amaziah did, that is, his other deeds and events, is written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." That work has not survived to today, and we do not know exactly what it was like.

The narrator of the book of Kings summarizes Amaziah's reign and directs the reader to other official records. This shows that he drew on sources from his own time. Right afterward he tells of the king's sad end: a conspiracy, his flight to Lachish, and his death.

For today: our lives also leave a record. Rather than being remembered for what we accomplished, let us strive to live with humility and faithfulness before God, who sees everything.
exp.14:37:
This verse records the death of Jotham, king of Judah. "Slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died. He was buried in the city of David, that is, Jerusalem, alongside the kings who came before him. His son Ahaz took the throne.

This is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes the end of each reign. Just before this, it says that Jotham did what was right, and that in his days God began to send against Judah Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel. That threat already points to hard times. Ahaz, the new king, would not follow his father's good example.

For today: our life is brief, and others will take our place. Even a good example does not guarantee that children will follow God, but it is worth living faithfully, praying for those who come after us, and teaching them to trust God for themselves.
exp.0:1:
It says that King Ahaziah fell through the latticed window (the "lattice") of an upper room in his palace in Samaria. He was injured and fell ill. Then he sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover. Baal-zebub was a false god of the Philistines.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. Ahaziah was the son of Ahab and was ruling over Israel. His family had already turned away from the true God. So, by seeking help from an idol, he ignored the LORD, and God sent Elijah to rebuke him.

When we are distressed or sick, it is easy to look for answers anywhere but in God. This passage invites us to bring our fears to Him first, with trust, and not to depend only on other sources of security.
exp.5:9:
This verse tells us that the king of Israel sent people to the place that Elisha, the man of God, had pointed out to him. The danger was there. "Warned" means that he had been alerted in advance. "Kept himself" means that he took care and stayed away from that place. And "not once nor twice" means that this happened many times.

The narrator shows that Syria was at war against Israel. Each time the Syrian king planned an ambush, God let Elisha know where it would be, and the prophet warned the king of Israel. In this way the king was saved. Later on, the Syrians discover that Elisha is the cause.

For today: God speaks with wisdom to look after us, and sometimes He does so through the advice of people who are faithful to Him. It is wise to listen humbly to warnings that agree with the Bible and to heed them in time, even when we do not fully understand the reason.
exp.8:2:
He says the young prophet must take the box of oil, pour it on Jehu's head, and announce that God has anointed him king over Israel. Then he must open the door and flee without delay. The source's word for the small oil vessel should be described with the verse's own word: the box of oil is the small container meant here, and "flee" means to run away quickly.

Elisha speaks to a young man from the company of the prophets. Israel was under the house of Ahab, marked by idolatry, and God was going to bring judgment on it. Anointing with oil was the sign that God set someone apart for an office. The urgency probably protected the young man and showed that his task was only to deliver the message.

For today: when God entrusts you with something, obey clearly and without evasion. You do not have to control the outcome; your part is to be faithful in delivering what he asked of you.
exp.0:3:
God, through Elijah, tells King Ahaziah that he will not get up from the bed where he lies sick: he is surely going to die. After giving this message, Elijah departed.

The LORD speaks, and Elijah is his messenger. Ahaziah, king of Israel, had been hurt in a fall and, instead of seeking the God of Israel, sent to consult Baal-zebub, a god of Ekron, a Philistine city. God responds with judgment because the king placed his trust in an idol, as though there were no God in Israel.

For today: when a crisis comes, whether of health or of another kind, the first thing we should do is turn to God in prayer, and not look for security in things that cannot save us.
exp.3:39:
He says they served the stew to the men, but when they tasted it they cried out, "Man of God, there is death in the pot!" and could not eat it. The phrase about the food being poured out means that the meal was served. The word for the stew is the pottage, or broth. The phrase about crying out means that they shouted. The expression about death in the pot shows that the stew was poisoned or dangerous.

There was famine in the land, and Elisha was feeding a group of disciples called "sons of the prophets." One man went out to gather herbs and put wild gourds into the broth without knowing what they were. The men, who speak here, were frightened and went to Elisha. The text does not say precisely what plant it was, only that it proved harmful.

Even with good intentions, we can make mistakes and cause harm without knowing it. This invites us to be humble, to recognize our errors quickly, and to bring them to God and to wise people. The account goes on to show that God cares for his people in their need.
exp.5:16:
Elisha asks God to open the eyes of his young servant so that he can see. God does so, and the young man discovers that the mountain is full of horses and chariots of fire surrounding Elisha.

The king of Syria had sent a great army to surround the city of Dothan to capture Elisha. When the servant saw the encirclement, he was filled with fear. Elisha had already told him that there were more forces on their side. Now God shows him that unseen reality. The Bible does not explain in detail what that vision was like.

When fear overtakes us, sometimes we see only the problem. We can pray, as Elisha did, asking God to give us faith to trust that he is present and cares for his own, even when we do not see him with our eyes.
exp.21:10:
This verse says that King Josiah, when he heard the reading of the book of the law, tore his clothes. In those days, tearing one's clothes was a public sign of deep grief, sorrow, or repentance.

The narrator tells how the scribe Shaphan read aloud to the king a book that had been found in the temple while repairs were being made. Many believe it was all of Deuteronomy or a part of it, though the text does not say exactly. Josiah understood that the people had turned away from what God had commanded, and so he feared God's judgment. Right away he sent to inquire of the LORD.

For today: when you read the Bible, let it truly confront you. If God shows you something you need to correct, do not justify it or ignore it. Respond with humility, ask for forgiveness, and take a concrete step to obey him.
exp.0:12:
This verse tells that King Ocaziah sent a captain with fifty soldiers for the third time to take Elijah. But this captain acted differently: he fell on his knees before the prophet and asked him to spare his life and the lives of his men. The phrase "man of God" means a prophet. The word "I pray thee" means "I ask you."

Ahaziah was sick and, instead of seeking the God of Israel, he consulted a false god. Elijah had confronted him, and the king wanted to capture him. The first two captains spoke arrogantly and ordered the prophet to come down; fire consumed them. This third one acknowledged God's authority. Then the angel of the LORD told Elijah to go without fear.

For today: God responds to humility. Approaching Him with respect and simplicity, and not with pride, opens the door to His mercy.
exp.9:29:
God tells Jehu that, because he carried out what He commanded against the family of King Ahab, his descendants will rule over Israel for four generations. "Doing what is right" means doing what is just, and "according to all that was in my heart" means according to what God had desired.

The LORD speaks after Jehu has destroyed the house of Ahab and the worship of Baal. But the text makes clear that Jehu did not turn away from the golden calves of Jeroboam, nor did he follow God's law with his whole heart. God acknowledges what Jehu did well, although his obedience was incomplete. Some understand that the promise shows God's kindness, and others that it also foreshadows the judgment that would come later.

Today we can learn that God sees and values obedience, but He wants a whole heart. It is not enough to correct only what is most visible; it is wise to ask God to show us the areas we are still holding on to.
exp.13:4:
It says that when Amaziah had the kingdom firmly in his hand, he put to death the servants who had killed his father, King Joash. The verse for the phrase about his rule being secured has been rewritten in plain terms: his reign was now secure, and to strike them down meant that he had them killed.

This is the account from the book of Kings, which tells the story of Judah. Amaziah began to reign after his father was murdered. The text makes clear that he did what was right, though not entirely. It then says that he did not kill the children of the guilty men, because the law of Moses forbade it (Deuteronomy 24:16). In this way it shows that he obeyed the law on that point.

For today: when someone has wronged us, we should seek justice without revenge or excess. God's law protects the innocent, and no one should pay for the faults of others.
exp.13:15:
This verse tells of the death of Jehoash, king of Israel. "Slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died. He was buried in Samaria, the capital, alongside other kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam (the second of that name) became king in his place.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings, who is not named. He summarizes the lives of the kings and how they ended. Earlier, the account spoke of Jehoash's war against Amaziah, king of Judah, and of how he carried treasures from the temple to Samaria. Now the account closes his story and moves on to the next king.

For today: no one remains in power or in fame forever. It is worth more to live today with humility, honoring God and caring for what He entrusts to us, than to accumulate things that will be left behind.
exp.8:9:
It says that God announces a terrible punishment for Jezebel: the dogs will eat her in the field of Jezreel, and no one will bury her. Then the young prophet opens the door and flees.

The one speaking is a young prophet sent by Elisha to anoint Jehu as king of Israel. He passes on the message of the LORD: the family of Ahab, who led the people into idolatry and shed innocent blood, would be judged. Jezebel was a central part of that wickedness. The prophet flees at once, just as he had been instructed.

For today: God sees injustice and does not let it go unanswered forever, even though he sometimes waits a long time. This invites us to live with humility and not to take vengeance into our own hands, trusting that God does justice in his own time.
exp.24:5:
This verse says that the Chaldeans captured King Zedekiah and brought him before the king of Babylon, who was at Riblah. There "they gave judgment upon him," that is, they passed judgment on him and set his punishment. "Brought him up" is the same as "took him" in the verse above.

The passage is a historical account from the book of Kings. The narrator tells of the fall of Jerusalem and of the last king of Judah. Zedekiah had fled by night, but he was overtaken on the plains of Jericho and his army deserted him. The book presents this fall as the result of the long disobedience of the people and their kings toward God. Riblah was in the north, far from Jerusalem.

For today: running away from the consequences does not remove them. It is better to listen to God in time, obey Him and trust Him, rather than look for ways out on our own once we have ignored His voice.
exp.17:20:
Here, Egypt is compared to a staff made of a bruised reed. A staff is a walking stick. If someone leans on it, the broken reed gives way, drives into the hand, and wounds it. Pharaoh is that kind of support for all who trust in him.

Rabshakeh, a high official of the king of Assyria, speaks from outside Jerusalem. He wants to discourage the people and King Hezekiah of Judah, who had rebelled against Assyria. He mocks their alliance with Egypt and tries to break their confidence. Although he says some true things about Egypt's weakness, his intentions are intimidation and pride.

Today we can ask ourselves what we rely on for our security: money, people, or plans. All of these can fail. Trusting in God gives us a firm support.
exp.2:7:
Someone asks which route they should take to attack Moab, and the answer is: by the road through the wilderness of Edom. Edom is the name of the region south and southeast of Moab. It was a long and difficult route.

The text does not give the names, but it is most likely that Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, asks and Joram, king of Israel, answers. Moab had rebelled against Israel, and Joram asked Jehoshaphat for help. Up to this point, the kings are planning the war, but they do not consult God. Afterward, the army runs out of water in the desert.

Today we can learn not to plan only with logic and strategy. Before choosing an important path, it is wise to pray and seek God's guidance. A good plan made without consulting God can lead us into very dry places.
exp.14:23:
This verse says that Pekahiah, king of Israel, did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, that is, as God sees it. It did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin. The quoted phrase in the source means the same as "in the sight of the Lord", meaning how God sees it.

This is the narrator of the book of Kings speaking, who judges each king by how faithful he was to God. Jeroboam had set up golden calves for worship and so separated the people from the temple in Jerusalem. Pekahiah reigned only two years and was killed by his captain Pekah. The text repeats this judgment about many kings of the north.

For today: bad habits or decisions we inherit do not correct themselves. We can ask ourselves what harmful custom we keep following only because others practiced it, and ask God for help to change.
exp.3:43:
This verse says that the servant set the bread before the hundred men, they ate, and there was even food left over, just as the Lord had said. The verse's wording "according to the word of the Lord" matches this.

The prophet Elisha, a man of God, had received twenty loaves of barley and new grain as firstfruits, that is, the first of the harvest. His servant doubted because it was very little for a hundred people. Elisha insisted, because God had already promised that they would eat and there would be some left over. This happened in a time of famine in the region, according to the context of the chapter.

For today: when God asks you to give or serve with the little you have, you can obey with confidence. He does not depend on how much you have, but keeps his word and can make it be enough.
exp.11:19:
This verse says that the servants of King Joash agreed together in secret against him and killed him. This happened in the house of Millo, as he was going down to Silla. The phrase "made a conspiracy" means they made a secret plan together among several of them. It is not known for certain where Silla was; the text only indicates that it was a place near that house.

The text is narrated by the author of the book of Kings. Joash had taken the gold from the temple to pay Hazael, king of Syria, and so keep him from attacking Jerusalem. Soon after, this betrayal came. The text does not explain the exact motive, so it is not wise to claim more than it says. The following verses name the murderers, and his son Amaziah reigned afterward.

For today: Joash trusted in money and in his own arrangements, and ended in ruin. We can learn to seek God first and to be faithful in difficult decisions, instead of relying only on quick solutions.
exp.1:12:
Elisha picks up the cloak that fell from Elijah when he was taken up to heaven. Then he turns around and stops at the edge of the Jordan River. The sentence that explains the old word for "stopped" and the word for "cloak" is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your readers see.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Elijah has just been taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, and Elisha, his disciple, is left alone. The cloak stands for the work of being a prophet, which Elisha must now carry on. He had earlier asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Now he must face the river without his master.

For today: sometimes God leaves us alone before a challenge that someone else used to face. Elisha did not stay behind weeping; he gathered up what Elijah left and went forward. Learn from those who taught you, but trust that the God they served is with you too.
exp.10:12:
She heard the noise of the guard and of the people, the verse says, and she came to the people who had gathered in the temple of the Lord. A loud, confused noise is what the word here describes. The name of God is the name the reader will see as the Lord. She heard the commotion and went to see what was happening.

The narrator tells how the priest Jehoiada had secretly crowned Joash, the young heir of David, after Athaliah had seized the throne by force. The people were celebrating the new king, and Athaliah, knowing nothing, went straight to the place where everything had been prepared.

For today: God is able to keep his promises even when it seems that evil is in control. We can trust that he works with patience, and that our hope does not depend on who rules today, but on his faithfulness.
exp.20:22:
The verse tells us that some servants, that is, close officials of King Amon, made a secret plan against him. "Conspired" means they agreed together in secret to harm him. They killed him inside his own palace.

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Judah. Just before this, he says that Amon imitated his father Manasseh: he worshipped idols and turned away from the LORD. This violent end came after that life far from God. The text does not explain why the servants conspired, so it is not right to invent reasons. Afterward, the people punished the conspirators and made Josiah king.

For today: following paths that leave God out leads to ruin. Let us examine which examples we follow and seek to walk with God from now on.
exp.18:10:
It says that the king of Assyria sends a message to Hezekiah. It reminds him that the Assyrian kings have laid waste to all the peoples they found, "destroying them", that is, bringing them to an end. It closes with a mocking question: "shalt thou be delivered?", that is, "will you really be saved?"

The one speaking is Sennacherib, king of Assyria, through his messengers. Jerusalem was under threat. He wants to frighten Hezekiah into surrendering and giving up his trust in God. He presents God as just one more of the gods of the conquered nations.

For today: when problems seem bigger than God, do not measure your situation only by what others have suffered. Do as Hezekiah did, who brought the threat before God in prayer (in the verses that follow), and trust that he is greater than any fear.
exp.11:16:
It says that Hazael, king of Syria (the neighboring kingdom to the north, also called Aram), attacked the Philistine city of Gath and captured it. Afterward he decided to march against Jerusalem. The phrase "set his face" is an old expression meaning that he firmly resolved to do it. "Gath" is Gath, and "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

Context: the one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings, who recounts the history of the kings of Judah. Joash had organized the repair of the temple with great order and honesty. Now the account shifts: a military threat arrives. In the following verse, Joash gives Hazael the sacred treasures so that he will not attack the city. The text does not explain every detail of why God allowed this.

For today: even after good accomplishments, trials can come. It is wise for our trust to rest in God and not only in what we have built or in quick solutions.
exp.1:10:
It says that while Elijah and Elisha were walking and talking, suddenly a chariot of fire appeared with horses of fire, and it separated them. Then Elijah was taken up to heaven by a whirlwind, that is, by a strong, swirling wind. The phrase "parted them both asunder" means that it separated the two of them, and "came to pass" means "happened."

Elijah, the prophet, was about to finish his service. Elisha, his disciple, had asked for a double portion of his spirit to continue the work, and Elijah told him it would be granted if he saw him depart. The account shows that God himself passes on the task, and that Elisha stayed alert until the end. Some understand the chariot as a sign of God's protection; the text only says that it was something real and astonishing.

For today: if you want to receive what God has for you, stay close to him and attentive to him, especially in moments of change. Trust that God continues his work even when the people you admire are no longer present.
exp.5:22:
He says the king of Israel ordered a great feast prepared for the Syrian soldiers. They ate and drank, and he sent them back to their master. After that, the raiding bands, meaning armed groups that carried out surprise attacks, stopped entering Israel.

Elisha the prophet had led those soldiers to Samaria, and the king of Israel wanted to kill them. Elisha told him no, and that he should give them food instead. The next verse shows that Syria later did attack with its whole army, so the phrase "came no more" refers to those small raids.

For today: answering kindness to someone who harms us can break cycles of violence. It will not always change the other person, but it lets us act with mercy, as Romans 12:20-21 teaches.
exp.6:16:
It says that the king put in charge of the gate of Samaria the trusted officer, the one on whose arm the king leaned. The people, running desperately toward the food, trampled him, and he died. "Prince" here means an officer or assistant of the king, and "trampled" means walked over and crushed. In this way what Elisha, the man of God, had said came true.

The context: Samaria was besieged and suffering from famine. Elisha announced that the next day there would be cheap food. This officer did not believe it and mocked him. When the Syrians fled and the people went out to plunder the camp, God's word was fulfilled, both the promise and the warning.

For today: God keeps his word, even when it seems impossible to us. Doubting with mockery closes the heart, but trusting prepares us to receive what he does. Today we can pray: "Lord, help my unbelief."
exp.11:12:
This verse says that the money people brought to the temple was not used to make luxury items for worship, such as bowls of silver, snuffers, basins (containers for washing or catching liquids), trumpets, any vessels of gold, or vessels of silver. The money was set apart only for repairing the building.

It is part of the account of the reign of Joash, king of Judah. The narrator describes how the repair of the temple, which had fallen into disrepair, was organized. Earlier, the priests had not carried out that task well. For this reason, care was taken that each offering was used for the necessary work, and the verses that follow say that those in charge acted with faithfulness.

For today: before spending what is given for the work of God, it is good to ask what is truly necessary. Being faithful and honest with the money of the church is worth more than wanting to appear impressive.
exp.9:17:
Jehu gathers all the people and tells them that Ahab, the king before him, served Baal a little, but that he will serve him much. The word "served" here means that Ahab gave worship to Baal. However, these words are not sincere.

Jehu, who had just wiped out Ahab's family, spoke as God had said through Elijah. According to the text that follows, it was all a trick: he wanted to make people believe he would worship Baal so that he could gather his followers and destroy them. It is a difficult episode, and the Bible tells it without approving of every method Jehu used.

For today: truth and loyalty to God matter. Jehu acted with deception and, later on, his heart did not follow the Lord fully. Let us ask God to give us a sincere zeal, with integrity and humility, not just appearances or ambition.
exp.14:0:
This verse tells us when Azariah, son of King Amaziah, began to reign over the kingdom of Judah. The date is marked by the reign of Jeroboam, king of Israel, in his twenty-seventh year.

"Began to reign" means that he began to rule.

In other places in the Bible, Azariah is also called Uzziah.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, telling the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. He uses the year of a king of the north to place the king of the south in time, because there were two separate kingdoms. Some scholars note that the dates of these reigns are hard to make line up, and they are explained in several ways.

For today: God acts within real history, with concrete names, dates and people. We can trust that he is also present in our own time and in our circumstances, even when we do not fully understand them.
exp.15:5:
At that time, according to the verse, Rezin, king of Syria, took back the city of Elath for his country and drove the Jews out of it. Then the Syrians settled in Elath and lived there "until this day," that is, until the time when the book was written. Elath was a port at the northern end of the Red Sea.

The narrator is the author of Kings, who evaluates the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. Ahaz practiced idolatry, and because of this Judah was weak in the face of its enemies. Losing Elath was a consequence of that turning away from God, and it sets up the next mistake: asking Assyria for help.

For today: when things become difficult, it is tempting to look for quick human solutions. Ahaz looked to other kings and not to God. Before seeking ways out on your own, pray and place your problems in the Lord's hands.
exp.9:2:
He says to choose among the seventy sons of Ahab the one they consider most capable and just, set him as king in place of his father, and fight for the house of their master.

Jehu is the one speaking, the man who had already been anointed to put an end to the house of Ahab. He writes to the leaders of Samaria, who had the princes, weapons, and a fortified city. Many understand that it was a challenge meant to test their loyalty and their courage. They, filled with fear, surrendered without fighting, since the kings before them had already fallen before him.

For today: fear can lead us to hand over what we ought to defend. Let us ask God for courage to decide according to what is right, and not only out of fear of those who hold power.
exp.4:14:
Naamán, who has now been healed of his leprosy, returns with his whole company to Elisha, the man of God. He stands before him and acknowledges that the only true God in all the earth is the God of Israel. "Now I know" means that he now knows this from experience. "Gift" is a present, and "your servant" is a humble way of referring to himself.

Naamán was a commander of the army of Syria, a foreign country. He had come sick and proud, but he obeyed the command to wash himself in the Jordan. Now he speaks gratefully and wants to give a gift. Elisha refuses it, as seen later, so that all the honor belongs to God and not to the prophet.

For today: when God helps you, do not keep the benefit to yourself alone. Acknowledge it with sincere words and gratitude, and let that experience strengthen your faith.
exp.6:9:
The lepers returned to the city of Samaria and called out to the guards at the gate. They told them that they had gone to the camp of the Syrians and there was no one there, not even a human voice. They saw only horses and donkeys tied up, and the tents left just as they were. The words for the Syrians and the gate guards are now clear from the verse itself.

The speakers are the four lepers who lived outside the gate. Samaria was suffering terrible hunger because of the enemy siege. They discovered that the Syrians had fled, and they decided to give word so that others could also be saved. Earlier, the Bible says that the Lord had made the Syrians hear a great noise of chariots and horses.

When we receive something good from God, we should not keep it to ourselves. Today we can share with others hope, help, or the good news of Christ, without waiting until it is too late.
exp.1:6:
This verse tells us that fifty men, members of the groups of prophets, came and stood, at a distance and in front. Meanwhile, Elijah and Elisha stopped beside the Jordan River. The word "men" in the verse refers to ordinary men, and "stood" means they took their place and stayed still.

The narrator describes the scene just before Elijah is taken up into heaven. The prophets of Jericho already knew that God would take Elijah away that day, and now they watch from afar. Only Elisha, who would not leave his master, stands beside him at the decisive moment.

For today: some only watch from a distance what God is doing, and others draw near with determination. We can ask ourselves whether we are merely spectators of our faith or whether, like Elisha, we are willing to persevere and stay close to God and his work, even when it costs us.
exp.21:19:
God tells King Josiah that he will be gathered to his fathers, that is, that he will die and be buried in peace. He will not see the evil that God will bring upon Jerusalem and Judah. At the end, the messengers carry this answer back to the king.

The prophetess Huldah speaks on God's behalf. Josiah had heard the words of the book of the law, he was distressed over the sin of the people, and he humbled himself. God announces that judgment will come, but that the king will not see it in his lifetime. Some scholars note that Josiah died in battle (2 Kings 23:29), and they explain "in peace" as a peace with God, or as a death before the fall of Jerusalem. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, let us respond with humility and not with indifference. God sees a tender heart and listens to it.
exp.20:0:
This verse introduces Manasseh, who became king of Judah while still a boy of twelve years old. He reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem, the longest reign of any king of Judah. His mother's name was Hephzibah.

It is part of the book of Kings, written by a narrator who reviews the history of the kings of Israel and Judah. Manasseh was the son of Hezekiah, a king who sought God. The verses that follow explain that Manasseh did the opposite of his father and led the people into idolatry. The author gives these facts to show how the wickedness of this reign weighed on the history of Judah.

For today: no one chooses the family they are born into or the age at which they receive responsibilities, but we do decide whom to follow. We can ask God to help us value what faithful people taught us and not let it be lost.
exp.10:13:
Athaliah looks and sees the young king standing by the pillar, as was the custom at coronations. Beside him are the officers and the trumpeters, and all the people celebrate and blow the trumpets. She tears her clothes and cries out, "Treason, treason!" The word "rejoiced" here means shouts of festivity, and "princes" means the leaders or officers.

The account is told by the narrator of Kings. Athaliah had seized the throne by killing the royal family. Jehoiada, the priest, had secretly protected Joash, the only heir who survived, and now he was crowning him publicly. She calls "treason" what was in fact the restoration of the throne to the rightful heir of David.

For today: when the truth comes to light, the one who lives in deception often accuses others. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our mistakes instead of defending ourselves with shouting.
exp.2:24:
It says that Israel's army, with its allies, destroyed the cities of Moab. Each soldier threw stones onto the good fields until they covered them, they blocked the springs, and they cut down the good trees. In the end, only Kir-hareseth was left standing, but the slingers (soldiers who threw stones with a sling) surrounded it and attacked it.

The account tells of the war of the kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom against Moab, which had rebelled. Elisha had announced the victory. This verse describes how it came about, with the land suffering total destruction. Some think this followed the rules of warfare of that time; the Bible here only narrates it, it does not applaud it.

For today: war leaves damage that lasts a long time. Before acting out of anger or a desire for revenge, let us think about the consequences, and seek peace whenever it is possible.
exp.15:12:
This verse tells that King Ahaz made several offerings on the new altar. He burned his burnt offering (an animal offered whole to the fire) and his meat offering (a grain offering). He also poured out his drink offerings (liquid offerings, such as wine) and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings (sacrifices of fellowship or thanksgiving) beside the altar.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. Ahaz had seen an altar of another people in Damascus and ordered a copy made in Jerusalem. The priest Urijah built it and obeyed. Then Ahaz moved the bronze altar that God had commanded. The account shows how the king placed his own ideas above the design God had given.

For today: there can be a great deal of religious activity without true obedience. Before copying trends or customs, ask what God says in his Word.
exp.7:20:
This verse says that King Joram of Judah went to Seir with all his chariots. The Edomites had surrounded him, so he rose by night and attacked them, along with the captains of his chariots. Even so, his army fled into their tents.

The text is a historical narrative, not a speech. It tells how Edom rebelled against Judah in the days of Joram, who had turned away from God. Although there was an apparent victory in the attack, verse 22 makes clear that Edom remained independent. Some scholars think Joram barely managed to escape the siege, but the text does not say this with certainty. God did not destroy Judah because of his promise to David.

For today: a momentary success does not always solve a deeper problem. When we turn away from God, the consequences can continue. But God is faithful to his promises, and we can return to him with humility.
exp.22:1:
This verse says that King Josiah went up to the temple accompanied by all the people: the leaders, the priests, the prophets, and the common folk, from the least to the greatest. There he read aloud, so that everyone could hear it, the book of the covenant that had been found in the temple. The inhabitants of the city are the people who lived there, and a covenant is a binding agreement or commitment with God.

This is part of the account of King Josiah of Judah. The book of the law was found in the temple, and when he heard it, Josiah realized how far the people had strayed from God. Many believe it was Deuteronomy or a part of it, but the text does not specify. That is why he gathered everyone to hear the Word.

For today: God's Word was not meant to be kept on a shelf, but to be listened to carefully and obeyed. Today you can set aside a moment to read it and ask God to show you what needs to change.
exp.1:22:
Elisha goes up from Jericho toward Bethel. Along the way, some young people come out of the city and mock him, shouting: "Go up, bald head!" The word for these young people can mean children or youths; their exact age is not known. Bethel is the place named in the verse.

Elisha had just received Elijah's place as prophet. Bethel was a center of idolatry in the northern kingdom. Some understand the words "go up" as a mockery of the fact that Elijah had gone up into heaven, as if telling Elisha to disappear too. This is a possible interpretation, but the text does not say so. The safest reading is that they despised God's prophet and his message.

For today: let us watch our words and respect people, especially those who carry God's word. Mockery is never a small game; it calls us to humility and a sound heart.
exp.24:22:
This verse tells us that the surviving army officers of Judah, together with their men, heard that Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as governor. So they went to see him at Mizpah. Four leaders are named: Ishmael, Johanan, Seraiah and Jaazaniah. The phrase "captains of the armies" means the commanders or leaders of the troops.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jerusalem had already fallen, and Babylon left the poorest people in the land, with Gedaliah at their head. These leaders were looking for guidance and a safe place. Later, Ishmael, who was of royal family, killed Gedaliah. That shows that not everyone who came had good intentions.

For today: when everything falls apart, let us seek direction with humility, but also with discernment. Not everyone who comes near us has a sincere heart. Let us ask God for wisdom and peace.
exp.23:5:
This verse says that King Jehoiakim died and was buried with his ancestors. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died. After him, his son Jehoiachin became king. The name Jehoiachin also appears in other passages as Jeconiah or Coniah.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who is summarizing the history of each king of Judah. Before this verse, he has explained why God would not forgive: Jehoiakim filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. Because of this, the kingdom of Judah was falling under the power of Babylon, and his son inherited a very difficult situation.

For today: Our decisions do not end with us, for their effects reach those who come after us. Let us strive to live with justice and mercy, thinking also of the good of our children and of those who will follow us.
exp.8:25:
Dice that God saw yesterday the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons, and promised to repay it on that same plot of ground. That is why Jehu orders Joram's body to be thrown there. "Plot of ground" is the family land; "recompense" is the punishment deserved; "blood" speaks of a violent death.

The speaker is Jehu, and he reminds his captain Bidkar of a judgment that God pronounced against Ahab, Joram's father. In 1 Kings 21, Ahab and Jezebel unjustly killed Naboth in order to take his vineyard. Now Jehu sees that word fulfilled. The texts do not mention the death of Naboth's sons in that passage; there only Naboth is spoken of, so some believe this detail has been added here.

For today: God sees the injustices that no one else notices. We can trust that he will take into account what is done in secret, and seek to live with justice, without taking advantage of the weak.
exp.20:20:
He followed the same path as his father Manasseh. He did the same evil things that Manasseh had done and worshipped the idols that his father had worshipped. The word "idols" refers to the images themselves, described as detestable to God.

Nobody speaks here directly. This is the account of the writer of Kings, who summarizes the brief reign of Amon, which lasted only two years. He wants to explain why his rule ended badly: he abandoned the LORD, and the people of his own household killed him. The text presents his way of life as a repeat of his father's mistake.

For today: what we live with at home shapes us, but each person answers to God. It is worth asking ourselves which inherited habits we should leave behind and which good ones we want to pass on to others.
exp.20:7:
He says God promised not to again drive Israel out of the land he gave to their ancestors, on one condition: that they keep and carry out everything he commanded, according to the law of Moses. To make Israel's feet move out of the land means to be expelled or sent into exile. A fortune-teller is someone who predicts the future by omens, and spirits of divination are the spirits they claimed to consult.

The Lord speaks, and he says this in the middle of a rebuke against King Manasseh. This king set up an idol in the temple and practiced sorcery, even after God's promise to put his name there. God recalls his promise, but also that it depended on obedience. The people did not listen, and so punishment would come, as the verses that follow announce.

For today: God is faithful to his promises, and he invites us to respond to him with sincere obedience. Ask yourself what you have let into your life that takes first place away from God, and surrender it to him today.
exp.22:25:
This verse says that, although King Josiah carried out an admirable reform, God did not turn away the fire of his anger against Judah. "Fierceness" means intensity, and the "provocations" are the offenses that made him angry. The cause mentioned is what Manasseh had done.

The author of the book of Kings tells this after praising Josiah. Manasseh, Josiah's grandfather, had led the people into idolatry and serious injustice (2 Kings 21). The people had sunk so low that judgment was already decided, and God confirms it in the following verse. Interpreters see here both the seriousness of sin and the faithfulness of Josiah, which was valued even though it did not prevent the punishment.

For today: our decisions leave marks on others. For that reason it is wise to obey God with our whole heart and without delay, and to do so even when we do not see immediate results, because God sees and values that faithfulness.
exp.4:15:
Elisha tells Naaman that he will not accept the gift. He uses a solemn oath: "As the Lord liveth, before whom I stand," which means he speaks as a servant of God, aware that God sees him. Naaman keeps insisting, and Elisha refuses.

Naaman, a Syrian general, has just been healed of leprosy by obeying the prophet's word. Grateful, he wants to repay him with a gift. Elisha refuses, probably to make clear that the healing was a gift from God and not something that can be bought. In this way the glory stays with God, not with the prophet.

Today we can serve others without seeking profit or recognition. When God works through us, it is good to act in such a way that people see his grace and not our merit.
exp.9:15:
Jehu says to Jonadab: "Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord." Then they lift him up into his chariot. Zeal means an intense and burning interest. The phrase "they made him ride" means that they put him in the chariot or helped him up into it.

Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of King Ahab, and he was already carrying out that task with great violence. Jonadab, son of Rechab, was a man known for his simple life and his faithfulness to God. Jehu wants him to come along and see his zeal. Later it becomes clear that Jehu deceives the worshipers of Baal. For this reason many think that his zeal was mixed with political ambition, although the Bible does not fully explain his motives.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our zeal for God is sincere or whether we use it to be admired. True zeal shows itself in obedience, humility and love, not in showing off.
exp.8:24:
Jehu orders Bidkar, his captain, to take the body of King Joram and throw it into the plot of ground that belonged to Naboth of Jezreel. He reminds him that when the two of them rode behind Ahab, the father of Joram, God pronounced a judgment against that house. The officer who accompanied Jehu is the one called "captain" here; the word used for the plot of ground refers to land received as an inheritance; and the phrase "in one end" means "at one side."

Jehu speaks as the one anointed to destroy the house of Ahab. Ahab and Jezebel had Naboth put to death so they could take his vineyard (1 Kings 21). Jehu sees in this moment the fulfillment of the word God spoke through Elijah. It is a harsh passage, and not everything Jehu did afterward was right, but here the focus is that God does not forget injustice.

For today: if you have suffered abuse or injustice, trust that God sees it. Leave vengeance in his hands, and seek to live justly.
exp.16:5:
It says that in the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom. He carried the Israelites off to Assyria and settled them in several places: Halah, Habor by the river of Gozan, and the cities of the Medes. The word "carried away" means that he took them away by force to another place, that is, he exiled them.

The author of the book, who is not named, tells of the end of the kingdom of Israel, the northern one. Hoshea had sought help from Egypt and stopped paying tribute to Assyria, and that brought on a siege lasting three years. The verses that follow explain the deeper cause: the people sinned against God and followed other gods.

For today: God is not indifferent when we set him aside. It is wise to examine where we place our real trust: in God, or in allies that seem more secure. Returning to him in time is always better than waiting until everything falls apart.
exp.14:32:
It says that Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign in Judah and that he ruled sixteen years from Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, whose name we do not know for certain. He notes the basic facts about each king: age, years of reign, and mother. In this way he places Jotham in the history of Judah and compares him with the kings of Israel. Some scholars think Jotham ruled alongside his father Uzziah, who was ill, and that this would explain certain differences in the dates.

For today: God sees a person's whole life, not only their offices. Even simple facts, such as a mother's name or an age, matter in his story. Today you can ask him that your daily faithfulness, even in small things, be upright before him.
exp.9:0:
This verse says that Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria (sons and male descendants of his family). Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of the city, to the elders, and to those who brought up the king's children, meaning the people in charge of raising and caring for the king's sons.

Jehu had just been anointed to put an end to the house of Ahab, and he had already killed King Joram. Now he issues a challenge with these letters: if they wanted to defend the dynasty, they should choose one of the sons and fight. Scholars discuss whether it was a test, a strategy, or a trap; the text says nothing more about his intentions.

For today: God does not leave injustice unanswered, even if it takes time. This invites us to ask which side we are on and not to lend our silence to what God has already judged.
exp.18:29:
It says that the people of Judah who survive, the small group that remains, will grow again like a plant. First they will take root downward, that is, they will become firm, and afterward they will bear fruit upward. The word "shall yet again take root" means they will go on to take root again, and "the remnant that is escaped" refers to the survivors.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah. Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. God promises that Assyria will not take the city. The sign of the three years shows that the land would recover little by little. God cares for a faithful remnant out of his own zeal.

For today: when you feel that you have little strength left, remember that God often restores gradually. Seek firm roots first in prayer and in his Word; the fruit will come in its time.
exp.22:3:
He says that King Josiah ordered the removal from the temple of all the objects that had been made to worship Baal, the image of Asherah (which the older version calls "the grove"), and the heavenly bodies, called "the host of heaven." He burned them outside the city, in the fields of the Kidron, and had the ashes carried to Bethel.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. Josiah had just read the book of the covenant, which had been found in the temple, and the people promised to obey God. Now he begins to clean the temple of idolatry. Bethel had been a rival center of worship, and carrying the ashes there probably showed that these idols had no value. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of this act.

For today: if we decide to follow God wholeheartedly, we must also remove from our lives whatever takes his place. This is obeying with deeds, not only with words.
exp.17:25:
Here three officials of Hezekiah ask the spokesman of the king of Assyria to speak in Aramaic, which they understand, and not in the Hebrew of Judah, so that the people standing on the wall will not hear. Aramaic was the language of diplomacy, while the Hebrew of Judah was the language of the people.

Context: Jerusalem is under siege by Sennacherib. Rabshakeh tries to break the people's trust and says that the LORD himself sent him. The officials want to negotiate in private and avoid panic. Rabshakeh refuses and speaks even louder in Hebrew to frighten everyone.

For today: when someone tries to sow fear or doubt about your faith, you do not have to listen to everything or let it wear you down. Guard what you hear, protect others from discouragement, and, as Hezekiah later did, bring your fears to God in prayer.
exp.0:15:
Here Elijah tells King Ahaziah what God had said. Since the king had sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover, God asks: is it not because there is no God in Israel? The word "bed" means the couch he had climbed onto. For that reason the king would not come down from the bed he had gone up on, but would surely die.

The prophet Elijah speaks on God's behalf. Ahaziah was sick from a fall and sought an answer from a false god. Earlier, two groups of soldiers sent to arrest Elijah died by fire. The third captain humbled himself, and the angel of the Lord told Elijah to go without fear.

For today: when sickness or fear comes, let us not rush first to any source that promises security. Let us seek God in prayer and in his Word, and then also seek wise counsel, remembering that He is our first and best help.
exp.23:7:
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he ruled in Jerusalem only three months. His mother's name was Nehushta, the daughter of Elnathan, who was also from Jerusalem. Some copies of 2 Chronicles 36:9 give a different age for him, and scholars explain that difference in several ways.

The author of Kings, whose name we do not know for certain, tells the story of the kings of Judah. Jehoiakim had died and his son inherited the throne just when Babylon was dominating the region. That is why the reign was so short and ended in crisis.

Today it reminds us that what we leave to those who come after us matters. When the next verse says that Jehoiachin repeated his father's evil, we see how much example influences. Let us ask God for help to live in such a way that our children and those who watch us find a good path.
exp.22:15:
This verse tells how Josiah, king of Judah, turned around and saw some tombs on the mountain. He ordered the bones taken out of them and burned them on the altar at Bethel to make it unclean.
