In this way what God had announced through a man of God, that is, a prophet, was fulfilled. The word "polluted" means to make something unclean, and "proclaimed" means to announce something publicly.

The narrator is the author of Kings. Josiah was clearing the land of idolatry. At Bethel, Jeroboam had set up an altar that rivaled the temple in Jerusalem. Many years earlier, a prophet from Judah had announced that a king named Josiah would do this (1 Kings 13:2).

For today: what God says comes to pass, even when a long time passes. We can trust his promises and also take his word seriously, removing from our lives whatever displaces him.
exp.24:1:
This verse says that Jerusalem was surrounded by the enemy army for a long time, until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah's reign. The word "besieged" means surrounded and shut in, unable to get out or receive help. According to the previous verse, the siege began in the ninth year, so it lasted about two and a half years.

The text is a historical narrative, not a speech. The writer of Kings tells how the kingdom of Judah fell before Babylon. Earlier, the prophets had warned the people to return to God, and the book presents this fall as the result of many years of disobedience. The verse shows that the outcome was not sudden, but that there was a long period of waiting and of opportunity.

For today: sometimes we live through long seasons of pressure and waiting. This passage invites us not to harden our hearts in the meantime, but to listen to God and seek him with humility while there is still time.
exp.9:9:
What it says: Jehu speaks to the people and asks them to recognize something: everything God said against the house of Ahab will certainly be fulfilled. "Not one word will fall to the ground" means that not a single word of God will go unfulfilled. He says that the Lord has done what he announced through his servant Elijah. "Know" here means "understand."

Context: Jehu had just been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab, a dynasty marked by idolatry and injustice. Elijah had already announced that judgment. Jehu uses these words to justify himself before the people. The Bible shows that God judged that house, but not everyone understands Jehu's violent methods in the same way, and later he himself is criticized for his conduct.

For today: God does what he says, and that encourages us to take his Word seriously, both his promises and his warnings. Let us trust him, but with humility.
exp.2:19:
The verse tells that the next morning, at the hour when the offering was presented, water came by the way of Edom (Idumea). The water was so abundant that the country was filled with it.

Elisha had said that God would give water without wind or rain, and that he would also deliver Moab into the hands of the kings. Israel, Judah and Edom were campaigning against Moab, and their soldiers were dying of thirst. How the water arrived is unknown; the text only says it came from Edom, and presents it as the work of God. The water also prepared the deception that is seen afterward.

For today: God can answer at exactly the right moment, even when we see no signs beforehand. Before the water came, the people had to obey and dig ditches. If you are waiting for help today, keep doing faithfully what God has already shown you.
exp.23:9:
What it says: This verse tells that, while Jehoiakim was reigning in Judah, the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, that is, his officials and his army, came up to Jerusalem. They surrounded the city with troops so that no one could go in or out. The word "besieged" refers to this: the city was put under siege.

Context: The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings, who is not named. He explains that Jerusalem suffered this crisis after years of disobedience by its kings. Jehoiakim did evil, just as his father had. Soon Nebuchadnezzar himself arrived and the young king surrendered. This was the beginning of Judah's fall to Babylon.

For today: Bad decisions, even when they are repeated out of family habit, have consequences. But we can also break the cycle. Today is a good time to ask God for direction and to choose a different path.
exp.7:19:
In the days of Joram, king of Judah, the people of Edom broke free from Judah's rule. They rebelled and set up a king of their own.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the history of the kings. Joram had married a daughter of Ahab and followed his evil ways. Even so, God did not destroy Judah, because of the promise he had made to David. Many understand this loss of Edom as a consequence of Joram's unfaithfulness, though the text does not say so in those words. His attempt to put down the rebellion did not succeed for long.

For today: turning away from God often brings loss and disorder in what once stood firm for us. But his faithfulness stands, and his patience invites us to return to him and to live with integrity.
exp.9:26:
This verse tells how they broke the sacred statue of Baal and tore down his temple. Then they turned it into a place of filth, a place for waste and refuse. And so it remained to this day, that is, until the time the book was written.

The narrator recounts what Jehu, king of Israel, did after tricking the worshipers of Baal and gathering them in his temple. He wanted to end that worship in the kingdom. Turning the place into something shameful showed complete contempt for that false god. However, the text makes clear that Jehu did not remove the golden calves of Jeroboam.

For today: it is not enough to remove the obvious idols. Let us also examine the small sins we tolerate, and seek to obey God with all our heart.
exp.16:2:
It says that Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, attacked Hoshea, the last king of Israel. Hoshea was placed under his control, as a servant, and he paid tribute, that is, money or wealth that a weak country handed over to a stronger one to avoid being destroyed. The phrase "became his servant" means that he came under his rule.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, recounting the fall of the northern kingdom. Israel was already weakened by its disobedience to God. Later Hoshea stopped paying and looked for help in Egypt, and that led Assyria to besiege Samaria. Interpreters explain the exact order of events in different ways, but the account shows a gradual fall.

For today: trusting in human and secret solutions, instead of sincerely returning to God, only sinks us further. When we are in trouble, let us first seek God and act with honesty.
exp.12:22:
It says that God felt compassion for Israel and cared for them with tenderness. He did this because of the covenant he had promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. For that reason he did not want to destroy his people or cast them out of his presence, up to the time when this was written. The words "had compassion" mean that he was moved with pity, and "had respect unto them" means that he looked upon them with attention and care.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks, not a character. Israel suffered greatly under Hazael, king of Syria, during the reign of Jehoahaz. Even so, the text explains that God did not abandon them, and the reason was not Israel's goodness but God's faithfulness to his promise. Later Jehoash recovers cities, as a sign of that care.

When you feel that your failures or your problems are pulling you away from God, remember that his love rests on his faithfulness and not on your perfection. Return to him with confidence.
exp.8:19:
Here the watchman, who is standing in the tower keeping watch, reports that the second rider also reached Jehu and did not come back. He also notices something in the way the chariot advances: it goes so fast and with such force that it reminds him of Jehu, the son of Nimshi. The watchman is the one who keeps watch; "furiously" means with great haste and force.

Jehu had been anointed to put an end to the house of Ahab. King Joram wanted to know whether he came in peace, but Jehu held the messengers back. The watchman describes what he sees from afar, not yet knowing what will happen. Some understand "son of Nimshi" as a reference to his grandfather, since Jehu was the son of Jehoshaphat and the grandson of Nimshi.

For today: God uses determined people to carry out his purposes. Ask him to give you courage and perseverance to obey him, but also self-control, so that your strength is guided by his justice and not by impulse.
exp.18:20:
It says God answers the king of Assyria with a word from the Lord. When it says "hath despised thee" and "hath laughed thee to scorn," it means "has despised you" and "has mocked you." The "virgin the daughter of Zion" is a poetic way of speaking of Jerusalem and its people. "Hath shaken her head at thee" is a gesture of mockery: Jerusalem shakes her head as she watches you flee.

The prophet Isaiah speaks on God's behalf to King Hezekiah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. Hezekiah prayed, and God answers that he heard it. God announces that the proud invader will be humbled.

For today: when you feel threatened or small in the face of something very large, pray sincerely as Hezekiah did. God hears, and the mockery of the proud does not have the last word.
exp.10:1:
It says that Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and sister of King Ahaziah, took Joash, son of Ahaziah, and secretly took him out from among the king's sons who were being killed. She hid him from Athaliah, along with his nurse, in a bedchamber. So they did not kill him.

It is part of the story in the book of 2 Kings. The narrator tells how Athaliah, when her son died, wanted to destroy the whole royal family so she could keep the power for herself. This threatened the line of David, from which God had promised that the king would come. Jehosheba, according to the account, was the wife of the priest Jehoiada, and she acted and saved the child.

God often takes care of his promises through brave and humble people. When you see an injustice or a danger to someone who cannot defend themselves, do not think your action is small. An act of courage and care, done in time, can preserve a life and a greater purpose.
exp.14:12:
He says that Shallum, son of Jabesh, began to rule the kingdom of Israel in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah (also called Azariah), king of Judah. His reign lasted only one month, and he ruled from Samaria, the capital.

The phrase "began to reign" means that he took the throne.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, relating the history of the kings. Just before this, God's promise to Jehu is fulfilled: four generations of his descendants would reign. With Zechariah, that line comes to an end. Shallum came to power through a conspiracy, and the text that follows shows that Menahem killed him. It was a time of great political violence.

For today: power taken by force does not last long. We can trust that God keeps his word and, instead of pursuing quick success at any cost, choose honest and stable paths.
exp.18:19:
Verse 20 tells how Isaiah, son of Amoz, sent a message to King Hezekiah. He said that the Lord, the God of Israel, had heard his prayer about Sennacherib, king of Assyria. Hezekiah had asked God for help with a sincere and urgent plea. The message was delivered through a messenger sent to the king.

The Assyrian king had surrounded Judah and mocked the God of Israel, comparing him to the gods of other nations. Hezekiah took the threatening letter to the temple and prayed that God would save them, so that all the kingdoms would know that the Lord alone is God. Isaiah, the prophet of God, answers with the word of the Lord. What follows is a message against Sennacherib.

For today: when you feel threatened or without a way out, bring your problem to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. God hears, even though his answer does not always come the way we expect or when we expect it.
exp.4:26:
Elisha announces a punishment for Gehazi: the leprosy that had been cured in Naaman would now cling to Gehazi and to his descendants. The sentence that explains "seed" (descendants) and "cleave" (to stick fast) must be rewritten for words in the verse above, so I will say instead that the disease would stay on him and his offspring forever, and that Gehazi left the prophet's presence with skin as white as snow, a sign of leprosy.

Elisha speaks as a prophet of God. He had healed Naaman without charging anything, to show that God's grace cannot be bought. Gehazi, his servant, ran after Naaman, asked him for money and clothing with a lie, and then lied to Elisha as well. Elisha knew what had happened, and the Bible presents this as insight given by God.

For today: do not use spiritual things for personal gain, and do not hide your faults with lies. It is better to confess with humility and serve with honesty, because God sees the heart.
exp.21:17:
This verse begins God's special message for King Josiah. God tells the prophetess to answer the king, who had sent people to ask what to do. The sentence is left open: "Because you heard the words of the book...", and it continues in the next verse.

God speaks through the prophetess Huldah. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and Josiah, on hearing it, understood that the people had disobeyed. God announces judgment on Judah, but the king receives a different answer because of his attitude. Scholars often think the book was all or part of Deuteronomy, though this is not stated with certainty.

For today: when God's Word confronts you, do not defend yourself or ignore it. Listen with a humble heart, for God sees and responds to those who come to Him with sincerity.
exp.16:1:
It says that Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom (Israel), did what was evil in the sight of God. But it adds that he was not as bad as the kings before him. "In the sight of the Lord" means "according to God's judgment."

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of Israel and evaluates it according to faithfulness to the covenant with God. Here it summarizes the reign of Hoshea just before the fall of Samaria to Assyria. The text does not explain exactly in what way he was "less evil"; some think that perhaps he did not stop the people from going to Jerusalem, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God does not settle for us being "less evil" than others. Comparing ourselves with others can give us false comfort. It is better to examine our hearts before God and turn back to Him with sincerity.
exp.0:16:
Ahaziah died just as God had announced through Elijah. Since he had no son to inherit the throne, his brother Joram began to reign in his place. The word "according to" in the verse matches the source's "según," and "LORD" is the name of God.

Ahaziah, king of Israel, had fallen, and instead of seeking God, he sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub, a false god of Ekron. God sent Elijah with a message of judgment, and here we see that it came true. The dates of the reigns in this period are calculated in several different ways, and scholars explain them in different ways.

For today: what God says comes to pass. When you are afraid or need direction, seek God first in his Word and in prayer, and not other sources that promise security.
exp.0:5:
The messengers of the king tell him that they met a man, who was Elijah, and that he sent them back with this message: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to seek an answer from Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore, the king will not get up from his bed, but will surely die. "Bed" is the word for the bed he lies in, and "surely" means for certain.

The speakers are the group of messengers sent by King Ahaziah, who had fallen and was injured. He sent to consult a false god about whether he would recover. God stopped the messengers through Elijah. They repeat faithfully what Elijah said, and so the king learns of God's judgment.

For today: when sickness or distress comes, do not run first to sources that promise security without God. Pray, seek his guidance in the Bible, and also turn to the counsel of wise people and of doctors, trusting that the Lord is enough.
exp.2:6:
It says that Joram, king of Israel, sent a message to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He told him that the king of Moab had rebelled and asked whether he would go with him to fight. Jehoshaphat answered yes, and said that he, his people and his horses were at Joram's disposal, as if they were one.

Moab had been paying tribute to Israel, and when Ahab died it rebelled. Joram wanted to recover that control and looked for allies. Jehoshaphat was a king who generally followed God, but here he agrees right away, without consulting the Lord. Later in this same chapter, he will only then ask for a prophet.

It is good to be loyal and generous with others, but before we commit to a plan, it is wise to pray and seek God's guidance. A hasty "yes" can lead us into problems we could have avoided.
exp.14:3:
Says that although King Azariah (also called Uzziah) did what was right before God, the high places were not removed. The high places were raised spots where the people worshiped and offered sacrifices. The phrase about "burning" means they burned incense. The people kept using those places instead of going only to the temple in Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing Azariah's reign. He praises his faithfulness, but points out a flaw: the worship was not fully purified. Then he tells that God struck him with leprosy. The text does not explain the cause here; another book, Chronicles, gives more detail.

For today: it is not enough to do many good things if we leave unattended something we know must change. Ask God to show you one area of your life that you keep tolerating, and surrender it to him with humility.
exp.2:22:
The Moabites saw the water red and thought it was blood. They believed the three allied kings (Israel, Judah, and Edom) had fought and killed one another. So they shouted: "Moab, to the spoil!", that is, go and gather the plunder. "They have turned against each other" means that they had turned against one another.

Speaking are the soldiers of Moab. The allied kings were without water, and Elisha had announced that God would fill the valleys with water without rain. With the morning sun, the water looked red, and the Moabites were overconfident. Their mistake cost them defeat.

For today: do not make important decisions based on what seems true at first glance. Appearances and desires can deceive us. Before acting, stop, pray, and seek the truth calmly.
exp.19:15:
Isaiah tells King Hezekiah to listen carefully to what God is about to say. The words "Hear the word of the Lord" are an invitation to be quiet and pay attention, because what follows is not the prophet's own opinion.

Isaiah had asked Hezekiah about some visitors from Babylon, and the king admitted he had shown them all his treasures. Now the prophet changes his tone: he no longer asks questions but speaks in God's name. What follows is a serious announcement about the future of the royal house and of Judah.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is wise to listen first, even when what we hear makes us uncomfortable. Before boasting about what we have or trusting in our own strength, we can ask ourselves what God thinks about it.
exp.23:3:
It says that God did not want to pardon Judah for the innocent blood that King Manasseh shed. Manasseh filled Jerusalem with the blood of the innocent. For this reason, the Lord decided not to overlook that sin.

The narrator is the author of Kings, who explains why judgment came upon Judah in the time of King Jehoiakim. Decades had passed since Manasseh, but the text points to him as the central cause of the kingdom's fall. The enemies that God sent were carrying out what the prophets had already warned. How this relates to God's response to Manasseh's later attitude (2 Chronicles 33) is something that is debated.

For today: God takes human life and injustice seriously. Today we can defend the weak, reject all abuse, and turn promptly to God with sincere repentance, without minimizing our sin.
exp.3:40:
Elisha asks for meal, throws it into the pot where the stew had been poisoned, and tells them to serve the food to the people. The text says there was no longer anything harmful in the pot. The word "harm" here refers to whatever in the stew was dangerous or deadly.

Elisha, the prophet, is at Gilgal during a time of famine. A man had gathered wild gourds without knowing what they were, and the disciples of the prophets were alarmed when they tasted the stew. The Bible does not explain how the meal changed the stew; it presents the event as the work of God through his servant.

For today: when something seems lost or spoiled, God can intervene in simple and unexpected ways. Place your situation in his hands with confidence, and act with wisdom and obedience, while continuing to ask for his help.
exp.14:18:
This verse tells that Pul, king of Assyria, invaded the land of Israel. Menahem, the Israelite king, paid him a thousand talents of silver so that he would support him and so secure his power on the throne.

The verse does not give a second name for the Assyrian king; many identify him with Tiglath-pileser III. A talent was a very large unit of weight.

Here no character speaks; this is the account of the writer of Kings. Menahem had taken the throne by violence, and his reign was evil in God's sight. Faced with the threat from Assyria, he did not seek the LORD but bought protection with money, and he raised that money from the wealthy people of the land, as the following verse says.

For today: when fears and pressures arrive, it is easy to trust in money or in human alliances to feel secure. This passage invites us to seek God first and not to rest our stability on what cannot give us true peace.
exp.3:37:
Elisha returned to Gilgal at a time of great hunger in the region. The sons of the prophets, who were a group of disciples, were gathered together with him. Then he orders his servant to set on a large pot and prepare a pottage, that is, a warm stew, for all of them.

The narrator tells this moment right after Elisha restored to life the son of the Shunammite woman. Elisha is the one who speaks, and he does so to feed the disciples who lived and learned alongside him. The famine makes food scarce, and what follows in the account shows how difficult it was to find.

For today: in times of scarcity, caring for others with what we have is an act of faith and love. Even when there is little, we can share the table and serve with simplicity.
exp.9:4:
The officials of Samaria answer Jehu with complete submission. The "steward" is the one who managed the palace, the "governor of the city" was the head of the city, and the "guardians" were the tutors who raised the king's sons. They tell him: "We are your servants, we will do whatever you command, we will not make any king; do what seems good to you."

Jehu had just challenged these leaders to choose one of Ahab's sons and fight for him. Seized by fear, they saw that not even two kings had been able to stop him. So they gave up. This answer later leads to the killing of the king's seventy sons. The Bible records the event, but it does not approve of their cowardice.

For today: fear can lead us to obey those we should not obey and to stay silent in the face of injustice. Let us ask God for the courage to decide according to what is right, not only according to who holds the most power.
exp.3:11:
This verse tells how Elisha the prophet asks his servant Gehazi to call the woman from Shunem. She comes and stands before him. The word "Shunammite" means that she was from Shunem, her town. The phrase "she stood before him" means that she came and presented herself.

Elisha speaks from the upper room that the woman and her husband had prepared for him to rest in when he passed through their area. He felt grateful for her kindness and wanted to reward her. That is why he sends for her, although he speaks to her through Gehazi. In that time it was common to use a servant as a messenger. The Bible does not explain why Elisha did not speak to her directly.

For today: when someone serves us with kindness, let us thank them in a concrete way. A sincere "thank you," or asking "how can I help you?", honors the one who gives without asking for anything in return.
exp.23:4:
This verse is the formula the author uses to close Jehoiakim's reign. It says that the rest of his deeds, everything he did, is recorded in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." That book is not the Chronicles in our Bible, but an official court record that we no longer have.

The author of Kings, who does not identify himself, repeats this phrase at the end of the story of each king. Here it stands between two ideas: God's judgment on Judah for the sins of Manasseh, and the growing pressure from Babylon. The author wants to explain why Judah falls: it was not chance, but the result of a deep sin, such as the innocent blood that was shed.

For today: our choices leave a mark, and sometimes their effects last for years. Let us live today with justice and humility, and turn to God to ask for forgiveness and guidance.
exp.24:21:
This verse tells that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, left behind in Judah a group of poor people without power. Over them he set Gedaliah, son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, as ruler. The phrase "set as ruler" means that he appointed him to lead them on Babylon's behalf.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. Jerusalem had already fallen and many had been taken into exile. Gedaliah came from a family that had served in the court of Judah. For that reason, Babylon could have seen him as an acceptable leader. The text does not explain all of Babylon's reasons, so it is better not to assume more.

For today: even when everything seems lost, God still allows a new beginning. Seek to be a leader, or a person who cares for others with humility and peace.
exp.3:3:
She is told to go into her house, shut the door on herself and her sons inside, and begin to pour oil into all the jars. Whenever one is full, she is to set it to one side. "Jar" here refers to a small container, and "pour" means to empty the oil out into the vessels.

The prophet Elisha is speaking. A widow in debt had cried out for help, because a creditor wanted to take her two sons as servants. She had only a little oil. Elisha asks her to use what little she has and to obey. The text does not explain why the door had to be shut; some think it was to do this in private, and others think it was to make room for faith.

For today: God often begins with the little we have. We can take a step of obedience, even when we cannot see how everything will be resolved, and trust that He will take care of us.
exp.14:28:
In the days of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, invaded the land. He captured several cities in the north (Ijon, Abel-beth-maachah, Janoah, Kedesh and Hazor) and also the regions of Gilead, Galilee and all the territory of Naphtali. Then he carried the people of these places off to Assyria, that is, he took them away by force.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who records the history of the kings. The preceding text says that Pekah did what was evil in the sight of the Lord and followed the sins of Jeroboam. In this way, the account presents this invasion as part of the consequences of the people's and their leaders' unfaithfulness, although the verse itself only narrates the event.

Today we can remember that decisions, good or bad, have consequences. It is wise to return to God in time and not to grow accustomed to what He disapproves of.
exp.9:27:
It says that Jehu put an end to the worship of Baal in Israel. His men took out the sacred statues and burned them, broke down the main pillar of Baal, and tore down his temple. They turned it into a place of waste, that is, into a public toilet or latrine, and it remained that way to this day, up until the time the account was written.

The narrator tells what happened after Jehu, anointed as king, wiped out the family of Ahab and the worshipers of Baal. God had commissioned him to judge that wickedness. But the text goes on with a warning: Jehu did not get rid of the golden calves of Jeroboam. He removed one idol but kept another.

We can make visible changes and still hold on to idols that are more comfortable for us. Let us ask God to examine our whole heart, not just what others notice.
exp.6:2:
This verse presents four men with leprosy who were sitting at the entrance of the city gate. They ask one another: "Why sit we here until we die?" The word "leprous" refers to people with a skin disease that cut them off from others.

Samaria was under siege by the Syrian army and suffered a terrible famine. Because of their disease, these men lived outside the city, without help. Elisha had just announced that God would provide food the next day, although an official doubted it. The men with leprosy knew nothing of that promise, but they decided to act.

When we feel stuck and without a way out, staying still is not always the best choice. We can take a step, even a small one, and trust that God can work even in our despair.
exp.10:16:
Jehoiada, the priest, makes a covenant in three directions. First, between God, the king, and the people, so that all of them would be the people of the Lord. Second, between the king and the people. The name of God is the one the verse shows as "the Lord." A covenant is a solemn commitment.

King Joash was a child, hidden for six years in the temple, because Queen Athaliah had taken power and killed the heirs. Jehoiada presents him as the rightful king and, after Athaliah's death, renews the commitment to God and puts the life of the country in order. Then comes the fall of the worship of Baal.

Today, a commitment to God is also lived out in concrete relationships. We can ask him for help to keep honestly what we promise at home, in the church, and at work, remembering that faithfulness to God and justice toward others go together.
exp.22:36:
He is said that Jehoiakim, king of Judah, did what was evil in the sight of God, just like his ancestors. The phrase about doing what was evil in the sight of the Lord means that he acted in a way that God considered wrong. The word "according to" means "in keeping with" or "just like." "His fathers" refers to earlier kings, not only his own father.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes the reign of each king with a spiritual evaluation. Jehoiakim was put on the throne by Pharaoh Necho and, according to the text, taxed the people to pay him. The book does not detail here what wrongs he committed; it only gives the final verdict on his life.

For today: it is not enough to simply copy what others did before us. We can ask ourselves which inherited habits, good or bad, we are repeating, and ask God for help to change what does not please him.
exp.16:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel served idols, even though God had clearly told them not to do so. To "serve" here means that they worshipped them and gave them their loyalty. The word "idols" is the one the Bible uses for false figures of gods.

The author of the book explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell before Assyria. It is a kind of summary of their failures. They imitated the neighboring nations and disobeyed a known command, given in the Law. God warned them again and again through His prophets, but they would not listen.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts: money, fame, comfort, or the approval of others. If God has already spoken to us in His Word, let us not wait for consequences before we obey. Let us return to Him today, with humility and sincerity.
exp.8:14:
This verse says that King Joram had gone back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Syrians had inflicted on him in the war against Hazael. Jehu, already acclaimed as king by his fellow officers, asks them that, if they agree with him, no one should leave the city. In this way, no one could go to Jezreel to give word of what was happening. The phrase about the sword-like wounds and the note about what the words mean are left out here since they refer to wording not found in the verse you are reading.

Jehu speaks as a commander of Israel's army. A prophet had just anointed him in secret to remove the house of Ahab from the throne. Jehu wants to act by surprise, before Joram finds out and prepares himself.

For today: when God gives us a task, it is good to act with resolve and without delay. But we must also examine our motives and seek to do what is right with humility, since Jehu later did not follow the Lord with his whole heart.
exp.6:4:
The verse says that they rose up at twilight to go to the Syrian camp. When they came to the outskirts of the camp, they found that no one was there.

The people of Samaria were under siege and suffering a terrible famine. The lepers, outcast and living outside the city gate, reasoned among themselves that staying put meant death, and going into the city also meant death. So they decided to take their chances with the enemy. What they did not know is that God had already caused the Syrians to hear the sound of a great army and flee, leaving everything behind.

For today: God often works before we arrive. When you find yourself with no way out, take the step you can with humility and trust, and you will discover that God was already going ahead of you.
exp.23:1:
God sent against Judah, the southern kingdom, armed bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites. His purpose was to destroy it. This fulfilled what God had already announced through his prophets. "Bands" refers to groups of soldiers; "Arameans" are the people of the land of Aram, which the King James Version calls Syrians.

The narrator of the book explains why Judah suffered these invasions. King Jehoiakim had rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar after serving him for three years. The verses that follow point to the sins of Manasseh, above all the innocent blood shed in Jerusalem. The text presents these attacks as the judgment of God, not as mere political misfortune.

For today: God speaks with seriousness, but also with patience, for he gave warning long before. If you sense a warning in his Word, do not ignore it. Draw near to him with humility and change course in time.
exp.19:2:
Hezekiah asks God to remember how he has lived. He says he has walked before God in truth and with a whole heart, that is, sincerely and without divided loyalty. When he finishes, he weeps greatly, with a loud and heartfelt cry.

The king Hezekiah speaks here, and he is seriously ill. The prophet Isaiah has just told him that he is going to die. Hezekiah turns toward the wall, probably to be alone with God, and prays. His request does not claim perfection; many read it as the sincere cry of someone who trusts in God's faithfulness. God hears him and grants him more years of life.

We can bring our pain before God with complete honesty, even weeping. He hears sincere prayers and is not troubled by our tears. Praying with an open heart is an act of trust.
exp.15:19:
This verse says that King Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, that is, Jerusalem. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is an old and gentle way of saying that he died. Then his son Hezekiah became the new king of Judah.

The speaker is the author of the book of Kings, which tells the history of the kings of Judah and Israel. It closes the account of Ahaz, a king who did things contrary to God and altered the temple under pressure from Assyria. With Ahaz's death one reign ends and another begins. The text does not explain here what Hezekiah will be like; that is told in the following chapters.

No government or wrongdoing lasts forever, but God continues to work from generation to generation. Today you can trust that, even if others have left a bad example, you can choose to walk in a different and faithful way.
exp.6:0:
Elisha announces a word from God: tomorrow, at this same time, food will be very cheap at the gate of Samaria. A measure of grain and a piece of silver are the units mentioned in the verse, and the reader can see them there. Fine flour is flour of the highest quality. "Hear ye" is the verse's own call to listen.

Elisha speaks as a prophet in the middle of a harsh military siege of Samaria, where there was extreme hunger. That is why his announcement seemed impossible. The context that follows shows that one of the king's officers doubted this promise.

For today: when your situation seems closed in and without a way out, remember that God can act in ways you do not expect. Trust his word and do not dismiss it because of doubts, even when you cannot see how it could come true.
exp.5:30:
Here the king of Israel makes a very strong oath: he asks that God punish him severely if Elisha, son of Shaphat, is still alive at the end of the day. "God do so to me, and more also" is an ancient oath formula. "Stand on him" means that the head stays attached to the body.

The king of Israel speaks (the Bible does not name him here). Samaria is under siege, there is terrible famine, and a woman has told him that they ate her son. Horrified and desperate, the king tears his clothes and vents his anger against Elisha, as if the prophet were to blame for everything.

For today: when suffering overwhelms us, let us avoid blaming others or getting angry at those who speak on God's behalf. Instead, let us bring our pain to God with humility and repentance, and seek his help rather than acting in anger.
exp.0:13:
Here speaks the third captain, who kneels before Elijah. He reminds him that fire from heaven had already consumed the first two captains with their fifties. So he begs him to spare his life and the lives of his men. The phrase "let my life now be precious in thy sight" means "let my life be precious in your sight" or "have mercy on me."

King Ahaziah, who was sick, sent soldiers to seek out Elijah because he had consulted Baal-zebub, a god of Ekron, instead of seeking the God of Israel. The first two captains came with a commanding order and without humility. This third one comes in a different way. Interpreters often see in the fire a judgment of God against that rebellion.

For today: God resists pride, but He responds to those who come near with humility. Before asking something of God, we can acknowledge who He is and draw near with respect and sincerity.
exp.12:13:
Elisha was very sick, and he died of that sickness. King Joash went to see him, wept before him, and called him "my father, my father," "the chariot of Israel and its horsemen."

The king of Israel speaks here. Although he did what was evil before God, he recognizes that Elisha, with his word on behalf of the Lord, had been more of a protection for the nation than any army.

These words also recall what Elisha said when Elijah was taken up to heaven.

Today we can value and thank the people who guide us in faith and pray for us while we still have them close. A timely word of gratitude means a great deal. And let us remember that our true security is in God, not in human strength.
exp.6:11:
Here the king of Israel gets up in the middle of the night and tells his servants that what seems like good news is really a trap. According to him, the Syrians know there is hunger in Samaria, so they left their camp and hid in the field. He thinks they are waiting for the Israelites to come out of the city so they can catch them alive and get inside.

There is a besieged city with terrible hunger. Four lepers discovered that the enemy camp was empty, and they told the gatekeepers. The king, distrustful and unable to see the hand of God, interprets everything as a military strategy. The Bible does not say he had any proof; it is his suspicion.

For today: when God works in an unexpected way, distrust can keep us from recognizing him. We can be prudent, like the king who ordered a check, but we can also ask God for eyes of faith to see his help, even when it comes in a surprising way.
exp.5:18:
Elisha speaks to the Syrian soldiers, who have just been struck blind through the prophet's prayer. He tells them that this is not the road or the city they are looking for, and that he will lead them to the man they are seeking. Then he leads them to Samaria. Some readers see in this a clever move by Elisha, since he himself was the man they were after, while others understand it as a way of speaking that is still true, because he does bring them before the king.

The king of Syria wanted to capture Elisha, and he sent an army to Dothan. God protected his prophet with an invisible army and blinded the soldiers. Elisha takes advantage of their confusion to bring them, without violence, into the heart of Israel's territory.

When we feel surrounded by problems or enemies, we can trust that God is at work beyond what we can see, and that he has ways of resolving the conflict without answering with violence.
exp.11:11:
It says that the money collected was used to pay the masons and stonecutters, and to buy timber and hewed stone. All of this served to repair the cracks or damage of the temple, the breaches in the house of the Lord. Hewed stone is stone cut and shaped for building.

Here the account in the book of Kings speaks, which tells of the reign of Joash of Judah. The temple had fallen into disrepair, and a chest had been placed to receive the offerings. The text stresses that the money was handled with order: they counted it and handed it over to those in charge of the work, who paid the workers and bought the materials. The verses that follow say that it was not diverted to luxury items.

For today: caring for what belongs to God includes doing it with order and honesty. If you handle money for your church or for a project, keep clear accounts and use it for what is necessary.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells that Elisha was passing through Shunem, a town in Israel. There lived a woman of standing, that is, a woman of good position and great respect. She urged him strongly to eat with her, insisting until he accepted her invitation. From then on, whenever Elisha passed that way, he would stop at her house to eat.

The narrator reports a new event that follows the miracle of the widow's oil. Elisha was a prophet, called a man of God. Here no one special speaks; he is simply introduced to this woman, whose hospitality opens the story that follows, where she recognizes that Elisha is a holy man and proposes preparing a room for him.

For today: practice simple hospitality. A shared meal or an open door can encourage a servant of God, a neighbor, or someone who is weary, and God sees that steady kindness.
exp.5:20:
This verse says: the king of Israel looks at the Syrian soldiers, who are now inside Samaria, and asks Elisha, "Shall I smite them, my father?" The word "smite" here means to kill or attack. Calling Elisha "my father" was a way of showing respect to the prophet.

Context: Elisha had led a Syrian army, which had been struck blind, to the capital of Israel. When God opened their eyes, they found themselves surrounded with no way out. The king, surprised and with power over them, asks the prophet for his advice. Elisha replies that they should not be killed, but should be given food and sent away.

For today: when we have the upper hand over someone who has wronged us, we can choose kindness instead of revenge. Sometimes an act of generosity opens the way to peace.
exp.24:4:
This verse says that the Chaldean soldiers (the Babylonians) pursued King Zedekiah and overtook him in the plains of Jericho. All his army, which had fled with him, scattered and left him alone. The phrase about "overtook" means the army caught him, and the plains are the low, flat lands near Jericho.

The book of 2 Kings recounts the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. There is no character speaking; it is the author's account. The city was under siege and suffering from hunger, and Zedekiah tried to escape at night. The book presents this fall as the result of years of disobedience by the people and their kings toward God, although the text of this verse only narrates the events.

When we lean on our own strength, plans, or allies, they can leave us alone at the most difficult moment. Today we can learn to listen to God in time, obey Him, and trust Him before the crisis arrives.
exp.0:0:
It says that when King Ahab died, the people of Moab rebelled against Israel. "Rebel" means to stop obeying an authority and refuse to pay what was owed to it. Moab had been under Israel's control, and with Ahab's death it saw an opportunity to break free.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, continuing the story of the kings of Israel. We do not know for certain who wrote the book. This sentence opens the account and shows that the kingdom of Israel had grown weaker. In the verses that follow, King Ahaziah seeks help from a false god instead of seeking the LORD.

When things grow weak around us, it is easy to look for quick and wrong ways out. Today we can choose the opposite: in moments of crisis, turn first to God in prayer and trust, before looking for support in other things.
exp.5:19:
Elisha asks God to open the eyes of the Syrian soldiers. They had been struck with blindness and led into Samaria. Now they regain their sight and discover that they are in the middle of the enemy capital, surrounded.

Elisha speaks in the midst of a war. The king of Syria had sent troops to capture him, but God left them blind. Elisha led them before the king of Israel, who wanted to kill them. However, the prophet asked that they be given food and allowed to go in peace.

God can open our eyes to see our situation clearly, and at times He places us in places where we receive mercy instead of punishment. Just as Elisha treated his enemies with kindness, we can ask God to help us respond with gentleness to those who harm us.
exp.21:14:
Huldah, the prophetess, answers the men sent by King Josiah. She tells them that what she is about to say comes from the Lord, the God of Israel. First she asks them to take a message to "the man that sent you," that is, to the king. The words "said" and "saith" may sound old-fashioned, but they simply show that God himself is speaking through her.

King Josiah was alarmed when he heard the book of the law that had been found in the temple. He ordered his men to inquire of the Lord. They went to Huldah, a woman known as a prophetess. She does not speak on her own, but passes on what God makes known to her. What follows is a serious message of judgment.

For today: when you read the Bible, hear it as the voice of God and not as merely an ancient text. If it shows you something you should change, respond with humility, as Josiah did, and without delay.
exp.19:12:
Hezekiah received the envoys from Babylon and showed them everything of value he had: silver, gold, spices and fine oils, as well as his armory and his treasures. The verse says there was nothing in his house or in all his kingdom that he did not show them. The spices and the precious ointment in that list are the same things the verse names, so no further explanation of those words is needed.

The narrator tells us that the king of Babylon, Merodach-baladan, sent letters and gifts when he heard that Hezekiah had been sick and had recovered. Hezekiah responds with pride or confidence in his riches. The text does not give his exact reason, but Isaiah will confront him right away, and other passages warn that this would bring consequences.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security. When God blesses us or heals us, it is easy to boast about what we have instead of giving thanks to Him. Let us practice gratitude and humility, remembering that everything we have comes from God.
exp.9:18:
Jehu gave orders to call together all the prophets of Baal, all his servants, and all his priests, and he insisted that none be missing. He told them there would be a great sacrifice to Baal, and that whoever failed to come would not live. The text makes clear that this was a trick, a deception meant to destroy those who honored Baal.

Jehu was the king whom God had raised up to bring an end to the house of Ahab. That family had led Israel to worship Baal. Jehu pretends to be devoted to Baal so that he can gather his followers in one place. His method was violent and deceitful, and the Bible tells the story without approving everything he did. Later it says that he did not follow God with his whole heart.

For today: God does not tolerate our keeping other gods in our hearts. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God, and set them aside sincerely, not with deception.
exp.18:1:
It says that King Hezekiah sent three messengers to the prophet Isaiah: Eliakim, who was over the household; Shebna, the scribe; and the eldest of the priests. All of them went covered with sackcloth, a rough cloth that was worn as a sign of grief and repentance. Eliakim was over the household, meaning he was in charge of the palace, and Shebna was the king's scribe.

The Assyrian army, through its spokesman Rabshakeh, had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. Hezekiah, distressed, first went to the temple and then asked Isaiah to pray and bring a word from God.

For today: when a crisis comes that overwhelms you, go first to God and also seek the support of mature believers who will pray with you. You do not have to carry the fear alone.
exp.11:8:
This verse tells how the high priest Jehoiada took a chest, drilled a hole in its lid, and placed it beside the altar, on the right side of the entrance to the temple. The priests who guarded the door put into it all the money that the people brought into the house of the Lord.

King Joash had confronted the priests because the temple was still in disrepair. Until then the money was not being used to repair it. So the system was changed: the priests would no longer handle that money, and the chest would allow the offerings to be gathered in a visible and orderly way. Afterward, the king's scribe and the chief priest would count the money and hand it over to the workmen.

For today: when money is handled in the church, it is good to have order, clarity, and more than one person overseeing it. This protects everyone's trust, and what is given in love truly serves the work of God.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that the king asked the woman what had happened, and she told him her story. Then the king ordered an official, that is, a court officer, to restore everything that was hers: her house, her lands, and the harvests from the years she was away from the country.

The narrator tells us that, while Gehazi was speaking to the king about Elisha's miracles, that very woman arrived, the woman of Shunem, asking for help with her property. According to the previous chapter, she had left because of a famine. Her arrival at that moment was very timely, and the text suggests that God was watching over her.

God can care for us in the details, even when we do not see how. We can cry out with confidence, do what is our part, and wait for Him to act in his time.
exp.20:13:
God says he will forsake the remnant of his inheritance, that is, the people of Judah who were left, whom he holds as his most precious possession. He will hand them over into the hands of their enemies, and they will become a prey and a spoil: they will be plundered and stripped by all their adversaries. To forsake means to leave alone, without protection.

The Lord speaks through his prophets in the time of King Manasseh. Judah had practiced idolatry and violence, and had shed much innocent blood. God announces judgment on Jerusalem, comparing it with Samaria, which had already fallen. It is the consequence of a long and persistent rebellion.

For today: God is patient, but he takes seriously sin that is not abandoned. Let us not harden our hearts; if God shows us something crooked in our lives, let us repent quickly and return to him while there is still time.
exp.14:13:
Menahem, son of Gadi, went up from the city of Tirzah and came to Samaria. There he attacked Shallum, son of Jabesh, struck him down, killed him, and took the throne in his place. The word "struck" here means that he struck him a fatal blow, and "killed him" means that he put him to death.

This is part of the historical account of the kings of Israel. Shallum had taken the throne through a conspiracy and reigned only one month. Earlier, the text recalls that God promised Jehu that his descendants would reign to the fourth generation, and that promise was fulfilled. Afterward, the northern kingdom falls into a spiral of violence, with kings removing one another from the throne. The passage does not approve of what Menahem did; it only tells what happened.

For today: power taken by force and deception never brings lasting stability. Let us seek to act with justice, and trust that God sustains what is his.
exp.23:18:
This verse says that Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, did what was evil in the sight of God. That is, he lived in a way that God considered wrong. The phrase "according to all that Jehoiakim had done" means that he followed the same example of that earlier king.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who judges each king according to his faithfulness to God. Babylon had put Zedekiah on the throne and changed his name, in place of Jehoiachin. Here the text presents his reign as part of the fall of Jerusalem. Some scholars think that Jehoiakim is Jehoiakim, though the text gives no further details.

For today: bad examples weigh heavily, but they do not have to rule over us. We can ask ourselves whom we imitate and ask God for help in choosing a better path.
exp.11:4:
This verse says that the priests were to receive the money that the people brought to the temple, each man from those of his acquaintance, and use it to repair the damage to the building. The word "breaches" refers to the gaps or openings in the walls, and the phrase "of his acquaintance" is understood here as people close to him (some take it to mean the people who served him).

King Joash of Judah is speaking. The temple had fallen into disrepair, and he orders that the offerings of the people be used to repair it. But the following passage shows that, up to the twenty-third year, the priests had not carried out the work. For this reason the king calls them to account and changes the system.

For today: what is given to God must be handled with diligence and clarity. Good intentions are not enough; what has been promised must be fulfilled. Let us examine whether, in our church or in our commitments, we are doing what we said we would do.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that already in the twenty-third year of Jehoash's reign, the priests still had not repaired the cracks and damage in the temple. The "breaches" are the gaps, that is, the holes or broken places in the walls and damaged parts of God's house.

The text is part of the account in 2 Kings 12. Jehoash had ordered the priests to use the people's offerings to repair the temple. More than twenty years passed and the work was not done. So the king called Jehoiada and the priests to account. The Bible does not explain in detail why they failed to do it; it only shows that the assignment was not carried out.

For today: good intentions or resources are not enough to serve God; what has been promised must be fulfilled, and accounts must be given with humility. Think of something you have left pending in your church, your family, or your spiritual life, and take one concrete step today to attend to it.
exp.3:21:
Here the Shunammite woman calls to her husband and asks him for a servant and a donkey, so that she can hurry to the prophet Elisha, the man of God, and come back soon. She does not tell him that the child has died.

Her son has just died in her arms. She laid him on the prophet's bed and shut the door. Her husband does not know what has happened, and so he asks why she should go today. She answers only, "It is well." The text does not explain why she stayed silent; some see this as faith, others as a wish to act without delay.

When grief comes, do not freeze. She, in the middle of her anguish, moved and sought God through his servant. Bring your pain to God as soon as you can, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.8:27:
It says that the servants of Ahaziah, king of Judah, carried his body in a chariot from Megiddo to Jerusalem. There they buried him with his ancestors, in the family tomb, in the city of David, which is the old part of Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab, and Ahaziah, who was of that house, was wounded while fleeing. The text does not say that Jehu ordered him to be buried, but it does show that his servants treated him with respect. Other passages, such as 2 Chronicles 22, tell some details of his death in a different way, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: even when a person's life ends tragically, God remains just and governs history. This invites us to choose our alliances carefully and to live in a way that honors God, because our decisions also affect those around us.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that the money collected at the temple was to be used to pay the carpenters, the builders, and the masons. It also served to buy timber and hewn stone, which is stone cut and shaped for building. Everything was for repairing the house of God.

King Josiah speaks with his secretary Shaphan. He instructs him to tell the high priest Hilkiah to hand over the people's offering to the men in charge of the work. The temple had fallen into disrepair, and Josiah, who wanted to honor God, ordered it restored. The verses that follow tell that, in the middle of that repair, the book of the law was found.

For today: caring for what belongs to God requires order, hard work, and honesty. We can serve in our church with concrete effort and by handling what is entrusted to us with integrity.
exp.12:0:
This says that Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, began to reign over Israel in the twenty-third year of Joash, king of Judah. He ruled from Samaria, the capital, for seventeen years. Today we would write "began to reign."

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah, and for that reason he dates each reign by the reign of the neighboring kingdom. Jehoahaz belonged to the family of Jehu, who had ended the house of Ahab. The verses that follow show that this new king did not bring the people back to God, and for that reason difficult days came under Syria.

For today: it is not enough to come from a good beginning or from a family that did something good. Each person must seek God for himself and turn away from the bad habits he has inherited or copied.
exp.8:26:
Ahaziah, king of Judah, saw that Jehu had just killed Joram, and he fled. Jehu ordered his men: "Strike him down in the chariot too." They wounded him on the ascent to Gur, near Ibleam. Wounded, he made it as far as Megiddo, and there he died.

Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab because of its wickedness. Ahaziah was king of Judah, but he had family ties to that house and was allied with Joram. That is why he was caught up in the judgment. Chronicles gives an account of his end with other details, and it is not entirely clear how to fit the two together.

For today: our alliances and companions shape us. Before you join yourself to something, ask whether it draws you closer to God or drags you along with those who despise him.
exp.24:17:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of Babylon, took as prisoners Seraiah the chief priest and Zephaniah the second priest, along with three guards of the entrance to the temple. The word in the verse is "vessels" and it seems to be an error or an old way of translating the temple gatekeepers or guards; the Hebrew text speaks of guardians of the threshold.

No one speaks in the first person; this is the account of the biblical historian. Jerusalem had just fallen to Babylon (in 586 B.C.). The Babylonians plundered the temple and carried off the religious and civic leaders. According to the account, they were brought before the king at Riblah, and there they were put to death.

For today: positions and sacred places do not protect us if the heart turns away from God. Today we can ask him to give us a sincere faith, not merely an outward appearance, and pray for those who lead the church, that they may be faithful.
exp.7:27:
It says that Ahaziah, king of Judah, joined Joram, king of Israel, to fight against Hazael, king of Syria, at Ramoth-gilead. The Syrians wounded Joram. The phrase "went to the war" simply means that he went to fight alongside him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, continuing the account of the kings. He has just said that Ahaziah imitated the wickedness of the house of Ahab, because he was son-in-law to that family. So his military alliance is no casual detail: it shows how his closeness to that family led him to share their ways and their fate.

For today: the friendships and alliances we choose influence us more than we think. It is worth asking ourselves whether the people we walk with bring us closer to God or pull us away from him, and asking him for wisdom to choose well.
exp.24:9:
The verse tells how the Babylonian army, which was with Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the king, broke down the walls that surrounded Jerusalem. The name "Chaldees" is another name for the Babylonians, so the army is the one from Babylon. Without walls, the city was left defenseless.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the end of the kingdom of Judah. Jerusalem fell around the year 586 B.C., after years of warnings from the prophets. The text shows that the city, the temple and the palace were left in ruins, and that the people were taken into exile. The Bible presents this as the result of the people's persistent disobedience.

For today: the walls gave security, but they could not save someone who turned away from God. We can examine where we place our trust and return to resting in the Lord, who remains our refuge even when everything around us falls apart.
exp.24:7:
It says that in the fifth month, on the seventh day, in the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan came to Jerusalem. He was the captain of the guard, that is, a trusted officer of the king of Babylon. He came as his servant, in other words, to carry out his orders.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, telling of the end of the kingdom of Judah. They had already captured Zedekiah, and now Babylon carries out its punishment on the city. The book presents this as the result of years of unfaithfulness to God. Jeremiah 52:12 gives the tenth day, and it is not known for certain why; it may have been a different way of counting, or the arrival and the burning may have taken place on different days.

For today: God speaks with patience, but his warnings are serious. Today you can listen to him with humility and correct your course in time, without waiting for everything to collapse.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that the child Joash was kept hidden for six years with his aunt Jehosheba and his nurse in the house of the Lord, that is, in the temple. Meanwhile, Athaliah ruled the land as queen. Hidden means kept out of sight, protected so that no one would find him.

It is the narrator of the book who tells this. Athaliah had ordered the whole royal family killed in order to keep power for herself, but Jehosheba saved Joash, the only heir of David who survived. In this way, God's promise about David's descendants still stood. In the next verse, the priest Jehoiada prepares the moment to present the child as king.

For today: even when evil seems to rule for a long time, God keeps working quietly. We can trust him in times of waiting and faithfully care for what he has entrusted to us, even when no one sees it.
exp.11:14:
It says that the men in charge of receiving the money for the repair of the temple were not required to account for how they spent it. That money passed directly into the hands of the workmen, and there was no need to watch over those in charge, because they worked with faithfulness. The word "á" is an old form of "a", and "hacían la obra" means they were doing the work of repair.

It is part of the account of the reign of Joash, king of Judah. The narrator describes how the priest Jehoiada and the overseers managed the offerings to repair the temple. The text does not say that the accounts were never checked out of carelessness, but rather that there was such proven trust that no checking was needed. What was received went directly to the work.

For today: integrity builds trust. If you handle money or responsibilities belonging to others, whether in the church, at work, or at home, aim to be so honest that your conduct speaks for you, while also being wise enough to give an account clearly.
exp.6:13:
They took two horses with their chariots, and the king sent them to the camp of the Syrians, telling them to go and see what had happened. The Syrians are the Syrians, and the haste with which they fled is the hurry they showed in running away.

The king of Israel speaks in the middle of a terrible siege, with famine in Samaria. He is suspicious and thinks the Syrians are pretending to withdraw in order to trap them. A servant suggests sending riders to check. What the king does not know is that God had already caused the enemy to flee, just as Elisha had announced.

Many times we are afraid to believe that God is already at work, and we assume the worst. This passage invites us not to stay frozen by doubt, but to take prudent steps, look honestly, and trust that God keeps his word, even when the situation seems hopeless.
exp.10:8:
This verse says that the captains of the guard obeyed exactly what the priest Jehoiada commanded them. Each one gathered his men: those coming on duty that sabbath and those finishing their shift. The verse describes the captains over the hundreds, and the verse notes that they all presented themselves before Jehoiada.

Here the narrator tells of a secret plan. Athaliah, the queen, had seized the throne of Judah and killed the royal family, but the young Joash survived and was hidden in the temple for about six years. Jehoiada organized the guards to protect Joash and proclaim him king. He used the sabbath shift change to gather more men without raising suspicion.

For today: coordinated and trustworthy obedience helps accomplish a just purpose. Ask yourself where God is calling you to be faithful and to do your part well, even when no one applauds you.
exp.24:25:
After the murder of Gedalias, it says, all who remained in Judah, from the least to the greatest, together with the army commanders, set out for Egypt. "The Chaldeans" is another name for the Babylonians. The word "went" here means they set out. They did it out of fear of retaliation from Babylon.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem and appointed Gedalias as governor. Ishmael, who was of royal blood, killed him. The survivors feared that Babylon would punish them. Jeremiah 42 tells that God had told them not to go to Egypt, yet they went anyway. The book ends on a note of light: King Jehoiachin is released.

For today: fear can lead us to decisions that seem safe but move us away from God's guidance. Before acting out of fear, let us pray, seek his word, and trust that He is still at work, even in dark times.
exp.12:18:
This verse says that Elisha, the prophet, became angry with King Joash of Israel. The king had struck the ground with the arrows only three times, and Elisha told him he should have struck it five or six times. Then he would have defeated Syria completely, until they were all destroyed. Now he would defeat Syria only three times.

Elisha was sick and near death. The king came to him weeping, and Elisha gave him a sign with arrows, which announced victory over Syria. But the king acted without much zeal, and he stopped. The text does not say why he did it; it only shows that his response was weak.

For today: God gives us promises and opportunities, and our faith shows in how we respond. Serve with enthusiasm and perseverance what God puts in your hands, without settling for the minimum.
exp.5:11:
A servant of the king of Syria answers that none among them is a traitor. He says that Elisha, the prophet who is in Israel, tells the king of Israel even the words spoken in the innermost room of the palace.

A servant of the king of Syria speaks. The king was puzzled because his military plans kept failing: Israel knew in advance where he would attack. He suspected a spy, but the servant explains that God was revealing everything to Elisha. The Bible does not say exactly how Elisha knew, only that he was God's prophet.

For today: nothing is hidden from God, and that can give us peace. If you live with integrity, you need not fear that He sees you; and if you are in distress, remember that He knows what no one else knows and can care for you.
exp.22:22:
This verse says that the Passover that King Josiah commanded to be kept was held in the eighteenth year of his reign, in Jerusalem, to honor God. The word "was held" in the verse is the plain modern wording for what the older text expresses as "was kept." The Passover was the festival in which Israel remembered its deliverance from Egypt.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book. He tells what happened after the book of the law was found in the temple. Josiah was moved when he read it and led the people to obey. The Passover was kept so faithfully that it is said no other like it had been kept since the days of the judges. This does not mean that there had been no Passovers before, but that none had been kept with such faithfulness.

For today: when we discover what God says in his Word, it is not enough to admire it. We can take a concrete step of obedience and remember with gratitude what he has done for us.
exp.5:15:
Elisha tells his servant not to be afraid, because there are more with them than with the Syrians.

Elisha speaks to his young assistant. The king of Syria had sent horses, chariots, and a large army to capture the prophet, and the servant got up and saw the city surrounded. Elisha did not deny the danger, but he trusted God. Then he prayed, and God opened the young man's eyes so that he saw chariots of fire all around.

For today: when fear makes you see only the problem, pray to see with faith. God does not always remove the difficulty right away, but he keeps caring for you and is closer than it seems.
exp.12:12:
This verse says that King Joash died ("slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying he died). His son Jeroboam took the throne, and Joash was buried in Samaria with the other kings of Israel. The phrases "was buried" and "sat upon his throne" close the account of his reign.

The speaker is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes Joash's reign before telling an episode involving the prophet Elisha. This Jeroboam is the son of Joash, not the first Jeroboam mentioned earlier. The author notes that Joash did what was evil in the sight of God, although he had strength in war.

For today: at the end of life, achievements and positions are left behind, and what matters is whether we walk with God. Today we can seek Him sincerely and correct whatever pulls us away from Him.
exp.14:24:
Pekah, son of Remaliah, who was a captain in the army of King Pekahiah, plotted against him in secret. He struck him down in Samaria, in the king's palace, with the help of Argob and Arieh and fifty Gileadite men. He killed him and became king in his place.

It is a historical account from the book of Kings. God does not speak directly here; the narrator tells how the reign of Pekahiah ended, a king who did evil and followed the sins of Jeroboam. The kingdom of Israel was then marked by violence and one coup after another.

For today: when a people or a person turns away from God, it often ends in betrayal and violence. Let us seek what is good with honesty, without gaining power or success by unjust means, and trust that God governs.
exp.1:7:
Elijah takes his mantle, that is, his prophet's cloak, and folds it together. With it he strikes the waters of the Jordan River. The water divides to one side and to the other, and the two men cross over on dry land. The word for "struck" means hit, and "on dry land" means without getting wet.

Elijah and his disciple Elisha are on the way to the Jordan, and Elijah is about to be taken up by God. Elisha did not want to be separated from his master. Fifty sons of the prophets watched from a distance. This miracle recalls when Israel crossed the Jordan with Joshua, and it shows that God was still working through his prophet. Some see here also a preparation for Elisha's succession.

God opens paths that seem impossible, and he often does so when we take a step of obedience. Stay close to those who walk with God and move forward faithfully, trusting that he will do what you cannot.
exp.15:2:
He says that Ahaz, king of Judah, did not follow the example of David. He followed the way of the kings of Israel, who had turned away from God. He even made his son pass through the fire, that is, he offered him in a pagan rite, probably burning him as a sacrifice (some think it could have been a ceremony of dedication, but the text calls it an abomination). Those practices belonged to the peoples whom God had driven out of the land.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. Ahaz ruled in a time of military pressure, with enemies nearby. Instead of trusting in the Lord, he imitated the customs of the neighboring nations. The text shows how far a people can fall when they forget their God.

For today: when we feel fear or pressure, it is easy to copy what the world does instead of trusting God. Let us ask Him for wisdom and faithfulness, and take care that nothing and no one takes the place that belongs to Him alone.
exp.3:8:
What it says: A woman tells her husband that she has noticed Elisha, who always passes by their house. She concludes that he is a man of God, and she calls him "holy." "Man" is the meaning of the word rendered here, and the old spelling of "to" is written differently in older texts.

Context: The speaker is the woman of Shunem, described as a woman of standing, that is, of good position and highly respected. She had already invited Elisha to eat with them several times. Over time, she recognized that he was not an ordinary traveler. For this reason she proposes to her husband that they build a small room for him, so that the prophet would have a place to rest.

For today: Faith shows in the details. She did not wait until she had great resources or a special occasion, but used what she had to serve with generosity. Ask yourself today to whom you can offer hospitality or support, without looking for anything in return.
exp.24:13:
The Babylonians carried off the bronze utensils that the priests used every day in the temple: the pots (cauldrons), the shovels (scoops for removing ashes from the altar), the snuffers or tongs, the spoons, and all the metal vessels used in the service. "Ministered" means they served in worship.

This is a historical account, written by the author of Kings. It tells of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, plundered the temple. The text presents this as the consequence of Judah's long-standing unfaithfulness. It lists even the smallest items to show that the looting was complete.

For today: sacred objects do not protect anyone on their own; what God looks for is a faithful heart. Examine whether your spiritual life depends on outward routines or on a sincere relationship with Him.
exp.13:18:
The people of Jerusalem formed a conspiracy against King Amaziah. He fled to Lachish, a city of Judah, but his enemies sent people after him and killed him there.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes the end of this king of Judah. This passage does not explain why they rebelled. However, 2 Chronicles 25:27 says the conspiracy began when Amaziah turned away from the Lord. Earlier, Kings tells how he proudly challenged the king of Israel and was defeated.

For today: pride and turning away from God can cost a great deal, even when at first everything seems to be going well. Today we can ask God for a humble heart and stay close to Him each day.
exp.16:21:
This verse says that the people of the northern kingdom, Israel, kept committing the same sins as Jeroboam and never turned away from them. Jeroboam was the first king of that kingdom, and he had set up golden calves for worship, drawing the people away from worship in Jerusalem. Over time, that practice became the path of the whole nation.

Here the writer of the book of Kings speaks, explaining why Israel fell. God had sent prophets for centuries to call them back, but they refused. That is why the exile to Assyria came, just as God had already warned.

For today: a bad habit that is repeated and accepted as normal can become a way of life. Let us ask God to show us what we need to leave behind, and let us respond quickly when he calls us to change.
exp.15:17:
King Ahaz removed two things from the temple: the covert for the sabbath that had been built there, and the king's outer entry. He moved or took them away "for the king of Assyria."

This is part of the writer of Kings' account of Ahaz's reign. He changed several things in the temple while he was under Assyrian control. It is not certain exactly what the covert and the passageway were, and various ideas have been proposed. The text suggests that he did this out of pressure or to please Assyria, not out of obedience to God.

For today: it is worth asking whether we are changing what belongs to God in order to make a powerful person happy. May fear of people not lead us to trim our faithfulness to the Lord.
exp.6:1:
He says that an officer very close to the king, the one on whose hand the king leaned, did not believe Elisha's word. Mockingly he asked, "If the Lord should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?" Elisha, "the man of God," answered that he would see it with his own eyes, but would not eat of it. Here "lord" means the king's officer or captain.

Samaria was under siege by the Syrians, and the famine was terrible. Elisha announced that the next day food would be cheap and plentiful at the gate of the city. The officer doubted, thinking that only a great miracle could bring this about. Later the account shows that God fulfilled his word, and that this man was trampled to death at the gate, without tasting the food.

God can act in ways that seem impossible to us. When we doubt with mockery or contempt, we lose the joy of trusting. Today we can choose to believe his word, even when we do not see how he will fulfill it.
exp.17:7:
He says that Hezekiah, king of Judah, defeated the Philistines. He went as far as Gaza and its territory, and he overcame them throughout the whole region, from the small towers where the watchmen stood guard to the walled cities.
