This is the biblical narrator's account of Hezekiah's reign. Just before this, he says that Hezekiah remained faithful to God, and that God was with him and made him prosper. His victories are presented as the fruit of that faithfulness. He also rebelled against Assyria, the dominant power. Then the fall of Samaria, the northern kingdom, is recounted.

For today: constant faithfulness to God gives us steadiness in conflicts. It does not guarantee a life without struggle, but it reminds us that God accompanies the one who stays close to Him and obeys Him.
exp.22:34:
King Jehoiakim gave Pharaoh the silver and gold he demanded. But he did not pay it from his own treasury.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the history of the kings of Judah. Pharaoh Necho had defeated Judah, set Jehoiakim up as king, and required a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. Jehoiakim pressed his people to meet the demand.

For today: when we have authority, let us not burden others with the weight of our debts or decisions. May those who lead serve with justice and care for others, not protect themselves at their expense.
exp.2:8:
These verses tell that three kings went out together to fight against Moab: the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom (today this region is called Edom). They took a long detour through the desert for seven days, and they ran out of water for the soldiers and for the animals that followed them.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Kings. Moab had rebelled against Israel, and Joram, king of Israel, asked Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, for help. They chose the route through the desert of Edom, and there the lack of water put them in great distress. Afterward Jehoshaphat asked whether there was a prophet of the LORD they could consult.

For today: sometimes we make plans without seeking God first, and our need brings us back to Him. It is better to consult Him from the start, but it is never too late to ask for direction.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that the priests agreed to two things: to stop receiving money from the people for their own use, and not to take on for themselves the work of repairing the damage to the temple. The word "consented" simply means that they agreed. The "breaches" are the damaged or broken parts of the building.

King Joash had noticed that, after twenty-three years of his reign, the temple was still in disrepair. So he confronted Jehoiada, the high priest, and the other priests. The text does not detail the underlying reasons, but it shows that the money was not being used for the repairs. Then the system was changed: Jehoiada placed a chest to collect the offerings, and in this way the money was handled with more order and transparency.

When something sacred is neglected, it is wise to correct it with humility and order. If we manage resources of the church or of others, let us do so with clarity and accountability. Honesty protects the work of God and strengthens trust.
exp.1:20:
He went out to the springs of the water, where the city's water rises, and threw the salt in there. Then he declared that the Lord had healed those waters, and that from now on there would be no death or sickness caused by them.

Elisha is the prophet who received the ministry of Elijah. The people of Jericho asked him for help because the water was bad and the land was not producing fruit. The salt is not a natural cure; the text makes clear that the healing comes from the Lord and from his word. Some see in the act a sign of purification, though the text does not explain it.

Today we can bring to God problems that seem to have no solution, dealing with their root and not only the surface. He can use the simple things we hand over to him with faith and obedience.
exp.10:4:
Here the priest Jehoiada gives orders to the military commanders. He tells them to divide into groups for guard duty. A third part, made up of those who came on duty on the Sabbath, was to guard the king's palace.

Jehoiada spoke this way because Athaliah, the queen, had seized the throne by killing the royal descendants. But little Joash, the king's son, had been hidden in the temple for six years. Now Jehoiada was carefully preparing, through a solemn covenant, the moment to present him as the rightful king. The Sabbath shifts allowed them to gather men without drawing attention, although the Bible does not explain every detail of the plan.

For today: doing what is right requires courage, but also order and good planning. Trusting God does not rule out organizing ourselves with wisdom, patience, and teamwork.
exp.22:30:
This verse says that Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he began to reign in Jerusalem, and that his reign lasted only three months. It also names his mother: Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. The phrase "began to reign" simply means that he started to rule as king.

Here the narrator of the book, who records the reigns of Judah, is speaking. Josiah, his father, had just died at Megiddo. The people chose Jehoahaz, and the following text tells that he did what was evil and that Pharaoh Necho imprisoned him. He is also called Shallum in other passages, though some scholars debate the detail.

For today: having a good father or a good inheritance does not guarantee a good path. Each person answers to God for their own decisions. Let us ask Him for wisdom to follow His will with firmness.
exp.21:7:
It says that the high priest Hilkiah told the secretary Shaphan that he had found the book of the law in the temple. Then he gave it to him, and Shaphan read it. The word for "scribe" referred to an official secretary of the king, and the word for "found" means discovered.

Hilkiah speaks during the repairs of the temple that King Josiah had ordered. Many believe the book was all or part of Deuteronomy, although the text does not say so exactly. After years of spiritual neglect in Judah, this reading would lead the king to recognize the people's disobedience and to seek change.

For today: sometimes God's word is kept and forgotten, even in religious places. It is worth opening the Bible regularly, reading it with humility, and letting it correct and guide us.
exp.7:18:
He says that, although King Joram did evil, God did not want to destroy Judah. He did so out of regard for his promise to David, his servant. "Cutting off" here means destroying or eliminating. "Lamp" was a way of speaking of a light that stays lit, that is, of descendants of David who would continue to reign.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who tells the story of the kings. Joram of Judah married a daughter of Ahab and followed the bad customs of the kingdom of Israel. The author explains why Judah continued to exist despite that sin: God is faithful to what he promised.

For today: our faith rests on the faithfulness of God, not on our good behavior. His patience is no excuse for sinning, but it is an invitation to return to him with confidence.
exp.19:3:
This verse tells us that the prophet Isaiah had not yet reached the middle court of the palace when God spoke to him again. The verse notes that the word "afore" in the King James wording is an older form of "before," and that the verse means God's answer came almost at once, before Isaiah had fully left.

King Hezekiah was sick unto death, and Isaiah had told him to set his house in order because he would die. Hezekiah turned his face to the wall, prayed, and wept bitterly. The narrator tells us here that God did not delay in answering and sent Isaiah back with a different message.

For today: God hears sincere prayers, even those we pray in tears and in private. He may not always answer as we expect or as quickly, but we can pray with confidence, knowing that he hears us and cares about us.
exp.6:14:
The king's messengers followed the trail of the Syrians all the way to the Jordan River. The whole road was covered with clothing and equipment that the soldiers had thrown away while fleeing in such a hurry. The messengers came back and told the king everything.

Samaria was under siege by the Syrian army and was suffering a terrible famine. Elisha had announced that God would provide plenty of food the next day. Four men with leprosy had discovered that the enemy camp was empty, because God had made the Syrians hear the noise of a great army, and they fled. The king doubted, and for that reason he sent scouts to investigate. This verse confirms that the news was true.

God keeps his word even when the situation seems impossible and we doubt. We can trust his promises, and at the same time act with simplicity, seeking the truth, instead of letting fear or discouragement defeat us.
exp.24:11:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, did not take away all the people of Judah. He left some of the poorest to work the vineyards and the fields. The word "husbandmen" here refers to those who farm and cultivate the land.

This is the voice of the book's narrator, who recounts the fall of Jerusalem in about 586 BC. Babylon destroyed the city and carried many into exile. The texts do not explain Nebuzaradan's reasons, but it is reasonable to think he wanted the land to keep producing rather than be left abandoned. The Bible does not say this in so many words, so it is an interpretation.

For today: even in times of loss and judgment, God does not forget the humble. We can be faithful in simple things, such as tending the land, and care with compassion for those who have the least.
exp.7:23:
Joram died, and he was buried with his fathers in the city of David, which is Jerusalem. "Slept with his fathers" is a gentle way of saying that he died. His son Ahaziah succeeded him as king.

The writer of Kings tells the story of the kings of Judah. Here he closes the account of Joram, who, according to the verses before, had turned away from God and saw Edom and Libnah rebel. Even so, his line continues on the throne, and that reminds us that God kept his promise to the house of David. What follows shows that Ahaziah had a very influential mother, Athaliah, and reigned only one year.

Our lives also come to an end, and what we leave behind influences those who follow. Today we can ask ourselves what example of faith and obedience we are leaving to our family.
exp.7:3:
This verse tells us that the king of Israel was talking with Gehazi, the servant of Elisha. He asked Gehazi to tell him all the amazing things, or miracles, that Elisha had done. "Man of God" is an older way of saying a prophet.

The narrator shows us a scene in the palace. The Bible does not say exactly which king he was, or when this conversation took place in relation to other events. What matters is that, while Gehazi was speaking about the raising of the woman's son, she arrived just at the moment to ask for her house and her land. In this way, God took care of her at the right time.

For today: even when we do not see how, God can order the moments of our lives. When you face a need, pray with confidence and keep doing what is right, because God cares for those who trust in him.
exp.3:30:
Elisha gets up and follows the child's mother. Gehazi, his servant, had gone on ahead and laid the staff (Elisha's walking stick) on the child's face, but there was neither voice nor hearing, that is, no sign of life. Gehazi came back and told Elisha, "The child is not awaked." Here "awaked" means woke up.

A woman from Shunem, who had cared for Elisha, lost her son. Elisha sent Gehazi with the staff, but she insisted that Elisha himself come. The text does not explain why the staff failed; some think Gehazi lacked faith or the right attitude, but the Bible does not say this clearly.

God does not act through objects or methods, but through His own will. Sometimes we do everything we know how to do and see no response. That invites us not to trust in formulas, but to seek the Lord with persistence, like this mother, who did not let go of Elisha.
exp.5:28:
This verse says that two women, facing a terrible famine, agreed to cook and eat their sons. They had already eaten one woman's son, but the other broke the agreement and hid hers.

A woman is speaking and appealing for justice to the king of Israel. Samaria was under siege by the army of Aram, and the hunger was extreme. This shows how far the people had fallen. The king tore his clothes, and it was seen that he was wearing sackcloth beneath them, a sign of grief. But instead of seeking God, he became angry with Elisha.

For today: in the middle of pain, it is easy to blame others or God. Instead, we can draw near to Him with humility, ask for His help, and let the crisis lead us to repentance rather than anger.
exp.18:3:
King Hezekiah had a hope: that God would hear the taunts of Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria, who had mocked the living God. The verse of the words "reproach" and "reprove" as meaning to insult and speak with contempt is set aside here, since those words do not appear in the verse. Hezekiah asks the prophet Isaiah to pray for the remnant, that is, for the people who were still left. The word "perhaps" shows humility: it demands nothing, it only trusts.

Hezekiah, king of Judah, speaks through his messengers. Assyria had conquered many cities and now threatened Jerusalem. Rabshakeh mocked the people's trust in God. The king, in distress and dressed in mourning, does not trust his own strength but seeks the prophet and asks for prayer.

For today: when you feel you cannot go on, do not carry the problem alone. Bring it to God with humility and ask other believers to pray with you. God hears, and a simple and sincere prayer has value before Him.
exp.16:27:
This verse tells how one of the Israelite priests, who had been taken captive from Samaria, went back to live in Bethel and teach the people how to fear the Lord. Here "fear" means to revere and worship with respect.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Kings. The foreign peoples that Assyria had settled in Samaria were being attacked by lions, and they believed this was because they did not know the God of that land. The king of Assyria ordered that a priest be sent to them. Bethel had been a center of worship with golden calves, so we do not know exactly what this priest taught.

For today: knowing about God is not enough; we must worship Him alone. The next verse shows that those people kept on with their idols. Check whether your faith is sincere or mixed with other loyalties.
exp.18:2:
This verse is the message that King Hezekiah sends to the prophet Isaiah. It describes the day as one of distress, of rebuke (correction or punishment), and of blasphemy (speaking with contempt of God). The phrase "the children are come to the birth, and there is not strength to bring forth" is an image of a woman about to give birth but without the strength to do it. It means the situation has reached a critical point and there is no way out through one's own strength.

Hezekiah speaks through his servants. The Assyrians, with their spokesman Rabshakeh, surround Jerusalem, mock the God of Israel, and threaten to destroy the city. The king tears his clothes, puts on mourning clothes, and goes to the temple. Then he asks Isaiah to pray. Some understand the "rebuke" to be the punishment for the sins of the people; others, that it is the humiliation before the enemy.

For today: when you feel without strength, do not shut yourself in with your distress. Bring it before God and ask someone of faith to pray with you.
exp.0:9:
Elijah answers the captain who has come for him: if he really is a "man of God" (a prophet sent by God), then let fire come down from heaven and destroy him and his fifty soldiers. And so it happens. The captain's "man of God" is the phrase he used to address Elijah, and the verse's note on the old wording is not needed for this reader.

King Ahaziah, sick after a fall, had sent to consult Baal-zebub, a false god of Ekron, instead of seeking the God of Israel. God sent him a message through Elijah. Rather than repent, the king sent soldiers to order the prophet to come down. The captain called him a "man of God," but with the tone of a command, as one who orders a servant of the Lord to obey the king. Some see here a challenge to God's authority.

God deserves our respect, not only in words but through a humble attitude. We can use spiritual titles and yet still resist his voice. Today it is worth asking ourselves: do I listen to God with reverence, or do I try to put him at my service?
exp.8:13:
This verse says that Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, plotted against Joram. The word "conspired" means that he secretly rose up against the king. The text makes clear that Joram was defending Ramoth-gilead, together with all Israel, against Hazael, king of Syria.

The narrator tells how Jehu, a military commander, was anointed king by a young prophet sent by Elisha. His fellow officers quickly proclaimed him. Meanwhile, Joram was not at the front but wounded and recovering in Jezreel. This aside explains why Jehu will have to go there.

Today, this passage reminds us that God works in his own time and that human power is not secure. We can trust that he governs history, and when he gives us a task, we should obey with seriousness and prudence.
exp.8:8:
God says he will do to the family of Ahab what he did to the families of Jeroboam and Baasha: he will utterly destroy them. The kings of those two houses had been idolaters, and their dynasties ended in violence (1 Kings 15:29; 16:3, 12).

A young prophet, sent by Elisha, speaks and anoints Jehu as king of Israel in the name of God. The message presents the fall of Ahab as God's judgment for idolatry and for the blood of the prophets shed under Jezebel. Some scholars debate how to evaluate Jehu's later violence, but this announcement is a word of judgment.

For today: God sees injustice and does not let it pass. We can trust that he will do justice in his time, and examine our own hearts so that we do not take his warning lightly.
exp.4:7:
Elisha, whom the Bible calls "the man of God," heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes out of fear and distress. So he sent him a message: "Why have you torn your clothes? Let Naaman come to me, and he will know that there is a prophet in Israel." Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief or despair.

The king of Syria had sent his general Naaman, who had leprosy, with a letter asking the king of Israel to heal him. The king thought it was a trap to start a war, and he was alarmed. Elisha speaks because God works through him, and God wants it to be seen that the power comes from God.

When a situation overwhelms us and we see no way out, we can remember that God has resources we cannot see. Instead of panicking, it is worth seeking Him in prayer and asking for His help.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that King Ahaziah sent a second captain with fifty soldiers to take Elijah. The captain spoke with an urgent command: "Come down quickly," that is, "come down quickly." "Man of God" is a way of calling a prophet.

Here the captain speaks, repeating the king's order. Ahaziah was sick and had consulted a false god, Baal-zebub, instead of the God of Israel. Elijah had announced judgment against him, and the king wanted to silence him by force. The captain spoke with more haste and pressure than the first one, and the text does not say he showed any respect for God. Some see here a judgment against those who defy God; others emphasize the lesson of the third captain, who humbled himself.

For today: when God speaks to us, let us respond with humility and not with pride or pressure. It is better to bow before Him than to try to impose ourselves on Him.
exp.3:36:
She went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground. Then she took up her son and went out. The verse says she fell at his feet and bowed herself to the ground, and then she took up her son and went out.

Elisha had just prayed and stretched himself over the child, who had died, and God brought him back to life. Elisha sent for the woman through his servant Gehazi and said, "Take up your son." She does not say a single word in this verse; her gesture speaks for her. It is a sign of gratitude and reverence before what God had done through the prophet.

For today: when God gives us an answer or rescues us from a difficult situation, it is worth pausing to give thanks with humility before moving on. A moment of sincere gratitude reminds us where the favor comes from.
exp.18:36:
This verse says that King Sennacherib of Assyria was killed while he was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch. His sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword (the phrase "with the sword" means with a weapon that has an edge) and escaped to the land of Ararat, a mountainous region to the north. After that, his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place.

It is part of the historical account in Kings. The narrator tells of the end of Sennacherib, who had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. After his army was defeated, he returned to Nineveh. The text does not say exactly how many years passed; it only shows that his end came. As for the god Nisroch, no one knows with certainty who he was.

For today: God is just and has the last word, even over the powerful. We can rest in Him when we see injustice, without seeking revenge, and trust that He knows how to act in His own time.
exp.16:14:
This verse says that the people of Israel rejected God's laws and the covenant He made with their ancestors. "Statutes" are his commands, and "testimonies" are his warnings. "Vanity" means something empty and without value; so by following empty things, they themselves became empty. Moreover, they imitated the neighboring peoples, exactly what God had forbidden them to do.

The author of the book explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell before Assyria. God had warned them many times through the prophets, but they would not listen. The text does not speak of a single mistake, but of a long path of disobedience.

For today: when we turn our backs on God, we are not free; instead we cling to things that cannot sustain us. Today we can ask ourselves which voices we are imitating, and listen to God again in His Word before our hearts grow hard.
exp.15:18:
This verse is the formula the writer uses to close the reign of Ahaz. It says the rest of his deeds are not repeated here, because they were already recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah," an official record from that period that is not preserved as a separate book. The phrase "which he did" simply means "carried out."

The narrator of Kings uses this formula at the end of each reign. Earlier he tells how Ahaz, under pressure from the king of Assyria, removed and altered objects and spaces in the temple. The exact use of the "tent of the Sabbath" and of the "king's private entrance" is not known with certainty. Right after this comes his death and the reign of his son Hezekiah.

For today: our decisions also leave a mark. Before giving in out of fear or pressure, let us ask what will be written about us and, above all, whether we are pleasing God.
exp.16:35:
It says that Jehovah, the God who brought Israel out of Egypt with great power and a stretched out arm (a way of speaking of his strength to save), is the only one they must fear, worship, and offer sacrifices to. "Fear" here means to revere and obey, not merely to be afraid. The phrase "to him" in this verse is simply the word "him" in the sentence.

The writer of Kings recalls what God commanded Israel in the covenant. He speaks after the fall of the northern kingdom, when Assyria carried the people away. The verse is that they worshiped other gods and forgot what God had done for them. The neighboring lands mixed their worship with that of Jehovah, and the text corrects this.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts. Remembering how God has helped us in the past encourages us to put him first, with gratitude and sincere obedience.
exp.4:23:
He says that Gehazi, on reaching a secluded place, took from Naaman's servants the silver and the garments. He stored them in the house and sent the men away so that no one would see. The phrases "when he came" and "he hid it" and "he sent them away" are not in the wording of this verse, so they are left out here.

The narrator tells what Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, did. Naaman, a Syrian commander, had been healed of leprosy, and Elisha refused to accept payment. Gehazi ran after Naaman and lied, saying that Elisha was asking for gifts. Now he hides what he obtained through deceit.

For today: what we have to hide often shows that something is wrong. God sees everything, as Elisha later showed. It is worth living with honesty, without seeking gain at the cost of the truth or of God's grace.
exp.5:5:
It says that Elisha, the man of God, asked the man where the axe had fallen. When the man showed him the place, Elisha cut off a stick and threw it into the water. Then the iron floated up. The phrase "did swim" means that it made the iron float. The words "cast it in thither" mean that he threw it there.

Elisha was with a group of the sons of the prophets who were building a place to live beside the Jordan. One of them had let the borrowed axe fall into the water, and he was distressed because it was not his own. Elisha answered with a miracle. The text does not explain how the stick acted; it presents the event as the work of God.

For today: God cares even about our small worries, such as a debt or a careless mistake. We can bring to him with confidence what we have lost or damaged, and also take responsibility for what others have lent us.
exp.11:0:
It says that Jehoash began to reign over Judah in the seventh year of Jehu, king of Israel, and that he ruled for forty years from Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zibiah and she was from Beersheba, a city in the south of Judah. The phrase "began to reign" means that he came to the throne. The word "was" in the verse is simply the past tense of "be."

Here the narrator of the book of Kings presents each king in an orderly way: when he began, how long he reigned, and who his mother was. Jehoash came to the throne as a child, after very dark times in the royal family. The next verse explains that he did what was right while the priest Jehoiada guided him.

For today: no one grows alone. Seek wise and faithful people who can guide you in your walk with God. But do not let your faith depend only on them; cultivate your own relationship with the Lord.
exp.4:0:
This verse introduces Naaman, commander of the army of Syria. He was an important man, respected by the king and very brave. It is said that the Lord, the God of Israel, had given deliverance (victory and rescue) to Syria through him. But there is a "but" at the end: Naaman was a leper, that is, he suffered from a serious disease of the skin.

Here the narrator of the book begins the story by presenting a foreigner, an enemy of Israel. It stresses that God works even with those who are not of his people. The following context shows that a young Israelite captive spoke to him about a prophet who could heal him.

For today: no one is free from some weakness, however successful they may be. Recognizing our need with humility opens the door to receiving help, even from humble people.
exp.0:2:
It says that God sent his angel with a message for the prophet Elijah the Tishbite. He was told to go out to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria and to ask them a question: is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?

The angel of the Lord speaks, and then Elijah is to repeat his words. King Ahaziah had fallen, was injured, and sent messengers to ask a false god whether he would recover. In doing so he set aside the true God of his people. The question is a rebuke.

For today: when illness, crisis, or fear comes, what we do first reveals whom we trust. We may seek medical help and counsel, but without forgetting to turn first to God in prayer.
exp.14:11:
The verse says that what God had promised Jehu was fulfilled: his descendants, down to the fourth generation, would reign over Israel. And so it happened. The words "was" and "spoken to" are the only parts of the quoted wording that need no change here, so the verse simply reads as it is.

The narrator makes this point right after the death of Zechariah, the fourth of Jehu's descendants on the throne. The promise came from 2 Kings 10:30, when God rewarded Jehu for carrying out his judgment against the house of Ahab. With Zechariah, the promised period ended, and then came the coup of Shallum.

For today: God keeps his word, both his promises and his warnings. We can trust that what he says is fulfilled in its time, even when we see so much disorder around us.
exp.21:3:
Here King Josiah tells his scribe Shaphan to go up to Hilkiah the high priest. He asks him to sum the money that the people had brought into the house of the Lord, the temple. That money had been gathered by the keepers of the door, that is, the men assigned to watch the entrance.

The word "sum" means to add up and count the money.

King Josiah speaks in the eighteenth year of his reign. The text presents him as a king who did what was right, like David. His concern was to repair the temple, which had fallen into disrepair. The next verse explains that the money would be used to pay the workmen and buy materials.

For today: Josiah made sure that what was given to God was handled with order and honesty. We can do the same in the church and in our own lives: manage with transparency what is entrusted to us, and devote time and resources to restoring what has been neglected in our relationship with God.
exp.4:1:
The verse tells that bands of Syrian raiders had gone out, and in one of their raids they carried off a young girl from Israel as a prisoner. She ended up serving Naaman's wife. The phrase "by companies" in the verse refers to groups of soldiers who attacked by surprise, and "carried away captive" means taken as a prisoner.

The narrator first introduces Naaman, a powerful general who is ill with leprosy, a serious skin disease. Now, almost in passing, he mentions a young girl who has no name, no power, and is far from home. The story that follows shows that her words will open the way to this man's healing.

Even in the midst of pain and injustice, God can use people who seem small. We can witness to our faith with kindness, even when our own situation is difficult.
exp.8:33:
Jehu, after killing Jezebel, went into the palace, ate and drank at ease. Then he gave orders that they should bury the body of this cursed woman, because she was a king's daughter. The word "cursed" here means someone under judgment and condemnation for her wickedness.

Jehu speaks as one anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab. Jezebel had promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted God's prophets. Jehu acknowledges that she was a king's daughter and wants to give her a dignified burial, but the body had already been devoured by dogs, just as Elijah had foretold. The passage shows that the word of God is fulfilled.

For today: God is patient, but he does not ignore injustice. We can trust that he has the last word, and in the meantime, treat every person with respect, even those who have wronged us.
exp.5:13:
This verse tells that the king of Syria sent cavalry, war chariots, and a large army. They came by night and surrounded the city. The phrase "surrounded" in the source means they encircled it on every side, so that no one could get out. The "men on horses" are the horsemen.

The king of Syria was at war with Israel, but his plans always failed because Elisha would warn the king of Israel. When he learned that Elisha was in Dothan, he sent men to capture him. It is the narrator who tells this event. Such a great military force against a single prophet shows how threatened the king felt.

Today, problems sometimes surround us like that army. Yet the story goes on and shows that God watched over Elisha. When you feel afraid, pray and remember that God is with you, even when you cannot see him.
exp.9:21:
Jehú orders the man in charge of the temple wardrobe to bring out special robes for all who serve Baal. That man obeys and hands out the garments. The phrase "had charge of the robes" means he was responsible for keeping and handing out those sacred garments.

Jehú is the king of Israel whom God had raised up to bring an end to the house of Ahab. He pretended he would worship Baal in order to gather all of Baal's servants into one place. The robes helped to tell them apart from the worshipers of the LORD, so that idolatry could be eliminated. Scholars debate whether all of his methods were right, since the text describes what he did and does not approve of everything he did.

For today: true faith does not stop at appearances. Religious clothing does not change the heart. Let us ask God that our worship be sincere and that nothing take the place that belongs to Him alone.
exp.3:0:
A widow who belonged to the community of "sons of the prophets" (a group of disciples and followers of the prophets) cries out to Elisha for help. She says that her husband has died, that he feared the Lord, and that now the creditor, that is, the person to whom they owed money, wants to take her two sons as servants to collect the debt. The word "cried" means that she called out for help with urgency.

The speaker is a desperate woman who comes to the prophet Elisha. Israelite law allowed a debtor or his family to work as servants to repay what was owed (Leviticus 25:39-41). She had no income and no protection, and her husband, though faithful, had left a debt behind.

For today: when need overwhelms us, we can cry out to God and seek help from people of faith. Being faithful does not free us from difficulties, but God hears the cry of those in distress and often answers step by step.
exp.0:11:
Elijah answers the king's second captain and tells him that, if he is truly a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume him and his fifty soldiers. And so it happens. "A man of God" means a man who speaks on behalf of God, and "consume" means to destroy completely.

King Ahaziah, sick after a fall, sought counsel from a false god instead of seeking the God of Israel. Elijah had announced his judgment. Now the king sends soldiers to give orders to the prophet, in a commanding tone: "Come down quickly." This captain showed no respect for the word of God. The third captain, by contrast, humbled himself.

For today: when God speaks, humility is the wise path. We can approach his Word with respect and not with pride, knowing that his authority is real and that he receives with grace the one who humbles himself.
exp.18:5:
Isaiah tells King Hezekiah, through his servants, not to be afraid. God says that he has heard the mockery of the servants of the king of Assyria. To speak with contempt against God is the sense of the insults here, and "master" in this verse refers to King Hezekiah.

The Assyrians had surrounded Jerusalem, and their spokesman, Rabshakeh, mocked God and said that he would not be able to save the city. Hezekiah, distressed, asked Isaiah to pray. The prophet speaks in God's name and assures him that the Lord has not overlooked those insults.

When you hear threats or taunts that fill you with fear, bring them to God in prayer, as Hezekiah did. He listens to them and is attentive to your situation. Trusting his word does not erase the problem at once, but it helps you face it with more calm.
exp.24:8:
This verse tells how Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, set fire to the temple (the house of the Lord), the king's palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He also burned the houses of the leading men, that is, the nobles and rulers. The phrase "burnt he with fire" means that he destroyed them by fire.

It is a historical account, not a speech. The writer of Kings recounts the fall of Jerusalem, around 586 B.C. According to the book, this happened after years in which Judah turned away from God and did not listen to the prophets. It is the most painful moment in the history of the kingdom.

For today: God is patient, but His warnings are real. Let us not harden our hearts when He calls us to change. Even so, this painful account is not the end of the biblical story: God continues to work, offering hope and restoration.
exp.5:1:
The sons of the prophets propose going to the Jordan River, each one cutting a beam, and building a larger place to live. "Let us dwell" means "let us live there," and the words "Go ye" are simply the reply "Go." Elisha gives them permission.

The ones speaking are the disciples of the prophets, a group that lived together in community and learned alongside Elisha. Their place had become too small, perhaps because the group was growing, though the text does not explain this. Notice that they do not act on their own: they ask for Elisha's approval, and then they urge him to come with them. He agrees to go with them.

For today: when you need to grow or make a change, plan it with hard work and humility. Seek the counsel of someone wise in the faith, and ask God to walk with you through each step, even in the simple tasks.
exp.16:15:
They abandoned all the commandments of God. Two calves were made of cast metal (the word "molten" means made from metal melted and poured into a mold). They also made "groves," which were poles or wooden objects used to worship the goddess Asherah, though some translate simply "Asherah images." They worshipped "all the host of heaven," that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and they served Baal, a Canaanite god.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, explaining why the northern kingdom of Israel fell before Assyria. King Jeroboam had set up the calves in Bethel and Dan centuries earlier. The text presents the fall as the result of a long and stubborn disobedience, not of a single mistake.

For today: God shares his place with nothing. Ask yourself which things draw you more than he does, such as money, fame, or comfort, and hand them over to him little by little in prayer, before they become habit.
exp.17:22:
The messenger of the king of Assyria makes Hezekiah a proposal: "Make a bet with my master, the king of Assyria." The word "pledges" here translates an expression that can also be understood as "make a bet" or "make a deal." Then he mocks him: I will give you two thousand horses, but I doubt you have enough riders to mount them.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a high official of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. Jerusalem was under siege, and he wanted the people to surrender. With irony, he mocks Judah's military weakness and its trust in Egypt and in God.

For today: many voices will tell us that our faith is weak or useless. Before letting ourselves be intimidated, let us remember that trust in God is not measured by what we see, but by who He is. We can pray and wait calmly, as Hezekiah did.
exp.3:17:
This verse tells how the child, the son God had given to the woman of Shunem, grew up. One day he went out to find his father, who was with the reapers, that is, the workers who cut the grain in the field.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The woman had been kind to Elisha, and he promised her a son, which she believed was nearly impossible. The child was born just as it had been said. This quiet detail of everyday life sets up what comes next: sudden pain and the child's death.

For today: ordinary life, like a walk out to the fields, can change in an instant. Value the people you love, and keep your trust in God both in the calm days and in the hard ones, for He cares for you in both.
exp.22:17:
Josiah gives the order that no one is to disturb a man's tomb. "Let him alone" means "leave him in peace." "Let no man move his bones" means that no one is to take them out of there. In this way the bones of the man of God from Judah and those of the prophet who had come from Samaria were respected.

Here King Josiah is speaking as he cleanses Bethel of its idolatry. He had burned the bones from other tombs on the altar, just as God had announced centuries earlier (1 Kings 13). On seeing the tomb of the prophet who had foretold all this, he decides to respect it. It is generally understood that the prophet from Samaria is the one mentioned in 1 Kings 13, although the text here gives no further details.

For today: God honors those who were faithful to him, and his word always comes to pass. We can trust his promises and also learn to recognize and respect the faithfulness of those who went before us in the faith.
exp.3:38:
One of the disciples went out into the field to gather herbs for the meal. He found a wild climbing vine and picked from it wild gourds, as many as his lap could hold. He came back, cut them into pieces, and put them into the pot of stew. He did this without knowing what they were.

We are in a time of famine, in Gilgal. Elisha, the prophet, had asked for food to be prepared for the group of disciples who were with him. This man wanted to help, but he acted without knowledge. The Bible does not say exactly what plant it was, only that it turned out to be harmful, as becomes clear afterward.

For today: wanting to help is good, but it is wise to inform ourselves and ask before acting, especially when others depend on us. And if we make a mistake, God can help us put it right.
exp.22:24:
This verse says that King Josiah was unique among the kings of Judah. None before him turned to the Lord with all his heart, all his soul, and all his might, following the law of Moses, and none after him matched him.

The narrator of the book of Kings is speaking here, summarizing the life of Josiah. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and the king removed idolatry and celebrated the Passover. However, the following verse makes clear that the judgment on Judah, because of the sins of Manasseh, was not held back.

For today: loving God with our whole being is a daily and complete surrender. Even though we cannot change everything around us, our sincere obedience always pleases God.
exp.18:33:
It says that God himself will defend Jerusalem and save it. The word for "defend" means to shelter, cover and watch over. God gives two reasons: first, for his own sake, that is, for his own name and honor, and second, for the sake of his servant David, because of the promise he made to David to keep his line.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah. King Hezekiah had prayed in anguish, because the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, was threatening the city and mocking the God of Israel. God answers that the enemy will not even shoot an arrow at it. Later, an angel struck the Assyrian army in a single night, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh.

When you find yourself surrounded by a problem bigger than you are, do as Hezekiah did: bring it to God in prayer. He is faithful to his character and to his promises, not to your merits. Rest in that.
exp.7:21:
This verse says that Edom broke free from the rule of Judah and never came back under its control; the author adds "unto this day," that is, until the time the book was written. It also says that Libnah, a city of Judah, rebelled at that same time.

The one telling the story is the author of Kings, who summarizes the reign of Joram of Judah. Earlier it is said that Joram married into the family of King Ahab and turned away from God (2 Kings 8:18). Many understand these rebellions as a sign of a kingdom growing weaker. The text does not explain in detail why Libnah rebelled, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: when our decisions turn away from God, sooner or later areas of life we took for granted begin to weaken. It is worth returning to Him with humility and rebuilding on His faithfulness.
exp.16:30:
They say the Avites made images of their gods, Nibhaz and Tartak, and that the people of Sepharvaim burned their own children in the fire as offerings to Adrammelech and Anammelech. The word "made" here means that they fashioned idols. It is not known for certain what these gods looked like; scholars debate this.

The book of Kings tells that Assyria brought people from other nations to Samaria after deporting Israel. Each group brought its gods and its customs. The biblical narrator explains in this way how religion became mixed in that land, and shows how serious the sin of worshiping idols was.

For today: it is not enough to say we believe in God if at the same time we place our trust in other things. We can ask ourselves what occupies the place of God in our hearts, and give it to Him sincerely.
exp.17:6:
It says that God was with Hezekiah, king of Judah, and that everything he undertook went well for him. It also says that he rebelled against the king of Assyria and stopped serving him, meaning he stopped paying tribute to him and submitting to him.

The author of the book of Kings, whom tradition does not identify with certainty, tells the story of the kings of Judah. Here he summarizes Hezekiah's reign: he trusted God and obeyed him. His rebellion against Assyria is understood as the fruit of that faithfulness. The account then goes on to tell that Assyria attacked Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and this prepares the conflicts that would come.

For today: trusting God and obeying him can lead us to refuse submission to whatever dominates us or pulls us away from him. This does not promise that everything will be easy, but it does mean that God accompanies the one who remains faithful.
exp.3:6:
She went and told Elisha what had happened with the oil. He gave her three instructions: sell the oil, pay what she owed, and live on what was left over. "Man of God" means a prophet. "Creditors" are the people to whom she owed money.

The woman was the widow of one of the prophets' disciples, and she was in debt. Her creditors were threatening to take her sons as slaves. Elisha had told her to gather empty vessels, and God filled every one she had. Here Elisha explains how to use that miracle. God did not merely supply what she needed; he covered the debt and left something over.

God often provides through concrete steps. After prayer and trust, we are called to act responsibly: to pay what we owe, to manage well what we receive, and to live with gratitude for what God leaves us.
exp.10:14:
Jehoiada, the priest, gives an order to the captains of the army. He wants them to bring Athaliah out beyond the ranges, that is, outside the sacred grounds. He also orders that anyone who follows her be killed with the sword. The text makes clear that he did not want her put to death within the house of the Lord.

Athaliah was the queen who had seized the throne of Judah. She cried out "Treason!" when she saw that Joash, the rightful child heir of David's line, was being crowned. Jehoiada directs all of this with care. He took care that the temple, the place dedicated to God, would not be stained with blood, even in the midst of such a tense situation.

For today: even when we face serious conflicts, we should act with respect for what is sacred and with self-control. May the end never make us forget reverence for God or order in how we act.
exp.1:14:
It says that the sons of the prophets, a group of disciples who lived in Jericho, saw Elisha from a distance by the Jordan. They concluded: "The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha." Then they went to meet him and bowed themselves to the ground. Their bowing was a way of recognizing his authority.

Elijah had just been taken up to heaven. Elisha took his mantle, struck the Jordan, and cried out, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" When the water parted, the disciples saw the sign that God was now working through him. It is these prophets who speak. Even so, they afterward hesitate and search for Elijah for three days.

For today: God continues to sustain his work even when the leaders change. Trust the same God and ask him to use you where you are.
exp.15:13:
This verse tells how King Ahaz moved the bronze altar, the one God had commanded to be used in the temple. He took it from the central place, the place "before the LORD," and set it to one side, toward the north. "Aquilon" is an old word that means north, so the verse here applies to the verse's "north side." "Forefront of the house" refers to the front of the temple.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Ahaz had seen a pagan altar in Damascus and ordered a copy made for the temple (vv. 10-13). That new altar took the main place, and the bronze altar was pushed aside. Many read this as a sign that Ahaz put foreign fashion and politics above what God had commanded.

For today: check what sits at the center of your life. It is easy to set God aside, to the north, while we adopt customs that seem useful. Ask him to take first place again.
exp.12:14:
Elisha, who is very ill, asks King Joash to take a bow and some arrows. The king obeys and takes them.

Elisha is God's prophet, now old and near his death. Joash, king of Israel, has come to visit him weeping, because he sees in Elisha the protection of his people, and Syria was a constant threat. Before he dies, the prophet prepares a symbolic act: with the bow and the arrows, God will show the king the victory that is coming over Syria.

God often asks us for small and simple steps of obedience before showing us what He wants to do. Joash took the bow without arguing. When you feel that God is asking you for something that seems small, do it with attention and faith, because He may be preparing something greater.
exp.21:18:
God tells King Josiah that he has heard him. When Josiah heard the words of the book of the law, he was moved, humbled himself, and wept. The verse says his heart was tender, which means it was responsive and not hardened. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of deep grief. Words meaning destroyed and cursed refer to falling under God's judgment.

Speaking through the prophetess Huldah, the Lord answers the inquiry that Josiah had sent. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and Josiah realized the people had disobeyed. God announces that judgment will come, but that Josiah will not see that disaster in his lifetime. Scholars do not agree on every detail, but the text shows that God responds to a humble heart.

For today: when God's Word confronts you, do not defend yourself or ignore it. Answer with humility and sincere repentance, trusting that God listens.
exp.21:0:
This verse introduces Josiah, who became king of Judah at the age of eight and ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. It also names his mother, Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah, from a place called Boscath.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, giving a brief summary as the story of a new king begins. Josiah was very young, since his father Amon had been killed (2 Kings 21:23-24). The text prepares the account that follows, where it says he did what was right before God and that later the book of the law was found.

For today: God can work in people of any age and with a difficult past. No matter how young you are or where you come from, you can begin to seek God and do what is right starting today.
exp.14:31:
This verse says that Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, began to reign in the second year of Pekah, king of Israel. It is a way of dating events by using the reigns of the two sister kingdoms, the northern one and the southern one.

The book of Kings is told by a narrator who marks when each king begins and how he governed. After closing the account of King Uzziah's reign in Judah, the story turns to his son Jotham. Some scholars point out that the year counts between the two kingdoms do not always line up at first glance, and there are several possible explanations, such as shared reigns or different ways of counting years.

God sees each generation and raises up those who carry on what is good. Jotham followed the upright example of his father. Today, what we do well can inspire those who come after us.
exp.2:15:
This verse tells how Elisha, after the hand of the Lord came upon him, gives a command on God's behalf: to dig many trenches in the valley. The word "ditches" in the verse means channels or pits for holding water. God asks them to prepare the place before they see the answer.

The king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom were with their armies in the desert, without water, on the way to fight against Moab. Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Elisha spoke. He asked for music, and then the word of God came. God promised water without wind or rain, and also victory.

For today: sometimes God asks us to act in faith before we see the solution. Preparing the "valley" may mean obeying, praying, putting our life in order, or taking a concrete step, trusting that God will fulfill what he promised.
exp.17:27:
Rabshakeh stood up and shouted loudly in Hebrew, the language of Judah. He said to everyone: "Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria." The words "Hear" and "stood" in the verse correspond to "hear" and "stood" in the verse.

Rabshakeh was a high Assyrian official sent by King Sennacherib to pressure Jerusalem into surrendering. Hezekiah's officials asked him to speak in Aramaic, so that the people on the wall would not understand. He did the opposite: he spoke in Hebrew to frighten everyone. He wanted to spread fear and take away their trust in God and in their king.

Today too there are loud voices that try to frighten us and make us doubt God. Before we let fear carry us away, it is wise to stop, pray, and remember what God has promised. His voice is not always the loudest, but it is the most certain.
exp.22:13:
This verse says that King Josiah destroyed the objects used for false worship. "Images" are pillars or sacred stones that were used to worship idols. "Groves" translates the word "Asherah," which probably refers to wooden posts or trees dedicated to a goddess. By filling the place with human bones, he made it ritually unclean, so that no one would ever use it again for worship.

It is part of the account in the book of 2 Kings, where the narrator tells of the great religious reform of Josiah, king of Judah. He wanted to remove the idolatry that Solomon and other kings had allowed, so that the people would return to obeying the LORD and his law.

For today: if something in our life holds the place that belongs only to God, it is wise to remove it with resolve and not merely hide it. Ask God to show you which things you must take out of your heart so that he may come first.
exp.13:21:
King Azariah, also called Uzziah, rebuilt the city of Elath, a port by the Red Sea, and brought it back under the control of Judah. This happened after his father, King Amaziah, died. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is a respectful way of saying that he died.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the reign of Azariah. His father had been killed, and the people made Azariah king while he was very young. The text shows that, after that difficult moment, Judah regained an important place for trade and defense.

For today: when something has been broken or abandoned, God sometimes calls us to rebuild with patience and responsibility, without simply staying fixed on the losses of the past.
exp.16:18:
What it says: This verse explains that Judah, the southern kingdom, also failed to keep the commandments of God. Instead of following his Word, they copied the customs and rules that Israel, the northern kingdom, had made up. "Statutes" are established laws or customs, and "But not even" means "but not even."

Context: The speaker is the author of the book of Kings, whose name is not known with certainty. He is explaining why Israel fell before Assyria. In the middle of that account, he warns that Judah, which still stood, was also heading down the wrong path. He wants the reader to understand that the fall was no accident, but the consequence of abandoning God.

For today: It is not enough to see the mistakes of others; we must also examine our own hearts. Copying customs that draw us away from God harms us. Let us ask him to help us be guided by his Word and not by what is simply common.
exp.9:32:
This verse tells which territories Israel lost. Hazael, king of Syria, conquered the whole region east of the Jordan River, "the rising of the sun," that is, the east. It names Gilead, and the lands of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh, from Aroer, by the river Arnon, as far as Bashan. "Struck" here means that he defeated them and took land from them.

The one telling this is the author of Kings, who summarizes the reign of Jehu. Jehu had destroyed the house of Ahab and the worship of Baal, but he kept the golden calves of Jeroboam and did not obey God with his whole heart. The text presents this loss of territory as the beginning of God's judgment: "the LORD began to cut Israel short."

For today: partial obedience leaves us vulnerable. Doing good things for God does not replace giving him your whole heart. Ask him to show you what area you are still holding back, and surrender it to him today.
exp.23:8:
He says that Jehoiachin, the young king of Judah, did what was evil in the sight of God. "In the eyes of the LORD" is the same as "according to God's judgment," and "according to all that his father had done" means that he followed the same wicked ways as his father, Jehoiakim.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. Jehoiachin was eighteen years old and reigned only three months, at a time when Babylon dominated the region. The following verse shows that Jerusalem was besieged. The book presents this as part of the consequences of the disobedience that had been building for years.

For today: what we learn at home weighs heavily, but it does not have the last word. We can ask ourselves which inherited habits we should leave behind and ask God for help to choose a different path, his.
exp.13:20:
After the people had killed King Amaziah, all the people of Judah took his son Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father. The phrase "made him king" is simply the wording of the verse. Azariah is also called Uzziah in other passages of the Bible.

Here no character speaks; this is the account of the writer of Kings. Amaziah had been the victim of a conspiracy and died in Lachish. The people did not leave the throne empty, and they placed his son on it, continuing the line of David. The text does not explain why they chose Azariah or who proposed him.

For today: when there is crisis or loss, God can continue to work through young people and through the community. We can encourage young people, pray for them, and accompany them wisely when they receive great responsibilities.
exp.12:15:
Elisha asks King Joash to put his hand on the bow, and the king does so. Then the prophet places his own hands over the king's hands. It is a simple gesture, yet a very close one: the prophet guides the king while he holds the bow.

Elisha is very ill and close to death. Joash, king of Israel, visits him weeping, because he sees that the nation is about to lose its protector. Elisha uses a symbolic act to announce victory over Syria. By placing his hands upon the king's hands, he shows that the power comes from God, not from the king. Some think it also expresses God's support for that action.

For today: God calls us to act in faith, and at the same time He sustains us. Take today the step that He shows you, knowing that you do not take it alone. And do it with all your heart.
exp.12:1:
It says that Jehoahaz, king of Israel, did what was evil in the sight of the Lord. He followed the same path of sin as Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin. Jehoahaz did not turn away from that path. The phrase "made Israel to sin" means that Jeroboam drew the whole people along with his bad example.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. Jeroboam's sins were mainly the worship with golden calves, which turned the people away from true worship. Jehoahaz was the son of Jehu, who had begun with zeal but did not finish well. The text shows that bad habits can pass from one generation to the next.

For today: examine which inherited customs or mistakes you keep repeating without questioning them. If God shows you something, turn away from it. He hears the one who humbles himself and prays, as happened later with Jehoahaz.
exp.19:6:
Isaiah tells the king's servants to prepare a mass made of figs. They take it, place it on the sore, and the king recovers. The "sore" is a wound or infected swelling. The "mass of figs" was a paste made of pressed dried figs.

King Hezekiah was very sick, and earlier God had told him through Isaiah that he would die. Hezekiah prayed weeping, and God promised to heal him and give him fifteen more years. Here Isaiah gives the practical instruction. We do not know for certain whether the figs had healing power in themselves. The text says that God is the one who heals, and that he used a simple remedy.

God can work through miracles, but also through ordinary means, such as medicine and the care of others. We can pray with confidence and, at the same time, accept with gratitude the treatments and advice that God places within our reach.
exp.5:27:
Here the king asks a woman what is wrong, and she reports something terrible: another woman proposed that they eat her son first and then the woman's own son. The phrase "Give thy son" means "give your son," and "we will eat my son to morrow" is a reference to the arrangement that they would eat the second child the following day.

The city of Samaria was under siege by the army of Syria, and there was extreme famine. The woman cries out to the king of Israel from the wall, seeking justice. He is horrified and tears his clothes, and it is shown that he was wearing sackcloth, a rough cloth of mourning, under his clothing. The Bible presents this as a painful consequence of a people who had turned away from God (Deuteronomy 28:53).

For today: when you see a crisis, do not grow accustomed to the suffering of others. Help the one who suffers, and bring your distress before God with humility, before looking for someone to blame.
exp.1:15:
The sons of the prophets tell Elisha that they have fifty strong men, ready to go and look for Elijah. They think the Spirit of the LORD may have taken him up and set him down on some mountain or in some valley. Elisha answers, "Ye shall not send," meaning "do not send anyone."

These men are disciples of the prophets at Jericho. They have just seen Elisha cross the Jordan as Elijah did, and they recognize that the spirit of Elijah rests on him. Their concern is sincere, but they do not accept that Elijah has already been taken. Elisha, who watched him depart, knows that searching for him is useless. In the end he gives in because of their insistence, and three days of searching find nothing.

For today: sometimes we insist on reviewing what God has already closed. We can respect those who have more clarity and trust what God has shown, without letting pressure move us to act against what we know.
exp.2:4:
After Ahab's death, Mesha, king of Moab, stopped obeying the king of Israel and rebelled. The verse notes that the word "But" in the verse is the word that opens this sentence, and that "when Ahab was dead" means the same as the time of Ahab's death. Moab no longer wanted to keep paying its tribute.

The narrator of the book tells us this event. Moab had been paying Israel a large number of lambs and wool, and Ahab, who kept that control, had already died. Mesha saw an opportunity to become independent. This prepares the account of the war that King Joram and Jehoshaphat undertake against Moab. Many understand that Israel's weakness came from its sin, although the text here only shows the fact of the rebellion.

For today: situations that seem firm can change suddenly. For that reason it is wise to rest our lives on God and not on power, money, or circumstances, which can come to an end.
exp.11:9:
This verse tells us that, when the chest was already holding a lot of money, the king's secretary and the high priest would come up to count it. The word "scribe" here refers to a royal secretary or clerk, and "high priest" is the chief priest. After counting the money, they would put it into bags.

The account is historical narrative, not a speech. Under King Joash, the temple had fallen into disrepair, and the priests had not carried out the repairs. So Jehoiada placed a chest with an opening beside the altar to receive the offerings. In this way the handling of the money was done openly and by two responsible people, one from the king and one from the temple.

For today: when money belonging to a church or to others is handled, it is wise to do so with order, transparency, and more than one person overseeing it. This protects trust and honors God.
exp.14:8:
This verse says that Zechariah, king of Israel, did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin. "Led into sin" means that he drew them into idolatry.

The narrator of the book gives a brief summary of each king. Zechariah ruled only six months over the northern kingdom, and his reign ended when Shallum killed him. The text does not detail his actions, but it judges him by the same standard as always: faithfulness to God. The sin of Jeroboam was setting up golden calves as centers of worship (1 Kings 12).

Today we can ask ourselves what bad habits we have inherited without questioning them. God invites us not to repeat what is harmful just because "it has always been done this way," and to seek Him with sincerity.
exp.14:27:
It says that Pekah, king of Israel, did what was evil in the sight of the Lord. He continued in the same sins as Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes each reign with a spiritual judgment. Jeroboam had set up golden calves for worship, and the kings that followed repeated that path. Soon after, the text tells how Assyria invaded the north and carried people into captivity, and how Hoshea killed Pekah. The text presents these falls as part of a people who were turning away from God, though it does not explain every detail.

For today: let us not thoughtlessly repeat the bad habits we have inherited. Let us ask God for light to recognize them and to change, because our decisions also influence others.
exp.0:14:
The angel of the Lord speaks to Elijah here and tells him to go down with the captain and not to be afraid of him. Elijah obeys, rises, and goes down with him to where the king was.

King Ahaziah was sick, and he had sent to consult Baal-zebub, a false god, instead of seeking the Lord. Two earlier groups of soldiers had already arrived with a commanding tone, and they were consumed by fire. The third captain, by contrast, humbled himself and asked for mercy. God responds to that attitude and assures Elijah that he can go without fear. Then Elijah gives the king God's message.

For today: God cares for those who obey Him and rejoices in humility. When you have to do something difficult, remember that He can give you courage and go with you, and draw near to Him with humility.
exp.12:11:
This verse is the closing summary of the reign of Joash, king of Israel. It says that his other deeds, his might, and his war against Amaziah, king of Judah, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. That book is not the Bible's Chronicles, but an official court record that we no longer have.

The author of the book of Kings uses this phrase to close the reign of each king. He wants to point readers to where more details can be found. Here he says it right after noting that Joash did evil in the sight of God and followed the sins of Jeroboam.

For today: achievements and fame are forgotten or filed away, but God looks at the faithfulness of the heart. Living in obedience to him is worth more than being remembered for what we accomplish.
exp.6:10:
This verse tells that the gatekeepers, that is, the guards who watched the gates of the city of Samaria, called out the news and carried it to the king's palace. The phrase about them calling out means they spoke loudly. The word for reporting it means they passed the news along.

Samaria was under a terrible siege by the Syrians, with extreme hunger. Four men with leprosy discovered that the enemy camp was empty and full of supplies. They told the gatekeepers, and these passed the message on to the palace. So the good news reached the king, although at first he doubted it.

For today: when we receive good news, such as the message of the gospel, we should not keep it to ourselves. We can share it simply with others, even if some doubt at first. Perhaps someone near you needs to hear it today.
exp.17:9:
It says that the Assyrians captured Samaria after a siege of three years. That happened in the sixth year of King Hezekiah of Judah, which matched the ninth year of Hoshea, the last king of Israel. The first part of the sentence, "they took it," is the same as "Samaria was taken," meaning that the city fell.

The narrator of the book of Kings recounts the fall of the northern kingdom, Israel. The verses that follow explain the reason: the people did not listen to God and broke his covenant. The date is recorded using the years of Hezekiah to show the contrast: Judah, with a faithful king, was still standing, while Israel fell. Scholars explain the exact calculations of these dates in several different ways.

God speaks patiently for a long time, but ignoring him has consequences. Today we can ask ourselves what we have put off and obey him without delay, trusting in his grace.
exp.3:1:
Elisha asks the widow what he can do for her, and he asks her to tell him what she has in her house. She answers humbly that she has nothing at all, only a jar of oil, which is a small clay vessel used to keep oil.

The speaker is Elisha, the prophet, and the widow was the wife of one of the sons of the prophets, a group of disciples who served God. Her husband died and left debts. The creditor, that is, the man who had lent him money, wanted to take her two sons as servants to collect the payment. She cried out asking for help.

When we feel we have nothing, God often begins with the little we do have. Put into his hands what is in your house: your time, your abilities, a sincere prayer. He can do a great deal with that.
exp.1:13:
Elisha picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah, struck the waters of the Jordan, and asked, "Where is the Lord God of Elijah?" When he struck the water, it divided to one side and to the other, and he crossed over.

Elisha speaks only after Elijah has been taken up into heaven. He had asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, and now he faces his first test as a prophet alone. His question does not sound like a mocking doubt; it is a plea of faith, a wish to see whether God would still act as he had before. When the prophets of Jericho saw him, they recognized that the spirit of Elijah rested on him.

God does not depend on one person to carry out his work. When you face a new season or a loss, take the step of faith and lean on the same God who helped others before you.
exp.9:24:
This verse tells how, when they had finished offering the burnt offering (a sacrifice burned up completely), Jehu commanded his guard and his captains to go in and kill all the worshipers of Baal, letting none of them escape. They did so, left the bodies there, and went on to the innermost part of the temple of Baal. The phrase "the city of the house" is hard to understand; some believe it refers to an inner enclosure or a fortified area of the temple.

Jehu was king of Israel, and he acted with deceit: he pretended he would serve Baal in order to gather his followers in one place. God had raised him up to bring an end to the house of Ahab and to the worship of Baal, which had led the people into idolatry. The Bible presents this act as judgment, but it also shows that Jehu did not follow God with his whole heart.

Today we are not called to use violence. We are called to remove from our lives, with firmness and without compromise, whatever takes the place of God, and to serve him sincerely, not only through outward actions.
exp.22:16:
Verse 17 tells how King Josiah saw a marker or stone beside a grave and asked what it was. The word "title" in the verse refers to the marker or sign that identified the tomb. The people of the city explained that the man of God was buried there, the one who had come from Judah and had announced what Josiah had just done at the altar of Bethel.

Josiah was cleansing the land of idolatry. About 300 years earlier, a prophet, whose name is not given here, had announced that a king named Josiah would destroy that altar (1 Kings 13). Now the prophecy was being fulfilled. That is why Josiah respected the tomb and ordered that the bones of the prophet not be disturbed.

For today: God keeps his word, even when it takes a very long time. We can trust his promises and remain faithful, even when we do not see results soon. It is also good to honor those who went before us in the faith.
exp.17:14:
It says that Hezekiah gave the king of Assyria all the silver that was in the temple of the Lord and in the treasures of the palace. The first sentence about the old wording is replaced: the verse uses "gave," and "found" means that it was discovered. It was a payment to make the enemy leave.

The account tells what King Hezekiah did when Sennacherib, king of Assyria, invaded the fortified cities of Judah. Hezekiah said to him, "I have sinned," and agreed to pay whatever he demanded. To gather the tribute he emptied the treasures of the temple and of the palace. The Bible does not explain in detail what he meant by "I have sinned"; some think it refers to his rebellion against Assyria. In the end, the Assyrian king attacked Jerusalem anyway.

For today: When we feel afraid, it is easy to want to buy peace with quick solutions that cost a great deal and guarantee nothing. Before giving in, it is wise to seek God and trust in Him, for only He gives true security.
exp.15:8:
This verse says that the king of Assyria listened to Ahaz's request. He went up with his army against Damascus, the capital of Syria, took it, and carried its people away captive to a place called Kir. He also killed Rezin, the king of Syria.

The account is told by the writer of Kings. Ahaz, king of Judah, was threatened by Syria and Israel. Instead of trusting God, he paid Assyria with silver and gold from the temple and the palace. Assyria responded, but that alliance left Judah under the control of a foreign power.

For today: when pressure comes, let us avoid quick solutions that pull us away from God. Human help may solve the immediate problem, but it has a cost. Let us seek God first in prayer, and ask him for wisdom before we decide.
exp.20:23:
After the servants of King Amon assassinated him, the people of the land put to death all those who had conspired against him. Then they made Josiah, Amon's son, king in his place.

This is part of the historical account in Kings, and the author of the book is the one telling the story. Amon had turned away from God, and his own servants killed him in his house. It is not known for certain who the people of the land were; many think they were influential citizens of Judah, but they are understood in several ways. They kept the kingdom from falling into chaos and placed Josiah on the throne, who later became a king who sought God.

For today: even in times of wickedness and disorder, God can bring something good. We can pray for our leaders and trust that He works even in dark situations.
exp.20:14:
It says that God is going to punish Judah because its people did what was evil in his sight and "provoked him to anger." This was not just something recent: it goes back to the time their ancestors came out of Egypt. Provoking God to anger means offending him again and again, until his patience is worn out.

God speaks, through his prophets, in the time of King Manasseh of Judah. Manasseh led the people into idolatry and shed a great deal of innocent blood. God announces that Jerusalem will suffer a judgment like that of Samaria and of the house of Ahab. This verse gives the reason: it is not an arbitrary punishment, but the result of a long history of rebellion.

For today: God is patient, but he is not indifferent. We should not let a small sin become a habit. Today we can ask him for forgiveness for something we have put off and change course with his help.
exp.14:10:
This verse says that the rest of what Zachariah did, as king of Israel, is not told here, but was written in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That book was an official record of the kings, and it has not survived today. The word "acts" refers to the deeds or the rule of this king.

The author of Kings summarizes each reign. Before this, he says that Zachariah did evil in the sight of God, followed the sins of Jeroboam, and was killed by Shallum. Afterward he recalls that what God had promised to Jehu was fulfilled: four generations of his sons would reign. Zachariah was the fourth.

For today: our lives also leave a record. God sees what we do and what we leave unsaid. It is worth asking ourselves what our life will leave written, and asking God to keep us from the evil paths that others pass down to us.
exp.19:20:
This verse says that King Hezekiah died. "He slept with his fathers" is an old, gentle way of saying that he died and was buried with his ancestors. After him, his son Manasseh became the new king of Judah. Hezekiah is spelled here in a different form.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who closes the story of Hezekiah. Earlier, Isaiah had told him that his descendants would be carried off to Babylon, and he said the word was good, thinking there would be peace in his days. The text does not explain his whole attitude, and it can be understood in several ways. Manasseh, his son, would reign afterward, and the Bible remembers him as a very wicked king.

For today: our life is short, and what we do influences those who come after us. It is worth asking whether we are teaching our children and others to trust God.
exp.17:30:
This verse says that the king of Assyria urges the people of Jerusalem not to listen to King Hezekiah. He offers them a deal: that they surrender, making peace and coming out to him, and in exchange they will be able to keep eating from their own vine and fig tree and drinking from the water of their own cistern.

The one speaking is Rabshakeh, an officer sent by Sennacherib, king of Assyria, while Jerusalem was under siege. His goal was to sow fear and doubt among the people so that they would stop trusting in Hezekiah and in the LORD. His offer sounds kind, but shortly afterward it reveals that it meant being taken far from their land.
