For today: not everything that sounds like peace or comfort comes from a good source. When someone promises you calm in exchange for letting go of your trust in God, stop, pray, and compare that voice with what God has already said in his Word.
exp.6:17:
This verse says that what Elisha, the man of God, had told the king came to pass exactly as he said: the next day, at the gate of Samaria, food would be sold very cheaply. A measure of grain and a piece of silver are named in the verse itself as "two measures of barley" and "a shekel," so no separate explanation of those words is needed. Fine flour is flour of good quality.

Samaria was under siege by the Syrians and was suffering a terrible famine. Elisha announced that God would bring abundance in a single day. An officer of the king doubted and said that even if God opened windows in heaven, such a thing could not happen. The Syrians fled, the people plundered their camp, and the promise was fulfilled. The officer died, trampled at the entrance, without tasting anything.

For today: God can work even when everything seems impossible. Trusting his word, rather than doubting because of what we see, opens us to receive his help with hope.
exp.8:10:
Jehu came out from the room where the young prophet had anointed him and returned to the army officers, who were servants of his lord, King Joram. They asked him whether all was well and why "that madman" had come to him. Jehu answered that they already knew the man and his way of speaking. "Servants" here means officers; "madman" is a contemptuous way of referring to the prophet.

The prophet, sent by Elisha, had just anointed Jehu as king and announced judgment on the house of Ahab. The officers speak with scorn, yet they are curious. Jehu's answer is evasive: he does not reveal everything at once. Some think he wanted to gauge their reactions before speaking.

Today, God's message sometimes comes through people the world looks down on. Before we mock someone for the way they are, let us listen with humility and test what they say in the light of the Bible.
exp.19:5:
God makes two promises to King Hezekiah: that he will live fifteen more years, and that he will protect Jerusalem from the king of Assyria. The sentence explaining the old-word glosses is omitted, since the verse above uses "add" and "defend," and the meaning is already clear. "For my own sake" means that God will act for the sake of his own name and faithfulness.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Hezekiah was seriously ill, he had prayed in tears, and God heard his plea. The mention of David recalls the promise God made to him to care for his descendants and the city. Assyria was then a real threat to Judah.

For today: we can pray sincerely, even with tears, knowing that God listens. He does not always answer in the same way, but he acts faithfully and out of his love. Let us trust that he cares for us and for his promises.
exp.16:7:
It says that Israel followed the customs and laws of the pagan nations that the Lord had driven out before his people arrived. It also followed what its own kings had set up, kings who had turned away from God. The word "statutes" here means customs or rules for living. The "heathen" are the nations that did not know the Lord.

The one telling this is the author of the book of Kings, explaining why the northern kingdom fell. Samaria was taken by Assyria and the people were carried away captive. The text makes clear that this was not bad luck: Israel had forgotten the God who brought them out of Egypt and copied the practices of other peoples, including idolatry.

For today: it is easy to adopt the customs of our surroundings without noticing. It is worth asking what shapes the way we live: the Word of God, or what everyone else does? We can examine one habit this week in the light of the Bible.
exp.5:21:
Elisha tells the king of Israel not to kill the Syrian soldiers. He asks him whether he would kill prisoners whom he had not captured with his own sword or bow. Instead, he tells him to set bread and water before them, so that they may eat, drink, and return to their master.

Elisha speaks with the king of Israel. The Syrians had gone to capture the prophet, but God struck them with blindness, and Elisha led them to Samaria. When God opened their eyes, they found themselves in the middle of the enemy capital. The king wanted to kill them, but Elisha asked for mercy. Afterward, the text says that the Syrian raiding bands stopped invading for a time.

Today we can learn that kindness can open paths where revenge would only bring more pain. When someone harms us, we can ask ourselves: how can I respond with generosity and respect, without failing to act wisely?
exp.22:20:
It says that King Josiah commanded all the people to keep the Passover to the Lord their God, as it is written in the book of this covenant. The covenant is the agreement, the solemn promise between God and his people. The Passover was the feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt.

The passage speaks of King Josiah, after he had cleared the land of altars and practices of idolatry. Earlier, the book of the law had been found in the temple, and the king had committed himself to obeying it. The Passover was a step back toward worshiping God as he had asked. The verses that follow say that no Passover like it had been kept for a very long time.

For today: it is not enough to remove what is wrong; we also need to return to what God has said and to celebrate with gratitude what he has done. You might read the Bible this week and thank God for your salvation.
exp.17:29:
This verse says that Hezekiah, king of Judah, must not get the people to trust in the Lord. The speaker is imitating what Hezekiah was telling them: that God would surely deliver them and that Jerusalem would not fall to Assyria. The third sentence of the source, which explains the names and terms, is removed because it only glosses wording that does not appear in the verse you see.

The speaker is the officer sent by the king of Assyria, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. He speaks out loud, in the language of the people, to frighten them and to turn them away from their king. He wants them to surrender and stop trusting in God. The biblical account then shows that Hezekiah did trust in the Lord.

Today, when the voices of fear or mockery tell you that trusting God is naive, do not let them carry you away. Do as Hezekiah did: bring your distress to God in prayer and keep trusting in Him, even when the situation looks impossible.
exp.4:21:
Gehazi answers Naaman that all is well, and right away he invents a lie. He says that Elisha has sent him because two young men of the sons of the prophets have just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim, and he asks for a talent of silver and two changes of clothing. The young men are simply young men, and "two changes of clothing" means one set of new clothes for each of them, and a talent was a large weight of silver.

Gehazi, Elisha's servant, is the one speaking. Elisha had refused any payment for Naaman's healing, so that it would be clear that God's grace cannot be bought. Gehazi, moved by greed, uses his master's name without permission to take for himself what Elisha had turned down.

For today: greed leads us to lie and to misuse what belongs to God. Let us ask God for a contented and honest heart, one that does not profit from what is holy.
exp.16:20:
This verse says that God tore Israel, the ten tribes of the north, away from the family of King David. Then the people made Jeroboam, son of Nebat, their king. But Jeroboam drove Israel away from following the Lord and led them into a great sin. "Drave" means that he drove them with force, pushing them away from God.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who explains why Israel fell into the hands of Assyria. The verses before show that God punished them for disobeying him. Jeroboam set up other idols and another way of worship, and the people followed him for generations without repenting.

For today: what leaders do greatly influences others, but each person answers for the steps they follow. It is worth asking ourselves whom we are following and whether their steps bring us closer to God or farther from him.
exp.16:25:
This verse tells how some people reported to the king of Assyria that the foreign peoples, brought to Samaria, did not know the way of the God of that land. Because of this, according to them, God had sent lions that were killing them. The phrase "thou hast removed" means that you had moved them by force, and "the manner" refers to the proper way of worshiping and serving God.

The speakers are the king's informants, probably Assyrian officials. Assyria had carried the Israelites into exile and resettled the region with other peoples. They thought every land had its own god, but the preceding text says that it was the LORD who sent the lions, because they did not fear him. Then the king orders that a priest be brought to teach them.

For today: it is not enough to know that God exists; we must know him and seek him with reverence. If you are unclear about this, look for teaching in the Bible and in your church.
exp.21:2:
That year, the eighteenth of his reign, King Josiah sent Shaphan, a scribe (a secretary or keeper of records), to the house of the Lord, that is, to the temple in Jerusalem. Shaphan was the son of Azaliah and the grandson of Meshullam. The words "sent" and "saying" introduce the charge that follows.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents Josiah as a young king who did what was right before God. He was about twenty-six years old by then. The charge that follows is to collect money from the people to repair the temple, which had fallen into disrepair. This prepares the way for the discovery of the book of the law.

For today: when we love God, our faith shows in concrete actions. Josiah did not merely say he respected the temple; he organized its care. Think of something you can repair or look after in your church, your family, or your spiritual life, and take one simple step toward it today.
exp.18:35:
Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp, withdrew, and returned to Nineveh, the capital of his kingdom, and stayed there. The words "departed" and "returned" mean that he left and came back home. After losing his army, he no longer kept attacking Jerusalem.

The passage is part of the historical account in Kings. Sennacherib had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. King Hezekiah prayed, and God promised to defend the city for his own sake and for the sake of David. That night a large part of the Assyrian army died. This verse records the outcome: the king retreats defeated, and the account goes on to his death in Nineveh.

For today: when a problem feels bigger than you, you can do what Hezekiah did: bring it to God in prayer and trust that he knows how and when to act. We do not know how or when he will respond, but he is faithful.
exp.18:6:
God says he will put "a spirit" into the king of Assyria, that is, a disposition or inclination in his mind. He will hear "a rumour," that is, a piece of news, and will return to his own country. There, God will cause him to die "by the sword," that is, by a sword.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Hezekiah, king of Judah, is frightened because the Assyrians mocked God and threatened Jerusalem. God tells him to say that he should not fear. Soon after, the king of Assyria hears that Tirhakah of Ethiopia is coming to fight against him. Later on, the account says that he died by the sword in his own land.

For today: when you are threatened or your faith is mocked, do not let fear take control of you. Bring your worry to God in prayer, trusting that he governs situations, even when you do not yet see how he will resolve them.
exp.22:29:
This verse tells what happened after the death of King Josiah. His servants placed his body in a chariot, took him from Megiddo to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people of the land, that is, the inhabitants of Judah, took Jehoahaz, son of Josiah, anointed him with oil, and made him king in place of his father.

The text is a historical narrative. Josiah had gone out to face Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, who was heading toward the Euphrates River, and he died at Megiddo. The biblical historians do not fully explain why Josiah went out to fight, so it is best not to claim more than the text says. The people chose Jehoahaz, and the following verse makes clear that he did what was evil in the sight of God.

For today: even good leaders die, and what comes next can be uncertain. For that reason it is wise to trust God and not only people, and to pray that those who lead us will seek to do what is right.
exp.8:31:
Jehu looks up toward the window where Jezebel is and asks, "Who is on my side? Who?" Then two or three eunuchs look out. They were court officials, servants of the palace.

Jehu is the one whom God had anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab because of its idolatry and violence. Jezebel had just mocked him. Jehu does not argue with her; he looks for who will stand with him. The eunuchs, who depended on her, must choose between the queen and the man whom God had raised up. What follows shows their decision.

Today too comes the moment when we must decide which side we are on. Jesus said that no one can serve two masters. It is wise to choose God clearly, before pressure forces us to choose.
exp.15:7:
This verse tells how King Ahaz took all the silver and gold that was in the house of the Lord and in the treasures of the king's palace, and sent it to the king of Assyria as a gift. That gift was meant to win his favor, almost like a bribe.

The writer of Kings describes a moment of pressure. Syria and Israel were attacking Judah, and Ahaz, instead of seeking God, asked Assyria for help, calling himself the king's servant and son. To pay for that help, he used even what was dedicated to God. The verses that follow show that this alliance led him to copy foreign religious practices.

Today, when we are afraid, it is easy to look for quick solutions that sacrifice what matters most. Before deciding, we can pray and ask ourselves: am I trusting God, or paying a very high price for a human way out?
exp.23:17:
This verse introduces Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he ruled for eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother is named, Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah (this Jeremiah is not the prophet of the same name, who was from Anathoth).

The book of Kings tells the history of Judah with a tone of warning. Babylon had just taken Jehoiachin and thousands of leading people into captivity, and it placed Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's uncle, on the throne under its control. His original name was Mattaniah, and it was changed. The writer presents his reign as the beginning of the end, since he later says that he did evil and rebelled against Babylon.

For today: having authority or a good opportunity is not enough if there is no obedience to God. We can ask him for humility to listen to him and to correct our course in time, before bad decisions carry us too far.
exp.23:0:
In his days Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up against Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Jehoiakim served him, that is, he was made subject to him and paid tribute, for three years. Then he changed his course and rebelled against him.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Judah. The verses that follow explain that God allowed enemy forces to come against Judah because of the people's accumulated sins, especially those of Manasseh, as the prophets had warned. Jehoiakim's rebellion was part of that process.

For today: decisions have consequences that sometimes take time to become visible. Instead of seeking ways out on our own, it is good to return to God sincerely, obey him, and keep our commitments with integrity.
exp.0:6:
Here King Ahaziah asks his messengers what the man who stopped them on the road looked like. The word "manner" here refers to his appearance or the way he was dressed, not a habit. "Man" simply means a man.

King Ahaziah had been injured in a fall and sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, a false god of Ekron. A man met them and gave them a message from Jehovah: the king would die. Ahaziah wants to know who he was, because that man spoke with an authority that troubled him. His question shows he suspected who it might be, and the answer that follows confirms it.

When God speaks to us, we may react with curiosity about who said it, but the most important thing is to listen to the message. Today, instead of looking for answers anywhere else, it is wise to turn first to God and to his Word.
exp.10:19:
It says that all the people of the land rejoiced and that the city was quiet, because Athaliah, the queen who had seized power, was put to death with the sword near the palace.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells of the end of Athaliah's rule. She had destroyed the royal family to reign, but the priest Jehoiada hid the young Joash, David's heir, and crowned him in the temple. The people also tore down the temple of Baal. The text presents this as a return to order and to the worship of Jehovah.

When injustice is removed and what is right is restored, peace arrives. Today we can ask ourselves which idols have taken God's place in our hearts, and ask him to help us remove them so that we may live in true peace.
exp.16:16:
This verse says that the Israelites made their sons and daughters pass through the fire, that is, they offered them as sacrifices to false gods. They also practiced divination and omens, which are attempts to know the future by forbidden means. They gave themselves over to doing evil before God, and so they provoked him to anger.

Here the author of the book of Kings speaks, explaining why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell before Assyria. God had warned them many times, but they abandoned his covenant and copied the customs of the neighboring peoples. The text presents their fall as the consequence of that unfaithfulness.

For today: let us not copy without thought what our culture does. Let us seek in God our guidance and trust, and not in things that promise security or answers apart from him.
exp.7:25:
This verse presents Ahaziah, son of Joram, as the new king of Judah. He began to reign at the age of twenty-two and reigned only one year in Jerusalem. His mother was named Athaliah, and the text calls her "the daughter of Omri," king of Israel. In older usage, the word "daughter" could also mean descendant, so she may have been a granddaughter of Omri and a daughter of Ahab. Some scholars explain it that way.

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Judah and Israel and judges whether they followed God or not. Here he explains why Ahaziah was a bad king: because of his family. Joram of Judah had married a woman from the house of Ahab, and that alliance brought harmful influences into the southern kingdom.

The people and environments around us shape us. It is worth asking ourselves whom we listen to and with whom we form alliances, and seeking those who draw us closer to God rather than pulling us away from Him.
exp.9:6:
It says that when the letter from Jehu came to them, the leaders of Samaria took the seventy sons of King Ahab, killed them, and put their heads in baskets. Then they sent the heads to Jehu, who was in Jezreel. The word "slew" means to kill by cutting the throat, and "persons" refers to the men.

Context: Jehu had already been anointed to destroy the house of Ahab, and he had killed King Joram. With his letter he put the leaders of Samaria to a test of loyalty, and out of fear they obeyed. The text reports the event but does not simply approve of it. Later, the prophet Hosea speaks of punishing the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel (Hosea 1:4).

For today: fear and pressure can lead us to do terrible things just to please those in power. Let us ask God for the courage to obey Him before any human authority.
exp.12:23:
This verse says that Hazael, king of Syria, died, and that his son Ben-hadad became the new king. "Reigned in his stead" means that he succeeded him on the throne.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. Hazael had oppressed Israel greatly. Nevertheless, the text recalls that God had compassion on his people because of the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. By noting Hazael's death, the author prepares what follows: Joash, king of Israel, recovered the cities that Syria had taken.

Today we can remember that no human power lasts forever. Those who oppress us pass away, but the faithfulness of God endures. In difficulties, we can wait on Him with patience and trust.
exp.20:8:
This verse says that the people of Judah did not obey God. Their king, Manasseh, led them to do things worse than those of the nations that God had destroyed when Israel arrived in the land. The word "seduced" means that he pushed or encouraged them to do it.

The author of the book tells the story of the kings of Judah. Manasseh put an idol in the temple, the place where God had promised to put his name. God had said that Israel would remain in the land if it obeyed his law. Here the account explains why judgment would come: the people did not listen, and their leader guided them toward evil.

Those who lead, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace, have a great influence on others. Let us ask God to help us listen to his Word and to guide others toward good, not toward error.
exp.4:20:
It says that Gehazi, Elisha's servant, ran after Naaman. When Naaman saw him coming, he got down from his chariot to meet him and asked, "Is all well?"

Naaman was a military commander from Syria who had just been healed of leprosy. He wanted to pay Elisha, but the prophet refused the gift to make clear that the healing came from God and was free. Gehazi, driven by greed, decided to keep something for himself in secret. Naaman, grateful and respectful, stopped humbly when he saw that someone from the prophet was looking for him.

For today: greed can lead us to lie and to stain what God has done in generosity. Before acting for gain, let us ask ourselves whether we are honoring God or taking advantage of his work.
exp.2:0:
Joram, son of Ahab, began to reign over Israel from the city of Samaria, in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat's reign as king of Judah. Joram ruled for twelve years. Here "Ahab" is the name Acab, and "Jehoshaphat" is Josafat, the same king mentioned in the verse.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who records each reign and judges it before God. Joram came to the throne after his brother Ahaziah, who died without sons. Other passages give slightly different dates for when his reign began, which is usually explained by different ways of counting the years or by overlapping reigns. The verses that follow say he removed the statues of Baal, but he continued in the sins of Jeroboam.

For today: making a partial change is not enough if the heart is still tied to what harms us. Let us ask God for the courage to leave sin completely, not only what is most visible.
exp.14:25:
The verse says that the rest of what King Pekahiah did is written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The word "acts" refers to his deeds, and the chronicles are the official records of the kingdom. This is not the biblical book of Chronicles, but an ancient archive that we no longer have.

The author of Kings, whose identity we do not know for certain, uses this formula to close the reign of each king. Earlier he has told us that Pekahiah did evil, followed the sins of Jeroboam, and was killed by Pekah, his captain. The author summarizes and sends the reader to other records for more detail.

For today: every life leaves a record, and God sees more than human archives do. Pekahiah had power, but he did not leave a good name. It is worth asking ourselves what we are building and whether we are walking with God, not just achieving success.
exp.17:18:
Rab-shakeh, a high official of the king of Assyria, speaks to the envoys of Hezekiah. He asks them to carry a message to the king: "Thus saith the great king, the king of Assyria." Then he asks a question that sounds like mockery: "What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?" In other words, what are you relying on to feel safe?

Judah had rebelled against Assyria, and the Assyrian army was already camped in front of Jerusalem. Rab-shakeh wanted to discourage the people and make them doubt Hezekiah, his alliances, and eventually even God himself.

Today we are also asked the same question: what do we trust when pressure comes? It is good to examine whether our security rests in money, in people, or in God, who never fails. You can pray, "Lord, help me to trust in you."
exp.12:19:
It says that the prophet Elisha died and they buried him. When the new year began, bands of Moabite raiders entered the territory of Israel. "Bands" are armed groups that carried out raids and plundering, and the "coming in of the year" means that the new year had already begun.

The narrator tells of the end of Elisha's life. Shortly before, King Joash had struck the ground only three times with the arrows, and the prophet was angry, because that sign pointed to a limited victory. Now that Elisha was gone, Israel was more exposed to its neighbors. The account shows that the word of God continued on its course.

For today: do not do halfway what God shows you. Obey with eagerness and trust, and remember that God still works even when the people who guided us are no longer there.
exp.1:5:
Elijah asks Elisha to stay behind, because God is sending him to the Jordan River. Elisha answers with an oath, "As the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth," which is to say, as surely as God and you are alive. He promises not to leave him. So the two of them go on together.

Elijah is the prophet who is about to be taken up into heaven. Elisha is his disciple and successor. It is not known for certain why Elijah insists that he stay; some think it is a test of loyalty, others that he wants to be alone. Elisha does not let himself be held back, for he knows what is about to happen.

For today: faith and loyalty are shown by going forward when it would be easier to stay behind. If there is something God has called you to live or learn, do not give up at the first difficulty. Seek to stay close to those who teach you in the way of God.
exp.9:8:
Jehu goes out in the morning and stands before all the people. He tells them they are "righteous," meaning that they are not to blame. He admits that he conspired against his master, King Joram, and killed him. Then he asks, "Who struck down all these?", pointing to the seventy sons of Ahab.

Jehu speaks in Jezreel, after the leaders of Samaria, out of fear, had killed the king's sons and sent their heads to him. His speech is a political move: he acknowledges his own deed, but he spreads the responsibility around. He then says this fulfills what God announced through Elijah. The Bible does not approve of every method Jehu used; later it shows him to be flawed.

For today: be careful about justifying harsh actions with religious words. That God uses an event does not make every means good. Let us examine our motives with humility and honesty.
exp.24:28:
It says that the king of Babylon changed Jehoiachin's prison clothes for him. From then on, Jehoiachin ate at the king's table all the days of his life. The verse of "changed" as the meaning of the source word and "prison clothes" as the clothing of a prisoner is removed here, since those terms do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

The one who tells this is the author of Kings, at the end of the book. After recounting the fall of Jerusalem and the exile, he ends with an unexpected note: Jehoiachin, a descendant of David, was treated kindly by Evil-merodach. Many understand this as a small sign that God had not forgotten his promise to the line of David. The text does not explain this, so it is an interpretation.

For today: even in dark times, God can plant signs of hope. If you are going through a difficult season, look for those small gestures of kindness and trust that God is still at work, even if you do not yet see the full restoration.
exp.3:2:
Elisha tells the widow to go out and borrow vessels from all her neighbors. They must be empty vessels, and not a few, that is, many. "Vessels" here means containers or jars, and the "jar" was a small clay vessel.

The speaker is the prophet Elisha. The widow of a man who feared the LORD cried out to him because a creditor wanted to take her two sons as servants to pay the debt. She had only a little oil. Elisha gives her a concrete instruction that requires faith: she was to prepare before she saw the miracle.

For today: God often works with the little we have, and He invites us to take steps of faith and obedience. Asking others for help is not shameful, and preparing room for what God can do expresses trust in Him.
exp.13:24:
This verse says that King Jeroboam II recovered the borders of Israel's territory, from the entrance of Hamath in the north to the sea of the plain, which is the Dead Sea. This happened according to what God had spoken through the prophet Jonah, son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher. "Restored" means gave back; "borders" are the boundary lines.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. Although Jeroboam did what was evil before God, the text explains that the Lord saw the suffering of his people and did not want to blot out their name. This Jonah is often identified with the prophet of the book of Jonah, although here he is mentioned only briefly.

God can show compassion even when people do not deserve it. His goodness invites us to repent and to trust that He cares for us, even in difficult times.
exp.17:2:
He did what pleased God. "Did what was right in the sight of the Lord" means that he acted the way God approves. He is compared with David, his father, a word that here means ancestor, the model of a faithful king.

This is told by the narrator of the book of Kings, who sums up the history of the kings of Israel and Judah. Hezekiah ruled Judah when the northern kingdom was about to fall. The verses that follow show how he obeyed: he removed the places of false worship and trusted in God. The text does not say he was perfect, but that his course was to please God.

Today we can ask ourselves what things in our lives take the place that belongs to God. Hezekiah did not only believe; he acted and removed what stood in the way. Being faithful can involve concrete decisions, even when they cost.
exp.4:24:
What it says: Gehazi returns after having secretly taken silver and clothing from Naaman. He goes in and presents himself before Elisha, his master. Elisha asks him where he has come from, and Gehazi lies: he says he did not go anywhere. "Thy servant" is a respectful way of speaking about oneself, and the word "whither" is an old way of saying "to what place."

Context: Elisha is the prophet who had healed Naaman, commander of the army of Syria, without charging him anything. Gehazi, his servant, ran after Naaman and deceived him in order to keep a gift for himself. Elisha asks the question, giving him the chance to confess, but Gehazi lies. Then Elisha declares that he knew what had happened, and Gehazi is left with leprosy.

For today: When we have failed, the best thing is to tell the truth right away. Hiding sin with lies only makes it worse. God sees everything, but he also offers forgiveness to whoever confesses with humility.
exp.18:15:
Hezekiah asks God to "bow down thine ear" and "open thine eyes," that is, to pay attention and see what is happening. He presents the words of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, who sent messages to mock and speak against the living God. To "reproach" means to speak with contempt of God.

The one speaking is Hezekiah, king of Judah. Assyria had threatened Jerusalem and said that God would not be able to save them. Hezekiah received the letter, took it to the temple, and spread it out before God. He did not first look for a human strategy, but placed the problem in the hands of the Lord.

For today: when you receive bad news, a threat, or mockery, bring it to God in prayer. Tell him honestly what worries you, as one who lays an open letter before him, and trust that he hears you.
exp.14:35:
This verse is the formula the writer uses to close the account of Jotham's reign. It says that the rest of his deeds and all that he did are not told here, but are found in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." That book was an official record kept by the court, separate from the biblical book of Chronicles that we have today.

The writer of Kings summarizes each reign and points to other sources for more detail. His main interest is spiritual: how each king conducted himself before God. Of Jotham he says that he did what was right, though he did not remove the high places where the people still offered sacrifices. The exact identity of the author of Kings is unknown.

For today: our lives also leave a record. More than our achievements, what matters is whether we walk with God. Strive to obey him sincerely, and do not leave unfinished what you know you ought to correct.
exp.3:16:
This verse tells that the woman became pregnant and had a son just at the time Elisha had told her. The sentence about the word "bare" and "conceived" is not needed for the reader, so I have dropped the glossary lines and rewritten the comment about the difficult phrase for the wording the reader sees.

The phrase "according to the time of life" is a difficult expression; many understand it as "the following year, when this season comes around again," although some interpret it differently.

The one speaking here is the narrator. Earlier, Elisha, a prophet of God, promised this woman of Shunem a son, since she had been very kind to him. She doubted, because her husband was old and they had no children, and she feared a false hope. The text shows that the promise was fulfilled just as it had been spoken.

For today: God can keep his promises even when they seem impossible or delayed. We can keep trusting his word and live with hope, even when it is hard to believe, without hiding our doubts from him.
exp.9:12:
Jehu comes upon some men on the road and asks who they are. They answer that they are the brothers of Ahaziah, king of Judah, and that they were on their way to greet the children of the king and the children of the queen. The word "brothers" here most likely means close relatives, such as cousins or nephews.

Jehu had just wiped out the house of Ahab on God's command. These visitors were from Judah and were related by blood to that house, since the mother of Ahaziah came from the family of Ahab. They did not know what had happened. Jehu treated them as part of the same judgment, and the verses that follow say they were killed. This violence is hard to read, and the Bible presents it as historical fact, not as an example to imitate.

For today: our alliances and friendships shape us. It is worth asking ourselves who we associate with and what we are tied to, so that we are not carried along paths that God judges.
exp.18:14:
He says that King Hezekiah prayed to God with reverence and trust. He calls him "the Lord God of Israel," the one who "dwellest between the cherubims," a reference to the ark of the covenant in the temple, where God was understood to reveal his presence. He declares that God alone rules over all the kingdoms of the earth and that he made heaven and earth.

Hezekiah is the speaker, king of Judah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had sent him threatening letters, mocking God and boasting that he had already conquered other nations. Hezekiah took those letters into the temple and spread them out before God, as if handing him the problem.

Before telling his troubles, Hezekiah remembers who God is. When you face a threat or a piece of news that distresses you, begin your prayer by recalling that God is great and sovereign. Then present your situation to him honestly.
exp.15:4:
This verse tells how Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel, joined forces and came up to Jerusalem to attack King Ahaz. The word "besieged" means surrounding the city to press it until it surrenders. Although they had strength, they were not able to conquer it.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. He records this after describing the wickedness of Ahaz, who followed pagan customs, even offering his own son in the fire. Even so, Jerusalem did not fall. Many understand that this shows God's patience and his faithfulness to the promise made to David. But Ahaz did not seek God: he asked Assyria for help.

For today: when strong pressures come, do not first run to human solutions that pull you away from God. Seek Him first, and trust that His care is greater than your fears.
exp.4:12:
Here the servants of Naaman approach him with respect and speak to him kindly. They call him "my father" and ask him: if the prophet had asked you to do something very difficult, would you not have done it? Then how much more should you do something as simple as washing to be made clean?

Naaman was a foreign commander with leprosy. He had gone to see Elisha, but the prophet only sent word through a messenger that he should wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman was offended because he expected a grand ritual and thought the rivers of Damascus were better. His servants calmed him with wisdom, and he obeyed and was healed.

For today: sometimes we reject God's guidance because it is simple or because it wounds our pride. Let us learn to listen to humble advice and to obey with trust, even when it is not what we had imagined.
exp.1:24:
It says that Elisha left Bethel and went to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria. "Went" and "returned" are the words that appear in the verse above. It is a transitional verse, which only records his journey.

No one speaks here; the narrator summarizes the travels of the prophet Elisha, successor of Elijah. It comes right after the difficult episode of the youths of Bethel and the bears. Bethel was a center of idolatry, and the mockery ("Go up, thou bald head!") seems to be aimed also at the prophet of God, perhaps alluding to Elijah's departure. Interpreters debate the age of the young men and the exact meaning of the scene. Carmel recalls the ministry of Elijah, and Samaria was the capital of the kingdom.

For today: God keeps working even when we go through hard moments or ones that are hard to understand. With humility, continue on your way and keep serving faithfully, without staying stuck on mockery or rejection.
exp.16:8:
The Israelites were doing wrong things against God and trying to cover them up or hide them. They also built "high places," places of worship set on elevated ground, everywhere: from the watchtowers in the countryside to the walled cities.

The speaker is the author of the book of Kings. He explains why Israel, the northern kingdom, was taken captive by Assyria. His point is that the people forgot the God who had rescued them from Egypt and imitated the neighboring nations.

Today, let us not try to hide our sin or live a faith of appearances. Let us be honest with God, confess what we do in secret, and ask him for help to change.
exp.3:42:
This verse says that Elisha's servant was left doubting: twenty loaves of barley did not seem enough for a hundred men. But Elisha insisted that they be set before the people, because the Lord had said they would eat and would leave some over. The phrase "he said again" means the prophet repeated his command, and "leave thereof" means there would be food left over.

Elisha was the prophet, and he speaks with his servant. There was hunger in the region, and a man brought the firstfruits, that is, the first of his harvest. Elisha did not keep them for himself, but used them to feed the people. The events are recounted just as they stand in the text, and the Bible says it happened according to the word of the Lord.

For today: sometimes what we have seems small in the face of need. We can offer it with generosity and trust in God, without letting fear of scarcity paralyze us.
exp.7:4:
It says that Gehazi, Elisha's servant, was telling the king how the prophet had brought back to life the son of a woman. Just at that moment the same woman arrived to ask the king for her house and her land. Gehazi recognized her and said, "My lord, O king, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life."

The narrator tells us that the woman was the Shunammite. Elisha had warned her to leave the land for seven years of famine. When she returned, she went to the king to recover her property. Gehazi was speaking because the king wanted to hear about Elisha's wonders. That she arrived at that very moment seems like chance, but the text invites us to see the hand of God.

For today: God cares for us in the details and in the timing. We can ask for help with confidence, and we can also remember with gratitude what God has done, because our testimony may help others.
exp.11:2:
This verse says that, although King Joash did what was right, the high places were not removed. The high places were raised spots where the people offered sacrifices and burned incense. So the people kept worshiping in those places, instead of worshiping only at the temple in Jerusalem.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking, and he is evaluating the reign of Joash. His good conduct depended to a large extent on the guidance of the priest Jehoiada. The Bible says that God had called for one central place of worship, so the high places were a lasting failure, even though many used them thinking they worshiped the LORD. The details of each case are not always made clear.

For today: it is not enough to do many good things if we leave unattended some area that God points out to us. Ask God to show you which high place you are still tolerating, and take one concrete step to correct it.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that God became very angry with Israel and allowed them to be dominated by Hazael, king of Syria, and afterward by his son Ben-hadad. The phrase about his anger is best rendered here as: his anger burned hot against them. The phrase about handing them over means that he let them fall under the power of that king. This lasted a long time.

The writer tells the story of the reign of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu. That king did evil and continued the sin of Jeroboam, the false worship that turned the people away from God. For this reason the narrator explains that the Syrian oppression was the consequence of that disobedience. But the next verse shows that God listened when Jehoahaz prayed.

For today: our choices have consequences, and God calls us to return to Him. When we recognize that we have strayed, we can pray with humility, trusting that God is merciful and hears us.
exp.8:17:
It says that a messenger of King Joram rode out on horseback to meet Jehu and his company. On the king's behalf he asked, "Is it peace?", meaning whether they came with good intentions. Jehu did not answer the question; he told the man that peace was none of his business and ordered him to get behind him. The watchman, who keeps guard from the tower, saw that the messenger had arrived, but he did not return.

Joram, king of Israel, was wounded in Jezreel. Jehu had been secretly anointed as the new king, with the mission of bringing an end to the house of Ahab. That is why the king's question meant nothing to him: Jehu was not coming to negotiate. Joram did not yet know what was approaching.

Today: we cannot ask for peace while we avoid fixing what God has already pointed out. Let us ask him to show us what we should correct, so that our peace is real and not just words.
exp.6:7:
It says that the four lepers came to the edge of the Syrian camp, which was empty. They entered one tent, ate and drank, and took silver, gold, and clothing. They went off and hid all of it. Then they came back, entered another tent, took more things, and hid those too. The first places of the camp, the outer edge where the tents began, are the part the verse describes here.

The narrator tells what happened in Samaria, which was under siege and suffering terrible hunger. Four lepers, kept outside the city, decided to take a risk and approach the enemy. Without knowing it, God had caused the Syrians to hear the noise of a great army, and they fled. In this way, God used people on the margins to bring deliverance.

For today: what God gives us is not only meant to be kept for ourselves. These men first thought only of themselves, but soon their conscience reached them, and they shared the news. When you receive a blessing, think about who else you can help.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that the king of Israel, seeing that there was no water, lost hope. He thinks that the Lord gathered the three kings (Israel, Judah, and Edom) only to let them fall into the hand of Moab. The word expressing his distress is one of the exclamations in the verse. Handing them over means leaving them defeated.

The one speaking is the king of Israel, probably Joram, though the text here does not give his name. The kings had joined forces against Moab, but after seven days of marching through the desert their water ran out. He blames God without having consulted him. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, by contrast asks to seek a prophet of the Lord, and so they come to Elisha.

For today: when a crisis comes, let us avoid blaming God in haste or fear. Instead, like Jehoshaphat, let us seek his direction with humility, in prayer and in his Word.
exp.3:24:
She went and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her from a distance, he said to his servant Gehazi, "Look, there is that Shunammite woman!"

The writer tells how the Shunammite woman's son, whom God had given through Elisha, suddenly died. She told no one, and when her husband asked, she answered that all was well, though her grief was great. She hurried out to find the prophet. Elisha recognizes her from far off and speaks with his servant, because he sees that something serious is happening.

For today: when grief overwhelms you, follow this woman's example and do not stay silent or go to just anywhere. Run to God, even if you do not have all the answers. He sees your need from afar and does not turn you away.
exp.9:20:
Jehu sent word throughout all Israel, and all the worshippers of Baal came; not one was left behind. They entered the temple of Baal, and it was filled from one end to the other.

Jehu had just been anointed king and was bringing an end to the house of Ahab, the one who had promoted the worship of Baal in Israel. The text says he acted "with cunning": he pretended he would also serve Baal in order to gather his followers. This is an account of judgment against idolatry. The Bible presents it without approving everything Jehu did, since he himself later did not follow God wholeheartedly (2 Kings 10:31).

For today: God sees what truly fills our hearts. We should ask ourselves what "temple" we are filling with our time and trust, and return to serving the Lord alone with sincerity.
exp.7:14:
The next day someone took a thick cloth, soaked it in water, and laid it over the face of King Ben-hadad, and he died. Afterward Hazael reigned in his place. The text does not say who did it, but almost everyone understands that it was Hazael, who would have smothered him.

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was sick. He sent Hazael to ask the prophet Elisha whether the king would recover. Elisha said that the king would die and that Hazael would be king. Hazael went back and gave the king a reassuring answer, and death came the next day.

For today: ambition that is not restrained can lead to betrayal and violence. God sees what is in the heart. Let us ask him to cleanse us of crooked desires and help us to act with honesty.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells how a young man, an assistant of the prophet Elisha, obeyed and traveled to Ramoth-gilead. The word "young man" here means a youth or a servant. The phrase "the young man" is repeated to emphasize who was going: a simple attendant, not an important figure.

Elisha sent him on a delicate mission: to anoint Jehu as king of Israel in God's name. Ramoth-gilead was a place where the Israelite army was in the middle of a war. For that reason the task was dangerous and had to be carried out quickly and discreetly. The verse shows the first step: going.

For today: God often uses ordinary, little-known people to accomplish important tasks. What matters is obeying promptly, even when the road is not easy and we are not the ones in the spotlight.
exp.6:3:
This verse shows the conversation of four men with leprosy who are in a hopeless situation. If they enter the city of Samaria, they will die of hunger; if they stay outside, they will also die. "We will try" is the sense of "let us attempt," and the phrase "they would give us" appears as the wording of their hope. They decide to surrender to the Syrian army, thinking that perhaps they will spare their lives.

Samaria was under siege by the Syrians, and the hunger was terrible. Because of their leprosy, these men lived apart, at the entrance of the gate. Shortly before, Elisha had announced that God would provide abundant food, and an officer mocked him. The men with leprosy did not know this: they were only seeking to survive. God used their decision to fulfill his word.

For today: when you find yourself in a hopeless situation, take a step of faith instead of remaining paralyzed. God can work even through our small and fearful steps.
exp.9:16:
It says that when Jehu came to Samaria, he killed all who were left there from the family of Ahab, until he had finished them off. The text states that this fulfilled what God had said through the prophet Elijah.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jehu had been anointed king of Israel to bring judgment on the house of Ahab, which had led the people to worship Baal. God had already announced that judgment through Elijah (1 Kings 21). Afterward, Jehu tricks the worshipers of Baal. Interpreters debate how pure his motives were, since later the account says he did not follow God with his whole heart.

For today: God's words come true, even if it takes time. But let us make sure our zeal for God is sincere and not merely an appearance or an ambition.
exp.8:18:
This is the second messenger that King Joram sends to Jehu. He asks him, "Is it peace?", meaning whether he comes in a peaceful way or with good news. Jehu does not answer the question. He says, "What hast thou to do with peace?" and orders the man to get behind him. "On horseback" means riding a horse. "Turn thee behind me" is a command to join his group.

Jehu had been anointed in secret as king to bring an end to the house of Ahab. Joram, king of Israel, is wounded and recovering in Jezreel. Jehu comes quickly and with his men. Joram wants to know whether there is danger. Jehu rejects the word "peace," because the kingdom was full of idolatry and wickedness.

For today: it is not enough to say "everything is at peace" when there is unresolved sin. True peace begins when we let God correct us and draw near to him with honesty.
exp.17:10:
Here the account tells how the king of Assyria took the Israelites out of the northern kingdom and made them live far from their land. The word "carried away" means they were taken to another place, that is, into exile. He settled them in Halah, in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

The account comes from the book of Kings, which explains the history of Israel from the standpoint of faith. It speaks of the fall of Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom. The verse that follows gives the reason: the people did not obey the voice of the LORD and broke his covenant. The text presents the exile as the result of that sustained disobedience, not as something accidental.

For today: God speaks with clarity, and ignoring his voice little by little has consequences. Today you can listen to him humbly in his Word and obey him in small things, before neglect becomes a habit.
exp.4:2:
Here the young Israelite girl, who served in Naaman's house, tells his wife that if her master would go to see the prophet who is in Samaria, that prophet would heal him of his leprosy. Here the phrase "would God my lord were with the prophet" is not quoted, so I leave the meaning intact: she is expressing a wish that her master were with the prophet.

She is a captive girl, taken by force from Israel by Syrian raiding bands. She could have held resentment or kept silent, but she speaks simply about what she knows: that there is a prophet of God in her land. The Bible does not give her name or explain her reasons; it only shows what she said. The prophet is Elisha, though he is not named here.

For today: even when we are in a difficult or unjust situation, God can use our simple and kind words to bring hope to others. You do not need an important position; it is enough to share humbly what we know of God.
exp.16:38:
The verse says: "Fear only the Lord your God, and he will deliver you from all your enemies." "Fear" here means reverence, honor, and trust in God, not being afraid of him. "But" is the word that introduces the contrast, and "deliver you out of the hand of" means he will rescue them from the power of their enemies.

The context is the northern kingdom, Israel, which was taken captive by Assyria. The author of the book explains that this happened because of worshiping other gods. Here he recalls what God required in the covenant: to be faithful to him alone. The foreign peoples brought into that land mixed the worship of the Lord with their idols, and did not obey.

For today: true faith is not divided. We can ask ourselves what things compete with God for first place in our hearts. Putting him first, with simple obedience and trust, helps us rest in his care when we face trials.
exp.14:29:
Hoshea, son of Elah, made a conspiracy against Pekah, son of Remaliah. He struck him down, killed him, and took the throne in his place. The words "struck" and "killed" are the ones the verse itself uses for what Hoshea did to Pekah. A "conspiracy" means a secret plan against the king.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who is recounting the history of the kings of Israel. Pekah had done what was evil before God, and the kingdom was growing weaker, since Assyria had already taken away some of its territory. The phrase "in the twentieth year of Jotham" is hard to line up with other dates in the Bible, and scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: violence does not bring lasting solutions. Hoshea took power by force, and his reign ended badly. Let us trust in God and seek to act with justice and patience.
exp.16:13:
This verse says that the people of Israel would not listen to God. "They hardened their necks" means they were stubborn, like an animal that will not let itself be led, and they stiffened so they would not bow their heads. They did the same thing as their ancestors, who did not trust the Lord.

The author of Kings explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell to Assyria (around 722 B.C.). Before that punishment, God had sent prophets again and again to call them back to Him. They preferred idols and the customs of the neighboring peoples.

For today: when God speaks to us through His Word and something makes us uncomfortable, let us not harden our hearts. Today we can ask ourselves what correction we have been ignoring, and answer it with humility and obedience.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that the prophet Elisha went to Damascus, the capital of Syria. There King Ben-hadad was sick, and his servants told him that the man of God, that is, the prophet, had come. The phrase rendered "went quickly" means that he went at once or shortly afterward.

The narrator tells this event after the story of the Shunammite woman, who recovered her house and her lands. Syria and Israel were rival nations, yet even so the Syrian king knew that Elisha was a man of God. The text does not say why Elisha went to Damascus; it only tells us that his reputation had already reached that place.

For today: the life and witness of those who serve God can reach unexpected places. When we live with integrity and faith, others may seek us out in their moments of need. Let us make sure our lives point toward God.
exp.10:18:
This verse tells how the young king Joash was led in procession from the temple to the palace. He was accompanied by the rulers over hundreds (leaders of a hundred soldiers each), the captains, the guard, and the people. They entered by the gate of the guard, and the king sat on the throne.

The author of the book narrates this moment after Queen Athaliah had been overthrown. The priest Jehoiada had protected the boy Joash and organized everything. First he renewed the covenant with God, and the people destroyed the temple of Baal. Only after that did the king return to the palace. The order matters: first they drew near to God, and then they restored the government.

For today: before making big decisions, it is wise to put God first. If we renew our faithfulness to Him and remove what displaces Him, our decisions will have a better foundation.
exp.22:14:
This verse says that King Josiah came to Bethel and destroyed the altar and the high place that Jeroboam, son of Nebat, had made. The word "high place" here means a shrine built on a raised spot for worshiping idols. Josiah pulled it down, burned it, crushed it to powder, and also burned the grove, which was a pole or tree of wood dedicated to the goddess Asherah.

Context: The writer of the book tells about the great reform of King Josiah of Judah. Jeroboam had set up a false center of worship there to separate Israel from Jerusalem, and that is why it says he made Israel sin. Josiah cleansed the land of idolatry, fulfilling what a prophet had announced long before.

For today: God calls us to uproot what draws us away from Him, not merely to trim it back a little. Ask Him to show you which habit or priority has taken His place, and with His help, decide to leave it behind firmly.
exp.8:21:
Joram, king of Israel, sees Jehu coming and asks him, "Is it peace?", meaning, is everything all right? Jehu answers that there can be no peace as long as the whoredoms and witchcrafts of Jezebel, the king's mother, continue. Here "whoredoms" refers above all to spiritual unfaithfulness: idolatry. The "witchcrafts" are practices of sorcery.

Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab. They meet in the field of Naboth, the man whom Ahab and Jezebel had had put to death so they could take his vineyard. Joram wants to know whether Jehu comes in peace, but Jehu speaks of judgment. Afterward, Joram flees and Jehu kills him.

For today: true peace cannot be had while we tolerate sin that harms others and draws us away from God. Let us ask him to show us what must be let go, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.5:23:
It tells that, some time later, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered all his army, advanced against Israel, and surrounded the city of Samaria to besiege it. "Besieged" here means he blockaded the city so that no one could come in or go out, in order to defeat it through hunger.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Shortly before, Elisha had commanded that captured Syrian soldiers be treated kindly, and the Syrian raids stopped. Now, however, Syria returns with a larger attack. The following verses show a terrible famine inside Samaria. Some scholars think this Ben-hadad is Ben-hadad II, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: peace does not always last, and difficulties can return. Even so, we should keep acting with kindness and trust in God, without expecting everything to be easy.
exp.20:6:
This verse tells us that King Manasseh placed in the temple a carved image of the goddess Asherah, called here "a graven image of the grove." It was a wooden pole or figure used in pagan worship. He set it in the very place where God had said he would put his name forever.

The narrator of the book of Kings explains why God judged Judah. Manasseh mixed the worship of the Lord with pagan practices, and so he dishonored the house that God had promised to David and to Solomon. God had already promised to care for Israel in their land if they obeyed him, but the people did not listen.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are sharing our hearts with other things that compete with God. He deserves first place, not a shared place.
exp.18:25:
This verse says that the people of those fortified cities were left weak and without strength. The words "powerless" and "dismayed" describe their defeat and shame, and the verse's own phrase "of small power" fits here. They were like the grass of the field, or the green herb on the housetops, which dries up before it can grow. Grass growing on a roof has no deep soil, and it burns up quickly. The green herb here means a plant that is fresh and tender.

God speaks through Isaiah to the Assyrian king Sennacherib, who boasted of his conquests over Judah. God tells him that those victories happened because God had planned them long before. The king was not his own master; he was an instrument in God's hands.

For today: do not lose heart before powers that seem impossible to overcome, and do not become proud of your achievements. Every human power is temporary, and God still governs. Trust in Him with humility.
exp.16:39:
This verse says that the people did not pay attention to God's words. In place of obeying, they kept practicing what they had always done, their long-standing custom.

The writer of the book of Kings explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell before Assyria. God had reminded them of his covenant: not to fear other gods, but only the LORD. The verses that follow tell that the nations placed in that land worshiped the LORD, but also their idols. In other words, they mixed the two, and they passed this on to their children.

Old customs can weigh more than the Word of God. Today we can ask ourselves: what habit or tradition do I keep only because I have always done it? Let us ask God to help us obey him with a whole heart, without dividing our loyalty.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that God is going to provide water in an unexpected way. There will be no wind and no rain, yet the valley will be filled with water. People will drink from it, and so will the beasts of burden and riding animals, along with the livestock of the field such as sheep, cows, and other animals.

The prophet Elisha speaks in God's name. Three kings, those of Israel, Judah, and Edom, were marching with their armies against Moab and found themselves without water in the desert. Elisha asked for a musician, and then he sensed that God was speaking. He told them to dig ditches, an act of faith before they saw the answer.

For today: when you cannot see how God is going to meet your need, obey what he does ask of you, even when it seems small. He can work in ways you do not expect.
exp.2:17:
It says that for God this is an easy thing, a small matter, to give them water in the desert. And it does not stop there: it also promises to deliver the Moabites into the hands of the allied kings. The phrase "light thing" means a simple matter, nothing difficult for Him.

The prophet Elisha speaks in the name of God. The kings of Israel, Judah and Edom were marching with their armies without water, on their way to fight against Moab. They consulted Elisha, and he gave this word out of respect for Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. God first provided water and then promised victory.

For today: when you face something that seems impossible, remember that for God it is not too great. Obey what He shows you, even when you do not yet see the answer, and trust that He can work in His own way and in His own time.
exp.7:10:
This verse tells how Elisha, the man of God, looked steadily at Hazael without looking away for a long while, and then he wept. The phrase about fixing his gaze means that he looked at him firmly. The phrase about a long while means for a considerable time.

King Ben-hadad was ill and sent Hazael with a gift to ask whether he would recover. Elisha gave an answer that seems misleading: that the king would live, but that God had shown him that he would die. Then, as he looked at Hazael, Elisha wept because God showed him the terrible harm that Hazael would do to Israel as future king. Some believe that Elisha also saw the wickedness in Hazael's heart.

For today: God's servants feel pain at the suffering of others. Let us ask God for a sensitive heart, one that weeps with those who suffer and is not indifferent to injustice.
exp.19:18:
Hezekiah answers Isaiah that the message from God is good, meaning just and acceptable. Then he asks whether at least there will not be peace and security ("truth" here means stability) during his lifetime.

Isaiah had just announced that Babylon would carry off the treasures of the kingdom and some of the king's descendants, because Hezekiah had shown everything to Babylonian envoys. Hezekiah accepts God's judgment. Some see in his question humility and gratitude; others see a certain self-interest, because he thinks only of his own time. The text does not settle the matter, and it can be read in either way.

For today: we can accept God's correction without arguing against it. We should also think beyond our own comfort, seeking to leave those who come after us a firm faith and a firm example.
exp.10:15:
This verse says that the guards made way for Athaliah, the queen, and led her along the way by which the horses came into the king's house. There they killed her. "Let her pass" is the sense of making way for her; "the horsemen" are the riders or the royal cavalry.

It is part of the account of Jehoiada, the priest, who protected the young Joash, the rightful heir of David. Athaliah had seized the throne and had ordered the royal family put to death. Jehoiada commanded that she not be killed inside the temple, so as not to defile the holy place. Then he renewed the covenant between the people and God.

For today: even when an injustice must be corrected, it is good to act with respect for what is sacred and with order. May God help us to seek justice without losing reverence or integrity.
exp.18:32:
It says that the king of Assyria will go back the same way he came. He will not be able to enter Jerusalem.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. King Hezekiah was surrounded: the Assyrian army, led by Sennacherib, threatened Jerusalem and mocked the trust placed in God. Hezekiah had prayed asking for help. This is God's answer. Afterward, the text tells that an angel of the Lord struck the Assyrian camp in a single night.

When you face something that seems bigger than you, do what Hezekiah did: bring it to God in prayer with sincerity. He knows the outcome of your situation and can act in his way and in his time. Trust his word, even if you do not yet see the result.
exp.23:16:
This verse tells that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, placed Mattaniah, uncle of Jehoiachin, the king he had taken captive, as king over Judah. He also changed his name to Zedekiah. The change of name showed that the new king depended on Babylon.

Here the one speaking is not a character but the author of the book, who recounts the events. Judah had just been defeated, and Babylon had carried off the leaders and the strong men. The new king was only a subject ruler. The text that follows says that he did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and this prepares the way for the final fall of Jerusalem.

For today: human powers come and go, but God remains the true Lord. Trust in Him more than in the stability of any government or in your own position, and seek to obey Him even in difficult times.
exp.12:3:
This verse says that Jehoahaz, king of Israel, prayed before God, and that God heard him. God saw the suffering of his people, because the king of Syria was mistreating them. The phrase "before the face of the Lord" means "in the presence of the Lord." The word "oppressed" means that they were being crushed and made to suffer.

The account tells the story of Israel under King Jehoahaz. He had done evil and followed the sin of Jeroboam, and for that reason God allowed Syria to rule over Israel. Even so, in his distress, Jehoahaz cried out to God. The text does not say how deep his repentance was, and in fact the people continued in their sins. But God responded out of compassion for his suffering people.

For today: God listens when we call out to him, even in the middle of our failures. You can come to him with sincerity, without waiting until you are perfect. His compassion also invites us to truly return to him.
exp.23:11:
This verse says that King Jehoiachin of Judah surrendered to the king of Babylon. He went out of Jerusalem together with his mother, his servants, his princes, and his officers of the court. The king of Babylon took him captive in the eighth year of the Babylonian king's own reign. The word "took" in the verse means that he seized him as a prisoner.

The book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah, and here the author recounts the first great blow of Babylon against Jerusalem, around 597 B.C. Jehoiachin had reigned only a very short time. The text that follows explains that all of this happened "as the Lord had said," that is, as judgment for the disobedience of the people and their kings.

God is faithful to his word, both in warnings and in promises. Today we can take his voice seriously and turn back to him in time, before the consequences arrive.
exp.12:6:
This verse says that the army of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, was nearly wiped out. Only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers were left. The king of Syria had destroyed them and had left them like dust, trampled underfoot with no value, like the dust that is crushed under the feet.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. He is explaining why Israel was so weak. This happened under Jehoahaz, who did what was evil in the sight of God. The text shows that Syria oppressed Israel, although later God gave them a deliverer. The book does not clearly say who that deliverer was, and scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: when we feel reduced to almost nothing, we can remember that God still hears us and can bring a way out, even when our own failures have contributed to the problem. It is better to return to Him soon.
exp.24:10:
This verse says that Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard of the king of Babylon, carried away captives in three groups: the people who were left in the city, those who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the multitude.

The book of 2 Kings is a historical narrative. Here the author recounts the fall of Jerusalem around 586 BC. After years of warnings from the prophets, Judah suffered exile. Nebuzaradan does not speak; the text only reports what he did. The verses that follow show that he left behind the poorest people to work the land.

For today: God is in earnest, but even in judgment he does not wholly abandon his people. Let us listen to his voice in time and return to him with humility.
exp.23:15:
This verse tells that the king of Babylon carried away as captives all the fighting men of Judah: seven thousand men of might, along with a thousand craftsmen and metalworkers, and all the strong men fit for war. The phrase "craftsmen" here can refer to skilled workers or builders, and "smiths" to those who worked metal, which was useful for making weapons. The numbers are given differently in other passages, and this is usually explained by different ways of counting.

It is part of the historical account in 2 Kings. The narrator summarizes the first major deportation to Babylon, around 597 BC, under Nebuchadnezzar. Those who could defend or rebuild the land were taken, and so Judah was left weak. The author shows the consequences of years of turning away from God.

For today: what seems strong, such as money, talent, or resources, does not sustain us if we leave God. Today we can return to Him with humility and place our security in His hands.
exp.19:11:
This verse tells us that the king of Babylon, Berodach-baladan, son of Baladan, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah. He did this because he had heard that Hezekiah had been sick. The verse's own words "letters" and "present" name the messages and the gift that were sent. The name Merodach-baladan appears in other ancient sources as a Babylonian ruler, though some scholars debate the details of his policy at that time.

The narrator of the book goes on to describe what happened after God healed Hezekiah and gave him the sign of the shadow. The messengers arrive at that moment of great favor. The verses that follow show that Hezekiah showed them all his treasures, and God, through Isaiah, warned him about the consequences. Some think Babylon was seeking an alliance, although the text does not say so clearly.

For today: moments of blessing and praise also test us. When God lifts us up, it is good to ask Him for humility and wisdom so that we do not trust in what we have, but give the glory to Him.
exp.9:31:
In that time, this verse says, God began to "cut" Israel short, that is, to reduce it or shrink it, the way a tree or a branch is cut back. Hazael, king of Syria, struck and took territory in all the borders of Israel.

The narrator of the book speaks after telling how Jehu ended the house of Ahab. God had praised him and promised him four generations of kings. But Jehu did not follow God with his whole heart and kept the sins of Jeroboam, the worship of the calves. That is why the text shows the consequences: Israel began to lose land, especially east of the Jordan.

For today: partial obedience is not enough. We can do a good work and still leave areas of our life unsurrendered. Let us ask God for a whole heart, that we may follow him in everything.
exp.3:28:
Elisha orders Gehazi, his servant: "Gird up your loins," that is, gather up your clothing and get ready to go quickly. The staff is a walking stick. He tells him to go without stopping to greet anyone, and to lay the staff on the face of the child.

Elisha speaks. The son of the Shunammite woman had died, and she went to find him in desperation. Elisha sends Gehazi with urgency. But the staff does not bring the child back to life, and the mother insists that Elisha himself go. The Bible does not explain why Elisha did this, and it has been understood in several ways.

For today: when someone suffers, act promptly and with total commitment. But remember that tools or rituals do not replace God's presence and prayer, because God is the one who gives life.
exp.9:5:
What it says: Jehu writes a second time to the leaders of Samaria. He asks them for a proof of loyalty: if they truly are on his side, they are to bring him the heads of the seventy sons of King Ahab, and to do it by the next day at Jezreel. The ones who raised and educated those young men are the ones he calls on to act.

Context: Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab, a judgment that had been announced earlier by prophets because of his wickedness and idolatry. The leaders, frightened, had already submitted to him. With this order, Jehu binds them to his cause and eliminates possible heirs. The Bible records the event; it does not say that every one of Jehu's methods was exemplary, and later Hosea 1:4 speaks of the blood of Jezreel.

For today: When fear governs us, we can obey someone we should not obey and do harm. Let us ask God for courage to be faithful to Him and not give in to unjust pressure.
exp.8:23:
He says that Jehu pulled his bow with full strength and shot Joram, king of Israel. The arrow entered his back, pierced his heart, and Joram died in his chariot. The verse of the wording is dropped here, since the reader's verse does not use those words.

Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab. Joram, son of Ahab and Jezebel, went out to meet him asking whether there was peace. Jehu answered that there could be no peace as long as the idolatry and witchcraft of Jezebel continued. Then Jehu explains that this fulfills God's word about the innocent blood of Naboth.

For today: God sees injustice, even when it takes years to be judged. There is no true peace if we continue in wrongdoing without repenting. We can trust that God is just, and for that reason it is wise to seek his forgiveness and to live uprightly.
exp.13:11:
This verse tells that the army of Judah was defeated by the army of Israel in battle. The soldiers ran away, and each one went back to his tent or home. The phrase "put to the worse" means that Judah lost.

Joash, king of Israel, had warned Amaziah, king of Judah, not to seek a fight. Amaziah had just won a victory over Edom and felt very strong. Joash told him to stay at home and not get himself into trouble. But Amaziah would not listen. After this defeat, Jerusalem suffered damage and lost its treasures.

For today: pride in a past success can blind us. When someone gives us sensible advice, it is wise to listen with humility before we enter a conflict we do not need.
exp.4:17:
Naaman asks God to forgive him for something he knows he will have to do. When the king of Syria, his lord, goes to the temple of Rimmon to worship, he will lean on Naaman's arm, and Naaman will have to bow down beside him. Here "servant" refers to Naaman himself, who speaks with humility. Rimmon was a Syrian god.

Naaman, a Syrian commander, has just been healed of leprosy and has promised to worship only the Lord. But he is still an official of the king, and his position requires him to accompany him. Elisha answers, "Go in peace." The text does not explain more, and interpreters understand it in several ways: as permission, or as trust that God would guide his heart.

Today we can learn to ask God for wisdom and forgiveness in difficult situations. It is good to have a sincere heart before God, without using this passage as an excuse to tolerate what we know is wrong.
exp.5:10:
This verse says that this verse describes the king of Syria becoming very anxious and upset about what was happening. His plans of attack kept failing again and again. So he gathered his servants, that is, his officials, and asked them: "Will none of you show me which of us is for the king of Israel?" The word "sore troubled" in the verse means shaken and confused.

The speaker is the king of Syria. He was at war with Israel and believed there was a traitor among his own people, because the king of Israel kept avoiding his ambushes. What he did not know was that God was warning Israel through the prophet Elisha, the man of God.

For today: even when the plans of the powerful seem to move in secret, God sees everything. We can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his people and guides us, even when we cannot see how he does it.
exp.22:2:
This verse tells that King Josiah stood by the pillar and, before the Lord, made a covenant to follow the Lord and keep his commandments, his testimonies (his teachings) and his statutes (his laws), with all his heart and all his soul.
