He promised to carry out the words of this covenant written in the book, and all the people joined in that commitment.

The narrator tells what Josiah, king of Judah, did. The book of the law had been found in the temple, and he read it to the people. Many understand it to have been all or part of Deuteronomy, though the text does not state this clearly. When they heard it, Josiah wanted to return to God, and for that reason he later removed the idols.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; we must respond with concrete decisions. Today you can choose one teaching from the Bible and begin to put it into practice with sincerity.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that King Menahem died. The phrase "slept with his fathers" is an old, gentle way of saying that someone passed away and was buried with his ancestors. After him, his son Pekahiah began to rule Israel.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the end of each reign. Menahem had paid a heavy tribute to the king of Assyria, collecting it from the wealthy people of Israel, in order to keep his throne. The text that follows makes clear that Pekahiah also did what was evil in the sight of God and followed the sins of Jeroboam.

For today: what we leave to those who come after us matters. Menahem passed on power, but also a bad example. We can ask ourselves what we are teaching by our lives to children, family members, and friends, and ask God for help in leaving a trace of faith and truth.
exp.17:23:
Here the spokesman for the king of Assyria mocks Judah. He says that they could not even defeat the least of the Assyrian officers, even if they trust in Egypt for chariots and horsemen.

"Turn away the face" means to force someone to retreat. A "captain" is a governor or military leader, and the "servants" here are officers or subjects.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a high-ranking officer of King Sennacherib, standing before the walls of Jerusalem. He wants to frighten the people and King Hezekiah into surrendering without a fight. He mocks their alliance with Egypt and also their faith in God. Later in the story, the account shows that God delivered Jerusalem.

Today it teaches us that voices of intimidation often exaggerate the power of our problems and minimize the power of God. Before you let fear defeat you, pray, remember the Lord's promises, and seek his help.
exp.17:0:
This verse tells us when Hezekiah began to reign over Judah, the southern kingdom. It was in the third year of Hoshea, who was king of Israel, the northern kingdom. Hezekiah was the son of Ahaz. The older spellings of the names are Hezekiah and Ahaz, and the phrase about beginning to reign simply means that he started to rule.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who is telling the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. Through dates he places each reign and compares them with one another. Here the presentation of Hezekiah begins, and the verses that follow say that he did what was right before God. Scholars debate how exactly some of the dates from this period fit together.

For today: although Hezekiah came from a father who had not honored God, he chose a different path. Your family background does not have to decide your future. Today you can choose to obey God and begin something new.
exp.18:24:
God asks the king of Assyria whether he has never heard that all of this was planned by Him long ago. What Assyria accomplished, such as destroying well-defended cities and leaving them as heaps of ruins, happened because God allowed it and directed it. The phrase "fenced cities" refers to cities with strong walls, and "ruinous heaps" means piles of rubble.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah to Sennacherib, king of Assyria. He mocked the Lord and boasted of his conquests as if they were his own achievement. Jerusalem was threatened, and God answers by reminding him that he is not the master of history.

For today: when you see power, success, or injustice around you, remember that God remains above all things. Do not let yourself be intimidated or filled with pride over your achievements. Trust in Him and stay humble.
exp.8:1:
Elisha gives instructions to a young prophet. When he arrives at Ramoth-gilead, he must look for Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi. He must make him get up from among his companions and take him to an inner room. A private room, set apart, where no one would see or hear what was about to happen, was meant by the word for it in the verse above.

Elisha speaks on behalf of God. Israel lived under the dynasty of Ahab, marked by idolatry and violence. God decided to anoint Jehu as the new king. It was done in private and in haste, because the moment was delicate and dangerous.

God works with order and wisdom, and often uses simple and little-known people, like this young messenger. Today we can learn to faithfully obey what God entrusts to us, even when it seems small, without needing recognition or understanding everything.
exp.3:34:
He says that Elisha got up, walked back and forth through the house, went up again, and stretched himself out on the child once more. Then the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes. "Walked back and forth" means he walked here and there, and "stretched himself" means he lay down stretched out over him.

A woman from Shunem had welcomed Elisha with kindness, and God had given her a son. The child suddenly died. She sought out the prophet, and he, after praying to the LORD, acted. The account does not explain why Elisha walked through the house or what the number seven means; it only tells that God brought the child back to life.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, keep praying and do not give up quickly. God can work in ways we do not expect, and sometimes he asks us to persevere while we wait for his answer.
exp.7:0:
Elisha speaks to the woman whose son had been brought back to life. He tells her to get up and go with her whole household to live wherever she can, because God has called for the famine, that is, he has sent it. That famine would come upon the land for seven years.

Elisha was a prophet in Israel. This woman, the Shunammite, had welcomed him with kindness, and God worked a miracle with her son (2 Kings 4). Now the prophet looks after her by warning her of the danger. She then obeyed and went to the land of the Philistines. The Bible does not explain why she chose that place.

For today: when God gives us a warning, it is wise to act with faith and obedience, even when it is hard to leave what is familiar. Trusting God also includes preparing ourselves with wisdom.
exp.11:10:
This verse describes how the money that people brought to the temple was used. Once it had been counted, it was handed over "into the hands of them that did the work", meaning the men in charge of directing the repairs. They used that money to pay the carpenters and builders who were repairing the house of the Lord.

The passage is not a speech but a narrative. It takes place in the time of King Joash of Judah, when the temple had fallen into disrepair. The priest Jehoiada placed a chest to collect the offerings, and the money was counted carefully and used only for the repairs. The text shows a transparent handling of what was given to God.

For today: if we handle money belonging to the church or to other people, we should do so with order, clarity, and honesty. Serving God also includes taking good care of what others entrust to our hands.
exp.17:19:
He says that Hezekiah is speaking only "mere words," that is, empty talk, when he claims to have a plan and strength for war. Then he asks: "On what do you rely?" since he has rebelled against Assyria. "Strength" means power or courage.

The speaker is Rabshakeh, a high-ranking spokesman of the king of Assyria, during the invasion of Judah. He stands before the walls of Jerusalem, speaking to Hezekiah's officials. He wants to intimidate the people and make them doubt their king and their trust, even in God. Although his words are arrogant, they raise a real question: what is Judah leaning on?

Today, in times of pressure, it is easy to trust in plans, money, or our own strength. The question "On what do you rely?" invites us to examine the heart. May our trust not be only words, but a real faith in God that shows itself in prayer and obedience.
exp.15:9:
Here, the narrator tells us that King Ahaz traveled to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. There he saw an altar that caught his eye, and he sent the priest Urijah a drawing and an exact model so that it could be copied.

It is the narrator of Kings who tells this story. Ahaz, king of Judah, was under the protection of Assyria, which had defeated Damascus and killed Rezin. Ahaz had paid for that support with silver and gold from the temple. Now, admiring a foreign altar, he wants to bring it to Jerusalem. The account presents this as a sign of his spiritual drift. Interpreters debate his exact motives, but the text shows that he copies what is foreign instead of following what God had commanded.

For today: let us make sure that what impresses us in the world does not replace what God has already taught us. Before copying a fashion or custom, let us ask what his Word says.
exp.22:4:
He says that King Josiah removed the "camoreos," an old word for priests who served false gods. The kings before him had appointed them to burn incense on the high places. He also removed those who offered incense to Baal, to the sun, to the moon, to the signs of the zodiac (probably the constellations), and to all the host of heaven, that is, the stars.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Kings. Josiah had just renewed the covenant with God after finding the book of the law. Since the people promised to obey the LORD, he cleansed the temple and the land of the idolatry that had spread for years.

Today we can ask what things hold in our hearts the place that belongs to God. Like Josiah, it is wise to decisively remove whatever competes with him, and not merely to promise faithfulness with words.
exp.2:26:
The king of Moab, named Mesha, saw that he was losing the war and could no longer break through the siege. Then he took his eldest son, the heir to the throne, and offered him as a sacrifice on the city wall. A burnt offering is an offering that is burned up completely. After this, there was great anger against Israel, and the Israelite army withdrew and returned to their own land.

The narrator of the book tells this, not a character in it. Israel, Judah and Edom were attacking Moab, and the city of Kir-hareseth was the last refuge. The text does not say whose anger it was: some think it was the wrath of the gods of Moab, others that it was an indignation or terror felt by the Israelites themselves at such an act.

Today we see how far human desperation can go when people trust in false gods. In the face of our troubles, let us turn to the true God, who never asks us to sacrifice anyone, but offers us his grace.
exp.21:15:
God says, through the prophetess Huldah, that he is going to bring disaster upon Jerusalem and its people. That disaster matches what the book the king Josiah had read says.

The book found in the temple, which many understand to be part of the Law (probably Deuteronomy, though the text does not say so with certainty), alarmed King Josiah. He sent his men to consult Huldah. She answered with the word of God: the people had abandoned the Lord and worshiped other gods, and the consequences warned of in the Law were real.

For today: God speaks in earnest, and his Word deserves to be heard with humility. If reading it confronts us, we should not ignore it; let us draw near to God with sincerity, as Josiah did.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that, although King Amaziah did good things, he did not remove the high places. The high places were raised sites where people worshipped, and there the people kept offering sacrifices and burning incense. The phrase "even so" shows that his obedience was real but incomplete.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. Amaziah reigned in Judah and followed the example of his father Joash, who also did what was right but left those places in place. The law called for worshipping God in the place He would choose, and the high places mixed that worship with questionable practices.

For today: it is not enough to obey God in almost everything. Ask Him to show you any habit or high place you are still tolerating, and surrender it to Him with humility.
exp.9:10:
It says that Jehu finished off all who remained of Ahab's family in Jezreel. He also killed his great men (the important leaders), his relatives, that is, his close friends, and his priests. He left no one alive.

Jehu had been anointed to punish the house of Ahab for its wickedness and idolatry. Earlier, God had announced this through Elijah. Jehu tells the people that this fulfills the word of the LORD. Interpreters debate whether Jehu acted only out of obedience or also out of ambition, since God later judges him for his violence in Jezreel (Hosea 1:4).

For today: God always keeps what he says, but we must obey him with a sincere heart, not for our own interests. Let us examine our motives when we serve him.
exp.11:1:
It says that King Joash did what pleased God, but with a condition: as long as the priest Jehoiada guided him. The phrase "did that which was right in the sight of the Lord" means that he acted rightly according to God, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of 2 Kings, who summarizes the reign of Joash. Joash came to the throne as a child, and Jehoiada had protected and trained him. The text that follows shows that his obedience was not complete, since the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places. Some think the phrase suggests that Joash changed after Jehoiada's death, and other biblical passages confirm this.

For today: thank those who guide you in faith, but make sure your love for God is your own. Ask God that your obedience does not depend only on other people, but on your personal relationship with Him.
exp.9:11:
And he arose and departed, and came to Samaria. And as he was at the shearing house in the way, this verse tells that Jehu set out and headed for Samaria. On the road he came to a place called the shearing house of the shepherds, a place where sheep were sheared, that is, where the wool was cut from the sheep.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Jehu had just put to death the family of Ahab, and the text stresses that in this way what God had said through Elijah was being fulfilled. This journey is one more step on his path, and at that place the next encounter with the relatives of Ahaziah takes place. Some scholars think the place had a proper name; others think it was simply a shepherds' house.

For today: God keeps his word, though it may take time. But we must be careful and not use religious zeal as an excuse for violence. Let us seek God's guidance with humility.
exp.5:7:
The verse tells us that the king of Syria was at war with Israel. He gathered his servants, that is, his advisers and officers, and asked them where he should set up his camp, meaning the place where his army would secretly position itself to prepare an ambush.

The writer of the book now presents a new scene. Before this, the prophet Elisha, called the man of God, had made an iron axe head float. Now it is shown that God was also revealing the enemy's secret plans to him, and so Elisha warned the king of Israel so that he would not fall into the trap. The text does not say that the Syrian king was going to attack by surprise, but the context suggests it.

For today: even when our plans or the plans of others seem hidden, God sees everything. We can trust that he cares for his people and ask him for wisdom to see danger in time.
exp.17:36:
This verse tells how three of King Hezekiah's officials, Eliakim, Shebna and Joah, returned to him with their clothes torn. Eliakim was the steward, or the one in charge of the palace household; Shebna was the scribe, or secretary; and Joah was the recorder, who kept the official records. They repeated to him the words of Rabshakeh, the spokesman of the king of Assyria.

Rabshakeh had challenged Jerusalem with mockery, saying that no god had delivered his people out of the hand of Assyria, and that the LORD would not deliver them either. Tearing one's clothes was a common way of expressing grief, distress or horror at a blasphemy. They had obeyed the king's order not to answer, and now they brought him the report.

When words reach us that frighten or wound us, we do not have to answer right away or argue. We can keep silent, bring the matter before the one who has authority, and best of all, lay it before God in prayer.
exp.18:12:
This verse is part of a message that the king of Assyria sent to Hezekiah, king of Judah. He mockingly asks where the kings of Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivah are. The point is that those cities were conquered, and their gods could not save them.

The one speaking is Sennacherib, through messengers. Assyria had conquered many peoples and was surrounding Jerusalem. With this letter he wanted to frighten Hezekiah and make him surrender. He placed the God of Israel on the same level as the idols of other nations. But Hezekiah did not respond with fear. He took the letter to the temple and spread it out before the Lord.

For today: when news comes that frightens you, or voices mock your faith, do as Hezekiah did. Bring your problem to God in prayer, honestly, and trust that he is Lord over all.
exp.20:11:
God announces that he is going to bring upon Jerusalem and Judah a disaster so great and so dreadful that whoever hears of it will be struck with horror. The phrase "both his ears shall tingle" means that the person's ears will ring from the shock; it is a way of saying the news will be terrible and hard to forget.

The Lord speaks through his prophets. King Manasseh led the people into idolatry and very wicked practices, even worse than those of the Amorites, the peoples who had lived in the land before. God had been patient, but this judgment shows that the sin of the king and the people had serious consequences.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also warns us in time. If today you feel that he is calling you to correct something, do not ignore it; come to him with humility and change direction while there is still opportunity.
exp.17:16:
The verse tells how the king of Assyria, Sennacherib, sent three of his senior officers from Lachish with a great army toward Jerusalem. Their titles were Tartan, Rabsaris and Rabshakeh. They stopped by the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller's field, the place where the cloth-washers worked.

King Hezekiah of Judah had already paid tribute to Assyria with silver and with gold from the temple. Even so, Assyria sent this army to press him. The one who speaks next is Rabshakeh, who gives a speech meant to intimidate and to break the people's confidence. Some scholars think those names were titles and not personal names, though this is not entirely certain.

When someone presses us, the pressure does not always ease even if we give in. Hezekiah learned that human solutions were not enough. Today we can bring our fears to God first and trust in Him.
exp.13:23:
He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, the first king of the northern kingdom, who led the people into sin. To lead the people into sin means that he took them into idolatry, since Jeroboam set up golden calves for them to worship. To turn away means to depart from or stop doing something.

The narrator of the book of Kings judges each king by how faithful he was to God. Here he summarizes the reign of Jeroboam II, which was long and prosperous politically. Even so, the text says that spiritually he continued on the evil path. The verses that follow show that God, out of compassion, used this king to restore the borders.

For today: success or comfort does not prove that we are right with God. It is worth examining whether we follow inherited customs or mistakes, and asking God to help us change course.
exp.22:7:
He brought together the priests who served in the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places where they had burned incense. This covered the whole kingdom, from Geba in the north to Beersheba in the south. He also tore down the altars that stood at the gate of Joshua, the governor of the city. To "defile" here means to make them unfit for worship.

This passage is the narrator of the book of Kings speaking. It describes the great reform of Josiah, carried out after the book of the law was found in the temple. The people had mixed the worship of God with the practices of other gods, and the king wanted to return to faithfulness to the covenant.

For today: it is not enough to leave the wrong things half done. Josiah cleared out even the corners. Let us ask God to show us hidden habits or idols in our lives, and let us remove them with determination, not only the most visible ones.
exp.3:10:
This verse tells how Elisha arrived one day at Shunem, went into the room that had been prepared for him, and rested there. The word "turned" means he went in to lie down to rest, and the "chamber" is a small room, a little upper room in the house.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the story. Elisha was the prophet who often passed through that town. A woman of Shunem, who saw in him a man of God, persuaded her husband to build him a simple room with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp. The text now shows that her kindness was truly useful, and that is why Elisha later wants to thank her.

For today: a simple act of hospitality, such as offering a place of rest to someone who serves or who is weary, can be a real way of honoring God. You do not need to do something great; it is enough to see a need and respond with care and generosity.
exp.9:35:
This verse says that Jehu ruled over Israel for twenty-eight years, and that his capital was Samaria. It is a short fact that closes the account of his reign.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks, summarizing the life of each king. Jehu had been anointed to put an end to the house of Ahab and to the worship of Baal. Even so, the passage before this verse tells us that he did not turn away from the golden calves of Jeroboam, nor did he keep the law of the Lord with his whole heart. His reign was long, but it was marked by a partial obedience.

For today: it is not enough to start well or to succeed for a long time. God looks at a heart given over completely. We can ask ourselves whether, in some area of our lives, we are obeying only halfway.
exp.11:18:
This verse is a closing phrase. The author says that the rest of what King Joash did is recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. With that, he shows us that there were other official records, which we no longer have today, and that here only the most important things were summarized.

The narrator of the book of Kings speaks here. We do not know with certainty who wrote it. Just before this, he tells how Joash, threatened by Hazael of Syria, took the treasures of the temple and the palace to buy his withdrawal. Then comes his death at the hands of his servants. It is a sad ending for a king who began well.

For today: our lives also will be written down. More than our achievements, what matters is whether we remain faithful to God to the end. Let us ask Him to sustain us, so that we do not trust in quick solutions, but in Him.
exp.18:23:
This verse says that the king of Assyria boasts of having dug wells in foreign lands and drunk their waters. He also claims that with the soles of his feet he dried up all the rivers of besieged places, that is, of fortified or walled cities. It is exaggerated language meant to say that nothing can stop him. Some translations render the last phrase differently, and some speak of the rivers of Egypt.

The prophet Isaiah passes on to Hezekiah God's answer to King Sennacherib. Sennacherib had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the Lord. Here God quotes the proud words of the king to show that his arrogance is in fact an insult against the Holy One of Israel.

For today: when we achieve something, it is easy to believe it was only by our own strength. This passage invites us to thank God for our accomplishments and to live with humility, remembering that He rules over all human power.
exp.23:13:
This verse tells that the king of Babylon carried away into exile almost all of Jerusalem's leaders and its most capable people: princes, mighty men of valour, craftsmen and smiths. Only the poorest of the people were left behind. The word "craftsmen" probably refers to skilled workers or specialists; the smiths were those who worked metal, important for making weapons. The number of ten thousand is explained in different ways, and the text gives other numbers further on, so these are probably counts of different groups.

The narrator of the book describes the first great deportation to Babylon, around 597 B.C., when King Jehoiachin surrendered. The author shows that this was no accident: it happened as the LORD had said, as a consequence of the people's long disobedience.

For today: God takes our decisions seriously, but he also remains faithful in the midst of the consequences. If you are going through a loss today, return to God with sincerity. He can use even the most humble, like those who were left behind, to continue his work.
exp.9:13:
Jehu orders that forty-two men be taken alive, and then they are put to death beside the pit of the sheepshearing house, a place where sheep were sheared. "Slaughter" here means killing by cutting the throat. Not one of them was left alive.

Jehu had just been anointed king of Israel to bring an end to the house of Ahab. He had already killed Joram, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah. These men were relatives of Ahaziah, and they came to greet him without suspecting anything. The Bible does not explain here whether God commanded this killing; later, Hosea 1:4 seems to criticize the blood that Jehu shed.

For today: religious zeal, even with good intentions, can become cruel and out of control if it is not submitted to God's mercy and truth. Before acting with force in God's name, it is wise to examine our hearts.
exp.19:19:
This verse is a final summary of the reign of Hezekiah. It says that the rest of his deeds, his might, and the work of the pool and the conduit, which brought water into the city, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. The word "conduit" refers to a channel or tunnel for water, and "might" means strength or power.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who closes the account of this king. Many believe the conduit is the tunnel that carried water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem, perhaps to withstand a siege, though the text gives no further detail. Earlier, Hezekiah had calmly accepted the hard word from Isaiah.

For today: our works also stand as a testimony. Let us prepare with wisdom and faithful labor, but let us remember that the most important thing is to trust God and accept his word, even when it is difficult.
exp.9:33:
This verse is a closing formula that repeats throughout the book of Kings. It says that the rest of Jehu's deeds, all that he did, and his might, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. That book is not preserved today, so we do not know for certain what it contained.

The narrator of the book of Kings summarizes here the reign of Jehu, which lasted twenty-eight years. Just before this, he tells how God began to cut Israel short, that is, to reduce and weaken it, when Hazael, king of Syria, took territories east of the Jordan. The author refers readers to other records to show that his own account is selective and highlights what matters spiritually.

For today: a person's fame and achievements are written down in some record, but what truly counts is how we responded to God. Ask yourself whether your life, beyond what you accomplish, reflects sincere obedience to the Lord.
exp.23:19:
This verse says that God's anger fell on Jerusalem and Judah, until the people were cast out from his presence, that is, carried off into exile far from the land and the temple. Zedekiah then rebelled against the king of Babylon.

The author of the book, whom Jewish tradition associates with Jeremiah though this is not certain, summarizes the final days of Judah. Zedekiah was the last king, placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar. Rebelling broke an oath made in the name of God, and that led to the fall of Jerusalem. The text presents the exile as the consequence of years of wickedness, not of a single mistake.

For today: God speaks to us patiently before the consequences arrive. If you feel that He is correcting you in some area, do not harden your heart. Listen to Him today, acknowledge your error, and change your course.
exp.13:16:
This verse states a simple chronological fact: Amaziah, king of Judah, lived fifteen more years after the death of Jehoash, king of Israel. It is a straightforward dating detail. The name Jehoahaz, the father of Jehoash of Israel, should not be confused with Jehoash, the father of Amaziah, king of Judah.

The book of Kings tells this history the way a narrator reviews the reigns of the kings. Earlier, Amaziah had challenged Jehoash of Israel, and Judah was defeated. This verse helps place the timeline: Amaziah outlived his rival, but his end was not peaceful, for he was later killed at Lachish after a conspiracy.

For today: living many years is not the same as living well. What matters is not how long our journey lasts, but how we walk it. We can ask God for humility and wisdom so that our years, few or many, are full of faithfulness.
exp.3:32:
This verse tells us that Elisha went into the room where the dead child was lying, shut the door so that he was alone with him, and prayed to the Lord. "Upon them twain" means upon Elisha and the child. The phrase "unto the Lord" refers to the name of God.

A woman from Shunem, who had taken good care of Elisha, lost her son, a child who had been born as a promise from God. She went to look for the prophet. Gehazi, his servant, had already tried to help with the staff (Elisha's walking stick), but nothing happened. Then Elisha himself went, and before acting, he sought God in private. The text does not explain why he shut the door; it could have been to pray without distractions.

When a situation overwhelms us, the first thing is not to look for formulas or quick solutions, but to step aside for a moment and pray. God listens and can act even where there seems to be no hope.
exp.2:2:
It says that Joram, king of Israel, clung to the sins of Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, and did not turn away from them. Jeroboam, son of Nebat, was the first king of the northern kingdom, and he set up golden calves for the people to worship (1 Kings 12:28-30). In this way he led Israel into sin.

The narrator of the book gives a summary of Joram's reign. Earlier he says that Joram removed the Baal statues that his father Ahab had made, which was a good thing. But he continued in the idolatry of Jeroboam. His reform was only partial, and for this reason the text judges him as someone who did evil in the sight of God.

For today: it is not enough to remove the most obvious things from our lives if we leave other things that keep us far from God. Let us ask Him to show us those less visible habits and help us to leave them behind completely.
exp.7:13:
Hazael leaves Elisha and returns to his master, King Ben-hadad of Syria. The king asks him what the prophet told him. Hazael answers, "He told me that you will surely recover." The word "master" here means his lord, the king, and the phrase "departed" means that he went away.

Ben-hadad was sick and had sent Hazael to consult Elisha. It is true that Elisha said the illness was not fatal, but he also revealed to Hazael that he would become king. Hazael gives only the reassuring part and keeps quiet about the rest. The next day the king dies, smothered with a wet cloth, and the text does not say who did it, though everything points to Hazael.

For today: a half-truth can be a lie. Let us be honest and complete when we speak, even when the truth is uncomfortable or leaves us looking bad.
exp.24:27:
It says that Evil-merodach, the king of Babylon, treated Jehoiachin, the former king of Judah, with kindness. The phrase "spoke kindly to him" means that he spoke to him with goodness and respect. In addition, he gave him a place of honor, higher than that of other kings who were also held captive or living there in Babylon. Here, "set his throne above" refers to position or rank, not just a seat.

The book of 2 Kings has no identified narrator; it tells the history of Judah up to its fall. This is the end of the book. Jerusalem had already been destroyed and the people were in exile. After so much sorrow, this small act of kindness toward a descendant of David appears. Many see it as a sign that God had not forgotten his promise to David, although the text does not say this directly.

Even in very dark times, God can open a door of hope. If you are going through a difficult season today, do not overlook the small signs of kindness: they can remind you that God is still at work.
exp.2:20:
When the Moabites heard that the three kings were coming to attack them, they gathered all the men able to fight. The phrase about those who could wear the belt of weapons refers to men old enough to carry arms, and the words "and upward" seem to mean from the youngest who could already bear arms up to the oldest. All of them took their stand at the border, ready to defend themselves.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom were marching against Moab, and they had run out of water. Elisha announced that God would provide water and victory. While Moab prepared with its own strength, it did not know that God had already acted.

For today: sometimes we prepare with great effort and fear, but God is already at work where we cannot see. Do your part with wisdom, but rest in the knowledge that He remains in control.
exp.19:8:
Isaiah answers King Hezekiah that God will give him a sign to confirm his promise to heal him. Then he asks him a question: does he want the shadow to move forward ten steps or to move back ten steps? The "shadow" refers to the shadow cast by a sundial, the dial of Ahaz. The "steps" were the marks or stairs on that dial; scholars do not agree on its exact form.

The prophet Isaiah speaks with King Hezekiah, who was seriously ill and had prayed to God with tears. God promised to heal him and add years to his life. Hezekiah asked for a sign, and God, through Isaiah, gives him a choice. It is a demonstration of God's kindness toward someone who needed encouragement to believe.

For today: when your faith feels weak, you can bring your doubts to God with sincerity. He is not angry with those who speak to him honestly, but knows how to strengthen the trust of his children.
exp.16:40:
This verse says that those people revered the Lord, yet at the same time they kept serving their idols. The word "feared" here means that they gave worship to him. The phrase "at the same time" describes this mixture, which passed from parents to children and grandchildren, and it continued the same "to this day," meaning up to the time of the writer.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, not a character in the story. He tells how Assyria brought foreign peoples to settle Samaria after carrying off Israel. They took on some of the worship of the Lord, but they did not give up their gods. The verse before reminds us that Israel also did not obey God. Scholars do not agree on the exact date of the phrase "to this day."

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give God a place of honor while letting other things rule our hearts. God asks for a sincere and complete faithfulness, not a half-hearted religion.
exp.18:26:
God tells the king of Assyria that He knows everything about him: when he sits down, when he goes out, and when he comes in, that is, his whole daily life. He also knows his rage and pride, directed against God.

Here God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had threatened Jerusalem and mocked the God of Israel. God answers his arrogance and reminds him that He directs history. Later He promises to restrain him and make him return the way he came.

For today: God sees everything we do and also what is done against his people. If today you feel threatened or treated unjustly, you can pray with confidence, knowing that nothing escapes God and that He acts with justice in his time.
exp.1:19:
Elisha asks for a new jar, that is, a clay vessel that no one has used, and for salt to be put in it. "They brought it to him" means they brought it to him right away, without arguing.

The people of Jericho had explained to Elisha, the prophet who followed Elijah, that the city was well located, but its water was bad and the land did not bear fruit. Elisha does not rely on the salt, which by itself does not purify a spring. It is a simple act, and in the next verse it is clear that the healing comes from God. Some think that the new vessel and the salt point to purity, but the text does not explain this.

Today: bring your problems to God honestly, as the people of Jericho did. Then obey, even when what He asks seems small or illogical, trusting that the healing comes from Him.
exp.13:14:
This verse is a closing formula. The author says that the rest of the deeds of Jehoash, king of Israel, including his war against Amaziah of Judah, are recorded in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That book is not the Bible we have, and it has not been preserved.

The speaker is the author of 2 Kings, who summarizes the reigns and refers readers to other records for more detail. He has just told how Jehoash defeated Amaziah, broke down part of the wall of Jerusalem, and carried off treasures from the temple. Then Jehoash dies. Scholars do not know with certainty who wrote those records.

For today: our lives too will one day be summed up. More than fame or power, what matters is living with humility and faithfulness to God, because He sees everything we do.
exp.1:11:
Elisha sees Elijah being taken up to heaven and cries out, "My father, my father!", calling him the chariot and horsemen of Israel. After that he no longer sees him. Then he takes hold of his own clothes and tears them in two pieces.

Elisha, the disciple of Elijah, speaks here. He had asked for a double portion of his master's spirit. Tearing one's clothes was a common way of showing deep grief. Calling him "father" shows affection, and "chariot of Israel" suggests that Elijah, through his prayer and his ministry, protected the people more than an army would. Then Elisha picks up the mantle and carries on the mission.

For today: it is natural to weep when someone who guided us in the faith is gone. But after weeping, Elisha gets up, takes the mantle, and trusts in the God of Elijah. Let us honor those who taught us, and let us move forward trusting in God.
exp.24:18:
When Jerusalem fell, the captain of the Babylonian guard seized several important men who were still in the city: an officer placed in charge of the soldiers, five men who stood close to the king, the chief secretary who enlisted and kept records of the army, and sixty men from the people of the land. The officer in charge of the soldiers was a military leader, and the king's close attendants were those who were always at his service.

The writer of Kings recounts the end of the kingdom of Judah, around 586 BC. Nebuzaradan, commander of Babylon's guard, went after the political and military leaders to take away any strength for further rebellion. According to the next verse, they were brought before the king of Babylon and put to death at Riblah. The book presents this as the result of the people's long disobedience.

For today: God takes justice and faithfulness seriously, but his word also calls us to return to him. Today we can examine whether we are listening to his voice in time, without waiting for the consequences to catch up with us.
exp.4:6:
He says that the king of Israel read the letter from the king of Syria and became deeply distressed. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief or alarm. He asked whether he was God, able to take life and give it, so that they would ask him to heal a leper. He thought the whole thing was a trap to start a fight with him.

The speaker is the king of Israel. The king of Syria had sent his general Naaman, who had leprosy, so that he might be healed. The king of Israel did not think of the prophet Elisha; he thought only about politics and the fear of war. Many understand that his reaction shows little faith.

When something frightens us, we tend to see only the problem and not God. Before we panic, we can stop and pray, remembering that God still has ways that we cannot see.
exp.17:35:
The text says that the people standing on the wall of Jerusalem kept quiet. They did not answer a single word to the insult they had just heard, because King Hezekiah had ordered them not to reply. "Kept quiet" means they stayed silent, and "order" is a command.

Rabshakeh, an official of the king of Assyria, was speaking loudly to frighten the people and make them doubt God. He compared the Lord with the gods of other nations that had fallen. Hezekiah knew that arguing on the wall would not help, so he asked for silence. The king's three envoys returned with their clothes torn, a sign of distress, and told him everything. Then Hezekiah brought the matter to God (2 Kings 19).

For today: not every attack deserves an immediate reply. When someone provokes you or fills you with fear, sometimes the wisest thing is to stay silent, breathe, and bring your worry to God in prayer before you speak.
exp.24:26:
This verse tells that thirty-seven years after Jehoiachin, king of Judah, was taken captive to Babylon, the new Babylonian king, Evil-merodach, lifted him out of prison. "Captivity" here refers to the exile, the time spent far from home as a prisoner. The phrase "lift up the head" means that he honored him and restored his dignity. This happened in the last month of the year, on the twenty-seventh day.

It is the end of the book of 2 Kings. The narrator, whose identity is not known for certain, has just recounted the fall of Jerusalem, the murder of Gedaliah, and the flight to Egypt. After so much disaster, the book closes with this small act of kindness. Many see it as a quiet sign that God had not forgotten the descendants of David, although the text does not say this in direct words.

For today: even in dark and long times, God can open an unexpected door. We keep trusting, with patience and hope.
exp.3:12:
Elisha tells his servant Gehazi to speak with the woman from Shunem. He instructs him to say that she has been very attentive and caring toward them, showing great concern for their needs. Elisha offers to help her: to speak on her behalf before the king or before the commander of the army. She answers that she lives content among her own people.

Elisha, the prophet, had been welcomed many times into this woman's home, and she had even prepared a small room where he could rest. He wants to repay her kindness. She asks for no favors or influence, because she feels secure and happy within her family and her community. Then Gehazi notices that she has no son.

For today: serve others generously without expecting a reward. And if someone wants to return your kindness, learn to receive it with humility and to live with a grateful and contented heart.
exp.8:29:
Jehu arrives at Jezreel after killing the kings Joram and Ahaziah. Jezebel learns of it, paints her eyes with a dark powder, a kind of ancient makeup, arranges her hair, and looks out from a window.

Here no one speaks; the text only narrates. Jezebel was the widow of King Ahab, famous for promoting the worship of Baal and for persecuting God's prophets. Jehu had been anointed to bring an end to the house of Ahab. Some think she adorned herself to keep up royal dignity in the face of her end; others, that she wanted to impress or provoke Jehu. The text does not make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we care more about appearance than about the heart. God asks us for humility and repentance, not a facade. Before it is too late, let us return to Him with sincerity.
exp.22:19:
It says that King Josiah killed the priests of the high places that were there in Samaria, the ones who led the worship of other gods on those altars. He burned human bones on the altars, and then he returned to Jerusalem. High places were shrines on the hills, and the priests who served there are the ones called "priests of the high places."

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Josiah leads a great reform to clear away the idolatry that Israel and Judah had practiced for generations. Burning bones defiled the altars according to the law, and it fulfilled what had been announced against the altar at Bethel. After the cleansing, he calls the people to keep the Passover. It is an account of severe judgment in its own time, not a model for acting with violence today.

For today: before seeking God with joy, it helps to remove whatever has taken His place in our hearts. Ask yourself what thing competes with your faithfulness to Him, and give it up with determination.
exp.4:16:
Naaman asks Elisha for permission to take back earth from Israel, as much as two mules can carry. ("Mules' burden" refers to the load that a pair of pack animals can carry.) He promises that from now on he will no longer offer burnt offerings or sacrifices to other gods, but only to the Lord.

Naaman speaks as commander of the army of Syria, just healed of leprosy in the Jordan. Elisha refused to accept his gift. So Naaman asks for something simple: earth. Many think he wanted to worship God on Israelite soil, since at that time people believed gods were tied to a particular land. The text does not explain this, so it is an interpretation.

For today: when God touches us, gratitude becomes a concrete decision. Naaman wanted to change his way of worshiping immediately. We can ask ourselves what real step we will take to honor God, even while we are still learning to follow him.
exp.18:9:
He says that the king of Assyria sends a message to Hezekiah, king of Judah. He warns him not to let himself be deceived by his God, that is, not to believe false hopes. Hezekiah was trusting that God would not allow Jerusalem to fall into the hands of Assyria, but the message presents this as an illusion. Being given into the hand of someone means coming under that person's power.

The one speaking is Sennacherib, king of Assyria, through his messengers. Rabshakeh, his officer, had returned to where the king was, who was fighting against Libnah. Upon hearing that an army was coming from Ethiopia, Sennacherib sent another letter to pressure Hezekiah into surrendering. His aim was to sow doubt and fear.

For today: when someone mocks your faith or tells you that God will not help you, do not stay alone with those words. Do as Hezekiah did: bring it to God in prayer and ask him to sustain you (2 Kings 19:14-15).
exp.1:1:
Elijah tells Elisha to stay behind in Gilgal, because the Lord is sending him on to Bethel. Elisha responds with an oath: "As the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth," which means "as surely as God lives and you live." He promises that he will not leave him. So the two of them go down together to Bethel.

Elijah is the prophet who will soon be taken up into heaven, and Elisha is his successor. We do not know for certain why Elijah asks him to stay; some think he is testing him, others that he wants to spare him the pain of the parting. Elisha does not separate himself from his master.

For today: faithfulness is shown by standing firm, even when it would be easier to fall behind. If you want to grow in faith, draw near to God and to those who teach you, and do not turn away when the road becomes hard.
exp.19:9:
Hezekiah replies that it is an easy thing for the shadow to move forward ten steps, because that is the normal course: the shadow always moves ahead. What is hard, and does not happen on its own, is for it to go back ten steps. The "steps" here are the marks or stairs on Ahaz's sundial.

Hezekiah was seriously ill, and God promised through Isaiah to heal him. He asked for a sign to confirm the promise. Isaiah let him choose between two options, and Hezekiah chose the harder one. Then Isaiah prayed, and God made the shadow turn back. How exactly this happened is not explained in the text.

God is not offended when we ask him for help to believe, and he usually responds with patience. But we can also trust that his word is firm even when we see no sign. Today, when faced with a promise that is hard to believe, we can pray honestly and ask him for faith.
exp.8:28:
This verse is the writer's note about when Ahaziah began to reign over Judah: in the eleventh year of Joram, son of Ahab, king of Israel. The word "eleventh" means the eleventh year.

The account in Kings is narrated by an author, not by a character in the story. The writer pauses the scene of Ahaziah's flight and death to place him in time. Later, 2 Kings 8:25 gives the year as the twelfth year. That difference is usually explained by different ways of counting the years of a reign, but this is not known for certain. Ahaziah was an ally of the house of Ahab and fell together with it.

For today: our friendships and alliances influence us more than we think. Let us ask God for wisdom to choose well those with whom we walk.
exp.10:3:
In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada sent for the commanders of the hundreds and the royal guards. He brought them into the temple, made a covenant with them, and had them swear their loyalty right there. Then he showed them the king's son.

The text is narrative; it is not a character speaking, but the narrator. Athaliah had been ruling for six years after having the royal family put to death. Jehosheba had hidden the young Joash in the temple. Jehoiada, husband of Jehosheba according to 2 Chronicles 22:11, decided to act with prudence and with the support of trusted leaders to restore the throne to the line of David.

For today: doing what is right requires patience, wisdom, and good allies. Jehoiada waited six years and acted at the right moment. If God places a difficult duty before you, pray, seek counsel from faithful people, and move forward with prudence, without rushing or giving up.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that the money collected at the temple must be handed over to the overseers of the work. They, in turn, will give it to the workers who repair the cracks or damage in the house of the Lord.

It is King Josiah who speaks, sending his scribe Shaphan to the high priest Hilkiah in the eighteenth year of his reign. The temple had fallen into disrepair, and the people had given offerings that the doorkeepers had gathered. The king wants that money to be used well to restore the place where God was worshiped.

For today: caring for what belongs to God calls for order, responsibility, and willing hands. Whether in the church or in our own lives, we can help repair what has been neglected, and manage honestly what others entrust to us.
exp.19:7:
Here the king Hezekiah asks Isaiah what sign he will have that God will truly heal him. He also wants to know whether in three days he will be able to go up to the temple, the house of the Lord. The words "sign" and "heal" are clear; "Hezekiah" is simply the same king's name.

Hezekiah was gravely ill, and God, through Isaiah, had promised him healing and fifteen more years of life. Although they had already placed a cake of figs on the sore, the king asked for confirmation. Some see in this a weak faith; others, a sincere desire for assurance. The text does not make it clear, and God does not rebuke him, but grants him the sign.

For today: when you doubt a promise of God, you can tell him honestly what you feel. He is patient with our questions and helps us to trust Him more.
exp.18:4:
This verse tells something simple: the servants of King Hezekiah came to where the prophet Isaiah was. The servants had been sent by Hezekiah with an urgent message, which is in the verse before.

Here the biblical account speaks. Jerusalem was threatened by the army of Assyria, and their envoy, Rabshakeh, had mocked the God of Israel. Hezekiah, distressed, did not rely only on his power as king. He sought a prophet and asked him to pray for the people who remained. Then Isaiah answered with a word from God: "Do not be afraid."

For today: when you feel surrounded by a great problem, do not carry the fear alone. Seek out someone of mature faith who will pray with you, and bring the matter to God yourself with sincerity.
exp.22:8:
The verse says that the priests who served at the high places, that is, the local shrines outside Jerusalem, did not come up to the altar of the Lord in the temple. Even so, they did eat unleavened bread together with their fellow priests. In other words, they did not regain their duties in worship, but they were looked after and given their provision.

The book of Kings here tells of the great reform of King Josiah, who cleared the land of idolatry and centralized worship in Jerusalem, following the law of Moses. Those priests had served at unauthorized altars, so they lost their place at the altar, but they were not abandoned.

For today: when God corrects a mistake, he may take away a place of service from us without taking away his care. Correcting firmly and at the same time caring kindly is a good example for the church and the family.
exp.16:17:
This verse says that God was very angry with Israel, the northern kingdom, and removed them from his presence. The phrase "removed them out of his sight" means that he drove them out of the land where God had placed them. Only the tribe of Judah was left, the southern kingdom.

The author of the book tells the story and explains why Israel fell to Assyria. Before this verse he lists their sins: they abandoned the commandments of God, made idols, worshiped Baal, and practiced divination. They also sacrificed their children in the fire. God had sent them warnings through his prophets, but they did not listen. Afterward, the text notes that Judah also did not fully obey.

For today: God is patient, but he takes our faithfulness seriously. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts. If he speaks to us, it is wise to return to him without delay.
exp.18:0:
When King Hezekiah heard the news, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the Lord. Tearing one's clothes and wearing sackcloth, a rough cloth, were signs of deep grief and humility. The Lord is the name of God.

The text tells what Hezekiah, king of Judah, did. He had heard the threats and mockery of the messenger of the king of Assyria, who scoffed at the God of Israel and threatened to destroy Jerusalem. Hezekiah did not respond with pride or with panic, but with brokenness, seeking God.

When bad news or a threat comes that is greater than we can handle, our first step can be to bring it before God. Before looking for a thousand solutions, we can come to Him with humility and sincerity, and ask for help from people of faith who will pray with us.
exp.15:16:
He says that King Ahaz dismantled part of the furniture of the temple. He cut off the borders of the bases (the bronze carts that held the basins or washstands), removed the basins, and took the "sea" (the large water basin for the priests) down from the twelve bronze oxen beneath it. He set it directly on the stone pavement.

It is a historical account, not a speech. Ahaz was a king of Judah who turned away from God and copied customs from Assyria. He had just replaced the altar of the temple with another one. The Bible says he did this "because of the king of Assyria," meaning out of pressure or in order to win his favor. The text does not detail all of his motives.

For today: when fear or pressure leads us to sacrifice what is sacred in order to please others, we end up losing what is valuable. Let us ask God for firmness so that we do not change what belongs to him.
exp.20:24:
This verse says that the rest of what King Amon did, everything he carried out, is recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah. The words "did" and "the rest" in the verse are the key words here, meaning his deeds and everything else about his reign.

The author of the book of Kings uses this formula when closing the account of each king. It tells us that he consulted official records from that period. That book was not preserved, and it is not the biblical book of Chronicles. Amon reigned only two years, did what was evil in the sight of God, and was killed in a conspiracy. Then his son Josiah took the throne.

Our lives also leave a record, and God knows it completely. Today we can ask what mark our daily decisions leave on our family and on others. Let us ask God for help to live in such a way that, when people remember us, they see faith, honesty, and love.
exp.3:31:
Its account says that Elisha came to the house of the Shunammite woman and found the child dead, lying on his bed. Some of the words are old: "come" means "having arrived", "behold" means "look" or "there he was", and "laid" means "lying down". The text embellishes nothing; it presents death as Elisha actually saw it.

The narrator then tells what happened after the mother insisted that Elisha go with her. Her son, born through a promise of God, had died. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, had gone ahead with the prophet's staff, but the child did not respond. Elisha does not arrive with a quick formula, but faces the situation up close.

For today: when you face something that seems without a way out, do not avoid it or cover it up. Bring it honestly before God and give time to prayer, because He can act where we see only loss.
exp.17:4:
This verse says that King Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. The phrase "put his hope" means that he leaned his whole life on God. It also says that, among all the kings of Judah, there was no one before him or after him who was like him in that trust.

The author of Kings, an unnamed narrator, tells the story of the kings of Judah. Here he explains why Hezekiah was so remarkable: he removed the forbidden places of worship and broke down the idols. He even broke in pieces the bronze serpent of Moses, called Nehushtan, because the people were worshiping it. Some see in the words "none like him" a comparison in terms of his trust, since the book says something similar about Josiah later on.

For today: trusting God sometimes means removing from our lives what we love or use in the wrong way, even things that were once good, so that nothing takes the place of God.
exp.16:31:
They said they feared the Lord, yet they appointed to the high places priests taken from among the common people, anyone at all, who were not chosen according to the law. There they offered sacrifices on their behalf. The high places were shrines set on elevated ground, where worship took place; common people means ordinary folk, not men chosen according to the law.

The author of the book of Kings tells what happened after the fall of the northern kingdom. Assyria brought settlers from several lands, and they mixed their own religion with the worship of the Lord. The narrator explains this to show that such divided worship was not true obedience, as he goes on to say: they did not truly fear the Lord.

For today: it is not enough to add God to our lives while still serving other things. Examine whether your faith shows in sincere obedience and in giving God first place.
exp.7:12:
Hazael is surprised by what Elisha tells him he will do. He asks, "But what, is thy servant a dog, that he should do this great thing?" Calling himself a "dog" was a way of saying that he felt insignificant and powerless. Elisha does not argue with him. He answers that the Lord has shown him that Hazael will be king over Syria.

Hazael was an officer of King Ben-hadad, and he had been sent to ask Elisha about his master's health. The prophet wept because he knew the terrible harm Hazael would do to Israel. The texts do not say that God forced him to be cruel; Elisha only reveals what would come. Afterward Hazael lied and killed Ben-hadad to take the throne.

For today: it is not enough to say, "I would never do that." Each of us can have a heart capable of causing harm if we give room to ambition. Let us ask God to examine our hearts and keep us from justifying evil.
exp.22:28:
Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, marched toward the river Euphrates to confront the king of Assyria. Josiah, king of Judah, went out to meet him, and Necho killed him at Megiddo.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings is speaking. Josiah was a faithful king who reformed the land, but before this, judgment on Judah had already been announced. The text does not explain why he went out to fight; some think he wanted to check Egypt, but the text does not make this clear. The report is brief and harsh.

For today: even good leaders and faithful people can face painful endings that we do not understand. Trust God without demanding complete explanations, and pray before entering battles that may not be yours to fight.
exp.12:21:
It says that Hazael, the king of Syria (also called Aram), made Israel suffer and oppressed the people of Israel throughout the reign of Jehoahaz.

The narrator of the book of Kings, who does not identify himself, summarizes here how Israel was doing. Years earlier, the people had turned away from God, and God allowed Syria to oppress them. This sentence sits between the story of the miracle at Elisha's tomb and the mercy of God that follows in the next verse. In this way it shows that the suffering was real, but it did not have the final word.

For today: even when we go through hard times, we can return to God with confidence. He sees our pain, He has compassion, and He does not abandon us completely.
exp.17:26:
Rabshakeh answers that his message is not only for Hezekiah's officials, but for all the people who are sitting on the wall. He tells them that they will suffer the worst if the city keeps resisting: they will have so much hunger and thirst that they will eat their own dung and drink their own urine.

Rabshakeh was a high spokesman of the king of Assyria, who had surrounded Jerusalem. The officials of Judah asked him to speak in Aramaic so that the people would not understand. He refuses on purpose and uses fear to break the morale of everyone, so that they will surrender.

For today: not everyone who speaks loudly tells the truth. When fear and threats press on us, let us remember that whoever intimidates wants us to doubt God. Before we react, let us pray and seek his Word.
exp.3:33:
Elisha goes up to the room where the dead child lies, and he stretches himself over him, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, and hands to hands. Little by little the child's body grows warm.

A woman from Shunem, who had generously hosted Elisha, had received a promised son through him. The child died suddenly. Elisha shuts the door, prays to the LORD, and then acts. The text does not explain why he did it this way; many see it as a gesture of total devotion and closeness. Life returns through the power of God, not through the method.

For today: when we pray for someone who is suffering, let us not do it from a distance. Let us pray with faith, and also draw near with presence, time, and care, knowing that only God gives life.
exp.4:18:
Elisha answers Naaman in few words: "Go in peace." Then Naaman went on his way for a short distance. The phrase about a short distance simply means he didn't go far. "So he departed from him" means that he took his leave and went away.

Naaman, a commander of the army of Syria, had just been healed of leprosy, and now he wanted to serve only the LORD. He asked for earth from Israel and voiced his concern: he would have to accompany his king into the temple of Rimmon. Elisha does not scold him or give him a list of rules. Some believe he blesses his sincerity; others think he simply leaves him in God's hands. The Bible does not explain it further.

For today: when someone begins to follow God, let us be patient and gracious. God continues to guide their heart, and it is not for us to demand perfect maturity all at once.
exp.10:9:
This verse tells how the priest Jehoiada gave the captains of the hundreds the spears (the "spears" and "shields" mentioned in the text) and the shields that had belonged to King David. These weapons were kept in the temple, the house of the Lord.

The account describes a very tense moment. Queen Athaliah had seized power in Judah, and Jehoiada had secretly protected the young Joash, the rightful heir of David's line. Jehoiada organized the guards to proclaim him king. By giving them David's weapons, he linked them to the legitimate royal house. The texts do not explain in detail why those weapons were there, so it is best not to add more.

For today: when we must do what is right in difficult times, God often uses faithful and prepared people. Serve with courage and order, using what God has already placed in your hands.
exp.12:7:
This verse is the formula the writer uses to close the reign of Jehoahaz. It says that the rest of his deeds, everything he did and his might (his acts of power or military strength), are written in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," a court record that we no longer have today.

The author of Kings narrates the history of Israel's kings and evaluates them before God. Jehoahaz followed the sins of Jeroboam, and his army was reduced by Syria. Even so, the text refers the reader to another book for further details and does not dwell on his achievements. Some think that his "might" is mentioned with a certain irony, since the kingdom was very weak, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: our accomplishments and our fame are recorded in human records, but what weighs most is how we live before God. It is worth asking ourselves whether our life, rather than impressing others, seeks to obey him.
exp.15:10:
This verse tells that the priest Urijah built a new altar, following exactly the pattern that King Ahaz had sent him from Damascus. He finished it before the king returned.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not God. Ahaz was king of Judah and was very unfaithful. He had asked the king of Assyria for help and, on seeing a pagan altar in Damascus, wanted to copy it for the temple in Jerusalem. Urijah, as a priest, was supposed to watch over the worship of the Lord, but he obeyed the king without objection. The text records no complaint from him.

For today: obeying those who have authority is good, but our first loyalty is to God. Before carrying out an order, let us ask whether it pleases the Lord, and have the courage to speak the truth with respect.
exp.17:17:
It says that the envoys of Assyria asked to speak with King Hezekiah, but he did not go out. He sent three of his officials: Eliakim, who was in charge of the palace (steward), Shebna, the secretary (scribe), and Joah, the one who kept the records and the affairs of the kingdom (recorder). The word "á" is the actual "a".

The narrator tells this scene during the invasion of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. Hezekiah had already paid a very high tribute, but Assyria still sent a great army. The Assyrian commanders stood before Jerusalem to frighten the city. The three men went out as representatives of the king, and soon Rabshakeh would begin to speak in order to shake the people's confidence.

For today: when strong pressure comes, do not face everything alone or on impulse. Seek counsel and faithful people, and remember that true confidence is tested when someone tries to shake it.
exp.13:7:
Amaziah, king of Judah, sends messengers to Jehoash, king of Israel. He says to him, "Come, let us look one another in the face." That is, "let us come and meet face to face." This is not a friendly invitation but a challenge to fight in battle.

Amaziah had just defeated the Edomites, and this filled him with pride. Many understand that he wanted to test his strength against Israel, his neighbor to the north. Jehoash answers him with a parable, warning him that his victory had made his heart proud and that he should not seek a harm that would ruin Judah too.

A success can become a trap if we believe ourselves invincible. When something goes well for us, let us give thanks to God and keep our humility. Before we get into an unnecessary conflict, let us think about who else we might drag down with us: family, church, or friends.
exp.8:35:
They came back and told him what was left of Jezebel's body. Then Jehu recognized that this fulfilled what the Lord had said through the prophet Elijah the Tishbite: the dogs would eat Jezebel's flesh in the territory of Jezreel.

The speaker is Jehu, whom God had anointed as king of Israel to put an end to the house of Ahab. Jezebel, Ahab's wife, had promoted idolatry and violence, as in the case of Naboth, whose vineyard in Jezreel was taken from him (1 Kings 21). Jehu sees in this end the fulfillment of a warning given years earlier.

For today: God keeps his word, even when it takes time. This invites us to take his warnings seriously and to trust that injustice will not have the final word.
exp.16:34:
This verse says that the Lord made a covenant with the people of Israel and gave them a clear command: they were not to fear other gods, nor bow down to them, nor serve them, nor offer sacrifices to them. "Fear" here means to revere and honor with deep respect. "Worship" means to prostrate oneself, and "sacrifice" means to offer gifts.

The author of the book explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell to Assyria. He recalls that God had commanded them to be faithful to Him. Then he speaks of the foreign peoples that Assyria brought into that land: they claimed to honor the Lord, but they also served their own gods. The text shows that God did not accept a mixed faith.

For today: review what things compete with God for your trust, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Ask Him for help to put Him first, not only in words, but in your daily decisions.
exp.19:4:
God tells Isaiah to go back to King Hezekiah and give him a message. God says he has heard Hezekiah's prayer, seen his tears, and will heal him. On the third day Hezekiah will be able to go up to the temple, the house of the Lord.

Hezekiah was seriously ill, and shortly before this Isaiah had told him he would die. The king wept and prayed, remembering that he had lived faithfully. Isaiah had barely left the palace when God spoke to him again. God presents himself as the God of David, recalling his promise to that royal line.

For today: we can pray honestly, even in tears, because God hears us and cares about our pain. He does not always answer in the same way or right away, but he always listens. If you are suffering today, bring your pain to him with confidence.
exp.17:28:
This verse says that the king of Assyria, through his spokesman, tells the people of Jerusalem not to let Hezekiah deceive them. According to him, Hezekiah will not be able to save them out of his hand. The word "deceive" means to make someone believe something false, and "deliver" means to rescue or save.

Rabshakeh, a high Assyrian official, speaks before the walls of Jerusalem. He speaks in Hebrew and out loud so that all the people can hear him. His aim is to frighten them and take away their trust in their king and in God, so that they will surrender without a fight. Later in the text, the account shows that God did watch over Jerusalem.

For today: when voices come to you saying there is no hope and that trusting God is a mistake, do not decide out of fear. Stop, pray, and compare what you are hearing with what God has promised in his Word.
exp.5:26:
The king answers the woman who is asking him for help: if the Lord does not save you, I cannot do it. He asks whether he could take anything out of the threshing floor, which is the granary or storehouse of grain, or out of the winepress, where the grapes were trodden to make wine. In other words, he has no food to give her.

The city of Samaria was under siege and the hunger was terrible. The woman cries out to the king as he passes by on the wall. Her words show her helplessness, although some read them also as bitterness toward God. Right after this, she tells him something horrifying.

For today: when you can no longer solve something with your own resources, turn to God with sincerity. And if someone asks you for help, do not stop at words; do what is within your reach.
exp.20:16:
This verse is the formula the writer uses to close Manasseh's reign. It says that the rest of his deeds, everything he did, and the sin he committed, are recorded in "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." That book was an official court record that has not survived to our day; it is not the book of Chronicles in our Bible.

The author of Kings speaks here, summarizing each reign and pointing to other sources for more detail. This comes right after describing Manasseh's wickedness: he shed much innocent blood and led Judah into sin. With this phrase his story is closed, and the account moves on to his death and to his son Amon.

For today: our choices leave a mark, especially on those who follow us. It is worth asking ourselves what influence we leave in our family, our work, and our church, and asking God to guide us to live in a way that blesses others.
exp.13:1:
This verse gives the basic facts about Amaziah, king of Judah: he was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddan, and she was from Jerusalem. The phrase "began to reign" means that he became king.

This book is a historical chronicle, so the one speaking is the narrator, not a character in the story. It presents each king with his age, the years of his reign, and his mother. Then it evaluates how he lived before God. Here the judgment of the verses that follow is being prepared: Amaziah did what was right, but not with a whole heart like David.

For today: God looks at a whole life, not only at the beginning or at the details of our résumé. We can ask ourselves whether we truly obey him, or whether we leave "high places" in the heart, habits we have not surrendered to God.
exp.11:20:
This verse names the two servants who struck down King Joash: Jozachar and Jehozabad. It says they struck him and he died. Then they buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Amaziah took the throne.

The words "they struck him" are the wording of the verse above, and "they buried him" is likewise just the verse's own phrase, so no separate explanation of them is needed.

The narrator of the book of Kings is summarizing the end of Joash's reign in Judah. Earlier, Joash had repaired the temple, but later he turned away (according to 2 Chronicles 24). The account in Kings does not fully explain the motives behind the conspiracy, so it is not wise to invent them. It only shows that his reign ended in violence, yet he was buried with the kings and the line of David continued.

For today: a good beginning does not guarantee a good ending. We can ask God for perseverance and stay close to Him every day, not only in moments of enthusiasm.
exp.4:9:
Elisha does not go out to receive Naaman; instead, he sends word through a messenger telling him to wash seven times in the Jordan River. He promises that his flesh will be healed and that he will be clean. The sentence explaining the old wording is removed, since the reader sees the King James text, which uses "flesh" directly and does not need a further gloss.

Naaman was a commander of the army of Syria, a foreigner who had leprosy, a disease of the skin. He had come with horses and chariots, expecting an important welcome. Elisha, a prophet of God, gives him a simple instruction. Afterward Naaman becomes angry because he expected something more spectacular.

God sometimes works through simple ways that wound our pride. Obeying what He directs, even when it is not what we imagined, opens the door to His blessing. Today we can ask ourselves: am I demanding that God act my way, or am I trusting what He has already told me?
exp.14:34:
This verse says that King Jotham did what was right before God, but the high places were not removed. These were places of worship on the hills where the people offered sacrifices and burned incense. It also says that Jotham built the higher gate of the temple in Jerusalem.

The book of Kings was written by an unknown author, who judges each king according to his faithfulness to God. Jotham was good overall, but the people still worshiped in places that the law of Moses did not approve, since the law called for worship at the temple. His work on the temple shows his concern for proper worship.

We can obey God in many areas and still leave one area untouched. Today it is good to ask him to show us that high place in our lives, that habit we tolerate, and to decide to surrender it to him with humility.
exp.12:24:
It says that Jehoash, king of Israel and son of Jehoahaz, defeated Ben-hadad, king of Syria and son of Hazael, three times. In this way he regained the cities that Syria had taken from his father in war.

The author of the book of Kings tells the story of Israel. Earlier, he explained that God was merciful to his people because of the covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Israel had suffered greatly under Hazael, and these victories show that compassion. Even so, the people remained far from God, and the text does not say that they had fully repented.

For today: God can restore what was lost, and he does so because of his faithfulness, not because of our merits. We can ask him for help with humility and give thanks for every recovery as a gift of his mercy.
exp.13:12:
It says that Jehoash, king of Israel, captured Amaziah, king of Judah, at Beth-shemesh. Then he went to Jerusalem and broke down part of its wall: from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate. It was four hundred cubits, about 180 meters approximately (a cubit measured close to 45 centimeters).

Breaking down the wall left the city without defense.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings speaks. Amaziah had challenged Jehoash to war and did not want to listen to his warning. Judah lost the battle, and its king was taken prisoner. Afterward Jehoash carried off treasures from the temple and the palace, along with hostages. The text shows the consequences of a pride that refuses to listen to counsel.

For today: before getting into a conflict, stop and listen to warnings and wise advice. Pride can leave us without protection and open breaches in the things we care for most.
exp.9:7:
