A messenger comes to Jehu to tell him that the heads of the seventy sons of King Ahab have arrived. Jehu orders them to be piled in two heaps at the entrance of the city gate and left there until morning.

Jehu, who had just been anointed to destroy the house of Ahab, had challenged the leaders of Jezreel and Samaria to show which side they were on. They killed the princes out of fear. The city gate was the public place where judgments were made and announcements were given. Jehu presented this as the fulfillment of God's word spoken through Elijah. His methods were violent, and later the text shows that his heart did not fully follow God.

God keeps what He says, but that does not justify everything people do. Let us ask God to give us sincere obedience and not only visible results.
exp.3:29:
The mother of the child says to Elisha, with an oath: "As the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee." That is, she swears by God and by the life of the prophet that she will not separate herself from him.

Her son, the one God had given her through Elisha, had just died. Elisha sent his servant Gehazi with the staff, but she was not satisfied with that. She wanted the prophet himself. Her insistence shows a faith that seeks God when everything seems lost. Afterward, the text tells us that the staff did nothing, and Elisha had to go in person.

For today: when pain comes, do not settle for half-measures, and do not turn away from God. Stay close to Him in prayer, with perseverance, even when you do not understand what is happening.
exp.5:32:
While Elisha was still speaking with the elders, the messenger arrived, and the man said, "This disaster comes from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?" Here "evil" means calamity or disaster, not wickedness.

Samaria was under siege and suffering a terrible famine. The king had sworn to kill Elisha, but Elisha already knew this and ordered the door shut. Many understand that the one speaking is the king, who arrives right behind his messenger. The text is not entirely clear, but the meaning is the same: it is the voice of despair and anger against God.

When suffering lasts a long time, it is easy to blame God and give up. But abandoning hope solves nothing. It is better to bring our complaint to God honestly and keep waiting on him, because in the next chapter he answers.
exp.7:24:
This verse tells us when Ahaziah began to reign over Judah. It was in the twelfth year of Joram, son of Ahab, who was king of Israel. Ahaziah was the son of Joram, the king of Judah. There are two kings named Joram: one reigned in the north (Israel) and the other in the south (Judah). The words "begin to reign" simply mean that he began to rule.

The author of the book of Kings, whose name is not given in the text, carefully records the reigns of both kingdoms. Here he notes that Ahaziah took the throne after his father. What follows explains that his mother was Athaliah and that he followed the evil ways of the house of Ahab, because he was related to it through her.

For today: close influences, such as family and friends, shape our decisions. Let us seek to surround ourselves with what draws us closer to God, and ask him for wisdom to choose well.
exp.20:19:
He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father Manasseh had done. The phrase "in the sight of the Lord" means "in the eyes of the Lord," that is, according to God's judgment. The verses that follow explain that Amon worshiped idols and turned away from the way of the Lord.

The Book of Kings does not have an author identified with certainty. Here the narrator evaluates each king of Judah according to his faithfulness to God. Amon was twenty-two years old and reigned only two years. His father Manasseh was known for his idolatry, although another account (2 Chronicles 33) tells that in his old age he humbled himself before God. Amon followed the bad part of his father's example, not the repentance.

Children often imitate what they see at home. If there are harmful habits in your family today, you are not obligated to repeat them. You can choose to follow God, and also set an example that others can imitate without risk.
exp.8:4:
The passage tells that the young prophet arrived at Ramoth-gilead and found the army's officers sitting together. He said he had a message and asked for the commander. Jehu wanted to know which of them he meant, and the young man answered, "To you." "Prince" here means an officer or military commander. "Servant" is a young helper.

The prophet Elisha had sent this young man with an order from God: to anoint Jehu as king of Israel. Anointing with oil was the sign that someone had been chosen to reign. The young man had to act quickly and then leave. That is why he asks a direct question to single out Jehu from the others.

For today: God knows how to call people by name, even in the middle of a crowd. If He speaks to you, listen carefully and respond with obedience, without letting noise or doubts distract you.
exp.6:8:
Four men with leprosy realize that the enemy camp is empty and that they have taken food and treasure for themselves. They say to one another that they are not doing right by keeping quiet on a day of good tidings, that is, of good news. They fear that if they wait until morning, some mischief will come upon them, that is, the punishment for their selfishness. They decide to go and tell the king's household.

The speakers are a group of lepers who lived outside the gates of Samaria during a terrible famine caused by the Syrian siege. God had made the Syrians flee, and these men were the first to discover it. While the city was dying of hunger, they kept the secret.

For today: if God has given us something good, such as hope, peace, or faith in Christ, let us not keep it only for ourselves. Think today of someone who needs it and share that good news with them kindly.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that Jehoram, king of Judah, followed the bad example of the kings of Israel, just as the family of Ahab did. He had married a daughter of Ahab, and that influenced him greatly. For this reason he did evil in the sight of the Lord, that is, what God regarded as sin. The phrase "he walked in the way" means that he lived according to that manner of acting.

The text is a historical account, written by a narrator who summarizes the reign of Jehoram. It explains why his rule was so bad: his marriage alliance with the house of Ahab. The verses that follow show that God, even so, did not destroy Judah, because of the promise he made to David. But there were consequences, such as the rebellion of Edom.

For today: the people close to us influence us more than we think. It is wise to choose our friends, partners and spouse carefully, and to ask God for firmness so that we do not lose our values.
exp.11:3:
Jehoash tells the priests that all the money that the people brought to the temple should be used to repair the house of God. This included dedicated things, the amount set for each person (the set payment is a fixed value), and voluntary offerings. The phrase about those who pass the account can be understood in several ways: it may refer to a census or to ordinary money.

The speaker is King Jehoash, who did what was right while he was guided by the priest Jehoiada. The temple was in poor condition, and the king wants the offerings to be used to fix it. Even so, the text that follows shows that by the twenty-third year the priests still had not carried out the repairs.

For today: giving generously is good, but it is also important to make sure that what is given is used faithfully and on time. If you manage your church's resources, be clear and responsible.
exp.17:8:
This verse says that in the fourth year of King Hezekiah of Judah, which was the seventh year of King Hoshea of Israel, Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, came up against Samaria and surrounded it, that is, he encircled it with his army to attack it and leave it with no way out. Hezekiah is the king named in the verse, and Hoshea is the last king of Israel.

The author of the book continues the story of the kings. Earlier he spoke of Hezekiah's faithfulness, the king whom God accompanied. Now he shows the contrast: the northern kingdom, Israel, falls because it had turned away from God, as the text explains further on. The siege lasted three years.

For today: God speaks with seriousness, but he also offers his care. If we have neglected our relationship with him, we can return today, before the consequences grow.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that King Josiah sent for the leaders of the people, and that all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem gathered with him. The elders here are the respected heads and authorities of the cities. The verse shows that he sent messengers with the order to come.

The text does not say who is speaking; it is the account of the writer of Kings. Shortly before, the book of the law had been found in the temple, and Josiah had been moved when he heard its words. Now he calls the leaders together so that all the people may hear that law and renew their commitment to God. The verses that follow show the result of this gathering.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is not enough to be moved in private. We can share it with our family or our church, and encourage one another to obey it together.
exp.13:22:
This verse says that Jeroboam, son of Joash, began to rule as king of Israel in the fifteenth year of Amaziah, king of Judah. He governed from Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and his reign lasted forty-one years. Notice that there are two kings named Joash: one ruled in Judah and another in Israel.

The author of the book of Kings records the reigns of both kingdoms, the northern and the southern, and that is why he notes in which year of one the other began. Jeroboam was a king who held the throne for a long time, and the account that follows explains that, although he did what was evil before God, God allowed the kingdom to recover territory, in keeping with the word of the prophet Jonah.

For today: God works even in the midst of imperfect governments. His mercy does not depend on our being worthy. Give thanks for his patience and respond with sincere obedience.
exp.19:0:
Here we are told that King Hezekiah became seriously ill, so ill that it seemed he was going to die. The prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz, went to see him with a message from God: "Set thine house in order," meaning to put the affairs of his family and his kingdom in order, because he was going to die.

Isaiah speaks, carrying God's word to the king. Hezekiah was a king of Judah who had sought to please God. The message was very hard, and the following verse shows that the king responded with prayer and weeping. The text does not explain all the details of the illness or the exact moment it happened.

For today: life is fragile, so it is wise to live in order, with our accounts clear before God and before our family. And when a difficult piece of news arrives, we can do as Hezekiah did: bring our sorrow to God honestly in prayer.
exp.2:12:
Elisha speaks harshly to the king of Israel and asks him what he has to do with him. He tells him to go to the prophets of his father and of his mother, that is, the prophets of Baal. The king answers no, because the Lord had called these three kings together to deliver them into the hand of Moab. The Moabites are the people of Moab.

The kings of Israel, Judah and Edom were on campaign against Moab and ran out of water in the desert. The king of Israel, son of Ahab and Jezebel, remembered God only in the crisis. Elisha confronts him for his idolatry, though afterward he helps out of respect for Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.

For today: it is easy to seek God only when there are problems. This scene invites us to draw near to Him with sincerity every day, not only in trouble, and to leave behind whatever pulls us away from Him.
exp.7:8:
Hazael takes a gift with the best of Damascus, carried by forty loaded camels, and goes out to meet Elisha. He comes before him and says that King Ben-hadad has sent him to ask whether he will recover from his illness. The gift was a present, and "went to meet him" means that he went out to receive him.

The king of Syria is sick and hears that the prophet Elisha is in the city. Although Syria was a kingdom that did not follow the LORD, the king seeks an answer from the God of Israel through his prophet. Hazael speaks as his servant, and for that reason he calls Ben-hadad "your son," as a sign of respect. The Bible does not say whether the gift was a payment or only a sign of honor.

For today: when life presses us hard, it is good to seek God, but let us do it with humility and sincerity, ready to hear his answer even when it is not the one we expected.
exp.15:14:
Here King Ahaz gives orders to the priest Urijah about how to use the new altar he had ordered copied from Damascus. On it the daily sacrifices would be offered: the morning burnt offering and the evening meat offering, along with the offerings of the king and of the people, together with their drink offerings (liquids poured out as an offering). The original bronze altar would be kept for inquiring, a phrase that is understood in several ways: seeking counsel from God, or the king deciding what to do with it.

It is King Ahaz who speaks, a man who had turned away from God and imitated the customs of other nations. Urijah obeys without question, though the change pulled worship away from the order God had set down in the law.

For today: obeying an authority must never lead us to abandon what God has said. Always compare what we are asked to do with the Word, and worship God as He teaches, not as is convenient.
exp.23:10:
This verse tells us that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came in person to Jerusalem while his armies had already surrounded it. "Servants" here means his officers and soldiers, and the city being surrounded means it was encircled by troops so that no one could go in or out.

The book of Kings is a historical narrative. Here the account speaks of the time of King Jehoiakim, of whom it is said that he did evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father had. The writer shows that Judah had fallen into a long-lasting unfaithfulness, and that the arrival of Babylon was not merely a political matter. The verses that follow say that all this happened "as the Lord had said."

For today: God takes our decisions seriously, and the consequences do not always come right away. Today is a good day to examine with humility what we ought to correct, without waiting for a crisis to force us to do it.
exp.16:23:
This verse tells that the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the cities of Samaria. They took the place of the Israelites and made their homes there.

Here the narrator of the book explains what happened after Assyria carried Israel away into exile. According to the earlier text, this happened because the people kept following the sins of Jeroboam and would not listen to the prophets. It was an Assyrian practice to mix conquered peoples together. What follows shows that the new inhabitants also did not know or honor the LORD.

For today: God speaks in earnest and is patient, but choices have consequences. Let us not allow custom or indifference to draw us away from Him. Let us listen to His Word today and obey it with humility, before sin carries us further than we expect.
exp.13:2:
It says that Amaziah, king of Judah, did what pleased God, but not with the whole heart of David, his ancestor. The phrase about doing what was right in the sight of the Lord means doing what is correct in God's eyes. His model was his father Joash, whose life of faith was good in part. Here "his father" is also used for David as a famous ancestor.

It is part of the account of the kings of Judah. The narrator compares each king with David, who was the measure of faithfulness. Amaziah obeyed, but with limits: the high places of worship were not removed. Some understand that his faith followed the example of Joash, who also fell short, though the text does not fully explain this.

Doing what is right is good, but God seeks a whole heart. Today we can ask ourselves whether we only copy the faith of others or whether we truly love God for ourselves. Let us ask him to help us obey him completely, without keeping any areas held back.
exp.14:36:
In those days, toward the end of Jotham's reign, the Lord began to send Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, against Judah. Here "the Lord" is the name of God, and "send" indicates that He allowed or directed these conflicts.

The narrator of the book of Kings speaks here, summarizing the history of the kings. Jotham was on the whole a good king, but the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places, something God had forbidden. This verse announces the troubles that would come upon Judah, which would be felt more strongly in the time of his son Ahaz. The text gives no further detail here.

For today: even when someone does many good things, the areas we leave uncorrected can bring consequences. Ask God to show you what you should put in order in your life, and trust that He still governs in the midst of trials.
exp.15:1:
This verse says that Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. "Did not do what was right in the sight of the Lord" means he did not do what pleases God. Unlike David, he was not faithful to him.

The author of the book of Kings, whose identity is not known for certain, presents each king and judges him according to his faithfulness to God. David is the standard of comparison. The verses that follow explain why: Ahaz imitated pagan practices and worshiped in forbidden places.

For today: God looks at the heart and at obedience, not at the customs of the surrounding culture. Ask yourself in which areas you follow what everyone does instead of what pleases God, and ask him for help to change.
exp.6:19:
This verse says that the king's officer experienced exactly what Elisha had announced. The people, in their desperation and rush to get food, trampled him in the city gate, and he died.

Samaria was under siege and suffering a terrible famine. Elisha, the man of God, prophesied that by the next day there would be food at a low price. That officer, one of the king's trusted men, mocked the prophecy and doubted that God could do it. The lepers discovered that the enemy army had fled, and the people went out to plunder the camp. God's word was fulfilled in both things: the abundance and the warning.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it seems impossible to us. Doubting with mockery distances us from his goodness; trusting with humility allows us to receive it.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that some men were burying a dead man when they saw a band of raiders coming. In a hurry, they threw the body into Elisha's tomb. As soon as the dead man touched the prophet's bones, he came back to life and stood up on his feet. The verse's note on two words is left out here, since the verse above already uses words like "band" and "suddenly" in its own wording.

The narrator tells this event after Elisha's death. Moab was attacking the land of Israel, and King Joash had received a rebuke from the prophet for his little faith. Even dead, Elisha still served as a sign that God was at work in Israel. The text says nothing more; what matters is that the power comes from God, not from the bones.

For today: God remains faithful even when the people who guided us are gone. Trust in Him, not in leaders. And live with faith, because your witness can give life to others even after you are gone.
exp.12:17:
Elisha again told the king of Israel to take the arrows. When the king took them, Elisha told him to strike the ground with them. The king struck three times and then stopped.

Elisha, the prophet, is sick and near death. The king is Joash, and Syria was oppressing Israel. Earlier, Elisha had given him a sign of victory with the arrow. This second action tested the king's heart. Elisha became angry because Joash stopped early, and for that reason his victory would be limited. The text does not say what the king was thinking, so his motive is not clear.

God gives us promises and opportunities, and he also expects a response of faith and perseverance. Let us not be content with doing the minimum. Let us pray and act with enthusiasm and steadfastness in whatever God entrusts to us.
exp.20:2:
It says that Manasseh rebuilt the high places, which were places of worship on the hills where the people worshiped in a forbidden way. His father Hezekiah had destroyed them. He also set up altars to Baal, a false god, and made a grove, which in other versions appears as an image of Asherah, a goddess whose worship used a sacred pole or tree. He also worshiped the host of heaven, that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars, and served them.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes the reign of Manasseh. He was twelve years old when he began to reign. The author compares him with Ahab to show how far Judah had fallen, and so explains why judgment would come upon the people.

For today: Spiritual progress does not sustain itself. Take care of what God has done in your family or your church, and do not let it be lost through carelessness.
exp.7:11:
Here Hazael asks Elisha why he is weeping. Elisha answers that he weeps because he knows the violence Hazael will bring against Israel: he will set their strongholds on fire, kill their young men with the sword, dash their children to the ground, and rip open the women who are with child.

Hazael was an officer of the king of Syria, Ben-hadad, who was sick. He was sent to consult the prophet. Elisha, a man of God, sees by revelation that Hazael will become king and will cause great suffering. His weeping shows that God does not take pleasure in the pain of peoples; the prophet feels the weight of what he announces.

For today: we can learn to feel compassion for the suffering of others, even when we cannot prevent it. Praying and weeping for those who suffer is part of a heart that resembles God's.
exp.22:10:
He says that King Josiah removed from the entrance of the temple the horses that earlier kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun. They were next to the room of Nathan-melech, an official of the court. "Eunuch" here means a palace official, and "suburbs" probably refers to some outbuildings or land next to the temple; the exact meaning is not certain. In addition, Josiah burned the chariots of the sun.

This is part of the writer of Kings' account of Josiah's great reform. He cleanses Judah from the worship of the heavenly bodies and of foreign gods that had crept even into the temple. The narrator wants to show how far the people had drifted from God and how complete Josiah's return to Him was.

Today we might ask ourselves what things in our lives have taken the place that belongs to God, even if they seem normal or we have lived with them for years. Josiah did not arrange them or set them aside: he removed them. Let us ask God for the courage to do the same.
exp.8:7:
It says that the whole family of Ahab will be destroyed. The phrase used for this is a bold, old-fashioned way of saying "every male," regardless of who he is. The reference to "the one who was kept" probably refers to someone who was protected or under guard, and "the one left alone" to someone who was free or without protection. Taken together, they mean that no one from that house would escape.

Here a young prophet, sent by Elisha, speaks. He anointed Jehu as king and gave him God's message. Ahab and Jezebel had promoted idolatry and killed the prophets of the Lord. This judgment came after a long time and many warnings.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it, even when he is slow to act. We can trust that he will judge with justice, rather than taking revenge ourselves, and remember that we should live with humility and obedience before him.
exp.20:1:
This verse says that Manasseh did what God considered evil. The phrase "in the sight of the Lord" means "in the eyes of God," that is, according to God's judgment. The "abominations" were detestable practices, above all idolatry. The "heathen" are the pagan nations that God had driven out of the land when Israel came to possess it.

The one speaking is the author of the book of Kings, who summarizes the life of Manasseh. He was a very young king, son of the faithful Hezekiah. The verses that follow explain his wickedness: he rebuilt the high places of worship to other gods, raised altars to Baal, and worshiped the stars, even inside the temple. The author wants to show that Israel imitated the peoples whom God had judged.

Today: let us not copy without thinking what the majority does. Even if we grew up in a good home, each of us decides whom to follow. Let us ask God to teach us to measure our customs by his Word.
exp.12:4:
God sent Israel a "saviour," and the Israelites were freed from the power of the Syrians (in the text, "Syrians" appears in the same form). They were able to live again in their "tents," that is, in their houses or dwellings, with the peace they had known before.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Kings. King Jehoahaz had prayed in his distress, and God listened. The text does not say who that saviour was. Some think of his son Jehoash, others of Jeroboam II, and others of Elisha. Even so, the people did not give up their sins, and this shows that God's mercy was undeserved.

For today: God listens to those who cry out to Him, even when their situation is partly the result of their own mistakes. But let us not take advantage of his goodness. When He gives us relief, the best response is to give thanks and truly return to Him.
exp.16:37:
This verse says that the people were not to forget the covenant, that is, the agreement or commitment that God made with them. Nor were they to fear other gods, meaning strange gods belonging to other nations. Here "fear" means to revere, honor, and serve.

The writer of 2 Kings explains why the northern kingdom, Israel, fell before Assyria. He recalls what God had commanded them since he brought them out of Egypt. The foreign peoples who were settled in that land worshiped the LORD and at the same time their own idols. The text shows that Israel did the same and did not obey.

For today: it is not enough to remember God now and then. We can ask ourselves what things occupy in our hearts the place that belongs to Him, and put Him first again each day.
exp.12:10:
It says that Joash, king of Israel, did what was evil in the sight of God. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin, and he kept living in them. The phrase "he walked therein" means that he lived this way as a settled pattern of life.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, evaluating each king according to his faithfulness to God. Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom, and he set up golden calves to worship, drawing the people away from the temple in Jerusalem (1 Kings 12). Nearly all the kings of Israel repeated that sin, and Joash did the same.

For today: it is not enough to inherit religious customs or simply to follow what others did before us. It is worth examining which harmful habits or patterns we have received, and asking God for help to leave them behind and walk in obedience.
exp.8:22:
Joram turns his chariot around and flees. As he escapes, he cries out to Ahaziah, king of Judah: "There is treachery, O Ahaziah!" Joram realizes that Jehu does not come in peace. 

Joram, king of Israel, is the one speaking here. He went out to ask whether there was peace, but Jehu answered him with accusations about the idolatry and sorceries of Jezebel, his mother. Jehu had been anointed to judge the house of Ahab. Joram understands that it is a coup and tries to save himself.

For today: when someone confronts us with the truth, it is easy to run away or blame others. It is better to listen in time, acknowledge sin, and turn back to God before it is too late.
exp.20:15:
This verse says that Manasseh, beyond the wickedness already recorded about him, killed a great many innocent people. He shed so much blood that it filled Jerusalem from one end to the other. The verse's wording means that the city was filled completely. Also, through his bad example he led all of Judah into sin, and the people did what was evil in the sight of God.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings explains why judgment would come upon Judah. Just before this, God announces through his prophets that he will hand the people over to their enemies. This verse shows one of the reasons: the violence and wickedness that Manasseh promoted. The text gives no details about who the victims were.

For today: those who hold authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, influence others by their example. Let us ask God to help us use that influence to protect and not to harm.
exp.2:11:
Jehoshaphat affirms that Elisha indeed has the word of the Lord, that is, that he speaks on behalf of God. So the three kings, the king of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah, and the king of Edom (Idumea), go down to seek him. The verb "went down" shows that they went to where Elisha was.

The three kings were marching against Moab and had run out of water in the desert. The king of Israel only complained, but Jehoshaphat, a king faithful to God, wanted to consult a prophet. A servant mentioned Elisha, who had served Elijah. Jehoshaphat recognizes Elisha's authority, and that is why the kings visit him. Later Elisha speaks harshly to the king of Israel, and it is understood that he listens out of respect for Jehoshaphat.

For today: when we are in difficulty, instead of only complaining, let us seek God's direction in his Word and with people of sincere faith who help us to listen to him.
exp.8:15:
Jehu rides in his chariot (or "rode in a chariot," as the older version has it) and sets out for Jezreel. There King Joram is lying, recovering from the wounds he received in the war against the Syrians. Also, Ahaziah, king of Judah, had come down to visit him.

The narrator tells how Jehu, already anointed by order of the prophet Elisha as the new king of Israel, acts against the house of Ahab. Joram, son of Ahab, is weak and unprepared. Ahaziah, of Judah, was related to that family. Jehu moves quickly and in secret, so as to surprise them before anyone can raise the alarm.

For today: when God places a clear task on your heart, do not put it off. Jehu acted with decision. But remember that we must obey with humility, asking God for a clean heart, not only for quick actions.
exp.22:33:
This verse tells how Pharaoh Necho of Egypt made Eliakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah in place of his father. He changed Eliakim's name to Jehoiakim. He also took Jehoahaz away as a prisoner to Egypt, and there he died.

The writer here is the narrator of the book of Kings. Judah had lost its independence and depended on Egypt. By changing the king's name, Necho showed that he was the one in charge. The text says that Jehoahaz did evil in the eyes of God, and the people had to pay the tribute that was demanded.

For today: human powers can seem strong, but they pass away. It is wise to place our trust in God rather than in those who rule, and to live with integrity even when others make decisions for us.
exp.4:25:
Elisha asks Gehazi whether his heart was not present when Naaman got down from his chariot to meet him. In other words, Elisha knew what had happened even though he was not there. Then he rebukes him: "Is it a time to receive money, and to receive garments, and oliveyards, and vineyards, and sheep, and oxen, and menservants, and maidservants?"

The prophet Elisha is speaking. Naaman, a Syrian commander, was healed of leprosy and wanted to pay, but Elisha would not accept anything. Gehazi, his servant, ran after Naaman, lied to get silver and clothing from him, and then denied having done so. Elisha confronts him because he was turning a gift from God into a personal business deal.

For today: God sees what we do in secret. If we serve God, let us avoid profiting from what He does by grace, and let us be honest instead of hiding our faults.
exp.8:6:
This verse says that Jehu, already anointed king, must destroy the family of Ahab, his current master. God says that in this way he will avenge the blood of the prophets and of all his servants, which was shed by Jezebel.

A young prophet sent by Elisha speaks, anointing Jehu with oil in the name of the LORD. Ahab and Jezebel had promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted God's prophets. This command is God's judgment after a long time of wickedness without repentance. How Jehu carried it out afterward is a matter of debate, since he acted with great violence.

For today: God sees injustice against his people and does not forget it. We can hand our pain over to him, trust that he will judge with justice, and not take revenge into our own hands.
exp.13:13:
It says that Joash, king of Israel, took all the gold, the silver, and the utensils he found in the temple of the Lord and in the treasures of the king's palace in Judah. He also took hostages, that is, people held to make sure Judah would not attack again. Then he returned to Samaria, his capital.

This is a historical account, not a speech. Amaziah, king of Judah, had provoked Israel to war (2 Kings 14:8-10), and he lost at Beth Shemesh. The text shows the consequences of his pride. Joash broke down part of the wall of Jerusalem and plundered even the temple. The Bible had already warned that Amaziah trusted in himself and not in God (2 Chronicles 25 develops this in more detail).

For today: pride often costs dearly. Before we get into a conflict out of vanity, it is wise to stop, ask God for direction, and listen to wise counsel. Humility protects us from losses that are later hard to recover.
exp.10:11:
Jehoiada the priest brings out the young Joash, the king's son, and places the crown on him and "the testimony." This word most likely refers to a copy of God's law, though some understand it in another way. They anoint him as king, and the people clap their hands and cry out, "God save the king!" "Clapping their hands" means applauding.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Athaliah, the queen mother, had killed the royal family to seize the throne. But Joash, a child, had been hidden for six years in the temple. Jehoiada, with the help of the guards, now presents him as the rightful king, a descendant of David.

For today: God can keep His promise even when everything seems lost. Trust that He cares for what He has promised, and be ready to serve Him with courage when it falls to you to act.
exp.18:28:
This verse says that God gives a sign to King Hezekiah. For two years the people will eat what grows up on its own from the land, without planting. The third year they will be able to plant, harvest, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit as normal.

God speaks through the prophet Isaiah. Assyria, under King Sennacherib, had invaded Judah and was threatening Jerusalem. The fields were probably damaged by the war. God promises to stop the invader and gradually restore the people. The sign announces that life will return to normal, and the next verse speaks of a remnant that will take root.

For today: when you go through times of scarcity or rebuilding, God can care for you step by step, not always all at once. Trust that He remains faithful while you wait and rebuild your life.
exp.7:15:
This verse says that Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, began to reign over Judah in the fifth year of Joram, king of Israel. The two kings had the same name, which can be confusing. The phrase "Jehoshaphat being then king of Judah" is hard: some think father and son reigned together for a time, but this is not certain.

The narrator of the book of Kings tells the story of the kings of Israel and Judah. After the death of Ben-hadad, he now turns his attention to Judah. The verses that follow explain that this Jehoram did evil because he married a daughter of Ahab and followed his bad example.

For today: the friendships and alliances we choose gradually shape our hearts. Before you join yourself to someone, ask whether they draw you closer to God or pull you away from Him.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that although God heard Israel's cry and gave them a savior, the people did not leave the sins of the house of Jeroboam. They kept living in them. "The grove" refers to the image of Asherah, a sacred pole or tree used to worship a false god, which still stood in Samaria, the capital.

It is the account from the book of Kings, which does not name its author. It tells that Jehoahaz, king of Israel, prayed when Syria oppressed them, and God had compassion. It makes clear that the relief did not produce a deep change. Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom, and his idolatry marked the kings who followed him. Who the "savior" was is not clear; different ideas have been proposed.

Today we can thank God for his help, but we should not stop at asking for relief. If God rescues us from a problem, he also invites us to leave behind whatever pulls us away from him.
exp.7:22:
This verse is the formula the writer uses to close the reign of Joram, king of Judah. It says that the rest of his deeds and all that he did are written in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." That book is not the Chronicles in our Bible, but an ancient court record that we no longer have.

The one speaking is the author of Kings, who summarizes and refers readers to other sources. Joram had suffered defeats: Edom broke away from Judah and Libnah rebelled. His reign was evil, since he married the daughter of Ahab and followed idolatrous ways (in the verses before). Here he only closes his story.

For today: our lives also leave a record, and what we do day by day counts. Let us live faithfully before God, so that our works, and not only our position or success, may deserve to be remembered.
exp.3:41:
A man came from Baal-shalishah and brought Elisha, the man of God, bread from the first harvest: twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain. Elisha ordered that all of it be given to the people so they could eat. The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, which was customarily offered to God.

The prophet Elisha speaks in a time of famine in the region. A large crowd had gathered around him, and there was little food. Later, when his servant doubted because there were a hundred men, Elisha replied that the Lord had said, "They shall eat, and have some left over." And so it happened. The text does not explain how it happened, only that the word of God was fulfilled.

For today: what we have may seem small, but when it is shared in faith, God can make it reach far. Today you can share your time, your food, or your help with someone, trusting that God cares for both of you.
exp.10:17:
After the covenant with God, the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They broke its altars and its images (statues) and killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars. Then the priest Jehoiada appointed guards (a guard) to watch over the house of the Lord.

It is a narrative, not a sermon. Athaliah, the queen, had promoted the worship of Baal in Judah. Jehoiada protected Joash, the young heir, and crowned him. After renewing the covenant of loyalty to God, the people removed the symbols of that idolatry. Afterward, the house of God was secured.

For today: it is not enough to say we want to follow God; sometimes we must remove what has taken his place in our hearts. And it is also wise to take care of what strengthens our faith.
exp.16:36:
What it says: God reminds his people that they must always carry out what he has written down: his statutes, his righteous decisions, his law, and his commands. To "put into practice" means to actually do them, not merely to hear them. "Other gods" are foreign gods, those that are not the true God. "Fear" here includes respect, reverence, and loyalty.

Context: The narrator of 2 Kings explains why Israel was taken captive by Assyria. He recalls the covenant that the LORD made with them when he brought them out of Egypt. Meanwhile, the peoples brought to Samaria were mixing their own religion with the worship of the LORD. The text contrasts that mixture with the faithfulness God had asked for.

For today: Ask yourself what things compete with God for your trust or your time. Choose one concrete biblical teaching today and practice it, instead of only admiring it.
exp.21:8:
Shaphan the scribe, the king's secretary, returned to King Josiah and reported that the workers had gathered the money that was in the temple. They had already handed it over to those who were overseeing the repair work. Giving an account of what had been entrusted is what he meant by reporting back. The overseers of the restoration are the ones who had charge of the work.

Josiah had ordered the temple to be repaired. Shaphan brings the report about the money and, on the same trip, also brings the book of the law that Hilkiah found. This report seems routine, but what follows changes everything: when the king hears the law, he tears his clothes in grief and humility.

For today: do your work with honesty and order, even in small things. God often uses faithful and simple tasks to open the way for something greater. And when His Word speaks to you, listen to it with humility.
exp.21:11:
This verse tells that King Josiah, after hearing the book of the law, gives an urgent order to five trusted men: the priest Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, the scribe Shaphan, and Asahiah, a servant of the king. It is a list of names that prepares the order given in the next verse. A scribe was someone who could read, write, and keep records.

Josiah has just heard the law and has torn his clothes, a gesture of grief and repentance. Now he acts: he sends his men to inquire of God. The book found in the temple was probably the law of Moses, or a part of it, though scholars debate which part.

When the Word of God confronts us, sadness alone is not enough. Josiah responds with humility and seeks direction. Today we can do the same: read the Bible with an open heart, and take concrete steps of obedience and prayer.
exp.18:16:
Hezekiah tells God that what Assyria has done is true: its kings laid waste the nations and left their lands in ruins. The phrase "Of a truth" in the verse he is speaking to is a way of saying "it is certainly so." "Nations" here means peoples or countries. Hezekiah does not deny the reality or make it seem smaller than it is.

King Hezekiah of Judah is speaking while Jerusalem is threatened by the Assyrian army. Sennacherib had sent a letter mocking God. Hezekiah brings it before the Lord in prayer. He acknowledges Assyrian power, but right away he sets it against the greatness of God, whom he calls Creator and the only God over all the kingdoms.

For today: when you face a big problem, you do not need to pretend it does not frighten you. You can honestly tell God how hard it is, and then ask him for help, remembering that he is still greater than any threat.
exp.16:28:
This verse tells us that the foreign peoples who lived in Samaria each made their own gods. They placed them in the houses of the high places, that is, in the shrines built on elevated ground, which the Israelites of Samaria had used before. Each group did this in the city where it lived.

The one telling the story is the author of 2 Kings. After Assyria carried the northern kingdom into captivity, the Assyrian king brought people from other lands to live there. An Israelite priest taught them to fear the LORD, but they did not give up their idols. The author points to this mixing of religions as something serious.

For today: it is not enough to add God to our lives while keeping other things we love more than Him. We can ask ourselves what holds first place in our hearts, and ask God to help us serve Him with complete loyalty.
exp.5:29:
He tore his clothes in grief and anguish when he heard the woman's terrible account. As he walked along the city wall, the people saw that he had sackcloth on underneath, right against his skin. Sackcloth was a coarse cloth worn in times of mourning or repentance.

The king is Joram of Israel. Samaria was under siege by the Syrian army, and there was extreme hunger. His grief was public, but the text does not say he repented before God. He immediately blames Elisha and threatens to kill him, so his sackcloth shows sorrow, though not a change of heart.

We can show sorrow on the outside, but God looks for a sincere heart. When crises come, instead of looking for someone to blame, let us come to God with humility and ask Him for help.
exp.18:34:
It says that, in a single night, the angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 soldiers of the Assyrian army that surrounded Jerusalem. At dawn, those who got up found the bodies lifeless. The first sentence about "struck" means he hit them with death, and the second about "Jehovah" is the name of God, so both comments are removed as they don't match the verse your reader sees.

The narrator tells how God fulfilled what he had promised through Isaiah. King Hezekiah had prayed with humility, since Sennacherib was threatening Jerusalem. God said he would defend the city for his own sake and for the sake of David. Afterward, Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, and there he died. The details of how that slaughter happened are not explained; the text only affirms that it was the work of God.

When you find yourself surrounded by problems you cannot solve, do as Hezekiah did: pray sincerely and trust that God is faithful to his promises, even when you do not know how or when he will act.
exp.13:6:
The verse tells how Amaziah, king of Judah, defeated ten thousand Edomites in the valley of salt. He also took the city of Selah, and he gave it a new name, Joktheel. The text adds that this name remained to the time of writing, that is, until the time when the account was written.

The narrator is the author of the book of Kings, summarizing the reign of Amaziah. This king had acted justly by following the law of Moses and not putting to death the children of the men who had murdered his father. Now his military strength is shown. But what follows reveals that the victory filled him with pride and led him to challenge Israel, with bad consequences.

For today: success can be a test. After an achievement, it is good to give thanks to God and to stay humble, because pride often prepares the next fall.
exp.0:17:
This verse closes the story of King Ahaziah with a phrase common in Kings: his other deeds are not told here, since they are written in the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel." That book is not the Bible we know; it was a court record that is not preserved today.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. He has just told how Ahaziah died, as God had announced through Elijah, because he sought counsel from Baal-zebub, a false god of Ekron, instead of seeking the God of Israel. Since he had no son, his brother Joram reigned. The narrator sums up his reign and refers the reader to other sources.

For today: when you are afraid or need an answer, do not first run to what has no power. Seek God in his Word and in prayer, and trust that his voice is more certain than any other.
exp.16:22:
This verse says that God removed Israel, the northern kingdom, from his presence. This happened just as God had warned through all his prophets. The people were taken captive from their land to Assyria. The phrase "to this day" shows that the author of the book wrote at a time when the Israelites had not yet returned.

The narrator of Kings explains why the northern kingdom fell, around 722 B.C. The verses before this one tell how Israel followed the sins of Jeroboam, who led the people away from the Lord. It was not a sudden punishment: God had warned them many times, and they did not want to turn back to him.

For today: God is patient and warns us clearly, but our choices have consequences. If you feel today that God is calling you to correct something, do not put it off. Respond with humility and return to him while there is still time.
exp.19:14:
Isaiah asks the king again what the envoys from Babylon saw in his house. Hezekiah answers with complete frankness: they saw everything, and he kept nothing back from them.

Here King Hezekiah speaks, questioned by the prophet Isaiah. The Babylonian messengers had come after his illness and recovery. Hezekiah showed them everything, and the text does not say for certain why; some think it was pride, others that he was seeking an alliance. Isaiah immediately announces that Babylon would carry off those treasures.

For today: let us not trust in what we have, nor boast about it. Before showing off our achievements, let us ask God for wisdom and humility to remember that everything comes from Him.
exp.8:30:
She says that as Jehu was coming in through the city gate, Jezebel spoke to him from the window. She asked him: "Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?" The verse of the old wording is that the word "peace" here means that things went well for him.

Jezebel speaks here, the widowed queen and enemy of God's prophets. Jehu had just killed King Joram on God's command. She reminds him of Zimri, a man who killed his own king and reigned only seven days before he died (1 Kings 16). Her question sounds like mockery or a threat; some think she meant to intimidate him. The text does not say for certain what her intention was.

For today: let us not trust our pride or our appearance to escape the consequences of our actions. It is better to draw near to God with humility and repentance while there is still time.
exp.15:15:
This verse says that the priest Urijah did everything that King Ahaz commanded him. In the ancient text, one of the unusual words refers to the north, and another refers to an offering burned completely on the altar.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book of Kings. Ahaz, king of Judah, had a pagan altar he saw in Damascus copied and placed in the temple. Then he moved the bronze altar that God had ordered. Urijah the priest did not oppose him. He obeyed the king, even though this pushed aside what God had established. Scholars see this as an example of religious leadership giving way to political power.

For today: obedience to human authority has a limit when it contradicts the will of God. Let us ask for courage to be faithful to God, with respect, even when it is difficult to say no.
exp.20:25:
Amon's burial and the succession of his son Josiah are described: the verse says that King Amon was buried in his tomb, located in the garden of Uzza, and that his son Josiah became king in his place. The two archaic spellings and the word for tomb in the source are not needed here, since the verse your reader sees uses "buried," "sepulchre," and "reigned," and the verse's notes on those words are omitted because they refer to wording your reader does not see.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Kings, who summarizes the end of Amon's reign. Amon was killed by his servants, and the people punished the conspirators and placed Josiah on the throne. It is not known with certainty who Uzza was or why that garden was a burial place; the Bible does not explain it. Josiah was still very young, and later he would be known as a king who sought God.

For today: even when a family's history has wounds or bad examples, God can raise up a new chapter. We can decide, with his help, to seek him and begin a different path.
exp.17:1:
This verse says that Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign as king of Judah, and that he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. It also says that his mother's name was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah. The spellings found in some older texts are not needed here; the names are simply Jerusalem and Zechariah.

Here the narrator of the book of Kings gives basic facts about each king. It comes after saying that Hezekiah began to reign in the time of Hoshea, king of Israel. These facts prepare the praise that follows: Hezekiah did what was right and removed idolatry. About Abi we know nothing more; some think her father was the Zechariah mentioned in Isaiah 8:2, but that is uncertain.

For today: God can use a young person who decides to seek him. Hezekiah's faith did not depend on his age or his surroundings, since his father Ahaz was a bad king. Today you too can choose to obey God, even when your family or your environment does not make it easy.
exp.5:25:
As the king of Israel was walking on the wall of Samaria, the besieged city, a woman cried out to him asking for help, saying, "Help, my lord, O king."

This woman was desperate. The army of Syria had surrounded the city, and the famine was terrible. She turns to the king because he was the one who should bring justice to the people. The verses that follow show that her complaint was horrible: an agreement to eat their children. The king responds helplessly and points to the LORD as the only one who can save.

For today: when pain overwhelms you, cry out without fear and seek help. But remember that no human leader or resource is enough; the firmest hope is in God, who hears those who cry out to Him.
exp.1:2:
It says that some young men from the group of prophets, who lived in Bethel, went out to speak with Elisha. They asked him whether he knew that on that very day the Lord would take his master away from him. The phrase "from your head" is a way of saying that Elijah would be taken from him, as someone who is above him and guiding him. Elisha answered that yes, he knew it, and asked them to keep quiet.

The "sons of the prophets" were communities of disciples who learned and served God. It seems God had already shown them what would happen. Elisha, meanwhile, kept following Elijah from place to place without letting go of him. His request for silence is not rudeness; he probably wanted to face that moment with seriousness and without distractions.

For today: when God prepares us for a difficult change, we do not need to discuss it with everyone. We can be quiet, pray, and stay faithful to what God has given us to do.

sum.5: Elisha helps the sons of the prophets by making a borrowed axe head float, and then shows that God protects him: he reveals the plans of the king of Aram and opens the eyes of his servant to see the heavenly armies. After Elisha leads the Arameans and God blinds them, Israel feeds them and sends them back home. Later, the siege of Samaria brings terrible famine, and the king, in despair, blames Elisha.
sum.22: King Josiah read the book of the covenant to the people, and everyone promised to follow God wholeheartedly. Then he tore down the idols and false altars in Judah and Bethel, and he held a Passover like none that had been kept in a long time. Even so, the judgment against Judah was not called off, and Josiah died at Megiddo; his successors did what was evil.
sum.12: Jehoahaz and his son Jehoash reigned over Israel, doing what was evil in the Lord's sight, and the Lord allowed Syria to oppress them. Yet the Lord listened to Jehoahaz's prayer. Elisha died after prophesying that Jehoash would defeat Syria only three times, and the Lord showed mercy to Israel because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
sum.16: Hoshea, the last king of Israel, rebelled against Assyria, and the Assyrian king conquered Samaria and carried the people away into captivity. The text explains that this happened because Israel had abandoned the LORD, worshiped idols, and refused to listen to the prophets. Assyria brought foreigners into the land, and they mixed the fear of the LORD with their own gods.
sum.7: Elisha warns the Shunammite woman that a seven-year famine is coming, and when she returns, the king restores her lands to her. Elisha announces that Hazael will become king of Syria, and Ben-hadad dies. In Judah, Jehoram and Ahaziah reign, and they follow the evil ways of Ahab, but God preserves Judah because of his promise to David.
sum.3: In this chapter, God works through Elisha to help people in their needs: he multiplies the oil of a widow who is in debt, gives a son to the woman from Shunem, and then brings him back to life. He also removes what is bad from a pot of stew and feeds one hundred men with a few loaves of bread.
sum.2: Joram, king of Israel, joins forces with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom to attack Moab, which had rebelled. In the desert they run out of water, so they seek out Elisha, who promises them water without rain and victory through the word of the LORD. In the end, Moab is defeated, but its king sacrifices his son, and Israel withdraws.
sum.6: Elisha announces that the next day there will be cheap food in Samaria, which was in severe famine, and a royal officer mocks the promise. Four men with leprosy discover that God has made the Syrians flee, and they carry the news to the city. The people plunder the camp, the word of God is fulfilled, and the unbelieving officer dies trampled.
sum.24: Babylon besieges Jerusalem, King Zedekiah is captured and punished, the city and the temple are burned, and the people are taken into exile, while a few of the poor are left behind. After the governor Gedaliah is murdered, many flee to Egypt. In the end, King Jehoiachin receives kind treatment in Babylon, a small sign of hope.
sum.0: King Ahaziah, sick after a fall, sent messengers to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, instead of seeking the God of Israel. Because of this, Elijah told him that he would die, and he showed that he was a servant of God when fire fell on two groups of soldiers. The third captain humbled himself, and Elijah confirmed the message to the king, who died.
sum.10: Athaliah killed the royal family to keep the throne for herself, but Jehosheba hid the young Joash in the temple for six years. Then the priest Jehoiada crowned him king with the help of the guard. Athaliah died, and the people returned to God in a covenant and destroyed the temple of Baal.
sum.1: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, with a chariot of fire, while Elisha, who refused to leave his side, watches everything and receives his cloak. With that cloak, Elisha parts the waters of the Jordan and heals the bad water of Jericho. At the end, some boys mock him in Bethel, and the text tells of a very harsh punishment.
sum.20: Manasseh began to reign at the age of twelve, and he led Judah into idolatry and witchcraft and into shedding much innocent blood, even setting up altars in the temple. Because of this, God announced punishment on Jerusalem. His son Amon followed the same evil and was assassinated, and Josiah was left as king.
sum.21: Josiah, a young king who did what was right in the sight of God, ordered the temple to be repaired, and there the priest Hilkiah found the book of the law. When he heard it read, the king tore his clothes and sought the word of God. The prophetess Huldah announced that judgment would come because of the people's idolatry. But because Josiah humbled himself, God promised that he would die in peace.
sum.9: Jehu eliminated the entire family of Ahab and the relatives of King Ahaziah, and then he tricked the servants of Baal into coming together so that he could kill them and destroy their temple. God praised him and promised that his descendants would rule to the fourth generation, but Jehu did not follow God wholeheartedly, and Hazael began to reduce the territory of Israel.
sum.8: Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu as king of Israel, with orders to bring an end to the house of Ahab because of its wickedness. Jehu kills King Joram and Ahaziah, and Jezebel dies just as God had said through Elijah. The chapter shows that God's word is fulfilled and that He judges injustice.
sum.19: Hezekiah became mortally ill and prayed, weeping, and God granted him fifteen more years of life along with a sign: the shadow moved back ten degrees. Afterward, the king proudly showed all his treasures to envoys from Babylon, and Isaiah announced that everything would be carried off to that land. Hezekiah accepted the word, thinking of peace in his own days.
sum.17: Hezekiah, king of Judah, does what is right: he removes the high places and the sacred pillars, and he trusts in God. Meanwhile, Assyria takes Israel captive for disobeying, and then threatens Jerusalem. The Assyrian messenger mocks the trust placed in God, but the people stay silent and wait.
sum.23:
Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon marched against Judah, and Jehoiakim rebelled against him. God allowed these enemies to come because of the sins of Manasseh.

Afterward, Jehoiachin was captured, Jerusalem was plundered, and many people were taken captive to Babylon. Zedekiah was left as king. He did evil and rebelled as well, showing that God's judgment was still moving forward.
sum.15: Ahaz, king of Judah, did not follow the Lord the way David had. He practiced idolatry and even sacrificed his own son in the fire. When Syria and Israel attacked him, he asked Assyria for help, sending them the gold and silver from the temple. He also copied a pagan altar from Damascus and changed the worship in the temple. When he died, his son Hezekiah became king.
sum.4: Naaman, a Syrian army commander who had leprosy, followed the advice of a young Israelite girl who had been taken captive, and went to the prophet Elisha. He became angry at the instruction to wash in the Jordan River, but he obeyed and was healed, and then he acknowledged the God of Israel. Gehazi, out of greed, lied and received leprosy as punishment.
sum.18: Faced with the threats and mockery of the king of Assyria, King Hezekiah humbled himself, asked Isaiah to pray, and brought the letter before God, begging him to save them so that everyone would know that he alone is God. God answered through Isaiah: he would defend Jerusalem, and that very night his angel struck down 185,000 Assyrians. Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, where his own sons killed him.
sum.13: Amaziah reigned over Judah and did what was right, but he did not remove the high places. His pride after defeating Edom led him to challenge Israel, and he lost to Joash. Later he was killed in a conspiracy. In Israel, Jeroboam II did what was evil, but God, seeing their affliction, saved them by his hand.
sum.11: Joash ruled in Judah and did what was right as long as the priest Jehoiada guided him, although the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places. He honestly organized the repair of the temple, but later he gave the sacred treasures to Hazael to prevent an attack, and his own servants killed him.
sum.14: This chapter tells how Judah, under kings like Azariah and Jotham, did what was right, though they left the high places in place. Meanwhile Israel falls into coups and kings who keep following the sin of Jeroboam. Assyria begins to weaken Israel, and the word of God spoken to Jehu comes to pass. The passage teaches that turning away from God brings instability and ruin.
